en: 1. Gaurava-Vilāsa: The first chapter, the Play of Devotion to Hari.
Now, the invocation:
I take refuge in the Lord Caitanya-deva,
writing this for the immediate delight of the Śrī-Vaiṣṇavas.
Having deliberated upon the necessary task and having gathered [the material] from all the scriptures together with the virtuous ones, // Hbhv_1.1 //
Gopāla Bhaṭṭa, the disciple of the blessed Raghunātha Dāsa, who is dear to the Lord, gathers these playful expressions of devotion for the joy of awakening.
And he gratified Rūpa and Sanātana as well.
May the devotees of Mathurānātha practice this work called *Bhaktivilāsa*, which has arisen from the playful manifestation of love and devotion for his lotus feet. (Hbhv 1.3)
May the Śrī-Vaiṣṇavas here in the Māthura-maṇḍala, who are established in ultimate devotion, be victorious!
May Kāśīśvara shine forth in Kṛṣṇavana, along with Śrī-Kṛṣṇadāsa, the lord of the world.
In that regard, the written pledge begins with the document together with its cause, followed by the taking of refuge in the venerable Guru;
then the Guru, the disciple, the examination and so forth, the Blessed One, and his Manu. (Hbhv_1.5)
The authority over mantras, the purification for the sake of attaining accomplishments (siddhi) and so forth, the consecration of mantras,
initiation (dīkṣā), the constant [practice] at the time of Brahmā, auspicious rising, purity,
the recollection of Kṛṣṇa at dawn and so forth, and awakening with musical instruments and the like. (Hbhv 1.6)
First, the removal of the withered offerings (nirmālya) and so forth; then the auspicious *ārātrika* lamp ceremony;
followed by the practice of friendliness (*maitrī*) and other virtues, as well as purification, sipping water (*ācamana*), and cleaning the teeth.
Bathing, the tantric twilight rituals (saṃdhyā) and so forth, and the consecration of temples and the like.
The fetching of tulasī and other items, bathing at home with warm water and so forth,
clothing, a seat, the vertical mark (ūrdhva-puṇḍra), and [the application of] śrī-gopīcandana and the like.
The mudrās such as the discus, the rosary, the twilight worship at home, the greatness of the Guru, and then the worship within the gateway and the interior of the temple of Kṛṣṇa.

The seat for worship, the placement of the water for the guest-offering and other articles, the warding off of obstacles, prostration to the venerable Guru and others, the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), and the purification of the vital breaths (prāṇaviśodhana). // Hbhv_1.11 //
The fivefold assignment of mantras (nyāsa) and mudrās, the internal worship through meditation on Kṛṣṇa, the steps of worship, the Śrīmūrti, and likewise the Śālagrāma stones; Hbhv_1.12 //

The discuses originating from the gates, the purifications, the worship of the pedestal, the invocation and so forth, their respective mudrās, and the offering of the seat and other requisites. (Hbhv 1.13)

The ceremonial bathing, the sounding of conchs, bells, and other musical instruments, the recitation of the Thousand Names, the reading of the Purāṇas, the wearing of garments, the sacred thread, and ornaments. Hbhv_1.14 //
Incense, the wood of the auspicious *tulasī*, sandalwood, and flowers; the leaves of *tulasī*; and the worship of the limbs, the secondary limbs, and the enclosures. (Hbhv 1.15)
Incense, lamps, food offerings, drinks, fire oblations, the ritual of bali-offerings,
mouth-rinses and the like, facial garments, and furthermore, divine perfumes and so forth.

The royal honors such as songs and the like, the great lustration ceremony (*mahānīrājana*), the sounding of conch shells and other instruments, the water-conch lustration, and hymns of praise. // Hbhv_1.17 //

Prostration, circumambulation, the offering of one's actions and so forth, recitation, supplication, the begging of forgiveness for offenses, and the wearing of the remains of offerings from various [deities]. (Hbhv_1.18)
The conch-water, the sacred ford, the worship of Tulasī, its clay and so forth;
the time for the prohibition of bathing with Dhātrī, and the acquisition of one's livelihood. (Hbhv 1.19)
At midday, the *śrāddha* for the Viśvedevas and others must be offered to Acyuta; there are faults in eating without worship, as well as in eating what has not been offered. (Hbhv 1.20)

The virtuous [avoid] eating the food offerings (naivedya), association with the wicked, lack of association with the good, going to evil ways, and the evil fruits such as derision and censure of Vaiṣṇavas. (Hbhv 1.21)

Devotion to the virtuous, the scripture of Viṣṇu, namely the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, as well as stories of His divine pastimes, the duties pertaining to the Lord, and one's own evening rituals. (Hbhv 1.22)
The avoidance of the falling of [unwholesome] karma, worship at the three times especially, nighttime duties, and furthermore, the vision of the fruits of worship, success, and so forth. (Hbhv 1.23)
The gift for the sake of Viṣṇu, various modes of service, the fulfillment of deficiencies,
the bed, the majesty of the worship, and likewise the wonder of the glorious Name.
Offenses against the Name, devotion, taking refuge in love, and so forth;
on the fortnights, Ekādaśī with its ancillaries, and the great Śrī-Dvādaśy-aṣṭaka. (Hbhv 1.25)

The rites to be performed during the twelve months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, the preliminary practices (puraścaraṇa), the mantra, and the characteristics of one who has attained accomplishment (siddha). Hbhv_1.26.

The manifestation of the form, the consecration of the image, the temple of Kṛṣṇa, the restoration of what is dilapidated, the marriage of Śrī Tulasī, and acts performed for no other purpose. (Hbhv 1.27)
In that regard, the cause for approaching the venerable guru is through the grace of Lord Kṛṣṇa and by association with His devotees;
having heard the greatness of devotion and desiring it, one should worship a true guru. (Hbhv 1.28)

Here, a succession of sufferings is experienced constantly, and in the next world, unbearable suffering is heard of from the scriptures; therefore, the wise person should desire to cross over even that.
And so it has been said in the Eleventh Skandha [BhP 11.9.29]:
"Having obtained this human birth— which is extremely difficult to attain at the end of many existences, which bestows purpose though it is impermanent here— the wise man,"
One should strive quickly lest one fall; for as long as there is time before death, every opportunity indeed exists for the supreme good.
And by the Blessed Lord Himself [BhP 11.20.17]: "The first human body, so easily obtained yet so difficult to obtain,
is a well-constructed boat with the teacher as its helmsman."
If a person does not cross the ocean of existence when impelled by a favorable wind such as myself, he is a destroyer of his own self.
Now, regarding the approach to the venerable Guru, it is stated in that very same work by the illustrious Prabuddha-Yogeśvara (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.3.21):
"Therefore, one who desires to know the highest good should take refuge in a Guru."
One who is proficient in verbal knowledge and in the Supreme Brahman, and who takes refuge in tranquility.
As stated by the Blessed Lord himself in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (11.10.5):
"One should worship a peaceful guru who knows me and whose very self is me. (Hbhv 1.33)
And in the *Kramadīpikā* [4.2]:

"A Brahmin whose host of enemies such as desire has been utterly destroyed, whose limbs are stainless, and who bears an intense devotion characterized by passion for the dust of the pair of lotus-feet of Kṛṣṇa..."

One who desires to thoroughly understand knowledge should take refuge in a teacher who knows the Vedas, whose path is purified by the scriptures and traditions, who is honored among the virtuous, and who is self-controlled, with body and mind fully inclined toward him.
Also in the Śruti [Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.12; Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2]:
"For the sake of knowing that, one should approach a guru alone, with fuel in hand, who is learned in the Vedas (śrotriya) and established in Brahman;
through a teacher, a person knows. (Hbhv 1.35)
Now, regarding the necessity of attending upon the guru, in the tenth book of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, within the hymn of the Vedas (Śruti-stuti), it is said [BhP 10.87.33]:
"By those who have conquered the senses and the vital breaths, yet whose wild horse of a mind remains unsubdued..."

Those who, having abandoned the feet of the Guru, strive here to cross over this excessively restless [world] through the exhaustion of mere means, are beset by hundreds of calamities; like merchants who have not secured a helmsman, they perish in the ocean. (Hbhv 1.36)
And in the Śruti [Kaṭhopaniṣad 1.2.9]:
"This wisdom is not to be attained by reasoning;
it must be taught by another who knows it well, O beloved, for the sake of right knowledge. (Hbhv 1.37)
Now, specifically regarding the characteristics of the venerable guru, it is said in the *Mantra-muktāvalī*:
"One of pure lineage, who is himself purified and devoted to his own appropriate conduct."
The forest-dweller should be free from anger, a knower of the Vedas, and a knower of all the scriptures.
Endowed with faith and free from malice, pleasant of speech and pleasant of appearance, pure, well-attired, youthful, and devoted to the welfare of all beings. (Hbhv 1.39)

The wise one, whose mind is free from arrogance, who is full [of virtues], self-reflective, endowed with good qualities, devoted to worship, firm in intellect, grateful, and affectionate toward his disciples. (Hbhv 1.40)
Capable of both restraint and grace, devoted to the fire-offerings and mantras, knowing the methods of reasoning and refutation, pure in soul, and an abode of compassion—
one endowed with such characteristics as these shall be a Guru, a treasure-house of dignity. (Hbhv_1.41)
And in the Agastya-saṃhitā:

"A worshiper of the deity is peaceful, free from desire even for sense objects, a knower of the supreme self, a proponent of Brahman, and skilled in the meaning of the Vedas and scriptures. (Hbhv 1.42)
That best of Brahmins is capable of both uplifting and destroying;
he knows the reality of mechanical devices and mantras, pierces their vital points, and is a knower of secrets.
One who has performed the preparatory rites (puraścaraṇa), mastered the mantras for the fire-oblation (homa), knows the ritual applications (prayoga),
is ascetic, and speaks the truth— such a householder is called a guru.
In the Viṣṇu-smṛti: A teacher who desires service, fame, or gain from a disciple is not a true guru;
rather, he is an ocean of compassion, perfectly fulfilled, and a benefactor to all sentient beings. (Hbhv 1.45)
Free from desire for anything, accomplished in all respects, proficient in all branches of knowledge,
and the dispeller of all doubts— a teacher who is not indolent has been sought out.
In the *Śrī-Nārada-Pañcarātra*, in the dialogue between the Blessed One and Nārada:
"A brāhmaṇa who knows all times should bestow grace upon all;
in his absence, the best of the twice-born—whose self is peaceful and who is permeated by the Blessed One [should do so]. (Hbhv 1.47)
One whose self is cultivated, who is omniscient, who knows the scriptures, who is devoted to virtuous actions,
and who is disciplined, having attained the threefold accomplishment, is consecrated for the office of an Ācārya.
Among those born of the kṣatriya, vaiśya, and śūdra castes, the kṣatriya is capable of showing favor;
and this is so even for a kṣatriya who is a teacher, provided he possesses such a disposition.
The Vaiśya should perform his duty, and he must always provide assistance to both [the Brāhmaṇa and the Kṣatriya] through a Śūdra of his own caste who is likewise qualified, O Great-minded One;
and the Śūdra’s assistance and consecration should always be performed by him.
Furthermore:
"If there is a teacher who is of the highest caste, venerable, and renowned—
whether he be in one's own country or elsewhere— one who desires what is auspicious should not perform this [act]."
But he who would act contrary to what exists, here or there, shall suffer ruin both in this world and the next; therefore, one should practice that which is declared in the scriptures.
One born of the kṣatriya, vaiśya, or śūdra castes should not be initiated in the reverse order of classes.
And in the *Padma Purāṇa* (6.253.26):
"A most excellent and highly fortunate brāhmaṇa is indeed the guru of men;
he is to be worshipped by all the worlds just like Hari. (Hbhv 1.53)
"Even if he is born of a noble lineage, initiated into all sacrifices,
and a student of a thousand branches [of the Veda], one who is not a Vaiṣṇava shall not be a guru. Thus,
a man who has received the initiation of Viṣṇu and is devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu [is the one to be honored].
One who is thus described by those possessing higher knowledge is a Vaiṣṇava; anyone other than such a person is a non-Vaiṣṇava.
In the ocean of reality, one who is a glutton, a procrastinator, and greedy for sense objects;
who delights in the doctrine of mere causes, is corrupt, speaks ill, and reviles virtuous qualities. (Hbhv 1.56)
One who has body odor, excessive hair, and serves a censured hermitage;
one with black teeth and black lips, and one who exhales foul-smelling breath.
Even if he is himself a lord, a teacher who is possessed of wicked characteristics and is addicted to accepting many gifts brings about the destruction of prosperity.
Now, regarding the characteristics of a disciple,
it is said in the *Mantra-muktāvalī*:
"A disciple should be of pure lineage, illustrious, humble, and pleasing to behold."
One whose speech is truthful, whose conduct is meritorious, whose intellect is vast, and who is free from hypocrisy.
Having abandoned desire and anger, he is devoted to the feet of the guru,
intent upon the deity day and night through body, mind, and speech.
Free from disease, having conquered all sins, endowed with faith, and constantly devoted to the worship of the twice-born, the gods, and the ancestors; Hbhv_1.61 //
A disciple who is young, whose senses are entirely restrained, and who is an abode of compassion—
one endowed with such characteristics as these— is qualified for initiation.
And in the eleventh book [BhP 11.10.6]:

"One who is not conceited, free from envy, skillful, devoid of possessiveness, firm in friendship, not hasty, desirous of knowing the truth, free from malice, and whose speech is not in vain. (Hbhv_1.63)
Now, regarding those who are to be disregarded, it is said in the Agastya-saṃhitā: "The lazy, the impure, the afflicted, the hypocritical, and likewise the miserly."
The poor, the sick, the angry, the passionate, and those craving sensual enjoyments—[these are the ones who do not see].
Those who are seized by envy and avarice, the deceitful, those who speak harshly, those who have acquired wealth through unjust means, and those who take pleasure in the wives of others; (Hbhv_1.65)
Those who are enemies of the wise, the ignorant who imagine themselves to be learned, those who have fallen from their vows, those of miserable conduct, the backbiters, and the wicked; Hbhv_1.66 //
"Eaters of much food, of cruel conduct, and evil-minded"—thus are these and others described as the most wicked, the lowest of men. (Hbhv 1.67)
Those who cannot be restrained from improper actions and who are unable to endure the teacher’s instruction—
such persons should be rejected and not admitted into discipleship.
For if these [offenses] are committed, they become vessels for reviling the deities; in this world, they become afflicted with skin diseases and are deprived of children and wives.
And at the end of their bodies, those hell-beings are reborn as animals.
In the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*, it is said:
"Jaimini, the Sugata, the nihilist, the naked one (the Jaina), Kapila, and Akṣapāda—these six are proponents of causal reasoning (*hetuvādin*). (Hbhv 1.71)
"Those lowest of men who act according to this [materialistic] view are called proponents of causality (hetuvādins); one should not bestow the Tantra upon them.
Thus, the examination of these two [teacher and disciple] consists of living together for one year.
One becomes truly wise precisely through the experience of the intrinsic nature of conventional reality.
Now, regarding the examination [of the suitability of a bridegroom], it is stated in the *Mantra-muktāvalī*:
"When the two have lived together for a year and have come to know each other's true nature,"
The status of being a teacher and that of being a disciple are not otherwise; this is the certainty.
And the Śruti says:
"One should not give [the instruction] to one who has not lived [as a student] for a year. (Hbhv_1.75)
In the *Sārasaṅgraha* as well:
"A true guru should examine the physical constitution of the disciple who has taken refuge in him. (Hbhv 1.76)
The faults committed by a minister accrue to the king, the sin of a wife falls upon her husband, and likewise, the sin earned by a disciple is certainly incurred by the teacher. (Hbhv 1.77)
In the *Kramadīpikā* (4.3), however, it says:
"One whose inner self is not crooked should satisfy him with his own wealth, even with his body, and with agreeable speech."

Then, after three years, when the Guru— being exceedingly steadfast— is satisfied by the disciple’s devotion as if he were the Lotus-navelled Lord (Viṣṇu), let him desire the initiation into the mantra.
Now, specifically regarding the procedure for serving the venerable Guru, it is stated in the *Śrī-Vyāsagītā* within the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"One should always bring water-jars, *kuśa* grass, flowers, and sacrificial fuel."
One should constantly perform the cleansing and smearing of one's limbs and garments with [cow dung].
One should never step upon his discarded flowers, his bed, his sandals, or his seat; nor should one step upon his shadow or his couch.
One should prepare the tooth-stick and other requisites, and announce the task to him.
One should not depart without having taken leave; one should have a taste for what is pleasant and beneficial [to the teacher]; and one should never place one's feet near him. (Hbhv 1.82)
One should always avoid yawning, laughing, and the like, as well as covering the throat with one's hand, and likewise slapping one's limbs in the presence [of others]. (Hbhv 1.83)
Furthermore:
One should always practice the conduct due to a teacher toward one's superior; likewise toward the teacher’s sons, his wives, and his own kinsmen. (Hbhv 1.84)
One should not perform the massaging of the limbs, the bathing, or the eating of leftovers for the teacher’s son, nor should one perform the washing of his feet. (Hbhv 1.85)
The wives of the teacher who belong to the same caste should be honored like the teacher himself;
however, those who do not belong to the same caste should be honored by rising from one's seat and by salutation.
Anointing, bathing, massaging the limbs,
and the dressing of the hair— these are the duties to be performed for the wife of one's teacher.
In the *Devī-āgama*, as spoken by the illustrious Śiva:
"One should never step over the bed or seat of the guru, his vehicle, his sandals, his footstool, his bath-water, or his shadow. (Hbhv 1.88)
One should set aside separate worship and non-duality in the presence of the Guru;
one should avoid bestowing initiation, giving explanations, and exercising authority in the presence of the Guru. (Hbhv 1.89)
In the words of Śrī Nārada:
"Wherever one sees the guru, there, with palms joined in reverence, one should prostrate on the ground like a tree whose roots have been severed. (Hbhv 1.90)
A disciple should never step over the seat, vehicle, sandals, shoes, clothing, or shadow of his guru. (Hbhv 1.91)
In the *Śrī-Manusmṛti*:
"One should not utter the name of one's guru alone, even in his absence;
nor should one imitate his gait, speech, or gestures. (Hbhv 1.92)
When the teacher’s own teacher is present, one should maintain the same steadfastness as toward one's own teacher;
nor, unless released by the teacher, should one pay homage to one’s own teachers.
As stated in the Śrī-Nārada-Pañcarātra:
"In whatever manner or wherever it may be, one should not take up [the name] alone;
one who has controlled the self should not utter the name of the Guru without devotion. (Hbhv 1.94)
First the *praṇava*, then the word "Śrī," followed by the name of Viṣṇu, and finally the word "Pāda" (Feet), while bowing the head with palms joined in reverence. (Hbhv 1.95)
Furthermore:
One should not issue commands to him out of delusion, nor should one transgress his command.
Nothing should be eaten without having informed the guru, nor likewise anything belonging to the guru.
And elsewhere it is said:
"One should go before him when he comes, and follow behind him when he goes;
one should not stand before the guru while he is seated or lying down. (Hbhv 1.97)
Whatever food, drink, or other pleasing and delightful object there may be,
one should offer it to the guru first and then consume it oneself every day.
In the *Śrī-Viṣṇu-Smṛti*:
"One should not do anything displeasing to the guru, even if struck or oppressed; one should not disregard his word, nor should one act in an unkind manner toward him. (Hbhv 1.99)
One should do what is pleasing to the teacher with one's life, with one's wealth, and with action, mind, and speech; such a person goes to the supreme goal.
In the Śrī-Nārada-Pañcarātra:
"He who speaks what is devoid of logic, and he who listens with injustice—both of them go to a terrible hell for an inexhaustible time. (Hbhv 1.101)
In the Vaiṣṇava Tantra:
"O Lord of the World, O Guru, protect me! I am scorched by the fire of saṃsāra and bitten by Time; I have come to you for refuge. (Hbhv 1.102)
In this matter, the wise should receive initiation from only one portion of the lotus feet of Śrī Vāsudeva, the crest-jewel of all the gods.
In the First Skandha (BhP 1.2.23):
"Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the qualities of Prakṛti; endowed with these, the one Supreme Person assumes here the various forms of this [world]."

For the sake of stability and so forth, the designations Hari, Viriñci, and Hara are used; indeed, among these, the names Hari and Viriñci are most auspicious for men whose bodies are composed of the quality of purity (sattva).
Moreover: "Furthermore,
even that water which has been poured from the tips of His toenails, offered as an arghya oblation by Viriñca, [sanctifies the world]."
Who indeed in this world, other than Mukunda, is the one who purifies even that which remains? Such is the true meaning of the word "Bhagavat."

Having heard that, the sages were struck with wonder and their doubts were dispelled; they placed even greater faith in Viṣṇu, from whom comes peace and from whom comes fearlessness. (Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam 10.89.15)
In the *Padma Purāṇa*, within the *Māhātmya of Vaiśākha* during the dialogue between Yama and a Brāhmaṇa (PadmaP 5.97.27):
"For the sake of deluding the world of moving and non-moving beings, let various ancient scriptures proclaim, until the end of the aeon, this or that particular deity as the supreme one."
In the final conclusion (siddhānta), however, it is determined that there is only one Blessed One, Viṣṇu, when all the operations of the scriptures have been subjected to analytical investigation.
In the *Nārasiṃha*: "Truth, truth, and again truth—I speak while raising my arm:
there is no scripture higher than the Veda, and no god higher than Keśava. (Hbhv 1.108)
For it is said in the Padma Purāṇa:
"An enemy becomes a friend, poison becomes wholesome, and unrighteousness turns into righteousness; when Hṛṣīkeśa is well-pleased, the opposite occurs when he is otherwise. (Hbhv 1.109)
In that very context, the words of the Blessed One are as follows:
"Even a sin committed for my sake conduces to merit;
conversely, even dharma, if practiced while disregarding me, becomes sin through my power. (Hbhv 1.110)

Therefore, it is said in the Śrī-Brahma-Nārada-Saṃvāda of the Skanda Purāṇa: "He who, abandoning Vāsudeva, worships another deity, indeed abandons his own mother and pays homage to a dog-cooker's wife. (Hbhv 1.111)
In that very same place, elsewhere it is said:
"He who, abandoning Vāsudeva, worships another deity—that deluded soul abandons nectar and consumes the halāhala poison. (Hbhv 1.112)
In the Mahābhārata:
"But he who, out of delusion, abandons Viṣṇu and worships another, is like one who casts away a heap of gold and desires to grasp a heap of dust. (Hbhv 1.113)
But he who, disregarding Viṣṇu, takes refuge in another deity, is like one afflicted by thirst who runs toward a mirage instead of the waters of the Gaṅgā. (Hbhv 1.114)
In the *Pañcarātra*:
"That evil-minded person who, out of delusion, once declares Viṣṇu to be equal to another inferior deity is an outcaste; he is not merely an outcaste—he is an outcaste. (Hbhv 1.115)
In the Vaiṣṇava Tantra:
"Even those whose minds are one-pointed, yet who perceive Viṣṇu as being on a par with others, shall not obtain again that exclusive devotion to Hari. (Hbhv 1.116)
And elsewhere it is said:
"But he who views the god Nārāyaṇa as being equal to deities such as Brahmā and Rudra will certainly become an heretic. (Hbhv 1.117)
If there are such floods of verses in the *Sahasranāmastotra* and other works,
then Viṣṇu, and no other, should especially be served by those who are devoted to living beings.
And likewise, in the Śrī Hari-vaṃśa, there is the speech of Śiva: "Hari alone is to be constantly worshipped by you who are established in goodness;
O brāhmaṇas, always recite the Viṣṇu-mantra and meditate upon Keśava. (Hbhv 1.119)
If statements concerning such greatness were collected from all sources, there would be the fault of excessive bulk in the work; therefore, only those that are required are being written here.
Now, regarding the greatness of the Śrī-Vaiṣṇava mantras, it is stated in the Āgama:
"The Vaiṣṇava mantras, such as the King of Mantras (Śrī-mantra-rāja) and others, [are received] through the grace of the guru."
Having attained all sovereignty through recitation, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Those men who have performed vast merit and intense austerity for thousands of years,
and who recite the Vaiṣṇava mantras, are purifiers of the world.
And in the Vaiṣṇava [scripture] it is said:
"By reciting Vaiṣṇava mantras, whatever person one sees with the eye or touches with the foot, that person is immediately liberated from great fear. (Hbhv 1.123)
Now, the greatness of the Viṣṇu-mantras is specifically written down in its essential meaning for the purpose of nourishing the majesty of the Śrī-Gopāla-mantra. (Hbhv 1.124)
Regarding the greatness of the twelve-syllable and eight-syllable [mantras],
it is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between the divine messenger and Vikuṇḍala:
"Together with its limbs, its mudrās, its ritual placements (*nyāsa*), and its seers and deities..."
The twelve-syllable mantra, together with the ritual of initiation, meditation, and the yantra.
Those best of men who recite the eight-syllable Lord of Mantras—
even a killer of a Brahmin is purified upon seeing them, for they are Viṣṇus themselves.
Having become bearers of the conch and the discus, wearing the *brahmāyu* garland,
those men dwell in the world of Viṣṇu in the form of Viṣṇu himself.
In that very same work, in the fourth book (*caturtha-skandha*) of the *Dvādaśākṣara* [Bhagavata Purāṇa 4.8.53]:
"And listen to me, O son of a king, regarding the supreme secret of recitation (*japa*), by practicing which for seven nights a man beholds the sky-dwellers (*khecara*s). (Hbhv 1.128)
In the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa [1.6.40]:
"The planets, such as the moon and the sun, return again and again;
but those who contemplate the twelve-syllable mantra do not return even today. (Hbhv_1.129)
Regarding the eight-syllabled [mantra],
as stated in the *Nārada-pañcarātra*:
"The three Vedas, the six auxiliary limbs, the meters, and the various gods."
Everything that exists within the eight syllables, as well as whatever else consists of speech.
The eight-syllable mantra is the essence of all the Vedāntas and the means of crossing the ocean of saṃsāra; it is the refuge for men who do not desire rebirth.
Where the illustrious one, perfected in the eight-syllable mantra, is honored,
there disease, famine, and thieves shall not roam.
Gods, dānavas, gandharvas, siddhas, vidyādharas, and others bow down to that great-souled man who knows the eight-syllable mantra. (Hbhv 1.133)
For it is evident that the Blessed One himself is indeed Nārāyaṇa manifest;
he revolves within [the practitioner's] mouths in the form of the eight-syllable mantra.
In the *Pādmottara-khaṇḍa* [PadmaP 6.226.18]:
"Thus, this eight-syllable mantra should be known as the accomplisher of all aims;
it is glorious, the remover of all suffering, the essence of all mantras, and auspicious. (Hbhv_1.135)
In the Liṅga Purāṇa:
"What is the use of many other mantras? What is the use of many other vows?
The mantra 'Namo Nārāyaṇāya' accomplishes all goals. (Hbhv 1.136)
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, he who at all times recites "Salutation to Nārāyaṇa" goes to the world of Viṣṇu along with his kinsmen.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
"The eight-syllabled great mantra is the supreme remover of all sins;
it is proclaimed to be the king among all Viṣṇu mantras. (Hbhv_1.138)
And in the dialogue between Śrī Śuka and Vyāsa:
"The mantra 'Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya' accomplishes all goals;
for those devotees who chant it, O dear one, it bestows the fruits of heaven and liberation. (Hbhv 1.139)
This alone is the supreme liberation; this is declared to be heaven.
This essence has been extracted from all the secrets of the Vedas.
In ancient times, it was proclaimed by Manu for the benefit of the Vaiṣṇavas by Viṣṇu himself;
it destroys all sins and bestows all desired objects.
"Salutation to Nārāyaṇa"— this alone is the true mantra for destroying the terrible poison of saṃsāra;
let those of truthful mind, joyful and free from passion, hear it.
With my arms raised high, I teach even more loftily.
Raising my arms aloft, I now speak to you with truth as my witness:
"O sons and disciples, listen; there is no mantra superior to the eight-syllabled one."
Therefore it is said in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"Whether sitting or lying down, or standing wherever one may be, one should take sole refuge in the mantra 'Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa'. (Hbhv 1.144)
In the *Tāpanī* scriptures [NṛsiṃhaTU 1.5.8], it is said:

"The gods indeed said to Prajāpati, 'O Blessed One, tell us the fruit of this Nārasiṃha King of Mantras in the Anuṣṭubh meter. He, Prajāpati, replied: 'He who [knows] this Nārasiṃha King of Mantras in the Anuṣṭubh meter...'"

He who studies constantly becomes purified by fire; he becomes purified by wind; he becomes purified by the sun; he becomes purified by the moon; he becomes purified by truth; he becomes purified by Brahman; he becomes purified by Viṣṇu;
he becomes purified by Rudra; he becomes purified by all; he becomes purified by all. (Hbhv 1.145)
In that very context, at the end [of the verse]: "A hundred uninitiated boys are equal to one initiated boy;
a hundred initiated boys are equal to one householder."
One hundred householders are equal to one forest-dweller;
one hundred forest-dwellers are equal to one ascetic;
and a full hundred ascetics are equal to one who recites the Rudra-mantra.
A hundred reciters of the Rudra-mantras are equal to one teacher of the Atharvaśiras and Śikhā. Furthermore,
this is the supreme abode of the teacher of the King of Mantras, where the sun does not shine,
where the wind does not blow, where the moon does not gleam, where the stars do not shine, and where fire does not burn.

Where death does not enter, where there is no suffering, but eternal bliss, supreme joy, peace, permanence, and constant auspiciousness—the Brahman adored by Brahmā and others, the supreme state meditated upon by yogis, having gone to which yogis do not return—that very thing is expressed by this verse: [The verse follows: "The wise perceive that supreme abode, free from darkness, beyond the reach of the senses, unmanifest, possessing the nature of light, and eternal; entering it, they do not return. (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.15)
The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu,
like an eye stretched across the sky.
The inspired poets, watchful and praising, kindle it.
That which is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Now, regarding the majesty of the Śrī Rāma mantras, it is said in the Agastya-saṃhitā:
"Among all classes of mantras, the Vaiṣṇava is declared to be the most excellent."
It bestows desired fruits within the Gāṇapatya, Śaiva, Śākta, and Saura [traditions].
Even among the Vaiṣṇava mantras, the Rāma-mantras yield greater fruit;
they are superior by tens of millions upon tens of millions of times compared to the Gāṇapatya and other mantras.
O best of Brahmins, even without initiation, indeed even without the preliminary rite (puraścaryā),
and even without the ritual of ritual placement (nyāsa-vidhi), they grant success through mere recitation alone.
Among the eight mantras, this six-syllable one yields its fruit without effort;
indeed, this six-syllable mantra wards off the great flood of sins.
It is proclaimed as the King of Mantras, the most excellent among all; it destroys the daily misfortune arising from fortnights, months, seasons, and years. (Hbhv_1.151)
It burns everything without exception, like fire consumes a mountain of cotton—even thousands of killings of Brahmins committed both knowingly and unknowingly. (Hbhv 1.152)
The theft of gold, the drinking of liquor, and violating the teacher’s bed—
indeed, even thousands of millions upon millions of minor offenses—
all of these perish through the recitation of the Rāma-mantra. (Hbhv_1.153)
And in the Tapanīya Śrutis:
"The Brāhmaṇa who constantly studies this Tāraka [mantra] crosses over evil."
He crosses over death; he crosses over the killing of a brother;
he crosses over the killing of all beings.
He crosses over cyclic existence;
he crosses over everything;
he becomes one who relies upon liberation.
He thus attains immortality.
Now, regarding the greatness of the Gopāla-deva mantra:
the mantras of Lord Kṛṣṇa, the manifest Bhagavān Hari—the seed of all incarnations—are the most powerful of all. (Hbhv 1.155)
And so it is stated in the *Bṛhad-gautamīya*, known as the *Śrī-govinda-vṛndāvana*:
"Among all the most excellent mantras, the Vaiṣṇava is said to be the best; specifically, the mantras of Kṛṣṇa are the sole means for both enjoyment and liberation. (Hbhv 1.156)
Furthermore, whichever deity belongs to whichever mantra,
that very deity is declared to be the essence of its seed-syllables (manu) as well, because there is no difference between them.
"Kṛṣṇa alone is the Supreme Brahman, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss;
by his mere remembrance, he indeed bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus, even there, he manifested his own divine lordship through the pastimes of a cowherd boy.
Among those, the most excellent mantras are the eighteen-syllable ones.
In the *Tāpanīya-śrutis*: "Om! Indeed, the sages said to Brahmā:
'Who is the supreme deity?'"
From what does death fear?
By whose knowledge is everything known?
By what does this universe transmigrate?
The Brāhmaṇa said to them: "Kṛṣṇa is indeed the supreme deity;
Death fears Govinda.
Through the knowledge of Gopījana-vallabha, everything becomes known."
"By *svāhā* this transmigrates.
To him they said:
"Who is Kṛṣṇa Govinda? Who is that beloved of the cowherd women? And who is *svāhā*?"

The Brahmin, the remover of sin, who is known through the Vedas as the Knower of Cows and Earth, the impeller of the arts of ignorance of the cowherd folk, and the master of their illusory power, said to them:
"All this is indeed the Supreme Brahman.
He who meditates upon it, tastes it, and worships it becomes immortal—he becomes immortal."
They said: "What is His form? What is His taste? Or how is He carried? Tell all that to those who desire to know it.
Then Hairaṇya said: "[He is] dressed as a cowherd, shining like a cloud, youthful, and seated upon the wish-fulfilling tree."
Furthermore, in that very same work, it says further on: "Devotion (bhakti) is the act of worship (bhajana).
This consists of the mental application toward that [Divine] alone, through the absence of any limiting conditions regarding this world or the next."
And this indeed is freedom from action:
the Brahmins worship Him, Kṛṣṇa, in many ways; though He is Govinda, they propitiate Him in many forms.
The beloved of the cowherd women, resting upon the *svāhā* [sacrificial exclamation], supported the worlds; he whose seed is his own causes the universe to tremble.
Just as the one wind, having entered the world, assumes five forms in each and every creature,
so too Kṛṣṇa, though one, [assumes many forms] for the sake of the welfare of the world.
"By means of sound, he shines forth as the five-footed.
Furthermore, in that very same [text], immediately after the description of the method of worship:
"The one controller, all-pervading, Kṛṣṇa, the praiseworthy..."
Though being one, he who shines forth in many ways—
to those wise ones who worship him seated upon his throne belongs eternal happiness, and not to others.
The eternal among the eternals, the conscious among the conscious,
the one who fulfills the desires of the many—
those wise ones who worship Him seated upon the throne.
Their accomplishment is eternal, and not that of others.
For those eternally liberated ones who worship this supreme abode of Viṣṇu without desires,
He, in the form of a cowherd, [reveals Himself] through their diligent effort.
At that very moment, one should manifest the state of the Self.
To Him who created Brahmā in the beginning, and who protects for him the sciences— that Kṛṣṇa,
the divine, the light of self-knowledge— [I bow].
One who desires liberation should indeed go for refuge.
To those who recite the five-word mantra of Govinda with the syllable *oṃ* interspersed,
He reveals His own form.
Therefore, one who desires liberation should practice for the sake of constant peace.
From him, other five sons were born to Govinda; they were the Manus of men,
beginning with Daśārṇa, who were [further] begotten by Saṅkrandana and the others.
They are practiced correctly by those desiring prosperity.
Furthermore, in that very same place it is said:
"That Brāhmaṇa said: 'He was meditated upon and praised by me incessantly; at the end of a parārdha, he became aware.
A man in the guise of a cowherd appeared before me.'"

Then, having been bowed to by me with a favorable heart, He granted me His own form consisting of eighteen syllables for the purpose of creation and vanished. Again, my desire to create manifested itself,
as those syllables revealed the form of the future universe.
Thus, here, *kā* is water,
*lā* is earth,
and *īta* is fire.
From the drop [came] the moon;
from its sound, the sun—I created them from the syllable *klīm*.
From Kṛṣṇa [came] space, and from the subsequent [syllable], the wind; thus I manifested the fragrant Vidyā.
Beyond that, and beyond that, all this—consisting of female, male, and so forth—is "this. // Hbhv_1.169 //
And so it is stated in the Gautamīya Tantra:
"The head of the Śruti declares that he created the universe from the syllable *klīṃ*;
from the letter *la* the earth was born, and from the letter *ka* the origin of water. (Hbhv_1.170)
From the vowel *ī* fire is produced; from the nasal sound (*nāda*) life-force (*āyus*) was born;
from the bindu arises space (*ākāśa*). Thus is the mantra consisting of the elements.
By the word "own" (sva) is meant the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), and by "it" (he) is meant the supreme nature of consciousness (cit-prakṛti).
The arising of their unity is the coloring that covers the face [of reality].
For this very reason, the dissolution of the universe occurs within its own source.
Furthermore, that same scripture states:
"By the sacrifice to this very one, Candra-dhvaja, having realized his self to be free from delusion, repeated the mantra situated within the *oṃkāra*; being devoid of attachment, he attained it.
The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu."
Like an eye stretched across the sky,
therefore one should practice this constantly.
And so forth, as stated further on in that same work: "From whose first step [comes] the earth, and from the second, the waters."
From the third [element] fire arises; from the fourth comes the bearer of fragrance (the wind).
From the fifth [stage] arises the emergence into the sky; one should practice that alone.
Viṣṇu, whose banner is the moon, went to that very supreme, imperishable state. (Hbhv_1.174)
Then there is that very state consisting of five steps, which is pure, stainless, free from sorrow, and in which all attachment such as greed has been entirely cast out.
That Vāsudeva is that from which nothing else exists.

"I, together with the hosts of Maruts, constantly satisfy that one Govinda, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss, who sits beneath the celestial trees of Vṛndāvana, by means of this five-line supreme hymn.
Thus,
and furthermore, immediately following the hymn—

Whoever should repeat this five-word mantra goes effortlessly to that state which is absolute, unmoving, one, swifter than the mind; even the gods did not reach it, for it was ahead of them. (Hbhv 1.177)
Therefore, Kṛṣṇa alone is the supreme deity; one should meditate upon him, taste him, and worship him—Om Tat Sat. Hbhv_1.178.
And in the *Trailokyasaṃmohana-tantra*, in the very context of the eighteen-syllable mantra spoken by the illustrious Mahādeva to the Goddess:
"He is the lord of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; he is the Lord of the World."
He has thousands of highly fortunate incarnations.
Among those incarnations, his childhood was exceedingly rare;
and various superhuman deeds were performed by him.
I shall proclaim his unsurpassed mantra, together with its limbs and sub-limbs, by whom everything is established in the power of both cursing and bestowing grace. (Hbhv_1.181)
By the mere knowledge of which a person may attain omniscience;
one desiring a son obtains a son, and one desiring merit obtains wealth. (Hbhv 1.182)
One certainly becomes a master of the meaning of all treatises; of this there is no doubt.
One may bring the three worlds under one's control and agitate the entire universe.
He too shall delude all and slay all his enemies;
what need is there for much speaking here? One who desires liberation shall attain liberation.
Just as the wish-fulfilling gem is supreme, just as the cow, just as Satī,
just as the twice-born, and just as the Gaṅgā, so too is this mantra the most excellent.
Just as the Vaiṣṇava scripture is entirely excellent according to its own tradition,
and just as well-refined speech is supreme, so too is this mantra the most excellent.
Moreover:
"Therefore, O Sovereign of the Gods, this mantra is recited by me every day;
there is nothing equal to it in this world of moving and unmoving beings. (Hbhv_1.187)
Also in the Sanatkumāra-kalpa: "There are thirty-three varieties of mantras concerning Gopāla;
among all those mantras, listen to this king of mantras. (Hbhv_1.188)
O bull among sages, you must preserve with great effort this mantra, which is perfectly serene, within the tantra called Sammohana. Hbhv_1.189.
By means of this king of mantras, Purandara attained the status of Mahendra, the lord of the gods, which was swiftly bestowed by Viṣṇu. (Hbhv 1.190)
Formerly, afflicted by misfortune due to the curse of Durvāsas,
he indeed regained the state of being fortunate through that very same [means].
What is the use of saying much here regarding the preliminary practices and means?
Even without them, by mere recitation alone, one obtains everything desired.
I bow to that Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇacaitanya, the supreme guru,
by taking refuge in whom even an ordinary person may somehow become the highest.
Now follows the determination of eligibility:
even for women, for chaste wives, and for Śūdras and others who possess right understanding, there is eligibility for initiation into the mantras of the Tantras. (Hbhv_1.194)

And likewise, in the *Smṛtyarthasāra* and in the *Vaiśākhamāhātmya* of the *Padmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Ambarīṣa (PadmaP 6.84.48, 52–54), it is stated: "Worship may be performed even by women and *śūdras* according to the path taught in the Āgamas."
Having contemplated Viṣṇu as her husband within her heart, she should perform her duties with faith.
And for the Śūdras, the worship of deities shall indeed be performed by name;
all should perform it according to the path of the Āgamas, which imitates the Vedas.
Women also have the right to perform the worship of Viṣṇu and other such rites, provided they are devoted to pleasing their husbands; this is the eternal Vedic revelation.
In the Agastya-saṃhitā, with reference to the Śrī Rāma-mantra-rāja:
"Śūdras who are most pure in their vows, righteous, and servants of the twice-born;
women devoted to their husbands; and others born of inverse or natural order [of castes]."
"All people, down to the outcaste (caṇḍāla),
are eligible for this," thus the Guru should deliberate when bestowing mantras such as those for the *siddha* or *sādhya* classes,
considering their own lineage or lack thereof, and whether they are children or adults.
The states of female, male, and neuter; the conjunction of zodiac signs and lunar mansions;
the time of sleep and awakening; as well as debt, wealth, and so forth.
Now, regarding the purification of the Siddhas, Sādhakas, and so forth, the *Saradā-tilaka* states:
"First, there should be five lines with their tips pointing east and west, and [five] running from south to north."
And with that many [units], the mandala shall consist of four groups of four squares.
In the directions, by means of the numbers two, three, eleven, nine,
two, six, eight, sixteen, fourteen, and five;
and in the subterranean realms, by means of the fifteen, three, and one lunar mansion (koṣṭha).
The wise one should write the letters arising from the script in their proper sequence.

In each of the four squares, one should write the first syllable of the mantra and so forth, up to the number of syllables in the birth-constellation and the eyes (two), using four compartments for each single square. (Hbhv 1.203)
Furthermore, within the individual squares of the grid, starting from the letter representing one's birth [sign] on the left,
the wise should understand the sequence of *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *ari* [according to their respective positions].
The *siddha* is accomplished in due time; the *sādhya*, however, through recitation and fire-offerings;
the *susiddha* by mere seizing; and the *ari* cuts off the very root.
A *siddha-siddha* [mantra] is effective according to what has been stated; a *siddha-sādhaka* is twice as effective;
a *siddha-susiddha* is effective with half the recitation; but a *siddhāri* destroys one's kinsmen.
The *sādhya-siddha* is doubled; the *sādhya-sādhya* is indeed useless.
The *susiddha* is tripled, while the *sādhya-ari* destroys those born of the same lineage.

Through the recitation of a *susiddha* mantra, one achieves success; through one that is superior in its qualities, a *sādhya*; through a *susiddha*, a *graha* (seizer); and an enemy of a *susiddha* destroys one's own lineage. (Hbhv 1.208)
An *ari-siddha* [yoga] kills one's sons; an *ari-sādhya*, however, kills one's daughters. An *ari-susiddha* kills one's wife, while an *ari-ari* kills the practitioner himself. (Hbhv 1.209)
And likewise, in the Tantra, there is an exception regarding specific mantras for this [rule]: "In the case of Nṛsiṃha, Arka, and Varāha, as well as the Prāsāda and the Praṇava."
And one should not at all examine the perfected ones (siddhas) and so forth regarding a Vedic mantra.

In the case of a three-syllable or a single-syllable mantra obtained in a dream, bestowed by a woman, or given as a garland-mantra, one should not examine its success or other such qualities at all. (Hbhv 1.211)
That one's own family is actually no family and so forth should be understood from other scriptures;
it is not written here for fear of prolixity and because it would be redundant.
Regarding the mantras that possess such powers as manifest the sovereign majesty of the illustrious Lord Gopāla, nothing whatsoever remains to be deliberated upon.

And so it is said in the *Kramadīpikā* (1.4): "Among all castes, as well as among those in the various stages of life, among women, and among those born under various names and signs of the zodiac..."
This mantra of Gopālaka swiftly bestows all desired fruits.
And in the *Trailokyasaṃmohana-tantra*,

concerning the eighteen-syllable mantra, the venerable Śiva has said: "In this case, there are no defects such as [conflict with] the scriptures, nor is there any consideration of vowels, consonants, and so forth."
Or rather, O beloved, no consideration of the zodiacal signs should be made regarding the Mantra.
"Some are cut, some are obstructed, some are intoxicated with pride;
some are soiled, some are paralyzed, some are pinned down, and some are even corrupted.
This one, however, is not possessed of these defects, for he is the supreme among the three worlds. (Hbhv_1.216) Thus it is said.
And generally, as it is stated in the *Bṛhadgautamīya*:
"Now I shall describe the Kṛṣṇa-mantras, which bestow both seen and unseen fruits;
by knowing which, sages indeed attained liberation with ease. (Hbhv_1.217)
Householders, forest-dwellers, ascetics, and celibate students;
women, Śūdras, and others—all are qualified for this.
In this [practice], there is no need for consideration regarding the purification of enemies and so forth, nor the characteristics of enemies, friends, and the like;
nor is there an abundance of exertion, nor any weariness in the accomplishment.
And like a fire [consuming] a heap of cotton, it destroys ignorance in a mere moment;
there is no deliberation here regarding those who are the accomplished, the to-be-accomplished, the well-accomplished, or the enemy. (Hbhv 1.220)
Since the mantra consisting of the syllable of Brahmā is the perfected mantra of them all,
Prajāpati attained the preeminent sovereignty over the gods as the husband of Śacī;
the deities regained heaven, and Bṛhaspati attained lordship over speech.
And so forth; in that very same context it is said:
"By devotion to Viṣṇu, what on earth cannot be accomplished with distinction?"
O Sage, from insects up to Brahmā, [all attain their state] through the grace of Govinda.
"Abodes of all prosperity and free from fear from any quarter everywhere"—thus, O Lords of Sages, some of your majesty has been described to you. (Hbhv 1.223)
Just as stars appear in the sky or like the formation of sand on the ocean,
by the mere realization of this, one attains the fourfold liberation.
Whatever other defects exist in these and other mantras—for that purpose, the ten purificatory rites for mantras are inscribed according to the Tantra. (Hbhv 1.225)
In the *Śaradā-tilaka*:
"Birth and life, as well as striking and confining;
then consecration, purification, and replenishment."
Satiating, kindling, and concealment—these ten are the consecrations of the mantra.
The extraction of mantras from the midst of the *mātṛkā* is known as their "birth.
A wise person should recite the syllables of the mantra, placing the *praṇava* (oṃ) between them. (Hbhv 1.227)
Those proficient in the *mantras* and *tantras* declare this to be "life": having written the syllables of the name of the person (*manu*), one should strike them with sandalwood water. (Hbhv 1.228)
The practitioner of mantra should strike each [syllable] with the wind [vāyu]; that is declared to be "striking" (tāḍana).
Having written that mantra, the practitioner [should worship it] with flowers born of the karavīra.

The practitioner of mantra should perform the striking with a number equal to the syllables of that mantra; by means of that, there is confinement, according to the procedure taught in one's own tantra, using a number equal to the syllables of the mantra. (Hbhv 1.230)
One should consecrate the mantra with *aśvattha* shoots for the sake of purification;
having contemplated the mantra with the mind, one should burn away [impurities] from the mantra with light.

The practitioner of mantra should purify the three roots within the mantra; this is the purification. The light-mantra (jyotirmanu) is considered to consist of the syllable *tāra* (oṃ), the sky (0), fire (3), the pair of manas (2), and the staff (1). With water from *kuśa* grass over which this has been recited, one should sprinkle the mantra syllable by syllable. (Hbhv 1.232)
This nourishing [of the mantra] is prescribed according to rule by means of that mantra;
the satiation of the yantra with water by means of the mantra is known as *tarpaṇa*. (Hbhv 1.233)
The conjunction of Tāra, Māyā, and Ramā is called the "illumination of the mind";
the concealment of the mantra being recited, however, is its non-disclosure.
Because the mantras of Kṛṣṇa possess power, they do not depend on ritual consecration;
nevertheless, this has been stated merely by way of a general reference.

Thus ends the first chapter, named "The Chapter on Reverence" (*gaurava*), in the *Śrī-Bhagavad-bhakti-vilāsa* composed by Śrī Gopāla Bhaṭṭa. ************************************************************************* 2. The Chapter on Initiation (*dīkṣika*)
I bow to that Śrīmat-Kṛṣṇacaitanya, the teacher of the world, who belongs to the second [category], the initiated (daikṣika).
Through whose compassion even a dog may cross the great ocean with ease.
Now, the procedure for initiation (*dīkṣā-vidhi*):
Here, following the *Kramadīpikā*, the procedure for initiation is written down.
For indeed, without initiation, there is never any qualification for worship. (Hbhv_2.2)
In the scripture:

"For the twice-born who have not been initiated, there is no entitlement here to their own duties, such as Vedic study and the like; [such entitlement] arises only after the initiation ceremony. (Hbhv 2.3)
Likewise, those who have not been initiated have no authority over the worship of mantras and deities and so forth; therefore, one should make oneself praised by Śiva.
In the *Skānda Purāṇa*, within the section on Kārttika, during the dialogue between Śrī Brahmā and Nārada:
"Those men are beasts in this world; what fruit is there in their living, by whom initiation into Hari has not been obtained, or Janārdana has not been worshipped? (Hbhv 2.5)
In that very place, in the dialogue between Śrī Rukmāṅgada and Mohinī,
and also in the Viṣṇuyāmala, it is said:
"O lady of beautiful thighs, everything performed by one who has not received initiation is useless."
A person who lacks initiation enters the womb of an animal.
Specifically, in the Viṣṇuyāmala:
"Whether out of affection or even out of greed, if one should accept [a disciple] without initiation, a curse from the deity shall fall upon that guru along with his disciples. (Hbhv 2.7)

And in the Viṣṇurahasya: "One who performs the ritual action of Hari’s worship with devotion, yet without knowing the procedure as prescribed by the injunctions, obtains only a hundredth part of the merit gained from performing it according to the injunctions. (Hbhv_2.8)
Because it bestows divine knowledge and brings about the destruction of sin, it is therefore called *dīkṣā* by the teachers who are experts in the reality [of the principles]. (Hbhv 2.9)
Therefore, having bowed to the Guru and offered everything one possesses,
one should receive the Vaiṣṇava mantra according to the prescribed ritual, preceded by initiation.
In the Skanda Purāṇa, in that very same section, during the dialogue between Śrī Brahmā and Nārada:
"Those ascetics who are devoted to action are indeed the best of men on earth—those by whom the initiation of Hari, which liberates one from all suffering, has been received. (Hbhv_2.11)
And in the Tantra-sāgara:
"Just as bell-metal attains the state of gold through the application of mercury, so too does the status of the twice-born arise for men through the procedure of initiation. (Hbhv_2.12)
Now, regarding the time for initiation— concerning the purity of the month, it is stated in the Āgama:
"The undertaking of a mantra in the month of Caitra yields much suffering as its fruit."
In Vaiśākha there shall be the acquisition of jewels, but in Jyeṣṭha death is certain.
In Āṣāḍha there is the loss of kinsmen; in Śrāvaṇa, it brings fear;
in Bhādrapada, there is the decline of progeny; but in Āśvina, there is auspiciousness everywhere.
In Kārttika there shall be an increase of wealth; in Mārgaśīrṣa it bestows auspiciousness;
in Pauṣa there may be a loss of knowledge; in Māgha there is an increase in intelligence;
and in Phālguna, mastery over all beings is proclaimed by the teachers. (Hbhv 2.15)
And in some places it is said:
"Prosperity will surely come in Śrāvaṇa, and likewise knowledge in Kārttika;
prosperity shall also come in Phālguna; one should avoid the intercalary month (malamāsa). (Hbhv 2.16)
In the Gautamīya [Tantra], the commencement of mantra practice should take place in Caitra, as it bestows all human goals;
in Vaiśākha there will be the acquisition of jewels, but in Jyaiṣṭha death is certain. (Hbhv_2.17)
In Āṣāḍha there will be the loss of kinsmen; in Śrāvaṇa one shall have a full lifespan;
in Bhādrapada there will be the loss of progeny; and in Āśvina there will be an accumulation of jewels.
In Kārttika there shall be the accomplishment of mantras; likewise it shall be so in Mārgaśīrṣa.
In Pauṣa there shall be affliction from enemies, while in Māgha there is an increase of intelligence. In Phālguna all desires shall be fulfilled; one should avoid the intercalary month (mala-māsa).
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in that very same section, within the dialogue between Śrī Rukmāṅgada and Mohinī, it is said:
"Initiation performed by men in the month of Kārttika cuts through rebirth;
therefore, one should undertake initiation in Kārttika with every effort. (Hbhv_2.20)
In the initiation for the mantras of the illustrious Gopāla, however, there is no fault;
for the teachers have stated that the initiation which was prescribed for the month of Caitra should indeed take place then. (Hbhv_2.21)
Now, regarding the purification of the day: it should be performed on Sunday, Thursday, Monday, as well as on Wednesday and Friday.
Now, regarding the purification of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra-śuddhi*), it is stated in the *Nārada-tantra*:
"Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, Ārdrā, Dhaniṣṭhā, and the three Uttaras."
Puṣya and Śatabhiṣaj are said to be the lunar mansions for initiation (dīkṣā).
And in some cases,
one should perform the mantra-consecration under the asterisms of Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, Svāti, Viśākhā, Hasta, and likewise under Jyeṣṭhā and the three Uttaras. (Hbhv 2.24)
Now, regarding the purity of lunar days (*tithi-śuddhi*),
the *Sārasaṅgraha* states:
"The second, the fifth, and especially the sixth [lunar days are auspicious]."
It should also be performed on the twelfth day, or even on the thirteenth.
And in some cases— the full moon day, the fifth, the second, the seventh, as well as the thirteenth and the tenth— are praised and grant all desires. (Hbhv_2.26)

Thus, initiation is praised when performed on a pure day during the bright fortnight, at the rising of Venus or Jupiter, in an auspicious astrological moment (lagna), and under favorable lunar and stellar conditions. Hbhv_2.27 //
Now, here is the exception (the specific rule) in the Rudrayāmala:
"At a sacred pilgrimage site, during an eclipse of the sun or moon, and on the days of the thread ceremony and the binding of the sacrificial post."
One should perform the initiation into the mantra; one need not purify the month, the lunar mansion, or other such factors.
For here, the strength of the ascendant, the moon, the stars, and so forth is always present;
thus, the mantra obtained here increases long life, prosperity, and progeny. (Hbhv_2.29)
There is nothing equal to the time of a solar eclipse;
whatever is performed at that time shall yield infinite fruit.
At a solar festival (parvan), there is no need for the purification of the month, lunar day, weekday, and so forth. (Hbhv_2.30)
When the ocean of reality is difficult to find, and the company of true gurus has been encountered even once,
and when their permission is obtained— that is the great occasion for initiation.
Whether in a village or a forest, in a field by day or at night,
whenever the Guru should happen to arrive by chance, then [the initiation] should be performed according to his command.
Whenever there is the desire [to receive initiation], then initiation is performed according to the command of the Guru.
There is no need for sacred pilgrimage sites, no vows, no fire-offerings, no ritual bathing, and no recitation of mantras;
rather, the performance of initiation occurs when a true Guru is encountered by one's own will.
Now follows the procedure for the construction of the pavilion.
Initiation is fourfold, categorized as *kriyāvatī* and so forth.
Among these, the *kriyāvatī* initiation is described here in brief.
Having consecrated the ground and worshipped the deities of the site (vāstu-devatā) therein,
one should construct a pavilion measuring seven cubits, complete with a beautiful altar.
It has eight banners and four gates, with arches made of milk-tree wood;
it is enriched with triple-stranded cords and encircled by garlands of *kuśa* grass.
Now follows the procedure for constructing the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa):
In that [direction], specifically the northern direction, the wise one should construct a square pit with three tiers (mekhalā), measuring twenty-four finger-breadths in size. (Hbhv 2.37)
One should construct the excavation together with the height of the three tiers;
outside of that excavation, one should certainly make a neck (kaṇṭha) of one finger-breadth.
In that regard, the height and width of the first girdle are four finger-breadths;
those of the second are three finger-breadths, and those of the third are two finger-breadths.
And on the western side, above the three girdles, one should fashion the *yoni*,
six finger-breadths in width and twelve finger-breadths in length.
One should fashion it one finger-breadth in height, with a hole in the middle,
shaped like the wielder of the mace (Viṣṇu), and provided with a girdle according to the rules.
For a homa of fifty [oblations], the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be one cubit in height and measure one fistful.
At a hundred oblations, the pit should be one *aratni* in measure; at a thousand, measured by a span (*pāṇi*);
at a hundred thousand, by four cubits (*hasta*); and at ten million, measured by eight of those.
One should make the excavation of the square pit such that its depth is likewise [the same as its width].

If a fire sacrifice (homa) is performed in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with fewer oblations than prescribed, it must be repeated; however, if the number of oblations is greater than required, no repetition is necessary.
The wise person should diligently construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) exactly according to the rules;
otherwise, many faults that cause great suffering will arise.
Thus it has been said by the Tantric masters: "A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) endowed with such characteristics bestows the desired fruit;
however, a pit that possesses deficiencies or excesses therein brings about many faults. (Hbhv 2.46)
Therefore, one who desires what is auspicious should act only after thorough examination;
or, in the case of a concise fire-offering ritual, a sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) measuring only a cubit [may be used].
Hārīta also says:
"If there is an excess or deficiency in the width, one will certainly be born with a short lifespan;
if there is an excess in the depth, one becomes a yogi, but if it is deficient, there is a loss of wealth."
If the sacrificial pit is crooked, there will be suffering; if the girdle is broken, death.
If the girdle is too high, there will be grief; if it is excessive, the loss of cattle;
if it is devoid of the [proper] base, the loss of one's wife; and if it is devoid of the neck-band, the loss of auspiciousness. (Hbhv 2.49)

The measurement of a finger is also stated: "Eight horizontal barley-corns or three vertical grains of rice are to be known as the measure of a finger, by means of the middle joint of the middle finger. (Hbhv 2.50)

Thus, the specific details regarding other matters, such as the preparation of the *srak* and *sruva* ladles, should be understood from another text; they are not written here for fear of excessive length. (Hbhv 2.51)
Now, the procedure for the initiation mandala:
Having sprinkled the pavilion with the five products of the cow and with scented water, one should duly draw the initiation mandala upon the altar. (Hbhv 2.52)
In its center is an eight-petaled lotus; outside of that, three circles;
then the zodiac signs; and then the pedestal provided with four legs.
Therefore, one should draw four walkways outside that [mandala] in the four directions, enriched with ornaments, sub-ornaments, and corners; then, [one should draw] the four gates.
Then, having performed the morning rites as part of the initiation (dīkṣā), the Guru should install [the deities] in their respective places,
as well as the conch and the ritual offerings, according to the manner described in the preliminary diagram.
Therein, first is the procedure for the installation of the jar:
having worshipped the gurus and Gaṇeśa, and having performed the worship of the pedestal,
one should place rice, unhusked grains, and likewise *kuśa* grass in the center of the lotus.
One should place the ten digits (kalās) of Fire, beginning with the letter 'ya', upon blades of kuśa grass;
having performed the placement and worship, and while reciting the Tāra mantra, one should place the water-pot as prescribed.
And they have been described as follows: Dhūmrārcis, Uṣmā, Jvalanī, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī, Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā, and also Havyavahā and Kavyavahā. (Hbhv 2.58)
Thus,

having assigned the twelve digits of the Sun in the pitcher (kumbha) using the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṭha*, joined with the letters beginning with *bha* and ending with *ḍa* in reverse order, one should worship them.
Now he writes about the placement (nyāsa) and so forth of the solar digits (sūrya-kalā) in that vessel (kuṇḍa), beginning with the words "by those starting with *ka*":
the twelve digits are joined with the phonemes (*arṇa*) starting from the letter *ka* and ending with the letter *ṭha*.
The particle *ca* is used for conjunction.
"They are also joined with letters beginning with *bha* and ending with *ḍa*.

Now, one might ask: "How can the twelve letters beginning with *bha* end with *ḍa*, given that they would reach *kṣa* in regular order? To this he replies: "By those moving in reverse," meaning by those obtained through inversion.

The meaning is as follows: having first joined each individual letter beginning with *ka*, recited in direct order (*anuloma*), with its corresponding single letter beginning with *bha*, recited in reverse order (*pratiloma*), within the solar digits (*sūrya-kalā*), one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and so forth.
The practical application (*prayoga*) is as follows: *kaṃ bhaṃ tapanyai namaḥ*, and so on. (Hbhv_2.59)
And they have been described as follows:
Tapanī, Tāpanī, Dhūmrā, Bhrāmarī, Jvālinī, Ruci, Suṣumṇā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā. (Hbhv 2.60)
Thus,
one should place white flowers, along with unbroken grains, white sugar, gold, gems, and likewise *kuśa* grass, into the interior of the jar while reciting the root mantra. (Hbhv 2.61)

Then, having meditated upon the fire in the form of the support (*ādhāra*) and the sun in the form of the vessel (*kumbha*) according to the method described, one should cast white flowers and so forth into the interior, the middle of that vessel—along with sugar. As it has been said:
"Having raised [the vessel], one should place a white flower together with sugar in its center."
One should cast gold, a gem, and a tuft of hair using the root mantra itself.
Thus,
whatever is written here that exceeds the meaning of the root text should be understood as following from the phrase "as previously stated" (*yathodita*) occurring earlier. (Hbhv 2.61)
One should fill the jar with pure water from a sacred ford according to the prescribed rite;
having placed the lunar clans (indukula) within the water along with their vowels, one should worship the sixteen [clans].
And they have been mentioned as follows:
Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭī, Rati, Dhṛti,
Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, and Aṅgadā.
Pūrṇā and Pūrṇāmṛtā.
Thus,
having cast the eight fragrances and the *kalās* into a conch filled with pure water,
one should invoke all of them and perform the *prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath) in due order.
The eight fragrant substances are also stated:
uśīra, kuṅkuma, kuṣṭha, bālaka, aguru, murā, jaṭāmāṃsī, and candana; this is the desired "eightfold fragrance" for Hari. (Hbhv 2.65)
Thus it is said:
"By some, this eightfold fragrance is considered to consist of sandalwood, camphor, agallochum, saffron, bezoar, kakkola, and the flesh of a monkey. (Hbhv 2.66)
In the same way, there are ten [syllables] born from the vowel *a* with the ten consonants beginning with *ka*;
those born from the vowel *u* begin with *ṣṭa*; and those born from the vowel *ma* begin with *pa*.

One should perform the placement of sixteen [syllables] upon the conch: four born from the *bindu* with the four [consonants] beginning with *ṣa*, and sixteen digits (*kalā*) born from the *nāda* joined with the sixteen vowels.
And they are said to be:

Creation (Sṛṣṭi), Prosperity (Ṛddhi), Memory (Smṛti), Intelligence (Medhā), Beauty (Kānti), Fortune (Lakṣmī), Fortitude (Dhṛti), Steadfastness (Sthirā), Stability (Sthiti), and Accomplishment (Siddhi). These ten digits (kalās) arising from the letter 'A' have been described. (Hbhv 2.69)
Old Age, Protectress, Peace, Sovereignty, Lust, and Desire;
Giver of Boons, Joy, Affection, and Longevity—these are the digits (kalās) born from the syllable *ukāra*.

The syllables beginning with *ma* give rise to the following *kalās*: Tīkṣṇā (the Sharp), Raudrā (the Fierce), Bhayā (Fear), Nidrā (Sleep), Tantī (the Cord), Kṣut (Hunger), Krodhanī (the Wrathful), Kriyā (Action), Utkārī (the Eructating), and Mṛtyu (Death). Hbhv_2.71.
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti;
Indhikā, Dīpikā, Recikā, and the supreme Mocikā.
Sūkṣmā, Sūkṣmāmṛtā, Jñānā, Ajñānā, Āyanī, Vyāpinī, Vyomarūpā, Anantā, and Nādasambhavā. // Hbhv_2.73 //

Thus, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of all the kalās one by one in sequence; having uttered their names in the dative case, ending with "namaḥ," together with their respective syllables. (Hbhv 2.74)
Prior to the consecration of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) and after the invocation (āvāhana) of those [deities],
one should recite the five verses in their proper places and worship those digits (kalās).
"Haṃsaḥ śuciṣat," beginning with that, then "Pratad viṣṇuḥ," after that "Tryambakam," then "Tat savituḥ," and finally "Viṣṇur yonim"—in this sequence. (Hbhv 2.76)
And one should pour that conch-water into the jar with the root mantra;
one should cover its mouth with sprouts of the *śakravallī*, mango tree, and so forth. (Hbhv 2.77)
Then, having covered that [pitcher] again with a vessel filled with flowers and other offerings,
and having wrapped it with a pair of cloths, one should then decorate the pitcher.
Now, the procedure for the worship of the Blessed One in the pitcher:

having invoked the supreme splendor into that pitcher according to the rule, and having performed the ritual of the limbs (sakalīkaraṇa), the preceptor should worship it with the seat and other offerings. (Hbhv 2.79)
And the sakalīkaraṇa has been described: "The sakalīkṛti is the placement (nyāsa) of the six limbs upon the limbs of the deity. (Hbhv 2.80)
And some say that even without all the ritual placements (*nyāsa*),
the making of one's own body possessed of limbs through that splendor is what constitutes being "sakalīkṛta" (made complete).

And thus, one should worship that Lord, together with his limbs, secondary limbs, and enclosures, within the pitcher according to the procedure for drawing [the deity], beginning from the front and continuing until the offering of food.
After the offering of the food oblation (naivedya), one should place earthen vessels containing seeds and sprouts, along with lamps, all around the mandala.

Now follows the procedure for the initiation-oblation (dīkṣā-homa): Then, for the sake of the oblation that is an ancillary of initiation, one should sweep around the entire sacrificial pit with a broom of *darbha* grass and smear it according to the rule.
Having scattered mustard seeds there and sprinkled [the site] with the five products of the cow,
one should worship Vāstupuruṣa in the center and his lords in the cardinal directions.
Having performed the drying and other rites for the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and having sprinkled it with water from kuśa grass,
one should scratch the ground and draw the mandala within it, together with the womb (yoni) and other features.
Having written the Śrī-bīja in the central womb and having worshipped it without eating,
one should place flowers and other offerings there and properly prepare a seat.
There, having invoked and worshipped Viṣṇu— the [deities] of Fortune, Death, and the Bath—
one should bring a bright fire in a vessel of copper or similar material and establish it in front.

Having worshipped the fire with perfumes and other offerings, one should contemplate it as being of the nature of the seed (retas) of Viṣṇu sporting with Śrī, and then worship that fire-pit with the Tāra mantra.

Having covered that fire with fuel sticks while reciting the mantra "vaiśvānara," and having kindled it with the mantra "cit piṅgala," one should worship that fire with the mantra "upatiṣṭhed agnim. (Hbhv 2.90)
One should place the tongue upon that [heart], and then assign the deities of the limbs to those six limbs;
having assigned the six forms, one should worship those eight.
And the seven tongues have been described:
Hiraṇyā, Gaganā, Raktā, as well as Kṛṣṇā, Suprabhā,
Bahurūpā, and Atirūpā— these are the seven tongues of Vasu.
Now, the deities of the limbs are known as Sahasrārcis, Svastipūrṇa, Uttiṣṭhapuruṣa,
Dhūmavyāpin, Saptajihva, and Dhanurdhara. (Hbhv_2.93)
And the eight forms are Jātavedas, Saptajihva, Havyavāhana,
the one known as Aśvodaraja, and another, Vaiśvānara.
And likewise Kaumāratejas, as well as those called Viśvadevamukha and Āhvaya.
Thus, having strewn grass around the fire and offered consecrated clarified butter according to the rule,
one should subsequently offer the *vyāhṛti* mantras and then offer again three times.
Then, one should perform for him the sacraments beginning with conception and ending with marriage in their proper order,
using the prescribed mantra and likewise offering eight oblations.
Thus, having worshipped the seat upon the consecrated fire,
one should invoke the deity there and worship him according to the ritual procedure beginning with perfumes and ending with lamps.
Having conceived that fire as the tongue of the deity, the wise one should offer one thousand and eight oblations of ghee, sugar, and milk-rice.
Then, having offered the great *vyāhṛtis* with clarified butter according to the rule,
the skillful one should present the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) to the planets, constellations, *karaṇas*, and so forth, as prescribed.
Now, regarding the quantity of the materials for the fire-oblation (homa) and so forth:
one karṣa of clarified butter is prescribed for the oblation, and one śukti of milk is likewise recorded;
the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are stated by the wise to be equal in measure to those.
An amount of honey, milk, and rice equal to that [the size of a jujube fruit] is prescribed;
curd should be one handful (prasṛti), and parched grain should be measured by a single fist.
And so forth.

Then, having prostrated and offered water for drinking as well as water for sipping (ācamana), and having performed worship up to the point of self-dedication (ātmārpaṇa), one should proceed according to the ritual prescribed for the written [mandala]. (Hbhv 2.102)
Now, regarding the rules for the teacher and the disciple and so forth:
having caused the disciple— who stands firm in his vows and is restrained in speech— to enter according to the ritual procedure,
the teacher should then project the Mātṛkā along with its limbs (aṅgas) upon that disciple’s body and instruct him in it.

Recalling the deity together with the enclosure as residing within the water-pot, the preceptor, having recited the mantra one thousand and eight times and having consumed something [to eat], should go to sleep. (Hbhv 2.104)
Seated upon a deer-skin over darbha grass, the disciple observing the vow, while recollecting the Mother Goddess and the Guru, should sleep there while muttering [the mantra]. (Hbhv 2.105)
Thus concludes the ritual duties of the preceding day.
Now, regarding the duties of that [current] day:
having performed the morning rites and worshipped the water-pot as before, the Guru proceeds.
Having offered the oblation and given the bali, one should perform other rites until the point of self-dedication.

Having joined the deities of the enclosure with the *saṃhāra-mudrā* into the black [deity], and having meditated upon him as consisting of nectar, one should dissolve the fire into oneself. (Hbhv 2.107)

Having visualized all the presiding deities of the banner, the archway, the directional jars, the pavilion, and so forth as being of the nature of consciousness (cid-rūpa), one should join them into the ritual jar (kumbha) and worship them. Hbhv_2.108 //
Therefore, one should worship the Guru, Gaṇeśa, and Viṣvaksena;
having dismissed [the deities] and touched the water-pot (kalaśa), one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Then, having observed the fast and performed his morning duties, the disciple—
clad in white garments and well-attired— should satisfy the Brahmins with material offerings.

Having circumambulated and prostrated before the guru while regarding him with the vision of the Blessed One, and having given him the prescribed sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one should offer up one's own body to him. (Hbhv 2.111)
Now, regarding the worship as an auxiliary to initiation (*dīkṣā*), it is said in the Tenth Canto [of the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*, 10.80.41]:
"This alone is the repayment to the guru that must be performed by true disciples."
Indeed, that which is the offering of all objects and one's own self to the guru with a state of complete purity; // Hbhv_2.112 //
Now follows the procedure for consecration:
having seated that disciple upon a throne in the bathing pavilion in the northern direction from the sacrificial hall, one should perform the rites of drying and so forth. (Hbhv 2.113)

Having performed the entire ritual of placement (nyāsa) upon the body of the disciple, beginning with the placement of the Mātṛkās and ending with the placement of the sacred seats (pīṭha), one should worship [the deity] with the seat-mantra (pīṭha-mantra).
Having placed yellow pigment (rocanā) along with auspicious unbroken rice and flowers upon the head of the disciple,
