one should lead the water-pot near him accompanied by musical instruments and the like.

Then, having offered prayers to Śrī-Kṛṣṇa and performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the disciple with the cloth from the water-pot, the preceptor should place its sprouts and other items upon the disciple’s head.
Thus it has been said:
"Having duly lifted up the jar and placed the celestial trees upon its rim, one should place it on the head of the child and mentally recite the Mātṛkā. (Hbhv 2.117)

Then, having sprinkled the disciple three times with water from the jar while reciting the root mantra, he should consecrate him while chanting the mantras, accompanied by the auspicious proclamations and blessings of the Brahmins. (Hbhv 2.118)
Now, the mantras for consecration are found in the Vaśiṣṭha-saṃhitā: "May the gods— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara— consecrate you."
Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, as well as the all-pervading Saṅkarṣaṇa.
May Pradyumna and Aniruddha be for your prosperity; likewise may Ākhaṇḍala, the lord Agni, Yama, and Nirṛti [be so]. (Hbhv 2.120)
May Varuṇa, Pavana, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), and Śiva, together with Brahmā—these guardians of the directions—protect you always. (Hbhv_2.121)
Fame, fortune, fortitude, intelligence, nourishment, faith, action, movement, intellect, modesty, form, tranquility, illusion, sleep, and creative ideation. (Hbhv_2.122)
May these, along with Rāhu and Ketu, being duly honored,
as well as the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas, consecrate you.
The seers, the sages, the cows, the mothers of the gods, the wives of the gods, the *dhruvas*, the *nāgas*, the *daityas*, and the hosts of *apsarases*. (Hbhv 2.124)
Missiles, all weapons, kings, vehicles, medicinal herbs, jewels, and whatever are the constituent parts of time; Hbhv_2.125 //
May the rivers, oceans, mountains, sacred fords, clouds, and streams consecrate you for the attainment of virtue, desire, and wealth. (Hbhv_2.126)
Now, the procedure for the recitation of the mantra:
Having put on his garment and sipped water, the disciple,
having gone to the sacrificial pavilion and bowed with devotion to the Guru, should sit to the right of the Guru.
The preceptor, having offered scents and other items equal in quantity to a man's daily food,
and having presented milk-rice (pāyasa) to Kṛṣṇa, should then perform the offering of a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali).

One should visualize that child as Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, adorned with the traditional mudrās and other ornaments, with palms joined in reverence, through the ritual depositions (nyāsa) beginning with the five limbs.
Placing the palm of his hand upon [the disciple's] head and on his right ear, he should recite the mantra, complete with the ṛṣi and other elements, three times. (Hbhv 2.130)
One should recite the long mantra for the disciple until it is mastered;
the disciple, contemplating the identity of the Guru, the deity, and the mantra, should recite it. (Hbhv 2.131)
Taking water together with unbroken grains of rice, the Guru should place it in the disciple's right hand while reciting this mantra: "May we be equal. (Hbhv 2.132)
The Guru should visualize the knowledge consisting of light departing from himself;
the disciple should visualize it as having arrived, thinking especially, "I am blessed. (Hbhv 2.133)
Having bestowed great favor upon the disciple, the Guru should place that milk-rice upon his head while pronouncing auspicious blessings. (Hbhv 2.134)
Having received that mantra from the Guru out of compassion, the disciple should recite it one hundred and eight times and then hear the rules of conduct (samayas).
Now, regarding the rules in the Śrī Nārada Pañcarātra:
one's own mantra should not be taught [to others], nor should it be spoken in a public assembly.
Likewise, this scripture should be kept secret and protected like one's own body.
One should have supreme devotion toward the Vaiṣṇavas, especially toward the teachers;
one should worship them according to one's ability and protect them when they are in distress.
Having received [the water] from the abode of Viṣṇu, one should carry it with bowed head;
then one should pour it into water so that it does not fall upon the ground.

One should meditate upon the deity Viṣṇu as abiding within the moon and the sun, situated in the midst of the cow, the aśvattha tree, and the fire, and residing within the bodies of the guru and the brahmins. (Hbhv 2.139)
Wherever one hears slander of the guru arising from envy, one should not dwell there; one should depart while keeping Hari in mind.
O Nārada, one should never dwell nor ever speak in any way with those who have reviled their guru or the Lord’s scripture.

During circumambulation, when setting out on a journey, and especially when making offerings, as well as at dawn and when traveling abroad, one should repeatedly recollect one's own mantra. (Hbhv 2.142)
If a wonder that causes extreme joy should arise suddenly, whether in a dream or before one's very eyes, it must not be told to anyone except the Guru.
In another *Pañcarātra* text: "I shall declare the observances (*samaya*) concisely from the *Pañcarātra*:
one should not eat fish, meat, nor the flesh of tortoises or pigs. (Hbhv 2.144)
One should not eat from a bell-metal vessel, nor from the leaves of the *plakṣa* or *vaṭa* trees.
One should not spit in a temple, and one should avoid sneezing there.
One should never enter an inner space with shoes on.
One should not eat on the eleventh day of either fortnight;
one should keep a vigil at night and especially worship the Lord.
And in the *Sammohana-tantra* it is said:
"One should conceal one's chosen deity; one should conceal one's own guru;
one should conceal one's own mantra; and one should conceal one's own rosary. (Hbhv_2.147)

Thus, it is held by some that initiation (dīkṣā) occurs only when the student has formally accepted the four hundred and twenty-four observances (samaya) previously prescribed by the Guru. Hbhv_2.148 //
And so it is stated in the Viṣṇuyāmala:
"The Guru, remaining vigilant, should examine the disciple for one year; he should cause him to hear the four hundred prescribed rules and things to be avoided. (Hbhv 2.149)

Rising during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should perform the awakening of Mahāviṣṇu, the ceremonial waving of lights (*nīrājana*) with musical instruments, and the morning bath according to the prescribed rules. (Hbhv 2.150)
Wearing a pair of pure, unwashed garments; the worship of the deity;
and always applying the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍraka*) with the clay of *gopīcandana*. (Hbhv 2.151)
The daily wearing of the five weapons, the service of the nectar of the feet, and the wearing of ornaments such as *tulasī* and jewel garlands; Hbhv_2.152.
One should worship the Śālagrāma stone and [other] images with devotion;
one should consume the remains of offerings (nirmālya) and Tulasī, and follow the injunctions regarding the speech of Tulasī.
The ritual twilight worship (saṃdhyā) should be performed according to the Tantric method, as indeed the binding of the topknot (śikhā-bandha) is required for the rite;
the libation (tarpaṇa) for the ancestors should be performed with the water from Viṣṇu’s feet alone;
and one should worship Hari with the royal services (mahārājopacāra) according to one's capacity. (Hbhv 2.154)

All daily and occasional rites, the performance of the purification of the elements (*bhūta-śuddhi*) and so forth, and all ritual placements (*nyāsa*) according to the prescribed rules, should be carried out without contradicting devotion to Viṣṇu. (Hbhv 2.155)
The devoted offering of fresh fruits, flowers, and the like;
the daily worship of Tulasī; and the worship of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam. (Hbhv 2.156)
Worship of Viṣṇu three times a day, the daily hearing of the Purāṇas, and the wearing of garments and other items offered to Viṣṇu. (Hbhv 2.157)
One should undertake all meritorious activities with the perception of the master;
therein lies the reception of the guru’s command and trust in what is spoken by the guru. (Hbhv 2.158)
The formation of one’s own respective mudrās, songs, dances, and so forth with devotion;
the sounding of conchs and other auspicious instruments, the performance of playful gestures of Hari;
and the daily performance of the fire sacrifice (homa) and the offering of oblations (bali) according to the prescribed rules. (Hbhv 2.159)
Welcoming the virtuous, honoring them, eating the remnants of their offerings, accepting the remains of their betel, and associating with Vaiṣṇavas. (Hbhv 2.160)
The desire to know the distinguished Dharma [arises] during the three days beginning with the tenth;
in this vow, there is necessarily well-being and contentment with whatever may come.
The performance of festival processions and other rites, the proper observance of the eight days [of the month],
and the conduct of Viṣṇu throughout all seasons according to the protocol for a great king.
The observance of all Vaiṣṇava vows, regarding the guru as the Lord himself, and the constant cultivation of *tulasī*—[these are the duties]. (Hbhv 2.163)
And the practice of attending to one's bed and so forth, as well as the contemplation of Rāma and others.
One should never sleep during the two twilights; nor should there be purification without earth;
one should not perform the ritual sipping of water while standing, nor sit upon the seat of one's guru.
In the presence of the guru, one must not leap over his shadow;
even when capable, one must not neglect the act of bathing or the omission of the worship of the deity.
One should cultivate the practice of rising from one's seat and so forth in the presence of deities and teachers;
likewise, one should avoid displaying erudition before a teacher or acting with arrogant foot-movements.
Applying a sectarian mark without mantras, rinsing the mouth without mantras, wearing dyed blue garments,

showing friendliness and so forth toward those who do not share one's faith, embracing false scriptures, attachment to the pleasures of trivial associations, and the consumption of liquor and meat. (Hbhv 2.168)
The consumption of intoxicating drugs, the eating of food such as lentils,
vegetables like the bottle-gourd (tumbī) and kalañja, the hoarding of food that has not been consecrated,
the undertaking of vows not dedicated to Viṣṇu, and likewise the recitation of mantras not dedicated to Viṣṇu; Hbhv_2.169 //

Performing malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) and the like out of one's power, the figurative application of secondary meanings (*gauṇopacāra*), being under the sway of grief and other emotions, and the observance of the *ekādaśī* fast on a day pierced by the lunar mansions of the quarters (*digviddha*)—[these are faults]. (Hbhv 2.170)
Likewise, in the vow [of celibacy], there is no distinction between white and black [actions] and no activity toward what is non-existent;
furthermore, one should avoid eating fruits and the like when capable, as well as performing ancestral rites (śrāddha) on the eleventh day.
On the twelfth lunar day, sleeping during the day, plucking Tulasī leaves,
bathing Viṣṇu during the day, and performing a Śrāddha with offerings not first presented to Hari [are prohibited].
On the anniversary of the death of elders, one should perform the Śrāddha with Tulasi; likewise, one should perform the Śrāddha for those who were not Vaiṣṇavas.
Even when drinking the nectar from the feet [of a Vaiṣṇava], one should perform the rite of sipping water (ācamana) for the sake of purification.
Worship of Vāsudeva while seated on a wooden seat;
idle chatter at the time of worship; and the worship of karavīra and other such [plants]. (Hbhv 2.174)
Using an iron incense burner and the like, applying the sectarian mark (puṇḍra) horizontally, performing worship with unrefined materials, and likewise due to a fickle mind; Hbhv_2.175 //
Prostrating with only one hand and so forth, seeing the Master at an improper time, and offering food and other items that are spoiled, such as those kept overnight—[these are faults]. (Hbhv 2.176)
Without counting, there is the recitation of mantras as well as the disclosure of mantras;
when the primary time is always impossible due to one's capacity, one adopts the secondary time. (Hbhv_2.177)
A Vaiṣṇava should always avoid accepting gifts from Viṣṇu;
the Guru should cause [the disciple] to hear these four hundred injunctions and prohibitions.
Once acceptance has been granted,
[the preceptor] should perform the worship of the deity preceded by the *nīrājana* rite, and then mutter the mantra into the disciple's right ear.
Thus it is said.
Then, having arisen, the disciple, his soul filled with fullness, should prostrate like a staff before the Guru, placing the Guru’s lotus-feet upon his own head. (Hbhv 2.180)

Then, having performed the ritual depositions (nyāsa) upon himself as well as the internal sacrifice (antar-yajana), the Guru should recite that mantra one thousand and eight times according to his own capacity for the sake of preserving his vital power.
The disciple, having given all that— such as the water-pot and other liquids— as well as other things according to his ability,
and having worshipped and bowed to the Guru, should honor and feed the Brahmins.
Strengthened by the auspicious blessings of the venerable guru and the brāhmaṇas,
and having obtained permission from them— the guru and the others— he should eat together with his kinsmen.
Thus, he who receives a mantra from a guru according to the prescribed rite of initiation becomes fortunate, long-lived, and one who has fulfilled his purpose.
And so it is said in the *Saṃmohana-tantra*, in the dialogue between Śrī Śiva and Umā:
"The mortal who acts in this manner has the divine powers (*vibhūtayaḥ*) in his very hand. Beyond this, O highly fortunate one, there is no other rite on the face of the earth."
By the mere practice of which Kṛṣṇa himself becomes directly pleased.
This tantric procedure has been explained for the most part in the *Prapañcasāra* and other such works;
now, the divine and puranic procedure for initiation (*dīkṣā*) is being written.

Now, O Goddess, hear from me the procedure for initiation as taught in the Varāha Purāṇa; it is the sacrifice to Viṣṇu, the God of gods, which destroys the five great sins and bestows sons and wealth. (Hbhv_2.187)
In this life, for that man on earth who is afflicted by poverty, disease, leprosy, and the like,
or who is unfortunate and childless,
there shall immediately arise fortune, long life, wealth, sons, and happiness. (Hbhv 2.188)
But having seen the deity in the mandala together with the goddess, O Goddess,
he who beholds Nārāyaṇa, the supreme deity, according to the prescribed rite, [attains the goal].
One should worship the deity shown by the preceptor—the mantra-form, not born of a womb—within a nine-naved [mandala] as well as upon the petals of a sixteen-petaled lotus. (Hbhv 2.190)
Especially on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārttika,
one should worship the God according to the prescribed rule on all such twelfth days.
O illustrious and auspicious lady, at the time of a solar transit, or even during an eclipse of the moon or sun,
whoever beholds the god Hari worshipped by their preceptor shall immediately attain satisfaction and the total destruction of all sins.
For he indeed becomes common to the gods; of this there is no doubt.
The teacher should conduct an examination of the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras for one year, based on their birth, purity, ritual actions, and so forth.
Then, having recognized those who have approached him, he should examine them with his heart;
and having understood that they too are devoted to himself as the Supreme Lord,
they should practice devotion toward their guru for one year, as unwavering as that toward Viṣṇu.
Then, when the year is complete, he should propitiate the Guru.
O Blessed One, by your grace we desire to cross the ocean of saṃsāra;
yet, O one whose wealth is austerity, we especially desire worldly prosperity in this life.
Having thus petitioned his guru as if he were Viṣṇu standing before him, and having honored him, the wise man, permitted by him, [should perform the rite] on the tenth day of the month of Kārttika.
Having consumed [the substance] produced from a milk-tree and consecrated by the Supreme Lord,
one should lie down upon the earth in the presence of the God of Gods.
Having seen dreams, the wise person should relate them before the Guru;
then the supreme Guru should speak of their auspicious or inauspicious nature.
Then, having fasted on the eleventh day and bathed, one should go to the temple.
And the guru should draw the mandala on the ground that has been prepared,
having marked the ground according to the rules with various characteristics.
The wise one, having drawn a wheel with sixteen spokes, or else with nine hubs,
or even with eight petals, should then display it.
One should carefully bind the eyes of the disciples with white cloth; then, according to their respective castes, one should cause them to enter with flowers in their hands.
When the wise one constructs a nine-naved mandala with colored powders,
he should then worship the god Indra in the east and in the eastern quarter.
Then the twice-born should worship Lokeśvara in the southeast, Agni in the southeast,
Yama in the south, Nirṛti in the southwest,
Varuṇa in the west, and Pavana in the northwest. (Hbhv 2.205)
Having placed Dhanada in the north and Rudra in the northeastern quarter,
and having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rule especially in the petals of the directions,
one should likewise worship Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord, in the lower petal.
Having worshipped Bala on the eastern petal, and likewise Pradyumna on the south;
having likewise worshipped Aniruddha on the west and the north, one should worship Vāsudeva, who grants peace from all sins. (Hbhv 2.207)
One should place the conch in the northeast and the discus in the southeast;
the mace is to be worshipped in the north, and the lotus in the northwest.
The wise one should worship the pestle in the southwest and likewise Garuḍa in the south;
he should then place Lakṣmī to the left of the God of Gods.
One should place the bow and the sword before the deity;
one should also worship the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha gem before the deity. (Hbhv_2.210)
Having thus worshipped Janārdana, the God of gods, according to the prescribed rule,
one should duly place eight jars in the circle of the directions and arrange the ninth jar there as the Vaiṣṇava vessel.
One should bathe those who desire liberation with a Vaiṣṇava jar;
likewise, one should bathe those who desire prosperity with an Aindra jar.
One should consecrate those who desire victory and majesty with the Āgneya rite;
likewise, one should perform the ceremonial bathing according to the Mṛtyuñjaya procedure and the Yāmya rite.
The rite for the Nairṛta [direction] is prescribed as sufficient for the complete destruction of the wicked;
then, the Vāruṇa [rite] is for peace, and the Vāyava [rite] is for the destruction of evil.
For one desiring the attainment of wealth, [the practice] is prescribed by Kauvera; for the cause of knowledge, however, it is by Raudra. These are the jars of the World-Guardians.
By bathing in each one of these, a man becomes freed from all sins;
such a person shall always possess unimpeded knowledge and be endowed with prosperity.
Furthermore, does a man who has bathed nine times become free from sin, instantly becoming like Viṣṇu, or rather, a king? (Hbhv_2.217)
Alternatively, one should worship the world-protectors in all directions according to their respective order, using their individual names in six distinct ways, according to the prescribed rule.
Having thus worshipped the gods and the world-protectors with a serene mind,
he should afterwards cause the examined disciples, whose eyes are bound, to enter.
Then, after they have been burnt by the fire-retention (āgneya-dhāraṇā) and fanned away by the wind,
and subsequently nourished by the moon (soma), the wise teacher should cause them to hear the rules (niyama).
One should not revile non-Brahmins, the gods, Viṣṇu, or a Brahmin; nor Rudra, Āditya, Agni, the guardians of the world, or the planets.
One should indeed pay homage to the Vaiṣṇava person who has been previously initiated. (Hbhv 2.221)
Having thus caused [the disciples] to hear the pledges (samaya), one should afterwards perform the fire offering (homa);
and having projected the principles of reality (tattva) into the bodies of the disciples, one should purify them.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One Viṣṇu, who possesses all forms; hūṃ svāhā!
One whose sacrificial fire is blazing should perform the oblation with the sixteen-syllable mantra and should carry out all the rites, beginning with the ceremony of conception (garbhādhāna).
Having removed the blindfold from the disciple and seated him before the God of gods after three sets of three oblations,
the Guru should generally impart the mantra to him according to the previously mentioned procedure. (Hbhv 2.225)

At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, the initiated king should subsequently cause the teacher to receive a guru’s fee (dakṣiṇā), consisting of elephants, horses, jewels, bracelets, gold, villages, and so forth. (Hbhv 2.226)
The wise man should cause [the teacher] to receive the middle [gift]; likewise, the middling man should cause him to receive the middling;
the other should cause him to receive a pair along with gold, according to the prescribed rule.
O Earth, when this is performed, the merit and majesty that arise are impossible to describe even in hundreds of years.
If one, having become the consecrated self of the guru, should listen to the Vārāha [Purāṇa],
by that [act] the Vedas, the Purāṇas, and all the mantras are well-collected.
They become as if recited at the holy site of Puṣkara, at Prayāga, at the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean, at Devahūta, at Kurukṣetra, and especially at Vārāṇasī. (Hbhv 2.230)
Whatever fruit may accrue to those who recite [mantras] during an eclipse or at the equinox,
that fruit is doubled for one who is initiated and listens [to it].
Even the gods, having performed austerities, meditate and say:
"When will my birth occur in the land of Bhārata, O bearer of beings? (Hbhv_2.232)
"And we shall become initiated; when shall we hear of the Boar?
When, having joined the sixteen-fold Boar within the body, shall we behold that supreme state, having gone to which there is no more rebirth? (Hbhv 2.233)
Thus do the wise speak and thus do they reflect in their minds:
"O Earth, when shall we behold the Vārāha sacrifice on the full moon day of Kārttika? (Hbhv_2.234)
This procedure has been taught to you by me, O Sustainer of Beings;
for it is indeed difficult to obtain in every respect even for gods, gandharvas, and yakṣas.
Thus, O Goddess, it is the sacred tradition that whoever knows this in its true essence, whoever beholds the maṇḍala, and whoever hears this—all such persons are liberated. (Hbhv_2.236)
Now, the concise initiation (*saṃkṣipta-dīkṣā*):
this procedure for the concise initiation is being written down for the benefit of people who are incapable of following the primary ritual manual (*mukhya-kalpa*). (Hbhv 2.237)
Then, when an auspicious moment has arrived, one should place a new water jar, adorned with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, within the Sarvatobhadra mandala.
It should be covered with cloth, filled with water, and provided with five sprouts;
it should contain all medicinal herbs, the five jewels, and the seven types of earth.

And seven types of earth are prescribed: earth from a horse stable, from an elephant stable, from an anthill, from a crossroads, from a royal gate, from a cow pen, and from the banks of a river; these are the earths traditionally taught. (Hbhv 2.240)
Thus,
having worshipped Kṛṣṇa, the preceptor should consecrate that jar one thousand and eight times with the kuśa-grass tuft while reciting the mantra to be given. (Hbhv 2.241)
Having consecrated the disciple with water as before, he should impart the mantra;
the disciple, for his part, should worship the guru with devotion and also honor the twice-born according to his ability.
Now, regarding the instruction in the *Tattvasāgara*:

"If someone here is unable [to perform the full ritual], having worshipped a lotus directly with its stalk, he should sprinkle his hand eight times with its water while reciting the root mantra. (Hbhv 2.243)
Having placed this [mantra] in the ear, one should recite it; this is the procedure for oral instructions (*upadeśa*).

During an eclipse of the moon or sun, at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), in a site of the perfected ones (*siddhakṣetra*), or in a temple of Śiva—the mere proclamation of the mantra is called an "instruction. (Hbhv 2.244)
In this very regard, there is a specific distinction stated in the Śrī-Nārada-Pañcarātra:

"For an embodied soul who is truly free from greed for wealth, who possesses only meager means, who is terrified by the fear of saṃsāra, and who is a devotee of Viṣṇu in accordance with reality... (Hbhv 2.245).

In the case of one who lacks ritual materials, the Guru should perform the rite of grace through speech alone, using either seeds accompanied by clarified butter in the fire, or with water alone. (Hbhv 2.246)
He who is impartial toward all beings, free from passion and devoid of envy,
whose senses are conquered, who is pure, skillful, and endowed with all limbs and members.
Through action, mind, and speech, he is always a giver of fearlessness even to those who are afraid; having attained the state of equanimity, he is there also permeated by the Blessed One.

One who knows the five times (*pañcakāla*), likewise understands the meaning of the *Pañcarātra*, and having fully realized the reality of Viṣṇu (*viṣṇutattva*)—which is both one and yet accessible through manifold divisions—may survey the entire earth; how much more so those who have approached him for refuge? (Hbhv 2.249)
Now, regarding the greatness of the bestowal of mantras,
as stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa* in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada: "In this world, [one obtains] fame, generosity, increase of progeny, wealth, and happiness."
Through the gift of knowledge, one who is characterized by goodness attains [the goal]; there is no doubt in this matter.
Just as the Supreme Lord is the highest among all the gods,
even so the gift of knowledge is traditionally held to be the supreme among all gifts.
Whatever sin has been committed by embodied beings, even throughout hundreds of lifetimes, all of that goes to destruction through the gift of knowledge. (Hbhv 2.252)
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift superior to the gift of knowledge;
by giving this, one attains auspiciousness, the supreme goal.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Initiation," in the *Śrī-Bhagavad-bhakti-vilāsa* composed by Śrī Gopāla Bhaṭṭa.
3. The Chapter on Purity (*Sauciya-vilāsa*)
The Third Vilāsa:
On Purity. I bow to the Great Lord Śrī Caitanya, whose infinite and wondrous sovereignty is beyond measure.
By whose grace even a lowly person may become a promoter of virtuous conduct.
The conduct and duties of a person who has received initiation and intends to worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa are here set forth in accordance with the Śrutis and Smṛtis. (Hbhv 3.2)
Now, having established that worship by one who has been initiated is obligatory:
"But he who does not daily worship the deity of the mantra with the mantra—the deity bestows upon him the undesirable fruit of all his ritual actions. (Hbhv 3.3)
Now, regarding right conduct (sad-ācāra):
since nothing whatsoever can be accomplished for anyone without right conduct,
therefore right conduct is necessarily required in all circumstances.
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (3.8.9):
"By a person who follows the conduct of the social classes and stages of life, the Supreme Person, Viṣṇu, is propitiated; there is no other path that causes Him satisfaction. (Hbhv 3.5)

Now, regarding the permanence of right conduct (*sad-ācāra*), it is stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* in the dialogue between the venerable Ālasa and Alarka: "A householder must always maintain the observance of right conduct."
For there is no happiness, either in this world or in the next, for one who is devoid of proper conduct.
In this world, sacrifice, charity, and austerity do not lead to the welfare of a person who acts by transgressing the conduct of the virtuous. (Hbhv 3.7)
And in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira:
"The Vedas do not purify one who is devoid of right conduct, even if they have been studied along with the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍ-aṅga*)."
At the time of death, the Vedic hymns abandon him,
just as birds with grown wings leave their nest.
Just as water in a skull or milk in a dog-skin bag becomes defiled by the fault of its container, so too is that which is devoid of right conduct inauspicious;
O King, one who lacks proper conduct is censured neither in this world nor in the next.
Thus, by means of this written record, the eternality of recollection and the other [mental functions] will be established;
likewise, the eternality of the practice of the virtuous (sad-ācāra), which consists of recollection and so forth, is also established.
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa [3.11.3], in that very context concerning the duties of a householder:
"By a man who possesses virtuous conduct, both worlds are conquered. (Hbhv_3.11)

The virtuous, however, are those whose defects have been extinguished; the word *sat* denotes the virtuous (*sādhu*). That which is their conduct is called *sad-ācāra* (the conduct of the virtuous). (Hbhv 3.12)
In the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, within the dialogue between Skanda and Agastya, it is said:
"Death afflicts that Brāhmaṇa who is habitually neglectful of Vedic study, who transgresses the conduct of the virtuous, who is indolent, and who eats the food of the wicked. (Hbhv_3.13)
Therefore, a twice-born man should always practice good conduct with diligence;
even sacred fords long for the company of those who possess good conduct.

And in that very same passage of the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*: "Dharma originates from right conduct (*ācāra*), and the virtuous are characterized by right conduct; the way of life of the good—that is what is intended by 'right conduct'. (Hbhv 3.15)
Therefore, one who desires their own welfare should always practice right conduct.
O King, even if one is devoid of all auspicious marks, if they possess excellent conduct, are full of faith, and free from malice, they shall attain all their desires. (Hbhv 3.16)
Furthermore:
O King, right conduct alone is the root of dharma and of one's lineage;
a being who has fallen away from right conduct is neither of noble birth nor righteous.
Furthermore:
Right conduct generates prosperity; right conduct increases fame.
Indeed, through right conduct life is prolonged, and right conduct destroys inauspicious marks.
O bull among kings, it is conduct alone, when practiced here, that yields the fruits of dharma, artha, and kāma for men;
therefore, O King, a wise man should always be attentive to it.
For that which is taught in the scriptures must be observed daily.
Now, regarding the daily duties there:
having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* while chanting "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa," and having washed his hands and feet, he should perform the cleansing of the teeth. (Hbhv 3.20)
Having sipped water (ācamana), discarded his night-garment, and put on another,
he should perform the sipping of water again according to the procedure for drawing [the mandala] in front of him.

Then, desiring supreme purification, having meditated upon the feet of the guru at the crown of his head, and having praised them while glorifying Kṛṣṇa and remembering Him, he should utter this: Hbhv_3.22.
Now, in this recitation of the morning remembrance:
Victorious is the Abode of Men, whose birth is from Devakī, who, amidst the assembly of the best of the Yadus, strikes down unrighteousness with his own arms!
Destroying the sins of all things stable and moving, he increases the god of love in the women of Vraja and the city by means of his face, which possesses the splendor of a beautiful smile.
I go for refuge to that unborn and eternal Hari, upon remembering whom one becomes a vessel for all auspiciousness. (BhP 10.90.48) (Hbhv 3.24)
His entire body is marked with the signs of enjoyment from the playful amorous sports of the clever cowherd girls;
he is the purifier of the words of the Vedas, yet remains inaccessible to them.
I take refuge in Brahmā, the thief of fresh butter.
In the Tenth Canto [BhP 10.46.46]: "The sound of the women of Vraja, as they sang aloud to the lotus-eyed one, touched the heavens."
And by means of the churning of curds, mingled with the sound of the churning-stick, that which brings ill fortune to the quarters is cast out. (Hbhv_3.26)
Thus one should recite again this "Four Verses" in accordance with the tradition of the virtuous, for the pacification of all faults and the attainment of auspiciousness. (Hbhv 3.27)
At dawn, for the sake of pacifying the great agony of fear of worldly existence, I remember Nārāyaṇa, whose navel is a lotus, who has Garuḍa as his vehicle,
and who is the cause of liberation for the noble elephant seized by a crocodile in the water.
He who has the discus as his weapon and eyes like the petals of a fresh lotus.
At dawn, I bow with my mind, my speech, and my head to the pair of lotus-feet of the Supreme Person,
Nārāyaṇa, who delivers one across the ocean of hell.
Of one who is devoted to the ultimate goal and whose supreme refuge is the Brahmins intent on the study of the Pārāyaṇa.
In the morning, I worship Him who grants fearlessness to those who seek refuge, so that He may destroy the fear arising from sins committed throughout all previous births—
He who [rescued] the lordly elephant whose feet had fallen into the mouth of a crocodile.
Bearing the conch and the discus, he brought about the destruction of sorrow.
To whoever recites these three meritorious verses every morning, Hari—the teacher of the three worlds—shall grant his own abode. (Hbhv 3.31)
Thus it has been written;
this may be found here and there in various legal treatises (*vyavahāra*).
However, one should contemplate the form and other attributes of Śrī Kṛṣṇa according to one's own desired preference. (Hbhv 3.32)
In this manner, one should perform the chanting and remembrance of the Blessed One and so forth;
for indeed, this constitutes the bathing in all sacred waters, which purifies both externally and internally.
And likewise, in the Skanda Purāṇa, in the words of Śrī Śiva addressed to Skanda:
"O son, by uttering 'Nārāyaṇa' even once, a person becomes as one who has bathed in all the sacred fords, such as the Gaṅgā, for three hundred kalpas. (Hbhv 3.34)
And elsewhere it is said:
"But he who, having risen from his bed, should glorify Madhusūdana, through that glorification, his sin goes to destruction without remainder. (Hbhv 3.35)
Thus, the greatness of recitation has been written first as the primary topic;
now, however, the greatness of mindfulness is being written about to some extent. (Hbhv 3.36)
Regarding that, first, his eternity is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*, in the *Bṛhatsahasranāmastotra* (6.71.100):
"Viṣṇu should be remembered constantly; he should never be forgotten."
All injunctions and prohibitions are but servants to these two alone.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*, within the context of Kārttika, in the words of the venerable Agastya:
"That is a loss, that is a great flaw, that is delusion, and that is confusion, for which even a single muhūrta or moment Vāsudeva is not meditated upon. (Hbhv 3.38)
And in the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*, within the account of the life of Śrī Dhruva, it is said:
"This alone is the supreme loss, this indeed is the calamity, and this is the ultimate misfortune—that one does not remember Vāsudeva. (Hbhv_3.39)

Those moments, those instants, those divisions of time known as *kāṣṭhās*, and those twinks of an eye that have passed without the remembrance of Viṣṇu—in them, he has been robbed by Yama. (Hbhv 3.40)
Thus,

even though it is eternal, its greatness should be understood by the wise— just like the New and Full Moon sacrifices— as being proclaimed in the scriptures through the granting of diverse fruits. (Hbhv 3.41)
Now, regarding the greatness of recollection (smaraṇa),
its superiority even to bathing in all sacred fords (tīrthas) has been stated by the followers of the Smṛtis as well:
The sevenfold bath is traditionally taught as being mantra-bath, the earthly, the fiery, the windy, the celestial, the watery, and the mental. (Hbhv 3.42)
The bath with water is indeed the mantra-bath; the touching of clay is the earth-bath;
bathing with ashes is the fire-bath; and bathing with the dust raised by cows is the wind-bath. (Hbhv 3.43)
When there is sunshine, that rain which falls is called the divine bath (*divya-snāna*).

Bathing in rivers and other waters outside is declared by the wise to be the Varuṇa bath (*vāruṇa*). That meditation on Viṣṇu performed with the mind is proclaimed as the mental bath (*mānasa*). (Hbhv 3.44)
Furthermore, because of the body's lack of capacity, all [actions] would result in equal fruits depending on time, place, and so forth; thus said Parāśara: Hbhv_3.45.
Among all forms of bathing, the mental bath is considered supreme by Manu and others;
by performing it, even twice-born householders are indeed liberated.
The supreme purifying power [of the mantra] is stated in the *Garuḍa-purāṇa* by the venerable Nārada,
and in the *Viṣṇu-dharma* by Pulastya:
Whether impure or pure, or even if one has reached any state whatsoever,
whoever remembers the Lotus-Eyed One is pure both externally and internally.
Even if he is afflicted by sins that are exceedingly difficult to overcome through the mind,
nevertheless, by recollecting Viṣṇu, he becomes pure both externally and internally.
In the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa (2.6.37–38): "Of all the various atonements consisting of austerity and ritual action, the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa is the supreme among them all. (Hbhv 3.49)
For that man in whom remorse indeed arises after a sin has been committed,
the one supreme expiation is the constant remembrance of Hari.
Furthermore:
"Moreover, the most fierce defilement of the Kali age, which brings the pain of hell to men, goes to immediate dissolution when he is remembered even once. (ViP 6.8.21) Hbhv_3.51.
In the *Bṛhan-nāradīya-purāṇa* (1.10.100), in the dialogue between Śukra and Bali:
"Hari removes sins even when remembered by those with wicked minds;
for fire indeed burns even when touched unintentionally. (Hbhv 3.53)
In that very context, at the conclusion of the discussion on expiation, [it is said]:
"Whether one is burdened by a great sin (mahāpātaka) or burdened by all sins, he is indeed instantly liberated whose mind is centered on Viṣṇu. (Hbhv 3.54)
In the *Brahma-vaivarta*:
"Whatever accumulation of sin has been committed through action, mind, or speech—even that in its entirety goes to destruction by remembering the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa. (Hbhv 3.55)

Therefore, it has been said by Śrī Parāśara in the *Skanda Purāṇa* in the context of Kārttika: "A man who remembers the one whose banner is Garuḍa will not see the most terrible path of Yama, nor the hells, nor Yama himself, even in a dream. (Hbhv 3.56)
In the sixth book [of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, 6.1.19], Śrī Śuka said:
"Those whose minds have been placed even once here upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, being enamored of His qualities..."
Those who have performed the required expiation do not see Yama, nor his noose-bearing attendants, even in their dreams.
Regarding his quality of being the liberator from all calamities,
it is stated in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa* (1.17.44) in the words of Śrī Prahlāda:
"The tusks of elephants are as hard as the tips of diamonds."
That these [trees] have withered is not due to my power;
rather, it is the majesty of the recollection of Janārdana that destroys the fall of great calamity.

And in the *Vāmana Purāṇa*: "The *viṣṭi* yogas, the *vyatipāta* yogas, and whatever other calamities arise from ill fortune—all such afflictions come to destruction through the remembrance of Viṣṇu. (Hbhv_3.59)
In the *Pādmapurāṇa*, within the *Māghamāhātmya* during the hymn to Devadyuti:
"I bow down to that Ananta, by the mere remembrance of whom there is neither delusion nor an evil rebirth, neither disease nor sufferings. (Hbhv_3.60)
The eradication of evil tendencies is described in the twelfth book [of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa,
12.3.47]: "Just as fire residing within gold destroys the base color produced by impurities."
In this way, Viṣṇu, abiding within the self, [destroys] the impure disposition of yogins.
The quality of bringing about all auspiciousness is found in the *Pāṇḍava-gītā*:
"Victory is theirs, success is theirs; whence can there be defeat for them?"
Those in whose hearts Janārdana resides, dark as a blue lotus, [are truly fortunate].
The fact that [the month of Kārttika] bestows the fruits of all meritorious deeds is stated by Agastya in the context of Kārttika in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Among gods, sacrifices, and austerities..."
Whatever fruit has been prescribed for men through gifts, pilgrimages, and vows, as well as through sacrifices and works of public utility— that same fruit is obtained by remembering Acyuta.
In the *Bṛhan-nāradīya-purāṇa*, it is established that in the Kali age, there is a deficiency or excess in Vedic rites; however, the efficacy of the ritual action remains intact.
In this matter, the mere remembrance of Hari alone bestows the complete fruit.
And in the Smṛti it is said:
"Whatever rite among the sacrifices might fail for those performing it through negligence, that becomes complete simply by the remembrance of Viṣṇu; such is the Vedic revelation. (Hbhv 3.65)
Regarding the superiority of all ritual acts in the context of the Kali age, the *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa* states:
"Among the gifts of the *tulāpuruṣa*, the *rājasūya*, and the *aśvamedha*... [NārP]...
O best of the twice-born, the fruit of [this] is never equal to the remembrance of Viṣṇu.
In the twelfth book [of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa,
12.3.48]: "By means of knowledge, austerity, restraint of the vital breaths, friendliness,
bathing at sacred fords, vows, charity, and the muttering of prayers..."
The inner self does not attain ultimate purity as long as the infinite Blessed One remains within the heart.
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (1.17.36), in the speech of Śrī Prahlāda to Hiraṇyakaśipu: "While You, the remover of all fears, reside within my infinite mind, where can fear remain for me?"
O dear one, when he is remembered, all fears arising from birth and old age depart.
In that very same place, elsewhere [ViP 2.6.40]:
"By the constant remembrance of Viṣṇu, one whose entire accumulation of afflictions is exhausted attains liberation; for such a person, the attainment of heaven is inferred to be an obstacle."
In the *Bṛhan-nāradīya-purāṇa* (1.1.65): "The excellent, the most venerable, the giver of boons, the ancient one,
who has illuminated all the worlds with his own radiance."
Having remembered the Primordial God, who grants all desired objects, a person shall proceed to the state of liberation.
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Salutations to that powerful Viṣṇu, by the mere remembrance of whom one is liberated from the bondage of birth and saṃsāra. (Hbhv 3.71)
In that very context of the Kārttika festival, as stated by the venerable Parāśara:
"At that very moment, a person is truly liberated from birth, suffering, old age, and the like, when they remember Hari with supreme devotion. (Hbhv 3.72)
Regarding propitiating the Blessed One,
the *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa* (1.1.77) states: "By whatever means possible, the imperishable Nārāyaṇa should be remembered."
Even for one joined with a heinous sin, [the Lord] will become gracious; of this there is no doubt.
Regarding the quality of leading one to the realm of Śrī-Vaikuṇṭha,
the Vāmana Purāṇa states:
[He is] Hari, who is without beginning or end, ageless and immortal.
Those men on earth who daily and constantly remember that all-pervading, supreme, and ancient Brahman,
they indeed go to the eternal and imperishable station of Viṣṇu.
In the *Pādmapurāṇa* (3.31.101), within the dialogue between the divine messenger Vikuṇḍala and the instruction of Yama’s messengers, it is said:
"Those beings who remember Keśava even once, even by chance, go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu, with the entire flood of their sins destroyed. (Hbhv_3.75)
In the *Viṣṇurahasya* of the *Brahmapurāṇa* (216.88):
"Even those men who constantly remember Janārdana, even if out of deceit, they too, upon casting off the body, go to the stainless world of Viṣṇu. (Hbhv_3.76)
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"But he who is free from desire and free from the sense of 'mine,' and remains intent on the meditation of Viṣṇu, attains that state where, having gone, one does not grieve. (Hbhv_3.77)
Regarding the attainment of similarity [with the Divine],
in the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*, within the section concerning Śrī Bindumādhava, during the hymn of Agnibindu:
"O Trivikrama, those who always cultivate You within their hearts..."
O lotus-eyed one,
even those who possess the splendor of a rain-cloud and whose forms are enveloped in garments shimmering like lightning touch upon your inconceivable beauty.
In the Śrī Bhagavad Gītā (8.5): "And at the time of death, whoever departs casting off the body while remembering Me alone, attains My state of being; there is no doubt about this."
In the tenth book [of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa], in the narrative of Pṛthu (10.80.11):
"Does the Teacher of the World not grant even his own self to one who remembers his lotus feet; how much less so the objects of wealth and desire, which are not his highest goal? (Hbhv 3.80)

O Maitreya, for one whose mind is fixed upon Vāsudeva— the Lord of Viṣṇu— during the recitation of mantras, fire oblations, worship, and so forth, even the status of Indra, lord of the gods, is merely a secondary obstacle; it is not the true fruit.
In the *Garuḍa-purāṇa*: "The constant remembrance of Hari is the root of great austerity, the source of a continuous stream of merit, and the sweet fruit of life. (Hbhv 3.82)
In the second book [of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, 2.1.6]:
"This much is the supreme attainment of birth for men through Sāṅkhya and Yoga, through the perfection of their own duty: at the end, the remembrance of Nārāyaṇa. (Hbhv_3.83)
Therefore, it was requested by the group of kings imprisoned by Jarāsandha in the Tenth Canto [BhP 10.73.15]:
"Instruct us in that means by which the remembrance of Your lotus feet may not cease, even for those wandering here in this world. (Hbhv 3.84)
Śrī Nārada also said:
"I have beheld Your pair of feet, which grant liberation to all people and are meditated upon in the hearts of Brahmā and others of unfathomable wisdom."
Meditating upon that support for crossing over those who have fallen into the pit of saṃsāra, I move about; may you favor me so that mindfulness may arise.
Thus,
he who wishes to cross that great ocean of the majesty of remembering Kṛṣṇa, which is difficult to traverse even with the intellect, is indeed deceived by Caitanya.
Then, having first drunk a little of the water from the feet, one should perform an ablution upon one's own head with that [water] taken together with *tulasī* leaves.
Then, having first bowed to the venerable guru at the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, while making a brief request, one should offer all one's duties and bow down. (Hbhv 3.88)
Now, regarding the morning salutation, the Vāmana Purāṇa states:
"To Him who is the auspiciousness of all that is auspicious, the most excellent, the bestower of boons, and the source of well-being..."
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa, one should perform all ritual actions.
Now, regarding the formal request (*vijñāpana*),
it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"O Hari, whatever ritual action such as a festival there may be, that [is performed] by you being impelled."
"I shall do what is to be known by you"—this is my petition.
O Viṣṇu, having been awakened in the morning by you, Hṛṣīkeśa,
whatever you command me to do, O Lord, that I shall perform at your command.
O primordial God, Śrīnātha Viṣṇu, who consists of the consciousness of the three worlds, having risen at dawn by Your very command for the sake of Your pleasure—
I shall continue the journey through saṃsāra.
O Śrī Nṛhari, O Inner Self, by Your command, as I continue on the journey of saṃsāra,
may [the obstacles of] rivalry, contempt, strife, and negligence—
O Infinite One, may fears not overcome me.
I know what is dharma, yet I have no inclination toward it;
I know what is adharma, yet I have no aversion to it—
because of You, O Hṛṣīkeśa, who abide within my heart.
I shall do exactly as I have been commanded.
Now, the verses of salutation from the Mahābhārata:
"Homage to the God who is the friend of Brahman, and to him who acts for the welfare of cows and Brāhmaṇas."
Salutations again and again to Kṛṣṇa, to Govinda, who acts for the welfare of the world.
In the Garuḍa Purāṇa:
"The end of whom is not known by the Asuras, gods, and Siddhas,
and who is contemplated within by all the sages as pure— "
I bow to that unborn, immortal Lord Vāsudeva, the witness of all, who dwells within the heart of every being and knows all.
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, it is said: "I bow to Him who is called Vāsudeva, the Person of Sacrifice, by the performers of sacrifice; and who is called Viṣṇu by those who know the Vedānta. (Hbhv 3.97)
Informing [the deity] in this manner, meditating, and reciting according to the rule,
the wise person should perform prostrations according to their ability, at least four in number.
Having fashioned the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) with the sacred gopīcandana according to the prescribed rule,
one should sit facing the east on an auspicious seat in a pure place.
And so it is stated in the Nāradīya-pañcarātra:
"Having gone out and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to rule, the wise man should enter again and sit down upon the prepared seat, facing the east. (Hbhv 3.100)
Having performed the purification of the elements (bhūta-śuddhi) according to the tradition and having duly practiced the breath-controls (prāṇāyāma), one should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa as described.
And so it has been said:
"In all minor offenses (upapātaka) and even in the great sins (pātaka), one should enter the first watch of the night and practice meditation on Viṣṇu. (Hbhv 3.102)
And likewise during the *Vaihāyasa-pañcarātra*, the practitioner who seeks success must constantly perform recitation and meditation for the remainder of the night until sunrise. (Hbhv 3.103)

Having divided the night into five parts, the practitioner should regularly perform the worship of the deities and other rites during the remaining portion, as well as recitation, fire-offerings, and meditation. (Hbhv 3.104)
Therefore, in the Viṣṇu-smṛti it is said: "The last watch of the night is called the Brāhma-muhūrta. (Hbhv_3.105)
Thus, that procedure and majesty regarding the washing of the feet, drinking water, and so forth shall be written hereafter; however,
for now, that [procedure] for meditation is written in brief.
In the *Tāpanīya* Śrutis (Ṛgveda Khila 1.9–11):
"The Lord has beautiful lotus-eyes, is cloud-like in hue, wears a lightning-bright garment, possesses two arms adorned with the *jñāna-mudrā*, and is garlanded with forest flowers. (Hbhv 3.107)
Surrounded by cowherds, cowherdesses, and cattle, seated beneath a celestial tree,
adorned with two ornaments, and situated in the midst of a jewel-lotus.
By meditating in one's mind upon Kṛṣṇa, who is served by the breezes touching the waves of the waters of the Yamunā, one is liberated from the cycle of worldly existence.
And in the *Sāradā-tilaka*, as taught according to the *Mṛtyuñjaya-saṃhitā*:
"One should meditate upon Govinda, the lotus-eyed one, who incessantly enchants thousands of cowherd girls in the beautiful Vṛndāvana. (Hbhv_3.110)
With their bee-like eyes drawn toward the lotus-face of the Self,
they were rendered helpless by the arrow of desire and long yearned for an embrace.
Bowed under the weight of their full, lofty breasts shimmering with pearl necklaces,
with their braided hair and garments disheveled, they speak with voices faltering from intoxication.
Adorned with quivering lower lips radiant with the luster of rows of teeth,
they captivated [the senses] with various amorous gestures imbued with deep emotion.
With the beauty of a full-blown blue lotus, a moon-like face, and a fondness for peacock-feather ornaments;
bearing the Śrīvatsa mark and the noble Kaustubha gem, clad in beautiful yellow garments;
his body worshipped by the lotus-eyes of the gopīs, surrounded by hosts of cows and cowherds—[I bow to Him].
I worship Govinda, who is intent on playing his melodious flute and whose limbs are adorned with divine ornaments.

Thus, that supreme meditation is proclaimed in the *Śrī-Gautamīya-tantra* and other such works; it should also be written down here before us, and one should practice whatever is desired therein. (Hbhv 3.115)
In the Bṛhat-Śātātapa-smṛti:
"The sin that perishes for a man through fasting for a fortnight is destroyed by men through a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). (Hbhv 3.116)
Whatever sin of men is destroyed by a thousand breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma),
that same sin is utterly destroyed in a mere moment by meditating upon Hari.
In the Viṣṇudharma:
"Even one who is addicted to every kind of sin, by meditating for a single moment on Acyuta, becomes a man of austerity, a purifier of those who purify the assembly. (Hbhv 3.118)
And in the Viṣṇu-purāṇa:
"One should meditate upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa during rituals such as ritual bathing;
for it is certain that this is the atonement for every evil deed. (Hbhv 3.119)
Regarding the quality of removing the defects of the Kali age, it is stated in the *Bṛhan-nāradīya-purāṇa* in the section on Kali (NārP 1.41.97):
"He who is the support of the entire world and whose nature is the ultimate reality..."
When the terrible Kali age has arrived, one who meditates upon Viṣṇu does not perish.
Regarding his authority over all dharmas,
it is stated by Agastya in the *Kārttika-māhātmya* of the *Skanda-purāṇa*:
"But what is the use of many sacred fords for him, or what is the use of many vows?"
He who constantly meditates upon the god Nārāyaṇa with undistracted mind.
The quality of bestowing liberation is stated in the *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa* in the section concerning the Kali age (*NārP* 1.40.52):
"Those men who are free from passion and who know that which is beyond and below..."
Those who constantly remember Nārāyaṇa, the preceptor of the gods,
have their consciousness purified of defilements by that meditation;
they do not drink the milk from a mother’s breast again.
Regarding the attainment of Śrī-Vaikuṇṭha,
it is stated by Śrī Brahmā in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"He who meditates upon Nārāyaṇa without weariness for even a single moment..."
Even he attains a good rebirth; how much more so one who is devoted to that [practice]!
In the *Pādmapurāṇa*, within the *Māhātmya* of Vaiśākha, in the dialogue between Yama and the Brāhmaṇa [PadmaP 1.96.78]:
"Those who meditate upon the divine Puruṣa and remember Acyuta attain the abode of Acyuta; this is the ancient Vedic revelation. (Hbhv 3.124)
Regarding the attainment of similarity of form (*sārūpya-prāpaṇa*),
it is stated in the eleventh book of the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* (11.5.48):
"By whom the kings Śiśupāla, Pauṇḍraka, and others— out of enmity— "

Śālva and others, their minds captivated by her gait, graceful gestures, glances, and so forth, meditated upon her while on their beds and seats; they attained a state of identity with her—what then can be said of those whose hearts are already full of passion? (Hbhv 3.125)
The state of being the supreme fruit by itself is stated in the Fourth Skandha [BhP 4.20.29], in the words of Śrī Pṛthu:
"Therefore, the saintly indeed worship You..."
O Blessed One, we know of no other cause for the virtuous than the recollection of your feet, which brings about the cessation of the arising of the delusions of the qualities of māyā. (Hbhv 3.126)
And in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the words of Brahmā:
"Having churned all the scriptures and having reflected upon them again and again, this alone is well-established: Nārāyaṇa is to be meditated upon at all times. (Hbhv 3.127)
Therefore, it is said in the *Nārāyaṇavyūhastava* of the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*:
"Salutations again and again even to those who have renounced worldly duties and wealth, who have come under the sway of devotion to Viṣṇu, and who meditate upon the Supreme Self. (Hbhv 3.128)
Thus,

the wise know that whatever majesty exists in recollection (smaraṇa) exists in its entirety in meditative concentration (dhyāna) as well; how great a difference could there possibly be between the two in terms of their general and specific characteristics?
Then, for the awakening of the Blessed Lord, one should go to the temple and, preceded by the sounding of bells and other instruments,
awaken Kṛṣṇa with hymns of praise, perform the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*), and offer this prayer: Hbhv_3.130.
In the Third Canto [BhP 3.9.25]:
"That Blessed One, possessing abundant compassion, with a smile born of increased love, caused his lotus-like eyes to blossom."
And having arisen for the sake of our universal victory, may the Ancient Person dispel our despondency with his honeyed speech.
O Keśava, remover of the suffering of those who have taken refuge in you, grant me your grace;
O Acyuta, deliver me once again by the gift of your glance.
Thus,
having entered the temple and reciting his beloved hymns of praise,
one should remove the floral offerings (nirmālya) of Kṛṣṇa, with the exception of the tulasī.
Now, regarding the removal of the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings), the *Atri-smṛti* states: "A wise person should always perform the removal of the *nirmālya* at the time of dawn."
Thirsty tethered animals, a menstruating maiden, and a deity with its floral offerings removed destroy previously accumulated merit. (Hbhv 3.134)
In the *Nārasiṃha-purāṇa*, the venerable Yama stated:
"The removal of garlands from a deity, the sweeping of a temple, and the bathing of all the gods are recorded as being equal to the gift of a cow. (Hbhv 3.135)
In the *Nārada-pañcarātra*:
"He who, having risen in the morning and performed his daily duties, discards the remains of the offerings (*nirmālya*) of the Lord,"
For him there is no suffering, nor poverty,
nor untimely death, nor even mere illness.
At the time of dawn, the remains of offerings (nirmālya) become a thorn;
in the morning, however, they become a great thorn by virtue of being present for even a single ghaṭikā.
One should recognize it as an exceedingly grievous wound, like a blow from a thunderbolt;
however, at the time of dawn, Hari endures that wound.
If a *ghaṭikā* has passed, it brings about a minor offense (*pātaka*);
if a *muhūrta* has elapsed, it is called a full offense.
It would be a minor transgression (atipātaka) during four ghaṭikās;
when three muhūrtas are completed, it is called a major transgression (mahāpātaka).
Beyond that, the killing of a Brahmin constitutes the five great sins (mahāpātakas);
once the blow has reached completion, there is no atonement thereafter.
Now, the expiation for a delay regarding the *nirmālya* is being stated:
if half a *muhūrta* has passed, one should perform a thousand-fold recitation (*japa*).
When a full muhūrta has elapsed, it is said to be "with a thousand" (sārdha-sahasra);
one should perform the second thousand during four ghaṭikās. (Hbhv 3.143)
When three muhūrtas have passed, one should perform ten thousand recitations;
when the watch [of the day] has reached completion, it is called *puraścaraṇa*.
If the watch has elapsed, no expiation is prescribed. (Hbhv 3.144)
Then, for the purpose of washing the lotus-like face,
hands, and feet, one should offer water for rinsing the mouth in his house and present a tooth-stick. (Hbhv 3.145)
Having given a tongue-scraper, wooden sandals, pure clay,
and water, he should further give a cloth for wiping the face.
Then one should offer the meritorious and auspicious Śrī-tulasī, which is dear to the Blessed One;
and its greatness should be written down beforehand in connection with that primary subject.
Now, regarding the greatness of offering a tooth-stick, it is said in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"By the gift of a tooth-stick, one attains the excellence of one's teeth."
By using a tongue-scraper, one becomes free from disease.
By the gift of sandals, one attains a desired state;
by the gift of a portion of clay to the Lord, one obtains unsurpassed land.

Then, having recited the verses for the auspicious lustration (*maṅgala-nīrājana*) and other pleasing stanzas accompanied by the sounds of great musical instruments, one should perform the lustration of the Lord known as "Auspicious," which brings welfare to the world. (Hbhv 3.150)
This *nīrājana* ceremony should be performed by all with bodies purified;
having arisen with supreme faith, it should always be witnessed by men.
This fulfills all the desires of both women and men, and brings about the pacification of all wretchedness, poverty, misfortune, and the like. (Hbhv 3.152)
Then, making an effort for the morning bath,
one should go outside at the end of the dawn for the purpose of bathing;
chanting the names of Kṛṣṇa, one should thereafter proceed to a sacred ford (tīrtha).
And so it is stated in the *Śukra-smṛti*:
"Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, having become pure and composed, and having assumed the *svastika* or other postures, one should meditate upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa. (Hbhv 3.154)
Then, having emerged from his dwelling, he should recite these names:
"O Śrī Vāsudeva, Aniruddha, Pradyumna, Adhokṣaja, Acyuta, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Ananta, Govinda, Saṅkarṣaṇa—homage be to you! (Hbhv 3.155)
Having gone to a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) or similar location, having set aside his bathing requisites there,
and having performed the duties of loving-kindness and so forth according to the rule, as well as the purification (śauca),
he should sip water (ācamana), cleanse the apertures of the body, and perform the bath as is appropriate. (Hbhv 3.156)
Now follows the procedure for the practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the other virtues,
as described in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa* (3.11.8–15) within the dialogue between Aurva and Sagara during the exposition of the duties of a householder:
"Then, having risen at dawn, O Lord of Men, one should void urine."
In the southwest, beyond the distance of an arrow-shot from the house, [he should sit].
One should void urine and feces at a distance from one's dwelling;
one should not discharge water used for washing the feet or food remnants into the courtyard of the house.
A wise person should never urinate upon his own shadow, the shadow of a tree, nor upon a cow, the sun, fire, or wind; likewise, he should never urinate upon his teacher or upon brahmins and others.
Not on ploughed land, nor in the midst of crops, nor in a cow-pen, nor in a crowd of people; not on a path, nor at river-banks and the like, O bull among men. (Hbhv 3.160)
One should not perform the evacuation or the discharge of feces or urine in water, nor on the bank of water, nor in a cremation ground. (Hbhv 3.161)
O King, a wise man should discharge urine and feces facing north during the day and facing the opposite direction at night, except in times of distress. (Hbhv 3.162)
Having covered the ground with grass and having his head wrapped in a cloth,
he should remain there for no very long time and should not utter anything at all.
Likewise, in the *Vyāsagītā* of the *Kūrma-purāṇa*:
"Having placed the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) upon his right ear, facing north, and having covered the ground with wood, leaves, clods of earth, or grass... (Hbhv 3.164).
One should discharge feces and urine while covering the head;
nor should one do so facing women, teachers, Brahmins, cows, deities, temples, or water at any time. (Hbhv 3.165)
Having observed the river and the celestial bodies, one should not set out with the wind, fire, or the sun facing forward, nor likewise with the fire or the moon facing forward.
In the *Kāśī-kāṇḍa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Skanda and Agastya:
"Then, to perform the necessary [rites], one should resort to the south-western direction;
one should go a hundred *dhanus* from a village, and four times that distance from a city. (Hbhv_3.167)
Wearing the sacred thread over the ear, facing north during the day and at both twilights, one should void urine and feces while observing silence; at night, one should face south.
One should not look toward the quarters of the horizon, the circle of the stars, or the stainless sky;
holding the penis with the left hand, one should rise up with diligence.
In that very same place, it says further:
"One should not void urine in a cow-pen, nor on an anthill, nor in ashes; nor in pits containing living beings, nor while standing, nor even while walking. (Hbhv 3.170)

One may discharge excrement at night or during the day, in shade or in darkness, and even amidst fears or when one's life is threatened, provided it is done facing a comfortable direction. (Hbhv 3.171)
In that very same passage of the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (3.11.16–18):
"One should not offer earth dug up by anthills or mice, nor earth from within water, nor what remains after cleansing, nor earth from a house that has become smeared. (Hbhv 3.172)
O King, one should avoid all these types of earth for the purpose of purification: that which is inhabited by living beings, and that which has been turned up by a plow. (Hbhv 3.173)
O King, one application of clay is for the penis, three for the anus, ten on the left hand, and seven on both hands; these are the applications of clay that bring about purification.
In the *Yama-smṛti*:
"Three [prostrations] should always be offered at the feet by one who desires purification. (Hbhv 3.175)
Furthermore:
"But after having cleaned one's nails, three lumps of earth should be applied. (Hbhv 3.176)
And in that very same section of the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*:
"One should apply one portion of earth to the private parts, five to the anus, ten to the left hand, and seven portions of earth to both hands. (Hbhv 3.177)
One should apply one portion of earth to each foot and three to the hands;
thus should a householder perform purification until the odor and the smear have vanished. (Hbhv 3.178)
This [purity] is doubled respectively for the three stages beginning with studentship;
and from the purity prescribed for the day, one should practice half during the night.

One should apply half that amount when afflicted by illness, half of that again when troubled by thieves and the like on the road, and half of that for women; however, one should not use less than this even when in good health.
For purification, earth as much as the size of a fresh *dhātrī* fruit is prescribed.
In the Śaṅkha-smṛti:
"But clay is prescribed as that which fills three finger-joints. (Hbhv 3.181)
In the *Dakṣasmṛti*:
"The first amount of clay is prescribed as half a handful;
the second and the third are proclaimed to be half of that. (Hbhv 3.182)
Now, regarding the skillful performance of voiding urine alone:
one application of earth is prescribed for the penis, three for the left hand, and two applications of earth for both hands.

In the Brahma-method, having taken water with both hands and thoroughly washed them, one should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana); then, being pure, one should remember the eternal Viṣṇu. (Hbhv 3.184)
In that very same passage of the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (3.11.19–21):
"With water that is clear, free from odor and froth, and devoid of bubbles, one should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana);
then, being composed, one should apply earth once more. (Hbhv_3.185)
Having performed the purification of his feet and having sprinkled water over his head once more,
he should drink water three times with that [water] and likewise rinse his mouth twice.
Then one should touch the apertures of the head and the crown of the head with earth;
one should also touch the arms, the navel, and the heart with water.
And regarding this, Dakṣa has stated the specific rule:
"Having washed both hands and feet, one should drink water that has been inspected three times;
then, using the base of the joined thumb and forefinger, one should wipe the mouth twice. (Hbhv 3.188)
Having first brought the three [fingers] together, one should thus touch the mouth;
immediately thereafter, one should touch the nostrils with the thumb and the index finger.
With the thumb and ring finger, one should repeatedly touch the eyes and ears;
with the little finger and thumb, the navel; and with the palm, the heart.
Then, with all fingers, one should touch the head, and finally the arms with the fingertips.

Likewise, in the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*, in that very same place: "Facing either east or north, well-seated on pure ground free from husks, charcoal, bones, and ashes, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*upaspṛśet*). (Hbhv 3.191)

A Brāhmaṇa should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with water that is neither hot nor frothy, which reaches the heart, without haste, using the Brahma-tīrtha, and which has been purified by his gaze. (Hbhv 3.192)
A king is purified by [water] reaching the throat; likewise, those of the ūrajas class [are purified] by water reaching the palate;
women and Śūdras are purified even by the mere contact with the mouth.
In the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti*:
"A twice-born man should not sip water that remains after washing his feet;
Baudhāyana declared that if he should sip it, he must pour it out upon the ground. (Hbhv 3.194)
In the *Bhāradvāja-smṛti*:
"One should sip water with the right hand alone, with the fingers joined;
having released the thumb and the little finger, one should discard the water without touching the lips. (Hbhv 3.195)
And in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, within the *Vyāsagītā*:
"After eating, drinking, sleeping, bathing, walking along a road,
touching the lips when they have lost their hair, and after changing one's garment."
Upon the discharge of semen, urine, or feces; upon speaking untruths;
at the beginning of spitting or commencing Vedic study; and likewise when coughing or wheezing occurs. (Hbhv 3.197)
Having approached a crossroads or a cremation ground, the best of the twice-born should likewise sip water for purification again, even if he has already sipped it, at both twilights.
Furthermore:

"Having covered one's head or neck, or even having one's lower garment or topknot hanging loose, or without having performed the purification of the feet—even if one has sipped water (ācamana), one remains impure. (Hbhv 3.199)
A wise person should not perform ācamana while wearing shoes, while standing in water, or while not wearing a turban;
likewise, a wise person should not do so under rain-showers or when the hands are still soiled with food remnants.
Nor [should one recite] with water not poured from both hands, nor without the sacred thread (*sūtra*),
nor while standing on sandals or a seat, nor with the knees outside [the body], nor likewise with the knees apart.
Now, regarding the Vaiṣṇava sipping of water: one should recite Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, and Mādhava while drinking three times;
and for the washing of both hands, one should likewise recite Govinda and Viṣṇu.
One should worship Madhusūdana for the first cleansing, and Trivikrama for the second.
In wiping the two lips, one should likewise visualize both Vāmana and Śrīdhara.
Furthermore, upon washing the hands, one should worship Hṛṣīkeśa;
on the feet, Padmanābha; and then, upon sprinkling the head, Dāmodara.

One should place Vāsudeva on the mouth, both Saṅkarṣaṇa and Pradyumna on the two nostrils, Aniruddha on the pair of eyes, Puruṣottama on the ears, Nṛsiṃha on the navel, and Acyuta on the anus. (Hbhv 3.206)

Then, one should sip water (ācamana) while reciting in sequence, using the vocative case ending for each name: "Salutation to Janārdana" at the heart, "to Upendra" on the head, "to Hari" on the right arm, and "to Kṛṣṇa" on the left arm, according to the prescribed rule. "Salutation to Ananta," likewise ending in the fourth case, [is recited for the feet]. Hbhv_3.207.
If one is unable [to perform the ritual], one should merely touch the right ear with the hand and likewise with speech;
or indeed, one may perform the touching of the right ear.
Now follows the rule for cleaning the teeth.
Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
"Having risen, having washed one's eyes, and having become pure and composed..."
And having consecrated it with the mantra, one should consume the tooth-stick.
And this is the mantra:
"O Lord of the Forest, bestow upon us longevity, strength, fame, splendor, progeny, cattle, and wealth, as well as sacred knowledge, wisdom, and intelligence. (Hbhv 3.210)
Regarding its permanence,
it is stated in the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*:
"Then, for the sake of purifying the mouth, one should take up a tooth-stick."
For even one who has sipped water is impure if he has not performed the cleaning of his teeth.
And in the Vārāha [Purāṇa]:
"But he who approaches me without having chewed a tooth-stick—by that single act, all the merit of his deeds performed throughout his entire life is destroyed. (Hbhv_3.212)
Now, regarding the days on which the use of a tooth-stick is prohibited,
Manu says:
"The fourteenth day, the eighth, the new moon, the full moon, and the sun's transit (saṅkrānti) [are forbidden]."
Among these, one should avoid women, oil, meat, and tooth-sticks.
Saṃvartaka says:
On the first lunar day, on the ninth, during the waning of the moon, on Sundays, and on Saturdays, one should avoid cleaning the teeth with a tooth-stick. (Hbhv 3.214)

Kātyāyana says: On the first day of the lunar fortnight, on the new moon, on the sixth, and especially on the ninth, the contact of a wooden stick with the teeth burns one's family unto the seventh generation. (Hbhv 3.215)
Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha says:
During a fast as well as at a śrāddha, one should eat [only] after cleansing the teeth;
indeed, the contact of the teeth with a wooden stick destroys seven generations of one's lineage. (Hbhv 3.216)
And elsewhere it is said:
"On the first, sixth, and ninth lunar days, as well as on the eleventh and on Sundays, the contact of a tooth-stick with the teeth destroys previously accumulated merit. (Hbhv 3.217)
Now, as a substitute in that regard,
since the cleaning of the teeth with wood is prohibited during these days, one should perform it with grass or with things other than wood. (Hbhv 3.218)
And so Vyāsa says:

"On the first lunar day (pratipad), the new moon (darśa), the sixth (ṣaṣṭhī), and the ninth (navamī), one should clean the teeth with leaves; on other days, however, the scraping of the tongue should always be done with a wooden stick. (Hbhv 3.219)
Paiṭhīnasi states:

"In the absence of [suitable] wood or when its use is forbidden, one should always perform the cleaning of the teeth with pure leaves or other materials; indeed, the scraping of the tongue should always be done in this manner. (Hbhv 3.220)
Now, regarding the exception in that very context:

the brushing of teeth with wooden sticks, which is prohibited on the first lunar day (pratipad) and other such days, may instead be performed with grass or leaves, except on the eleventh day (ekādaśī) when it is not yet full (amā).

For this very reason, there is another statement by Vyāsa: "In the absence of tooth-sticks, or when the lunar day is prohibited, one should perform the cleansing of the teeth with twelve mouthfuls of water. (Hbhv 3.222)
In the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, in that very same place:
"Since a man becomes a partaker of impurity when his mouth has been stale, he should therefore diligently perform the cleansing of the teeth for the sake of purification. (Hbhv 3.225)
Even during a fast, one should not be defiled by cleaning the teeth or applying collyrium, nor by perfumes, ornaments, fine garments, flower garlands, or ointments. (Hbhv 3.226)
Now, regarding tooth-sticks, it is stated in the Smṛti: "All thorny trees are meritorious, while milky trees are said to bestow long life."
And those that are pungent, bitter, and astringent bestow strength, health, and happiness.
Furthermore:
One should avoid using *palāśa* wood for a tooth-stick, as well as sandals;
and one should also carefully avoid the *vaṭa* and the *aśvattha* trees. (Hbhv 3.228)

In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, within the *Śrī-Vyāsagītā*: "A tooth-stick that is twelve finger-breadths in length and as thick as the middle finger, which has its bark intact—one should not hold it by its tip. (Hbhv 3.229)
That which arises from a milky tree, that which originates from the *mālatī*,
or the auspicious *apāmārga* and *bilva*, and especially the *karavīra*.
Having avoided the forbidden items and having taken one [item] as prescribed, the knower of the rules should indeed consume it after avoiding a sinful day. (Hbhv 3.231)
One should not split the tooth-stick, nor should one hold it with the tips of the fingers;
having rinsed it and used it, one should discard it in a clean place with a concentrated mind.
And in that very same section of the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*: "The tooth-stick should have a circumference equal to the tip of the little finger, be with its bark, free from blemishes, straight,
twelve finger-breadths in length, and fresh."
Or one may also fashion an auspicious tongue-scraper in the shape of a bow.
And in the *Rāmārcana-candrikā*:

"The scraping of the teeth is performed with a twig measuring one span (*vitasti*)," according to such mantras; [one should do so] in the morning with a twig of milk-tree (*kṣīrī*) wood or the like, avoiding the *vaṭa*, *khadira*, *palāśa*, *arka*, mango, and *bilva* trees.
Having eaten, one should perform six mouthfuls of rinsing (gaṇḍūṣa) twice with the fingers— excluding the thumb—
on the Nandā, Bhūtā, and Aṣṭamī lunar days, but certainly not on the Navamī, Ārka, Saṅkrānti, or Pāta days.
Then, after grooming the hair and so forth, and having sipped water (ācamana) according to the rule,
the twice-born man, having recollected the Praṇava and the Gāyatrī, should tie his topknot (śikhā).
And so it has been said:
"One should not arrange one's hair while facing south or upwards;
rather, having recollected the syllable *oṃ* and the *gāyatrī*, one should bind [the hair] up to the hairline. (Hbhv 3.236)
Now, regarding bathing,
it is stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (3.11.25) at that very place: "In rivers, streams, ponds, and waters dug by the gods..."
One should bathe for the sake of daily rites in mountain springs and waterfalls.
One should perform the bath with water drawn from wells, or on the ground;
or one may bathe with drawn water, or on the ground if [water] is unavailable.
Now, regarding the necessity of bathing, Kātyāyana states: "Just as one bathes during the day, so should one who is not ill bathe daily in the morning."
The body is utterly impure, endowed with nine apertures;
it flows [with impurities] day and night. Morning bathing is the means of purification.
Dakṣa says:
For forest-dwellers and householders, bathing occurs in the morning and at midday; for the ascetic, it is three times a day; but for the student, it is once. (Hbhv 3.240)
And all [the monks] together may perform it at once; however, if they are unable, they may do so without the ritual water (udaka).
Furthermore:
