For those engaged in ritual action who are unable [to bathe fully], bathing without the head is always permissible;
alternatively, there may be cleansing with a wet cloth or even with the hand.
And Śaṅkha says:
"A man who has not bathed is indeed unfit for recitation, oblations, and other such rites. (Hbhv 3.243)
In the *Vyāsagītā* within the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:

"The sinfulness of men in performing ritual acts is traditionally held to exist without the morning bath; especially so in the case of fire-offerings (*homa*) and recitation (*japa*). Therefore, one should perform the bath. (Hbhv_3.244)
In the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*:
"Since a man is drenched by perspiration, saliva, and the like, and is overcome by sleep, he becomes fit for the recitation of mantras, hymns, and so forth, only after his morning bath. (Hbhv_3.245)
And in the *Padma Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Devahūti and Vikuṇḍala (*PadmaP* 3.31.55–56):
"That man who eats without having bathed is always an eater of impurity;
the ancestors and deities turn their faces away from him, who is unbathed and impure. (Hbhv_3.246)
A man who neglects bathing is sinful; a man who neglects bathing is impure.
One who does not bathe experiences hell and is born among such beings as male insects.
Now, regarding the greatness of bathing,
in the *Udyoga-parvan* of the *Mahābhārata*, in the speech of Śrī Vidura [5.37.29], it is said: "Ten virtues attend one who is habituated to bathing."
Strength, beauty, purity of voice and complexion, pleasant touch, fragrance, and cleanliness; majesty, delicacy, and excellent women. (Hbhv 3.248)
And in that very same *Pādmapurāṇa* (3.31.54–58):
"One who bathes daily does not experience the suffering of the torments of Yama;
by daily bathing, even men who have committed sins are purified. (Hbhv_3.249)
O Vaiśya, the morning bath removes both external and internal impurity;
a man who is freed from sin by the morning bath shall not go to hell. (Hbhv 3.250)
Furthermore, those who perform ritual bathing in a river here on a festival day go to hell by that very act; they are not born in evil wombs.
O best of the Vaiśyas, for men who are purified by the morning bath, bad dreams and evil thoughts always become fruitless. (Hbhv 3.252)
In the Atri-smṛti:
"Through bathing, there shall be clarity of mind; the gods are always favorably disposed toward one;
[one gains] good fortune, prosperity, happiness, nourishment, merit, knowledge, fame, and fortitude. (Hbhv 3.253)
Morning bathing, especially so, removes great sins, misfortune, calamity, evil thoughts, grief, suffering, and the like. (Hbhv 3.254)
In the Kūrma Purāṇa, in that very same place:
"They praise the morning bath, for it indeed produces both visible and invisible results;
by the morning bath, sins are purified—of this there is no doubt. (Hbhv 3.255)
And in the Kāśī-khaṇḍa it is said:
"Since this body is always impure, one becomes purified by bathing at dawn;
for it is perforated by nine apertures and flows [with waste] day and night. (Hbhv 3.256)
Morning bathing is praised as the cause of mental clarity and the promoter of enthusiasm, intelligence, good fortune, and the perfection of physical form.
But that bath which is performed every morning when the pair of beautiful dawn-auroras has appeared, they say is equal to the Prājāpatya penance; it destroys great sins. (Hbhv_3.258)
The morning bath removes sin, misfortune, and exhaustion;
it bestows contentment, nourishment, and the removal of impurity as well as bad dreams. (Hbhv 3.259)
The wicked do not approach a person who bathes in the morning at any time;
therefore, one should perform the morning bath, which yields both seen and unseen fruits. (Hbhv 3.260)
In this context, both the mere bath and the morning bath are enjoined;
although these two, when combined, are to be understood as distinct, they are nevertheless [both required]. (Hbhv 3.261)
Now, the procedure for bathing:
Having gone to a sacred ford (tīrtha) and having placed washed garments, kusha grass, and earth upon the bank, one should bathe according to the respective rules for each.
One who performs daily or occasional rites while wearing unwashed clothing does not obtain the fruit; if performed in such a state, the rite becomes fruitless.

Having washed his feet and hands and sipped water (ācamana), and having respectfully made a formal resolve (saṅkalpa) and recollected the Gaṅgā and other sacred sites, he should offer the arghya water-oblation to the holy ford.
O you whose voice is like the roar of the ocean, who hold the staff in hand, the destroyer of asuras, creator of the world, and crusher of the world; I bow to you, O Lord of the Gods!
Having recited this mantra, one should perform the ritual bath at the sacred ford;
otherwise, the Lord of the Ford himself takes away half of the fruit thereof.
Having bowed, one should then request this permission for the purpose of bathing at the sacred ford:
"O God of gods, Lord of the world, wielder of the conch, discus, and mace;
O Viṣṇu, grant me permission to resort to your sacred ford. (Hbhv 3.267)
Thus,
having taken earth according to the prescribed rule and having entered the water of a sacred ford,
one should face the current in a river; elsewhere, one should face the sun.
Having performed the binding of the directions according to the ritual and having consecrated the sacred sites,
one should invoke the Blessed Gaṅgā from the solar orb.

The gods, yakṣas, as well as nāgas, and the hosts of gandharvas and apsarases.

And for those living beings who are without support, and those who are devoted to sinful ways—

To Yama, the King of Dharma, to Death, to the Ender,

In the *Pādma Purāṇa*, within the *Māhātmya of Vaiśākha* [5.87.30,
33], in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Ambarīṣa:

One should draw the shape of a svastika using white, yellow, red, and black [powders].
And regarding that, there is a statement in the *Pañcarātra*:
"One should indeed have the five-colored powders prepared for the sake of the mandala; the white [powder] may be made from rice-grain flour or from barley. (Hbhv 4.41)
Red [pigment] arises from saffron, vermilion, red chalk, and the like;
yellow from yellow orpiment, or sometimes from turmeric;
black from burnt green barley mixed with green and yellow [pigments]. (Hbhv 4.42)
Then, having installed banners, flags, and so forth upon the temple of Hari, a man devoted to the Blessed One should decorate it with various ornaments. (Hbhv 4.43)
Now, regarding the majesty of raising the banner: whoever raises a banner atop a temple with devotion shall dwell in the station of Brahmā and sport together with Brahmā. (Hbhv 4.44)
In the *Bṛhan-nāradīya* [1.19.2]:
"He who performs the supreme hoisting of the banner in the temple of Viṣṇu is honored by Viriñci (Brahmā) and the other gods; what is the use of further words? (Hbhv_4.45)
And right there, at the front [of the banner], it is said:
"O best of Brahmins, as long as the cloth of the banner moves with the wind, for that long the nets of sins are destroyed; of this there is no doubt. (Hbhv_4.46)
Whether one is burdened by a great sin or burdened by all sins,
by setting up a banner in the house of Viṣṇu, one is liberated from all sins.
Those righteous ones who rejoice upon seeing the banner raised are all likewise liberated from millions of great transgressions.
Thus, whatever has been declared in the *Bṛhan-nāradīya* and whatever else is marvelous—
the entire majesty of the raising of the banner (*dhvajāropaṇa-māhātmya*)— should be observed here in its entirety. (Hbhv 4.49)
Now, regarding the greatness of hoisting banners,
it is said in the *Dvārakā-māhātmya*:
"He who constructs a temple for Kṛṣṇa and adorns it with banners..."
His dwelling is always indeed in that world, and not elsewhere.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"And by giving an auspicious banner in the temple of Keśava, the twice-born attains the world of Vāyu for many groups of years. (Hbhv 4.51)
Just as she is shaken by the wind in the abode of Keśava,
so too is every sin shaken away from his body.
Now, regarding the greatness of offering a garland of salutation and erecting a plantain pillar,
it is said in that very same *Dvārakā-māhātmya*:
"O King, he who offers a garland of salutation in the temple of Kṛṣṇa..."
It is served by hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens and honored by the leaders of the gods.
He who builds a temple for Kṛṣṇa adorned with plantain pillars rejoices, accompanied by Apsarases; the King of the Gods welcomes him.
Now, regarding the consecration of the seat, vessels, clothing, and so forth:
therein, whatever vessel made of copper or other materials, whatever clothing and such belonging to the Lord,
and whatever seat and so forth— all that one should purify according to the prescribed rules.
Regarding that, the consecration of the footstool is described in the *Nārasiṃha*:
"One should rub the footstool of Kṛṣṇa with a *bilva* leaf."
And by washing with warm water, one is liberated from all sins.
Now, regarding the purification of vessels made of metal and other materials, the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* states:
"For vessels of udumbara wood, [purification is by] acid; for those of tin and lead, by alkaline substance."
The purification of bell-metal vessels is by means of ashes and water, and that of liquids is by means of overflowing.
And in the *Vāyu Purāṇa*:
"With a paste of gems, diamonds, corals, pearls, conch-shells, and stones, or again with a paste of white mustard seeds or sesame seeds... (Hbhv 4.58).
Those made of gold, silver, conch, stone, mother-of-pearl, and gems;
as well as those made of bell-metal, iron, copper, brass, tin, and lead. (Hbhv 4.59)
Objects that are unstained are purified by water alone;
however, those defiled by the leavings of a Śūdra must be cleansed three times with alkaline substances, acids, and water.
Thus,
if a bowl or other utensil is extremely defiled, one should purify it for the purpose of hospitality;
otherwise, one should employ it for its exchange or for another task of the master.
By reversing this, one should offer something else in return;
thus does this noble conduct shine forth everywhere in the world.
"The purification of copper, iron, brass, tin, and lead must be performed as appropriate with alkaline substances, acids, and water. (Hbhv 4.63)
Śaṅkha states:
One should prescribe the purification of copper, lead, and tin with acidic water, and that of bell-metal and iron with alkaline substance.
Furthermore:

"The purification of a vessel defiled by birth-impurity, food-leavings, or contaminated by liquor and the like, occurs through twenty-one cleansings; however, for bell-metal, heating is not required. (Hbhv 4.65)
And elsewhere it is said:
"Copper is purified by acid, provided there is no coating of impurity;
however, that which is smeared with impurity is purified by heating once again. (Hbhv 4.66)

Items defiled by a Brahmin, a woman who has recently given birth, a corpse, feces, urine, or a woman in her menses, as well as whatever else one might endure, should be cast into the fire. (Hbhv 4.67)
Therefore, Devala says:
"The purification of metals is by burning, or by ashes, or by cow dung;
that of stones is by burning, or by digging, or even by water. (Hbhv 4.68)
Wooden objects are purified by planing, as well as by earth, cow dung, and water;
however, earthen vessels are held to be purified by burning.
Earthenware that has been touched by intoxicating liquors, urine, feces, spittle, pus, or blood cannot be purified even by re-firing. Hbhv 4.70.
Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
"When one among a collection of vessels is damaged, the purification prescribed for that very item is declared to effect the purification of the common substance. (Hbhv 4.71)
Now, regarding the purification of garments and other items,
Śaṅkha states:
"First, one should cleanse a soiled woven garment with water and alkaline substances."
Or, having dried it with rays of light, one should collect it by means of the wind.
For woolen cloth, fine silk, linen, cotton, and skins,
purification shall take place through drying, sprinkling, and other such means when the degree of impurity is slight.
One should wash those very [utensils] smeared with impurities using white mustard seeds, pastes of grain, pastes of leaves, juices, and the bark of fruits. (Hbhv 4.74)
Having cleaned pillows and other cushions, as well as flowers, jewels, and garments, one should repeatedly wipe them slightly with the hands in the sun.
And afterwards, having sprinkled them with water, one should declare, "They are pure";
likewise, one should properly purify those [utensils] that are excessively stained with impurities.
Śātātapa states:
"Objects dyed with safflower, saffron, or lac-dye are purified by washing, as are those touched by a Caṇḍāla. (Hbhv 4.77)
Yama says:
Bones and teeth are purified by winds, by the waters of the hair of black antelopes, by earth, and by cow's urine; and linen garments are purified by white mustard seeds.
Śaṅkha says: For [utensils] made of ivory or horn, [purification] is by means of a paste of white mustard seeds;
for fruit-vessels, it is with cow-hair; and for bone [vessels], it should be as in the case of horn.
Furthermore:
[The same applies] to resinous exudations, molasses, and salts;
likewise to safflower, and to wool and cotton.
"Purity is declared to result from sprinkling," so said the Blessed Yama.
"The purification of large quantities of grain and clothing is by sprinkling with water;
however, for small quantities, purification by washing with water is prescribed. (Hbhv 4.81)
The purification of skins is like that of clothes, and the same applies to items made of split bamboo;
for vegetables, roots, and fruits, purification is held to be the same as for grain.
Grass, wood, and straw are purified by sprinkling;
a house by sweeping and smearing with cow-dung; and an earthen vessel by re-firing. (Hbhv 4.83)
Furthermore:

"In all purifications of objects, as long as the odor and the stain caused by contact with impurity do not depart from that which has been smeared by it, so long must earth and water be applied. (Manu 5.126)
Bṛhaspati:
For cloth, bamboo, leather, and the like, purification is traditionally held to be washing;
however, for that which is extremely defiled, one should discard that portion and cut it away for the sake of purification.
Viṣṇu:
Regarding earth, leaves, grass, and wood defiled by dogs, bones, Cāṇḍālas, or crows, purification is prescribed by means of the rays of the moon and sun, and by the wind. (Hbhv 4.86)
Baudhāyana says:
A seat, a bed, a vehicle, boats, a path, and grass—these, as well as things constructed of baked brick, are purified by wind and sun. (Hbhv 4.87)
Now, regarding the preparation of grains and other items, Baudhāyana states: "Grains, as well as vegetables, roots, and fruits, [are purified] by being sprinkled with water."
Either by the removal of that alone, or by the process of dehusking.
Śaṅkha says:
The boiling of clarified butter and oil, and the immersion of cow’s milk;
one should rinse the vessels with water, as well as the vegetables, roots, and fruits.
In the Brahma [posture],
one should wash away with water the many impurities that have flowed forth.
Having set aside the spoiled portion of the crops— whether rice, vegetables, roots, or fruits— one should then sprinkle them with water.
Bṛhaspati says:
The purification of clarified butter and oils is by heating; that of milk products is by immersion;
however, solid substances such as milk and curd are purified by merely removing the impure portion.
Likewise, ghee that has not melted should be melted by heating;
however, if there is a defect in the container, one should transfer the liquid from one vessel to another.
Clarified butter, milk-rice, milk, sugarcane juice, molasses, buttermilk kept in a Śūdra’s vessel, and likewise honey—these do not become defiled [by contact]. (Hbhv 4.94)
Furthermore, Manu [5.143] states:
"But if one who holds a substance in his hand is somehow touched by something defiled by leavings, he shall attain purity by sipping water (ācamana) without setting that substance down. (Hbhv 4.95)
Thus,
other methods of purifying substances should also be understood by Vaiṣṇavas based on the Smṛti scriptures; enough with elaborating on each of those.
Then, for the purpose of worship,
the Vaiṣṇava, having prostrated before Mahāviṣṇu and requested his permission,
should gather the sacred Tulasī, flowers, and other materials as prescribed. (Hbhv 4.97)
And as for the statement of Hārīta:
"If any twice-born ones indeed take up a flower after having performed their bath, the deities do not accept it; it turns to ashes like wood. (Hbhv 4.98)
Thus, this refers specifically to the midday bath,
since it is stated in the *Pādmapurāṇa* (5.98.7) in the section on the greatness of the month of Vaiśākha:
Having cut a *tulasī* leaf without having bathed for the sake of a deity or in a rite for the ancestors, all that becomes fruitless; one is purified by the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Now, the procedure for bathing at home:
while performing the bath in one's own house, having washed the feet and hands,
and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) and meditate upon Hari.
Then, having recollected the Gaṅgā and other sacred rivers, the virtuous person should invoke all the holy fords (tīrthas) into a full vessel with water mixed with *tulasī*.
And this is the invocation mantra:
"O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī—be present in these waters! (Hbhv 4.102)
Thus [it is said].
Alternatively, the wise man should invoke the Gaṅgā herself, who embodies all sacred fords,
using twelve names into a water vessel.
The twelve names are:
Nalinī, Nandinī, Sītā, Mālinī, Mahāpagā,
Gaṅgā, Tripathagāminī, and [the others born from] the water-offering at Viṣṇu’s feet.
Bhāgīrathī, Bhogavatī, Jāhnavī, and Tridaśeśvarī.
And in the *Padma Purāṇa*, in the section on the greatness of Vaiśākha (5.95.17–18):
"Your names are indeed Nandinī and Nalinī in the Vedas; you are Dakṣā, Pṛthvī, Vihagā, Viśvagāthā, and Śivapriyā. (Hbhv 4.105)
The great goddess Vidyādharī, as well as Lokaprasādinī,
Kṣemaṅkarī, Jāhnavī, Śāntā, and Śāntipradāyinī.
Then, having sipped water and requested permission from the Guru as before,
one should contemplate the Gaṅgā falling from the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa onto one’s own head.

And so it is said in the Śrī-Nārada-Pañcarātra: "One should meditate upon the Lord Vāsudeva, who is established in Himself, the lotus-eyed one, the embodiment of the mantra, resembling infinite suns, and possessing four arms. (Hbhv 4.108)
Holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus, clothed in yellow garments,
dark-complexioned, with a peaceful countenance, gracious, and with eyes granting boons.
His limbs are anointed with divine sandalwood paste, his lotus-face possesses a charming smile,
and he wears flaming makara-shaped earrings encrusted with many jewels.

The god is surrounded by a forest garland, worshipped by Nārada and others; he is endowed with armlets and bracelets, radiant with a golden crown, beautiful in every limb, and adorned with all ornaments. (Hbhv 4.111)
One should contemplate a stream falling from his lotus feet onto one's own head, entering one's body through the aperture of Brahmā (brahma-randhra);
by means of that, one should wash away all impurity residing within the body. (Hbhv 4.112)
At that very moment, the practitioner becomes free from passion and resembles crystal;
this bath is considered by the mantra-knowers to be more than a thousand times superior [to ordinary bathing]. (Hbhv 4.113)
Thus, one should recite the words beginning with "Nārāyaṇa" once;
furthermore, at the time of bathing, one should remember the name of that Great Lord. (Hbhv 4.114)
And so it is said in the Kūrma Purāṇa: "The waters were produced from Nārāyaṇa, and they indeed are his abode;
therefore, at the time of bathing, a wise person should remember the god Nārāyaṇa. (Hbhv 4.115)
Thus,
one should bathe even with warm water, or likewise with *āmalaka* fruits,
sesame seeds, and oils, while avoiding the days that are prohibited.
Now, regarding bathing with warm water,
the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* states:
"Water is pure by its very nature, and especially so when in contact with fire."
Therefore, the virtuous praise bathing with warm water.
And Yama says:
"Water is always pure by its very nature, and especially so when heated by fire;
therefore, warm water is traditionally held to be purifying at all times. (Hbhv 4.118)
And as it was said by Śaṅkha:

"The purification of the body for one who has bathed with water heated by fire or likewise with water from the sun's heat should be understood [as mere cleanliness], but the fruit of the ritual bath would not arise. (Hbhv 4.119)
Thus, that [rule] refers to the domain of optional (*kāmya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites;
for this very reason, it was stated by Garga:
One should perform the occasional bath with cold water, as well as the optional one; likewise, one may practice the daily and spontaneous baths according to one's preference.
Now, regarding the prohibited days therein,
Yama says:
"Upon the birth of a son, at the transit of the sun (saṅkrānti), and during the eclipses of the moon and the sun..."
And upon touching that which is untouchable, one should certainly not bathe with warm water.
Vṛddha-Manu says:
"He who bathes with hot water on the full moon day or likewise on the new moon day incurs the sin committed by killing a cow; of this there is no doubt in this world. (Hbhv 4.122)
Now, regarding the bath with *āmalaka* fruits, Mārkaṇḍeya says therein:
"Viṣṇu is pleased by *āmalaka* fruits, especially on the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*)."
A man desiring prosperity should always perform his bath with *āmalaka* fruits.
On the seventh [tithi], a man should not touch oil, nor should he wear indigo-dyed clothing;
he should not bathe with *āmalaka* fruit, nor should he engage in quarreling.
Bhṛgu says:
One should avoid bathing with garlands on the sixth, seventh, ninth, and thirteenth lunar days, as well as on the day of a solar transit (saṅkrānti) and on Sundays. (Hbhv 4.125)
Yājñavalkya states:
"For one who bathes with *dhātrī* fruits on the new moon day, or on the seventh or ninth lunar days, his splendor, lifespan, wealth, and sons shall diminish. (Hbhv 4.126)
Now, regarding the sesame bath (*tila-snāna*), Bṛhaspati says:
"The sage Vyāsa has declared that bathing with sesame seeds may be performed at all times. (Hbhv 4.127)
According to the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: likewise, on the seventh lunar day, the new moon, the sun's passage into a new sign, and during eclipses,
one who desires wealth, sons, or a wife should not touch anything that has been touched by sesame seeds.
Now, regarding the oil-bath,
it is said in that same [text]:
"Oil [used for bathing] on the sixth lunar day is detrimental to longevity, as is [bathing with oil] on the fourth days and on the festival days (parvan)."
Yogī-Yājñavalkya says:
If an unwise man bathes on the tenth lunar day without having first inquired about oil, four things perish for him: life-span, progeny, fame, and wealth. (Hbhv 4.130)
He who, out of delusion, anoints himself with oil on the first lunar day, the sixth, the new moon (kuhū), or likewise on an empty (riktā) lunar day, is deprived of four things.
On the fifteenth, the fourteenth, the seventh, during the sun's transit,
on the twelfth, the seventh, and the sixth, one should avoid contact with oil.
Furthermore:
On the seventh, ninth, and first lunar days, as well as specifically on the eighth, the fourteenth, and the new moon day, one should not touch oil. (Hbhv 4.133)
Furthermore:
Whether one has bathed or not, cooked oil does not become defiled.
Furthermore, in the Atri-smṛti:

"If a twice-born man voids excrement or urine after being smeared with oil or ghee, he becomes pure by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). (Hbhv 4.135)
Then, having removed his upper garment and bathed according to the rules,
he should perform the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite with a handful of water brought up to his nose.
Then, having performed the consecration as before with water from the feet of the guru and others,
the consecration should be performed with water mixed with *tulasī* using a conch shell.
Now, regarding the greatness of the consecration with *tulasī* water, it is stated in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"A Vaiṣṇava person indeed purifies himself during the consecration with *tulasī*."
O twice-born one, at that very moment, his body becomes composed of all the sacred fords.
By bathing with water from Tulasī leaves, especially on the Ekādaśī day,
one is liberated from all sins, even if one should be a slayer of a Brahmin.
Having performed an anointing with the clay from that site, he bathes day after day;
he obtains the fruit born of bathing that results from the final purificatory bath of ten horse-sacrifices.
They know water mixed with a *tulasī* leaf to be equal to the Gaṅgā; he who constantly carries it upon his head has the Jāhnavī herself worn there.
Having placed the water for the feet along with a *tulasī* leaf in a copper vessel, and having held a conch, one should sprinkle it upon one's own head while reciting the root mantra. (Hbhv 4.142)
Regarding its greatness, it is stated in the *Kārttika-māhātmya* of the *Padma-purāṇa*:
"Having placed the water from a *śālagrāma* stone— which is joined with the discus of Dvārakā—
into a conch shell, one should pour it into a copper vessel for the purpose of bathing."
Accompanied by a *tulasī* leaf, it destroys even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Thus,
having wiped the fluids from his limbs with a cloth other than the bathing-garment,
he should put on two garments as an undergarment and an upper robe.
Now, the procedure for wearing clothing: regarding this, Atri says—
whether it be unwashed, washed by a washerman, or even washed the day before;
One should discard the saffron-colored robe, the soiled garment, and the loincloth.
And one should never, under any circumstances, wear clothing that is still damp.
One may be naked or wear soiled garments; likewise, one may be naked with a half-cloth, naked with a double-layered cloth, or naked with a red robe.
One who wears sewn garments is naked; likewise, one with a greasy cloth is naked.
One with two lower fringes, one without an upper garment, and one who is simply unclothed is also naked.
One should not even contemplate Śrauta or Smārta rites while naked;
by performing them out of delusion, one goes downward, for that is remembered as being demonic (āsura).
During recitation, fire-offerings, and fasting, one should wear washed garments;
likewise, at ancestral rites and similar occasions, one should be adorned, pure, silent, and have the senses subdued.
Gobhila says:
One should not eat wearing only a single garment, nor should one perform the worship of the gods.
In the Trailokyasammohana-pañcarātra,
one should always wear white clothing and should strictly avoid red.
Aṅgiras states:
"The wool of sheep, even when touched by semen or a corpse, is not defiled; it is purified by the rays of the wind, fire, sun, and moon. (Hbhv 4.153)
And elsewhere it is said:
"Whether cut or mended, or even burnt, woolen cloth does not become defiled;
indeed, with a woolen garment, a man should perform the ancestral rite (śrāddha)."
What is given to the ancestors at Gayā is declared to be equal [to other offerings] and becomes inexhaustible for them.
O King, one should not use a mended garment for rites dedicated to the gods; nor should one wear one that is burnt, torn, or belongs to another. (Hbhv_4.155)
For that garment which has not been washed, which is said to be like crow-dung, and which has been brought from a washerman, shall not be pure. (Hbhv 4.156)
However, any garment that has been touched by insects, or upon which excrement has been cast, or urine, or even sexual intercourse, one should avoid that garment. (Hbhv 4.157)
O best of kings, woolen cloth is always pure;
it is highly commended for the rites performed for the ancestors, the gods, and human beings.
Whether washed or unwashed, burnt, mended, or brought by a washerman—
even if smeared with semen, urine, or blood— it is nonetheless supremely pure.
Fire, woolen clothing, and likewise the *kuśa* grass of a Brahmin—for these four, no fault was established by Brahmā Parameṣṭhin. (Hbhv 4.160)
Furthermore, elsewhere it is said:

"One should wear two pure garments, an undergarment and an upper robe, which are white, uncut, and with beautiful borders; then, seated upon a seat, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana). (Hbhv 4.161)
Now, regarding the seat,
the *Bahvṛca-pariśiṣṭa* states:
"One should have a white seat for ascetics made in the shape of a tortoise."
But for others, one should have it made four-sided and square.

A wise person should always avoid a seat made of cow dung, one that is broken, or one made of *palāśa* or *paippala* wood, as well as one bound with iron, even if it is made of *arka* wood. (Hbhv 4.163)
Now, the procedure for the seat is described in that very same [text]:
"Giving, sipping water, fire-offerings, eating, and the worship of the deity..."
One should not perform Vedic recitation or the libation of water while standing with feet apart.
But he who has placed his feet upon a seat, or upon his knees or his shanks,
having performed the *avasthika* posture, is called one with "stretched-out feet" (*prauḍhapāda*).
Thus,
having placed his feet upon the ground, sat down, and sipped water while holding *darbha* grass,
he should apply the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* and other marks with *śrīgopīcandana* and similar substances. (Hbhv 4.166)
Therein, first of all, one should cleanse the two lotus-feet of the Blessed One with unguents, and all the limbs with the remains of the offerings (nirmālya) out of devotion.
Regarding this, it was said by the Blessed One in the *Brahma-purāṇa*:
"O Lotus-seated One, one should always wear sandalwood paste adhering to a *śālagrāma* stone on all limbs for the sake of attaining supreme purity. (Hbhv 4.168)
Thus,
thereafter, the Vaiṣṇava should duly apply twelve vertical marks (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) upon the twelve limbs using the twelve names beginning with Keśava. (Hbhv 4.169)
Now, the procedure for the twelve tilakas is found in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa (6.225.45–47):
"One should meditate on Keśava on the forehead, and then on Nārāyaṇa on the abdomen."
One should place Mādhava on the chest and Govinda in the hollow of the throat.
One should place Viṣṇu on the right side of the belly, Madhusūdana on the right arm,
Trivikrama on the neck, and Vāmana on the left flank.
One should place Śrīdhara on the left arm, Hṛṣīkeśa on the neck,
Padmanābha on the back, and Dāmodara on the hips.
But the water used for washing that [image], one should place upon the head with the mantra "Vāsudeva."
Furthermore:
"The *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* on the forehead is prescribed as the foremost for all;
its application is ordained specifically in the sequence beginning with the forehead. (Hbhv 4.174)
Having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to tradition, one should place the Kirīṭa mantra upon the head for the accomplishment of all aims. (Hbhv 4.175)
Now, the Kirīṭa-mantra:
Oṃ, to the one who wears a crown, armlets, necklaces, makara-earrings, and holds a discus, conch, mace, and lotus in His hands; who wears yellow garments;
whose chest is marked with the Śrīvatsa; who, together with Śrī and Bhūmi, causes the radiance of His own self-effulgent light to shine; and who possesses the splendor of a thousand suns.
Homage, homage! Hbhv_4.176.
Thus,
regarding the necessity of the vertical mark (*ūrdhva-puṇḍra*),
it is stated by the Blessed One in the *Pādma-purāṇa*:
O Four-faced One, for the sake of my pleasure, for the sake of auspiciousness, or for the sake of protection,
my devotee, being composed, should always wear the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) which dispels fear at the time of my worship and fire-oblation, both morning and evening. (Hbhv 4.177)
In that very same work, the *Śrī-Nāradokti*, it is said:
"Sacrifice, charity, austerity, fire-offering, Vedic study, and libations to the ancestors—all these become fruitless if performed without the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*. (Hbhv 4.178)
In that very same [text], in the Uttara-khaṇḍa:

"But he who performs any rite whatsoever while devoid of the *ūrdhva-puṇḍra*—all his acts, such as sacrifices (*iṣṭa*) and public works (*pūrta*), shall be fruitless; of this there is no doubt. (Hbhv 4.179)
But he who performs the twilight rituals and other duties while devoid of the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* marks—every such act is eternally demonic, and he goes to hell. (Hbhv 4.180)
Furthermore:
"That lowest of men who applies the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) upon the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), having destroyed the mark which is the abode of Viṣṇu, goes certainly to hell. (Hbhv 4.181)
For this very reason, it is stated by Śrī Nārada in the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"That body of human beings which is fashioned without the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* should not be looked upon at all; it would be like a cremation ground. (Hbhv 4.182)
In the Padma Purāṇa:

"On whose forehead a gentle vertical mark (*ūrdhva-puṇḍra*) made with clay is seen, even if he is an outcaste (*cāṇḍāla*), he is a pure soul and certainly worthy of worship; of this there is no doubt. (Hbhv 4.183)
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"One should not apply the horizontal sectarian mark (tiryakpuṇḍra) even when death has arrived;
nor should a man utter any name other than that of Nārāyaṇa. (Hbhv 4.184)
One should wear the remains of Viṣṇu’s offerings, the remnants of incense, and the ointment;
one should apply the Vaiṣṇava mark (puṇḍra) produced from Gopīcandana.
In that very context regarding the month of Kārttika:
"If the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) is not seen upon the forehead of a man, one must not even look at him; having seen him, one should gaze at the sun. (Hbhv 4.186)
Elsewhere also it is said:
"The *ūrdhva-puṇḍra* is prescribed for Vaiṣṇava Brahmins;
however, others should have the *tri-puṇḍra*—so the knowers of Brahman understand. (Hbhv 4.187)
If a brahmin’s triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is not seen along with his vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), one should perform a bath with one's clothes on after either touching or seeing him. (Hbhv 4.188)
One should not apply the *tripuṇḍra* upon those who bear the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*;
for a mortal who has applied the *tripuṇḍra*, his ritual acts do not lead to the pleasure of Hari. (Hbhv 4.189)
Therefore, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa it is said:
"Resembling an aśvattha leaf, likewise having the shape of a bamboo leaf, and resembling a lotus bud—this triad is known as the deluding [mudrās]. (Hbhv_4.190)
Now, regarding the majesty of the vertical mark (*ūrdhva-puṇḍra*),
in the *Skanda Purāṇa* within the context of the month of Kārttika:
"He on whose forehead a bright vertical mark made with clay is seen..."
Even a Caṇḍāla whose self is purified attains the eternal Brahman.
In the vertical mark (ūrdhva-puṇḍra) resides Lakṣmī; in the vertical mark resides glory;
in the vertical mark resides liberation; in the vertical mark resides Hari.
In the Padma Purāṇa:
"He on whose forehead a gentle upward-mark (ūrdhva-puṇḍra) is seen with joy—even if he is a Cāṇḍāla, he is a pure soul and is certainly worthy of worship; of this there is no doubt. (Hbhv 4.193)
In that very same section, in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā [6.225.2–3, 5, 7–10]:
"In the center of the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, which is broad and most beautiful, Janārdana, the God of gods, is seated together with Lakṣmī. (Hbhv_4.194)
Therefore, the body of one upon whose person the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* is worn becomes the pure and auspicious temple of the Blessed One.
A Brahmin who wears the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* is honored in all the worlds;
having ascended a most excellent celestial chariot, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. (Hbhv_4.196)
Upon seeing one who wears the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, one is liberated from all sins;
or, by bowing with devotion, one obtains the fruit of all possible gifts.
If one feeds a Brahmin who wears the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* at a *śrāddha* ceremony, his ancestors will remain satisfied for ten million kalpas; of this there is no doubt. (Hbhv 4.198)

O lady of auspicious countenance, he who wears the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* and performs a *śrāddha* ceremony shall obtain the fruit of a *śrāddha* performed at Gayā for thousands of millions of kalpas.
Whatever sacrifice, charity, practice of austerity, recitation, fire-oblation,
and so forth one performs while wearing the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), its merit is infinite.
In the Śrī-Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"Even if he is impure or lacks proper conduct, and even if he commits sin in his mind, a man who is marked with the vertical *ūrdhva-puṇḍra* shall always remain pure. (Hbhv_4.201)
In that very regard, the word of the Blessed Lord is as follows:
"Wherever a mortal dies while wearing the *ūrdhva-puṇḍra*, even if he be a dog-eater (*śvapāka*), he is honored in my world, seated upon a celestial chariot. (Hbhv 4.202)
If a mortal wearing the vertical *ūrdhva-puṇḍra* eats food in anyone's house,
I shall then deliver twenty generations of his family from hell.
Now, regarding the procedure for applying the *ūrṇā* mark with *tilaka*:
in the venerable *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*,
it is said that one who, having looked at a mirror or even in water, should apply it with diligence—
O highly fortunate one, he who wears the vertical *ūrṇā* mark attains the supreme goal.
A length of ten finger-breadths is said to be the most excellent;
nine finger-breadths would be middling, and eight finger-breadths is beyond that [the lowest].
One should perform [the ritual] with these various finger-divisions, but one must not touch [the object] with the fingernails.
In the *Padma Purāṇa*, in the *Uttara-khaṇḍa*, at that very place [6.253.21, 40–43]:

“Those of great fortune who are single-mindedly devoted and delight in the welfare of all beings should apply the *puṇḍra* in the shape of Hari’s foot, including the space between the toes. (Hbhv_4.207)
The dark [color] is said to bring peace; likewise, the red brings subjugation.
They say the yellow brings prosperity, while the auspicious white brings liberation. (Hbhv 4.208)
Circular, horizontal, without gaps, short, long, extended, thin, curved, deformed, with a bound tip, cut at the root, or displaced from its position. Hbhv_4.209 //
They say that a sectarian mark (*puṇḍra*) which is impure, dry, smeared, fashioned with a finger, foul-smelling, or unbearable is useless. (Hbhv 4.210)
Starting from the base of the nose up to the forehead, one should smear it with clay;
the three parts of the nose are designated as the "base of the nose" (nāsā-mūla). (Hbhv 4.211)
Having begun from the middle of the eyebrows, one should fashion the space between them.
In that very same place [6.253.26–7, 24]:
"That lowest of the twice-born who makes a vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) without leaving any space between [the lines], indeed drives away both Viṣṇu and Śrī who reside therein. (Hbhv 4.213)
Those lowest of the twice-born who apply an unbroken vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) will have the footprint of a dog permanently upon their foreheads; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, a very beautiful vertical mark (puṇḍra) in the shape of a staff, provided with a gap at the top, should always be made by Brahmins and by women of auspicious appearance. (Hbhv 4.215)

One should know that the temple of Hari is the beautiful vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) extending from the nose to the hairline, provided with a hollow in the center; that indeed is the temple of Hari. (Hbhv 4.216)
Brahmā is situated on the left side and Sadāśiva on the right;
one should know Viṣṇu to be in the middle; therefore, one should not smear [the ointment] on the middle.
In the *Vāyu Purāṇa*, regarding the offense of improper service:
"He who performs the worship of Hari without wearing the vertical *puṇḍra*, or he who worships the god Janārdana while wearing a horizontal *puṇḍra*... (Hbhv 4.218).

The fault has been stated [in the scriptures] by such passages as: "By means of an accidental vertical *puṇḍra*, by ashes applied horizontally on the limbs, and by not wearing the conch and discus," and so forth. (Hbhv 4.219)
And there is a Śruti in the Hiraṇyakeśī branch of the Yajurveda:
"He who maintains within himself the treading upon the feet of Hari becomes dear to the Supreme; he is meritorious."
He who wears the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) with a hollow in the center becomes a partaker of liberation.
Thus ends the traditional rule regarding the application of the *tilaka* with the fingers.
The ring finger is said to bestow desire; the middle finger becomes the granter of longevity;
the thumb is declared to grant nourishment; and the index finger is the giver of liberation.
Now, regarding the clay for the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*,
it is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa* (6.225.35–38) at that very same place:
"On a mountain peak, on a riverbank, at the root of a *bilva* tree, or by a body of water..."
And on the banks of the Sindhu, at an anthill, and especially in a field sacred to Hari.
One should take the clay from that place where the bathing water of Viṣṇu flows constantly, for the purpose of applying the *puṇḍra* marks. (Hbhv 4.223)
At Śrīraṅga, on Veṅkaṭādri, at Śrīkūrma and auspicious Dvārakā, at Prayāga, on Nārasiṃhādri, at Vārāha, and in the Tulasī grove; Hbhv_4.224 //
Having devoutly taken clay together with the water from Viṣṇu’s feet, and having applied the *puṇḍra* marks upon one's limbs, one shall attain union (*sāyujya*) with Viṣṇu. (Hbhv 4.225)
In that very same [text]:
"But one should fetch the earth from that very place which is divine in the field of Hari. (Hbhv 4.226)
And it is said by the venerable Nārada in the Pādma [Purāṇa]:
"Whether one is a killer of a Brahmin, a killer of a cow, a rationalist, or a perpetrator of every sin, one becomes purified at that very moment through contact with Gopīcandana. (Hbhv_4.227)
Whoever gives a piece of Gopīcandana to a Vaiṣṇava,
by that act one hundred and one generations of his lineage shall be saved.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*:

"If one whose body is marked with the conch and discus, who bears a cluster of flowers upon his head, and whose limbs are smeared with *gopīcandana* is seen, then whatever sin has been committed [is destroyed]. (Hbhv 4.229)
For one who possesses these five in the home—the clay from Vṛndāvana, Tulasī, a conch, a Śālagrāma stone with its discus mark, and [the other two]—whence can there be any fear of sin? (Hbhv 4.230)
And in the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*, it is said by Śrī Yama:

"Where is that fragrance in sandalwood (*śrīkhaṇḍa*)? Where is such a celestial complexion? Where indeed is that purity found in any sacred ford (*tīrtha*) as it is in the sandalwood of the illustrious Gopīs? (Hbhv 4.231)
Now, the greatness of the *gopīcandana* vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) is stated by Nārada in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"He who [takes] the clay originating from Dvāravatī..."
Taking [the clay] in his hand, he should always apply the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) upon the surface of his forehead; thus,
the fruit of his ritual action shall always be multiplied ten millionfold.
Even if one is devoid of ritual action, devoid of mantra, devoid of faith, or deprived of the proper time,
if one applies Gopīcandana upon the forehead—
One always experiences that fruit of karma as its exhaustion.
O Lord of the twice-born, if a brahmin always wears a beautiful sectarian mark (puṇḍra) made from Gopīcandana on his forehead— whether by night or by day, at all times—
the merit he gains is equal to that which is obtained at Kurujāṅgala during a solar eclipse, or likewise at Prayāga at midday.
O Lord of Birds, he attains that and dwells in the abode of Viṣṇu like a god.
In whichever house Gopīcandana remains, and where a person wears it on his forehead with devotion,
Hari dwells in that house forever.
O bird, the slayer of Kaṃsa was endowed with faith.
Whoever would always wear upon their forehead the sacred mark originating from the City of Kṛṣṇa— which removes the sins of the Kali age and is joined with the mantra of Hari— [attains liberation].
If one were not enveloped by evil, one would not see Yama.
O bird, he who at the time of death applies Gopīcandana to his arms, forehead, heart, and head,
goes to the world of the Lord whose abode is the lotus.
If a killer of a cow's calf were to become a slayer of a Brahmin.
The planets do not afflict one, nor the hosts of Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, Piśācas, Uragas, Bhūtas, or Dānavas,
when the Gopīcandana is worn as a mark upon the forehead.
He in whom [this] abides by the grace of Hari.
In the *Padma Purāṇa*, the venerable Gotama said:
"O Ambarīṣa, perform the act of looking [at me] for the sake of destroying great sin—those by whom the auspicious mark of *gopīcandana* has been applied daily upon the forehead. (Hbhv 4.239)

And in the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the illustrious Yama said to his messengers: "Listen! He whose forehead is marked with gopī-candana must be avoided from afar with great effort, like a blazing firebrand. (Hbhv_4.240)
Thus,
then, upon that very [forehead], the Vaiṣṇavas should fashion a beautiful vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) using the clay from the root of the glorious Tulasī plant. (Hbhv 4.241)
Now, regarding the greatness of the sectarian mark made from the clay at the root of the sacred *tulasī*:
those men who take that clay and apply it as a mark upon their foreheads have established the standard for proceeding toward liberation. (Hbhv 4.242)
And in that very same *Kārttika-māhātmya*, within the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, it is said:
"O Nārada, sin does not touch the body of one on whose forehead the *puṇḍra* made with Tulasī clay is seen, even while [the sin] is being committed. (Hbhv_4.243)
In the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"For those people who apply the *puṇḍra* mark with *tulasī* clay day after day, the sins committed over a year vanish by the mere sight of them. (Hbhv 4.244)
Thus, O Blessed One, the remains of offerings (nirmālya) and ointments from above it should be worn in that same manner; for in this way, the tilaka is said to be of three kinds. (Hbhv 4.245)
Then, for the pleasure of Hari, one should wear the Nārāyaṇī mudrā,
as well as the marks of the Fish, the Tortoise, and so forth, and the weapons such as the discus.
Now, regarding the constant wearing of the mudrās as recorded in the Smṛti:
one is marked with the conch and the discus on both shoulders.
One should worship Hari constantly; otherwise, the worship is not accomplished.
In the *Āditya Purāṇa*:
"A base Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of the conch, the discus, the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*), and so forth, the king shall cause to be mounted upon a donkey and banish from the kingdom. (Hbhv 4.248)
In the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*, as spoken by the Blessed Lord:
"The qualification for all ritual acts is enjoined only for those who are pure;
and one should understand that purity arises from bearing my weapons. (Hbhv 4.249)
And in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa:
"A Brahmin who is devoid of the most beloved marks of Hari, such as the conch and the discus, falls away from all dharmas and goes to hell. (Hbhv_4.250)
And in the Śruti, in the Yajus-Kaṭha branch, it is said:
"That great-souled one who, wearing the upright *puṇḍra* and bearing the *cakra* on his arm, meditates upon the supreme Viṣṇu..."
Through sound and mantra, one should always abide in the heart upon that which is higher than the highest, greater than the great.
And in the Atharvaveda:
"May we, marked by these signs of the Wide-Striding One, become fortunate in the world."
Those who are marked [by this] go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
And so forth. For this very reason, the *Brahma Purāṇa* states:
"He who, upon seeing [an object] marked with the weapons of Kṛṣṇa, does not show it respect..."
The merit accumulated over twelve years comes to naught through a fruitless [life].
Now, regarding the greatness of wearing the *mudrās*,
in the *Skanda Purāṇa* within the dialogue between Śrī Sanatkumāra and Mārkaṇḍeya:
"O best of Brahmins, that devotee of Viṣṇu who is marked with the signs of the conch, the discus, and so forth..."
He indeed goes to the world of Viṣṇu, which is free from burning and dissolution.
Regarding this, it is said here:
"What can Yama do to one whose body is eternally marked with the weapons of Nārāyaṇa, even if that person is burdened by ten million sins? (Hbhv 4.255)
Whatever fruit is said to be obtained by those dwelling at Śaṅkhoddhāra for ten million years,
that same fruit is attained by [inscribing] the conch on the right arm every day.
Whatever fruit is obtained by the constant vision of Puṇḍarīkākṣa at Puṣkara,
one obtains that same fruit by placing a lotus upon a conch shell.
In the Kali age, Gadādhara bestows the merit of Gayā every day upon that person in whose left arm a mace (gadā) is seen depicted.
And whatever was said regarding the fruit of beholding Kṛṣṇa at Ānandapura, near Cakrasvāmī, that same fruit is obtained when the discus is drawn with a mace. (Hbhv 4.259)
In the words of the Blessed Lord:
"Furthermore, whatever man in the Kali age takes up the clay originating from my city, or the marks such as those of the Fish, the Tortoise, and so forth, and applies them... (Hbhv 4.260)
"O best of the gods, let it be known that I have entered his body; no opening whatsoever should be made by anyone desiring his own welfare. (Hbhv 4.261)
He in whose body my signs of incarnation are seen—a mortal who cannot be recognized as such by mortals—is surely my own body. (Hbhv 4.262)
In the Kali age, the evil of that embodied being arises in the form of good deeds, for his weapons are inscribed upon his body.
He who is marked by both of these signs— the fish-seal and the tortoise— has his own splendor deposited within his very body.
One who constantly bears upon their own body the conch, the lotus, the mace, the discus, the fish, and the tortoise,
brings about an increase in merit.
It brings about the destruction of evil accumulated over hundreds of births.
In that very same [work], in the dialogue between Śrī Brahmā and Nārada, it is said:
"The armor marked with Kṛṣṇa’s weapons is impenetrable by gods or dānavas;
it is invisible to all beings, including enemies and rākṣasas. (Hbhv 4.266)
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Durgā, Sāvitrī,
and the beloved of Hari dwell eternally in the body of that person whose form is marked with the conch shell.
The Gaṅgā, Gayā, Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, Puṣkara, and other such sacred sites always and eternally abide in him whose body is marked with the [Buddha’s] footprints. (Hbhv 4.268)
O lover of the Kali age, wherever the mark of the Kaumodakī mace appears on the left arm,
there the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean should be seen every day.
If a mace is held in the right hand and a discus stands below it,
then the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, are present there together with Kṛṣṇa.
The three fires, the three gods, and the three steps of Viṣṇu always dwell within the body of that person in whom the Sudarśana resides.
Furthermore:
"He in whose hand is a Nārāyaṇī seal marked with the weapons of Kṛṣṇa, and who holds authority over the upper worlds—he is to be known as the lord of the thirty [gods]. (Hbhv 4.272)

But for one who performs rites for the gods, the ancestors, daily duties, occasional rites, or those for specific desires while employing the Kṛṣṇa-mudrā, it becomes inexhaustible every single day. (Hbhv 4.273)
Neither planets, nor constellations, nor zodiac signs cause affliction for one who holds in hand a seal made of metal, marked with the eight syllables. (Hbhv 4.274)
In the *Vārāha-purāṇa*, as spoken by Śrī Sanatkumāra:
"What will he achieve by going to holy places such as Prayāga, if his body is already marked with the weapons of Kṛṣṇa by means of the clay of Gopīcandana? (Hbhv 4.275)
When one perceives another's body marked with signs such as the conch and so forth,
then the Lord of the World, being pleased, removes that person's sin.
He in whose body the conch, discus, mace, and lotus are drawn day after day, morning and evening, is Acyuta himself.
In the Kali age, having endowed himself with the weapons of Nārāyaṇa, he indeed performs meritorious deeds that are equal to Mount Meru. (Hbhv 4.278)

O twice-born one, when a person performs a *śrāddha* with devotion, marked by the conch and other signs, even if it lacks the prescribed ritual details, it becomes complete and equal to a *śrāddha* performed at Gayā for the ancestors. (Hbhv 4.279)
Just as fire, when intensely fanned by the wind, consumes wood,
so indeed do sins burn away upon seeing the weapons of Kṛṣṇa.
In the *Brahmī* [section], within the *Śrī-Brahma-Nārada-Saṃvāda*:
"A seal engraved with the name of Viṣṇu, endowed with the eight-syllable mantra, and joined with symbols such as the conch and other weapons, whether made of gold or silver... (Hbhv 4.281).
O beloved of the Kali age, he who especially in the Kali age wears [this] of the Blessed One shall be equal to Prahlāda; it cannot be otherwise.
Furthermore:
Keśava himself, together with the ancestors, eats the food of that householder in whose home a Brahmin with a conch-marked body partakes. (Hbhv 4.283)
O Nārada, if one who is marked by the weapons of Kṛṣṇa dies in a cremation ground, his destination is said to be the same as that which is proclaimed for one who dies at Prayāga.
In the Kali age, his body is eternally adorned with the weapons of Kṛṣṇa;
therein Indra and the various other gods take refuge.
Keśava constantly removes thousands of offenses from that man who performs the worship of Hari and is marked with the weapons of Kṛṣṇa.
Having fashioned an image out of wood marked with the weapons of Kṛṣṇa,
he who indeed brands himself with them is a Vaiṣṇava for whom there is no equal.
A man marked by the weapon of Kṛṣṇa is not defiled by the sins committed during the Kali age through association with heretics, the fallen, those who have lost their caste, or atheists.
Furthermore:
"That image which is marked with eight syllables, made of metal, and adorned with conch shells, lotuses, and so forth, is worshipped by gods and asuras. (Hbhv 4.289)
In former times, during the Kṛta age, the Nārāyaṇī mudrā was maintained by Prahlāda,
as well as by Vibhīṣaṇa, Bali, Dhruva, and Śuka.
O lover of the Kali age, by Māndhātṛ, Ambarīṣa, and the twice-born led by Mārkaṇḍeya,
having marked their bodies with weapons such as conch shells and other signs,
they worshipped Keśava and obtained their great desired fruit. (Hbhv 4.291)
Furthermore:
Hari dwells in the body of that person upon whose form the conch, lotus, discus, or other [emblems] have been drawn with the clay of Gopīcandana. (Hbhv 4.292)
In that very same place, it is stated by the venerable Sanatkumāra:
"He whose body bears the marks of the conch and so forth, who possesses the Nārāyaṇī mudrā, and who wears a garland made of dhātrī fruits or produced from tulasī wood... (Hbhv 4.293).
When the weapons are applied to the body of a brahmin by means of the twelve-syllable mantra, he indeed becomes a Vaiṣṇava equal to me.
Furthermore:
He on whose body the Nārāyaṇī mudrā is marked with signs such as the conch,
and whose entire body is marked with weapons originating from Nārāyaṇa;
No evil can enter him; indeed, he possesses the Vaiṣṇava armor.
And elsewhere it is said:
"In the Kali age, those twice-born ones who possess these marks of a devotee of the Lord become, in the world of mortals, capable of both cursing and bestowing grace. (Hbhv 4.296)
Now, the procedure for wearing the mudrās is stated in the *Gautamīya*:
"One should wear the discus on the right arm and the conch on the left, or [the conch] on the right."
One should hold a mace in the left hand, and below the mace, one should further hold a discus.
Likewise, he should hold a conch above [the left shoulder], a lotus on the right,
a sword at his chest, and a bow with an arrow upon his head.
Thus, a devotee of Viṣṇu should first wear the five weapons:
the fish on the right hand and likewise the tortoise on the left hand.
And so it has been said:
"A Brahmin should indeed wear the Sudarśana on his right arm;
others [should wear] the fish, the lotus, the conch, the lotus, and likewise the mace. (Hbhv 4.300)
Thus,
according to the practice of traditional scholars and as one pleases,
one should bear the marks such as the conch and the discus on all limbs. (Hbhv 4.301)
Out of devotion to one's own chosen deity, one should also wear its characteristic marks.
And the discus and conch are held by some even as they are joined together.

In this manner, a wise person should daily wear the marks of the discus and other symbols with the sacred gopīcandana; indeed, those [symbols] were originally forged from heated metal for the purpose of lying down and other such acts.
Now, the characteristics of the wheel and the other [emblems] are as follows: a wheel should have twelve spokes, six angles, and be joined with three concentric circles;
it should turn clockwise, and such is the conch of the illustrious Hari as remembered in tradition.
The mace, the lotus, and so forth are considered by the wise to be established in the world;
or else, O Blessed One, they may be mudrās marked with the names [of deities] such as the eight-syllable mantra.
Now, regarding the wearing of garlands and so forth:
thereafter, one should wear a garland offered to Kṛṣṇa, fashioned from *tulasī* leaves, lotus seeds, *tulasī* wood, or the fruits of the *dhātrī*. (Hbhv 4.307)
A Vaiṣṇava should wear ornaments made of Tulasī wood on his head, ears, arms, and hands, as he pleases. (Hbhv 4.308)
Now, regarding the procedure for wearing a garland,
it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Having offered a garland made of Tulasī wood to Hari..."
He who subsequently wears the garland himself is indeed the best of devotees.
That fool who does not offer a garland made from *tulasī* wood to Hari, yet wears it himself, certainly goes to hell. (Hbhv 4.310)
Having washed it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and consecrated it with the root mantra,
and having indeed consecrated it eight times with the Gāyatrī, one should fumigate it;
then, with supreme devotion according to the rule, one should worship it with the Sadyojāta [mantra].
O garland produced from Tulasī wood, beloved of the people of Kṛṣṇa!
I wear you around my neck; make me dear to Kṛṣṇa.
O Goddess of gods, just as you are the beloved of Viṣṇu and always dear to the devotees of Viṣṇu,
so make me always dear to the devotees of Viṣṇu.
The verbal root *lā* is taught in the sense of giving; since you, O beloved of Hari, give to me and to all devotees, for that reason you are called *mālā*.
Having thus offered the garland according to the prescribed rite upon the neck of Kṛṣṇa,
the Vaiṣṇava who indeed wears it shall go to the abode of Viṣṇu.
In that very context concerning Kārttika:
"If one does not wear a garland made of dhātrī fruits around the neck, he should not be known as a Vaiṣṇava, even if he is devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu. (Hbhv 4.316)
In the *Garuḍa-purāṇa*:
"Those rationalists of sinful intellect who do not wear the garland do not return from hell, being consumed by the fire of Hari’s wrath. (Hbhv 4.317)
Therefore, it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"One should not discard a garland of tulasī, especially a garland of dhātrī fruits, which destroys even the greatest sins and bestows virtue, desire, and wealth. (Hbhv_4.318)
Now, regarding the greatness of wearing a garland, it is said in the Agastya-saṃhitā:
"He who worships Hari while adorned with a garland of *tulasī* remains from the sacred offerings (*nirmālya*) shall [attain the highest state]."
Whatever one does, all that shall yield infinite fruit.
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
Those who have garlands of tulasī and lotus seeds clinging to their necks, or those who have shining vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) upon the surface of their foreheads;
Those whose arms are marked with the conch and the discus are indeed Vaiṣṇavas who quickly purify the world.
Moreover:
he whose pair of arms is marked with the signs [of Viṣṇu], and in whose speech is the chanting of the names of the Supreme Person (Viṣṇu).
I am the servant of him who bears upon his head an exceedingly straight sectarian mark (puṇḍra), and around whose neck is a garland of lotuses and jewels.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, in the words of the Blessed Lord:
"He who wears a garland made of *tulasī* wood around his neck—whether he be impure or of improper conduct—comes to me alone; of this there is no doubt. (Hbhv 4.322)
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"He on whose body a garland made of dhātrī fruits or one produced from tulasī wood is seen is indeed the best of Bhāgavatas. (Hbhv 4.323)
He who wears around his neck a garland made of Tulasī leaves, especially one brought forth from Viṣṇu, is worthy of salutation by the dwellers of heaven.
A garland made of Tulasī leaves or even fashioned from Dhātrī fruits grants liberation to sinners; how much more so, then, for those who serve Viṣṇu? (Hbhv 4.325)
In that very context concerning Kārttika:
"Furthermore, he who, having placed a garland of *tulasī* around his neck, worships Janārdana, obtains merit equal to ten thousand cows for every single flower. (Hbhv 4.326)
As long as the garland of *dhātrī* fruits remains rolling upon a man's throat,
for that long Keśava rolls with affection upon his body.
In the Kali age, for as many hairs as the garland of Dhātrī fruits touches the body of men,
for that many thousands of years shall they dwell in the abode of Keśava.
For as many days as a man wears the garland of Dhātrī in the Kali age,
for that many thousands of yugas shall his residence be in Vaikuṇṭha.
Whoever wears a pair of garlands made from *dhātrī* and *tulasī*,
and carries them around the region of the neck, shall dwell in heaven for ten million kalpas.
And in the *Garuḍa* and the words of Mārkaṇḍeya it is said:
"Whoever wears a garland made of *tulasī* leaves that has been cast off by Kṛṣṇa obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices for every single leaf. (Hbhv 4.331)
The enemy of the Daityas bestows daily the fruit arising from Dvārakā upon that man who wears a garland made from Tulasī wood.
Having offered a garland made from *tulasī* wood to Viṣṇu, that man who wears it with devotion indeed possesses no sin whatsoever. (Hbhv 4.333)
O Kṛṣṇa, son of Devakī, that man who wears a garland made from the wood of the tulasī plant is always delighted in mind;
for him there is no need for expiation, nor is there any impurity in his body. (Hbhv 4.334)
In that mortal whose head is adorned with an ornament made from *tulasī* wood, and who bears it on his arms and hands, Hari is ever present within his body. (Hbhv 4.335)
Adorned with garlands of Tulasī wood, one should perform meritorious acts;
in the Kali age, what is performed for the ancestors and the deities becomes ten millionfold.
But when the messengers of the King of the Dead see a garland made of Tulasī wood, they flee far away, like a leaf blown by the wind.
If one wanders adorned with garlands of tulasī wood,
there shall be no bad dreams, no ill omens, and no fear arising from weapons anywhere.
Now, regarding the procedure for the twilight worship (sandhyopāsana) at home:
thereafter, one should perform the rites such as the twilight worship according to the prescribed rules;
therein, the libation (tarpaṇa) to the gods and others should be performed with the water from the feet of Kṛṣṇa alone.

Carrying the remains of the offerings made to Viṣṇu upon the head, and even offering libations with the water used for washing his feet to the ancestors and the deities, is considered equal [to other forms of worship] by the Vaiṣṇavas. (Hbhv 4.340)
Regarding the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsti*), there is this statement of Vasiṣṭha:
"The twilight worship performed at home is said to have a single-fold merit; in a cow-pen it is ten-fold;
by a river it is a hundred-thousand-fold; and in the presence of Viṣṇu, it is infinite. (Hbhv 4.341)
Now, regarding the worship of the venerable guru: one who intends to perform worship should first bow down with devotion to Kṛṣṇa, who is present as the guru,
and worship him after offering some small gift.
In the Smṛtimahārṇava:
One should not look upon a king, a physician, or a teacher with empty hands; nor should one look upon a son, a pupil, or a servant without bringing a gift. (Hbhv 4.343)
Furthermore, it is stated by the illustrious Blessed One:
"First, having worshipped the guru, and then performing my own worship, one attains perfection; otherwise, it shall be fruitless. (Hbhv 4.344)
And Śrī Nārada said:
"But he who, while the guru is present, should worship another in his presence, falls into a miserable state; that worship of his is fruitless. (Hbhv 4.345)
In the Śrutis [Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.23]:
"For that great-souled one who has supreme devotion for the Lord, and for the teacher just as for the Lord, these truths that have been declared indeed shine forth. (Hbhv 4.346)
In the eleventh chapter [11.17.27], in the words of the Blessed Lord:
"One should know me as the teacher; one should never despise him.
One should not find fault with him with the notion that he is a mere mortal, for the guru embodies all the gods. (Hbhv 4.347)
And in the Tenth Canto [BhP 10.80.34]: "I, the Self of all beings, am not so pleased by sacrifice, progeny, austerity, and tranquility as I am by service to the guru."
In the seventh book [of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, 7.15.26]:
"The learning of one who harbors a false notion toward his guru—the manifest Lord and the bestower of the lamp of knowledge—is like the bathing of an elephant. (Hbhv_4.349)
Elsewhere it is also said:
"The deities diminish the devotion of the practitioner toward the guru, so that the disciple, being certain of his devotion to the guru, might bypass Viṣṇu. (Hbhv 4.350)
In the *Manu-smṛti* (2.153):
"The ignorant one is indeed a child, while the giver of the mantra is the father;
for they call the ignorant one a 'child' and the giver of the mantra a 'father. (Hbhv 4.351)
Furthermore: "The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is the god Maheśvara;
the Guru alone is the Supreme Brahman; therefore, one should always worship him. (Hbhv 4.352)
In the Vāmana-kalpa it is said:
"The mantra is the Guru in person; the Guru is remembered as Hari himself. He whose Guru is pleased—for him, Hari himself is pleased."
One should never sit on a seat that is equal to or higher than that of the guru.
In the *Viṣṇurahasya*:
"Therefore, one who worships the guru with all effort, according to the rules, as non-different from [the Lord], shall obtain the fruit of liberation. (Hbhv 4.354)
In the *Viṣṇudharma* and the *Śrī-Bhāgavata*, it is said that the service of the guru is the most excellent of all dharmas;
there exists no purifier superior to that dharma. (Hbhv 4.355)
Whatever causes of misfortune there may be for oneself, such as desire, anger, and the like—
a person shall indeed conquer all of this directly through devotion to the guru.
In the *Pādmapurāṇa*:
"O best of the people, those who always worship their guru with a sense of superiority toward their own father become guests of Brahmā in this world. (Hbhv 4.357)
In that very same hymn by Devahūti:
"If my devotion to the Guru is equal to my devotion to Hari, by that truth may Hari reveal Himself to me. (Hbhv 4.358)
In the *Āditya-purāṇa*: "Whether ignorant or learned, the Guru alone is Janārdana;
whether situated on the path or off the path, the Guru alone is always the refuge. (Hbhv_4.359)
And elsewhere it is said:
"When Hari is angry, the guru is the protector; when the guru is angry, there is no one at all.
Therefore, with every effort, one should propitiate the guru alone. (Hbhv 4.360)
In the Brahmavaivarta [Purāṇa] it is also said:
"Even if they strike, curse, or act in opposition out of anger, teachers are to be honored; one should lead them home after bowing. (Hbhv 4.361)
That birth is praiseworthy, that day is blessed, and that auspicious hour is meritorious, on which one bows to the Guru after having attended upon him with devotion. (Hbhv 4.362)
Those who reject a teacher who has come down through the tradition—
even when such teachers have died, flesh-eating spirits will not consume those ungrateful ones.
By him whose awakening has been defiled, his own wickedness has been made manifest;
he by whom the Guru was abandoned has already abandoned Hari.
And elsewhere:
"But that lowest of men who, having approached a teacher, acts contrary to his instructions out of delusion, shall be cooked in hell for ten million eons."
In the *Pañcarātra*:
"One who has been initiated with a mantra taught by a non-Vaiṣṇava shall go to hell;
he must be made to receive [initiation] again, correctly, from a Vaiṣṇava guru. (Hbhv 4.366)
In the Agastya-saṃhitā:
"O best of sages, those most sinful and lowest of men who do not carry out the command of their guru shall have no deliverance from the sufferings of hell. (Hbhv 4.367)
Those disciples who have constantly disregarded their gurus to be honored are indeed fallen from the prosperity of sons, friends, wives, and other such riches.
Those who, out of delusion, revile their teacher and speak harshly to him,
will indeed be born as pigs for even hundreds of lifetimes.
Those fools who are hostile toward their gurus and are constant performers of evil—for them, there will undoubtedly be as much merit as there is demerit. (Hbhv 4.370)
Therefore, having first worshipped the guru with a mind fixed on Kṛṣṇa,
the wise man should perform three prostrations, no fewer, like a staff falling to the ground.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, in the *Śrī-Vyāsagītā*:
"The clasping of the teacher's feet should be performed with crossed hands;
the left foot is to be touched with the left hand, and the right foot with the right. (Hbhv 4.372)
Thus,
having then obtained permission from the feet of the venerable Guru, the practitioner,
before entering the previously consecrated abode of Hari, should set aside his sandals. (Hbhv 4.373)
And likewise, Āpastamba says:
"In the fire-sanctuary, in a cow-pen, in the presence of gods or Brahmins, during the recitation of prayers, and at the time of eating, one should avoid wearing sandals. (Hbhv 4.374)
Thus,
having gone to the courtyard of the temple of the venerable Blessed One,
he should wash his hands and feet and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice.
And so it is said in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:

"One should perform rites such as the worship of the gods, as well as the salutation of the guru, after having properly performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana); one should do the same for the act of eating. (Hbhv_4.376)
Thus ends the section titled "The Ornament of the Śrī-Vaiṣṇavas" in the *Śrī-Bhagavad-Bhakti-Vilāsa* composed by the venerable Gopāla Bhaṭṭa.
The Fourth Vilāsa.
************************************************************************* Fifth Vilāsa: The Vilāsa of the Superintendent (Adhiṣṭhānika)

I bow to the presiding Lord Śrī Caitanya Prabhu, by whose grace even a child may cross the ocean of the ritual sequence of worship, which is infested with the crocodiles of various philosophical systems. Hbhv_5.1 //
Sanātana: Salutation to Śrī Caitanya.
"Bāla" means ignorant;
in another sense, it means a child.
The various kinds of views themselves are the "grasping" (grāha); it is pervaded by them.
The sequence of worship is the "method" (vidhi), or rather, the sequence of the method; that very thing is the ocean (arṇava). (HbhvC 5.1)
The secret ritual for the worship of the illustrious Lord Gopāla, derived from the eighteen-syllable yantra and observed in the *Kramadīpikā*, is now being written.
Sanātana: The procedure for worship—the method of adoration—by means of the eighteen-syllable mantra is now being written.

Although there is no difference in the ritual of worship even when using the ten-syllable mantra and others, nevertheless, this is stated with regard to the distinctions in the placement of mantras (*nyāsa*) and so forth.
Thus it has been written:
"Even though hidden, [the text] having been examined—that is, revealed—by the *Kramadīpikā* composed by Śrī Keśavācārya;
therefore, the sense is that it should be written according to what is stated in the *Kramadīpikā*. (HbhvC_5.2)
Since the Blessed One is always to be honored even by brahmins according to the path taught in the scriptures (āgama), he should therefore be depicted primarily according to scriptural injunctions.
And so it is stated in the Viṣṇuyāmala:
"In the Kṛta age, the path declared in the Śrutis prevails; in Tretā, that cultivated by the Smṛtis; in Dvāpara, that spoken in the Purāṇas; and in Kali, that originating from the Āgamas. (Hbhv_5.4)
For the Brahmins born in the Kali age are impure and resemble Śūdras;
their purification occurs through the path of the Āgamas, not by the Vedic way.

Sanātana: By the phrase "through the path of their scriptures" (*āgama-mārgeṇa*) and "by the Vedic way" (*śrauta-vartmanā*), the intended meaning is that even they must perform worship according to the scriptural injunctions alone.
Thus, it is said in the Eleventh Canto [BhP 11.5.61]: "Listen likewise even in the Kali age to the prescriptions of various *tantras*.
Regarding this, Śrīdhara Svāmin’s feet state: "By the phrase 'according to the prescriptions of various *tantras*', he shows the predominance of the *tantra*-path in the Kali age. (HbhvC 5.3–5)
Now, for the worship of the doors:

having offered water for the feet and other offerings to the deities of the door of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, one should then worship them with fragrances and flowers according to their respective positions and in due order.

Sanātana: Regarding those deities of the door of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—the name of the deity preceded by *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending in the dative case, followed by "namaḥ"—this is the application here, as it is to be written further on: *śrī-kṛṣṇa-dvāra-devatābhyo namaḥ*.

The meaning is that having offered water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and so forth with this mantra, one should worship them again specifically with fragrances (*gandha*) and other articles.

In the same way, further on as well, the formula "Obeisance to the attendants of Śrī-Kṛṣṇa along with their retinues," and so forth, should be understood. One should worship the attendants of Kṛṣṇa together with their retinues on the ground in front of the door;
before them, Garuḍa; and above the door, the Goddess of the Door (Dvāra-śrī). (HbhvC 5.6–5.7)
One should worship Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍaka on both sides of the eastern gate,
and Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ at the southern and western gates respectively.
Having likewise worshipped Jaya, Vijaya, Bala, and Prabala on the north, and the Vāstupuruṣa at the threshold with pairs of oblations, one should proceed.

Sanātana: Thus, the procedure for the worship of all [deities] has been written in general. Now, he writes specifically regarding that which was stated as "according to place" and "according to sequence," beginning with "at the front of the door," meaning at the two doors.

There too, first, one should worship— that is, offer sacrifice to— the attendants (pārṣadas) of Śrī Kṛṣṇa together with their entire retinue upon that pedestal (pīṭha) which has the form of the earth in front of the door.
Immediately thereafter, one should [worship] Garuḍa in front of that door.

Although the worship of the Door-Śrīs is stated in the *Kramadīpikā* to occur immediately after the principal worship, nevertheless, by the use of the suffix *-ktvā* in the word *iṣṭvā*, it is indicated that this takes place precisely prior to the worship of Caṇḍa and the others;
likewise, this is established by the practice of the virtuous (*sad-ācāra*).
Furthermore, because the word "dvandva" (pair) is written first, the application should be understood as a dual compound, namely: "Obeisance to Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa.
Then, one should worship Gaṅgā and Yamunā at the interior sides of the door.
On its two sides, one should worship the Śaṅkha treasure and likewise the Padma treasure.

Sanātana: Inside the door, within its interior, on both sides of that—that is, on both sides of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā—one should worship Gaṇeśa in the southeast corner of the temple, Durgā in the southwest, Vāṇī in the northwest, and likewise Kṣetrapāla in the northeast. (HbhvC 5.10–11)
Sanātana: One should worship Gaṇeśa in the south-eastern corner (āgneya-koṇa).
Thus it is stated in the *Krama-dīpikā* (7.103–106): "All these attendants have been described; furthermore, they are the venerable associates (pārṣada) of Viṣṇu."
On the pedestal at the front of the door, the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) is to be worshipped, and before him [the other deities].
Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa are in the east; Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ are in the south; Jaya and Vijaya are in the west; and Bala and Prabala are in the north.
Having worshipped the Goddess of the Door (Dvāraśrī) above, one should worship these [deities] in pairs at the door;
there, the Vāstupuruṣa is to be worshipped in the center of the pedestal of each door.
On the inner sides of the doors, one should worship the river Gaṅgā and the river Yamunā;
in the corners, one should worship Vighna, Durgā, and Vāṇī within the sacred field (kṣetra).
Thus,
leaning against the door-jamb with his left [hand], contracting his limbs,
and without touching the threshold, he should enter the house, placing his right foot first. (Hbhv 5.12)

Sanātana explains: "Leaning against the left door-post"—meaning resting upon the door-post situated on his own left side—"slightly touching his limbs," meaning with his limbs slightly contracted; "without touching the threshold" (dehalīm), which means without overstepping it;
"placing the right foot first," meaning by way of placing the right foot first.
"Entering the house"—that is, the temple of the Blessed Lord, the abode of Hari—as stated in the previous verse;
the worshipper should enter its interior slowly. And likewise, in the *Sāradā-tilaka*: [verse 5.12]... [the worshipper] should proceed.
Touching slightly with his left hand the branch [of the door], crossing the threshold,
and contracting his body, the Guru should enter within with his right foot.
Sanātana: "The Guru" is as stated in the *Dīkṣā-vidhāna* (HbhvC 5.13). Now, regarding the majesty of entering the house and its significance, it is described in the *Haribhakti-sudhodaya*:
Entering the abode of Viṣṇu for the sake of worship with great devotion,
the wise man shall never again enter the prison-house of his mother’s womb.
Now, regarding the worship within the house: one should worship Vāstupuruṣa and Brahmā in the southwest;
seated on a seat, one should worship those various deities elsewhere, except in the temple of the Blessed One. (Hbhv 5.15)
And the mantra for its worship is stated:
"The name of the deity preceded by the *praṇava* (OM), ending in the dative case and followed by *namaḥ*;
this is declared to be the worship mantra for all rites of veneration. (Hbhv 5.16)
Thus,
standing before Kṛṣṇa and having performed the binding of the directions,
one should scatter flowers and unbroken grains in all directions with the mantra prescribed therein. (Hbhv 5.17)

Then, for the purpose of worship, one should consecrate and honor the seat with the seat-mantra (āsanamantra) and sit upon it in either the lotus posture (padmāsana) or the auspicious posture (svastika). Hbhv_5.18.
