In that regard, the worshiper of Kṛṣṇa should generally face the east during the day, but face the north at night; however, he may remain with a steady posture facing [the deity] directly.
And in that regard, the eleventh book [of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa] states:
"Seated facing either the east or the north, or else facing directly toward the deity who is firm. (Hbhv 5.20)
Now, the mantra for the seat:
for the seat-mantra, Merupṛṣṭha is the seer (ṛṣi), Sutala is the meter (chandaḥ), and Kūrma is the deity; its application is through the consecration of the seat. (Hbhv 5.21)
O Earth, by you the worlds are supported; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu.
May you support me always, and make this seat pure. (Hbhv 5.22)
Now follows the rule for the seat (*āsana*), as stated in the *Nārada-pañcarātra*: "It may be made of bamboo, stone, wood, earth, grass, or leaf-sprouts."
A wise person should avoid a seat that brings about poverty, disease, or suffering;
neither a black antelope skin nor a woolen blanket is prescribed as a seat other than these.
And elsewhere it is said:
"One should prepare a soft seat from black antelope skin, tiger skin, silk, cane, cloth, deerskin, or a woolen blanket. (Hbhv 5.24)
Now, specifically regarding the rules concerning defects in the seat, it is said in the Nārada-pañcarātra:
"From a bamboo seat they say poverty arises; from a stone seat, the occurrence of disease."
On the ground there is the arising of suffering; in a wooden seat, misfortune.
On a seat of grass there is loss of fame; on a seat of leaves, mental distraction;
on a seat of darbha grass, the destruction of disease; and on a blanket, liberation from suffering. (Hbhv 5.26)
Furthermore, in the Śrī Bhagavad-gītā (6.11):
"Having established a firm seat for oneself in a clean place—neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, antelope skin, and kusha grass, one after the other. (Hbhv 5.27)
Thus it is said:
"Then, having sat down as described, one should place the requisites for worship, such as the conch and so forth, at their respective locations according to the tradition. (Hbhv 5.28)
Now, regarding the placement of the vessels:
the wise practitioner should place the conch with its stand to the front-left of himself;
right there he should also set down the vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings, and at the door, he should arrange them in their respective places.
One should place the vessels for tulasī, incense, flowers, and so forth on the right side, and a jar filled with water on the left side. (Hbhv 5.30)
To the right, one should place a lamp of ghee and a lamp of oil to the left;
other requisites should be set down within the range of one's own vision on the ground.
And for the purpose of washing the hands, a single bowl should be placed behind oneself. (Hbhv 5.31)
Now, regarding the vessels and their greatness,
it is stated in the Devīpurāṇa:
"They are of various and diverse forms, and some are shaped like lotuses."
One should fashion bowls that have the luster of a conch shell or a blue lotus.
One should have the vessels fashioned from jewels and other materials, provided with girdles and bases, according to their beauty and as they may be obtained. (Hbhv 5.33)
Furthermore, O Sage: by means of a swan-patterned vessel, one obtains all desired things;
likewise, by offering an *arghya* with a silver vessel, there shall be long life, sovereignty, and auspiciousness.
Through a copper vessel one obtains good fortune, and through one made of clay, the merit arising from dharma.
In the Vārāha [Purāṇa]:
"Whatever vessel is given—whether made of gold, silver, or bell-metal—I prefer copper above all of them. (Hbhv 5.35)
Copper is the purifier of purifiers, the most auspicious of auspicious things, the purest of the pure, and the means of liberation from saṃsāra. (Hbhv 5.36)
For those who have been initiated and are purified, one devoted to my ritual practice must always perform this with copper; in this way, O Earth, it shall be dear to me.
Thus,
some desire that the vessel for the *madhuparka* be other than copper, due to the defect of its contact with cow-products and the like in copper vessels. (Hbhv 5.38)

Likewise, some maintain that the conch alone should be the vessel for the *arghya*; for it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa: "Having placed water together with flowers, water, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) into the conch, one offers the *arghya* to the God. (Hbhv_5.39)
Now, regarding the placement of the auspicious jar:
for the sake of auspiciousness, one should place before the Blessed One a divine water-jar filled with water, provided with a lid, and accompanied by fruits and other offerings. (Hbhv 5.40)
And so it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"At the time of worship, one should place a divine water-pot together with a *karaka* vessel, filled with fruits and camphor; this is exceedingly dear to Kṛṣṇa. (Hbhv_5.41)
Thus it is said.
Furthermore:
"Whoever should place a water-pot filled with water and camphor before Kṛṣṇa..."
For an eon, his great-grandfathers do not look upon him with ill-will.
Then the practitioner should place the vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings;
into the *arghya* vessel, he should put sandalwood paste, flowers, unbroken rice, barley,
the tips of *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, and *dūrvā* grass, as well as white mustard seeds.
And some indeed assert that there are eight substances here, beginning with water.
For it is said in the *Bhaviṣya*:
"Water, milk, tips of *kuśa* grass, curd, unbroken rice, sesame seeds, barley, and white mustard seeds—thus the eightfold *arghya* is proclaimed. (Hbhv 5.44)
And in the vessel for the water for the feet, one should place these four substances: a lotus, dūrvā grass, śyāmāka grain, and the leaf of the *viṣṇupatrī*. (Hbhv 5.45)
In the same way, for the purpose of water for sipping (ācamanīya), the wise man should place three substances—
jātī fruit, cloves, and kakkola— into the vessel.
And into the vessel for the madhuparka, one should place these five substances: cow’s curd, milk, clarified butter, honey, and sugar-candy. (Hbhv 5.47)
Some virtuous ones maintain that there are only three substances in this bowl.
As it is stated in the Śrī-Viṣṇudharma:
"Clarified butter, curd, and likewise honey are prescribed as the madhuparka."
And in the *Ādivārāha*:
"In an udumbara vessel, one should place curd, ghee, and honey equal in measure for me;
however, if honey is unavailable, one should mix it with jaggery. (Hbhv 5.50)
O lady of beautiful hips, in the absence of ghee, one should mix it with parched grain;
likewise, in the absence of curd, one should mix it with milk.
In their absence, one should offer flowers and so forth while cultivating the meditative visualization of each respective [deity].
However, Nārada says that it is filled with pure water alone.
One should consecrate these vessels eight times with the root mantra using a single vessel;
furthermore, one should perform the protection of those vessels by means of the Cakra-mudrā.
Indeed, one who begins the worship, seated upon the prescribed seat,
should recite that auspicious rite of peace which is esteemed by the virtuous for the purpose of worship.
Now, the auspicious rite for peace:
Oṃ, may we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O worshipful ones.
With steady limbs, may we praise [thee] and, with our bodies, attain that lifespan ordained by the gods.
May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan and all the gods grant us well-being;
may Tārkṣya with his unimpaired wheel-rims grant us well-being.
May Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
Reciting thus: "Oṃ, may there be peace; may there be peace in the worship of the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa."
Thus:
Now, for the removal of obstacles:
"May those spirits depart who dwell upon the earth."
May those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva.
Having uttered this, the wise one should ward off all terrestrial obstacles with three strikes using the heel of the left foot, accompanied by the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra).
By means of that same upward progression through three successive levels of the palm,
the practitioner of mantras, possessing divine vision, should expel and drive away the celestial beings from the intermediate space.

Then, having prostrated before the venerable Guru and others, one should bow to the lineage of Gurus with palms joined in reverence, saluting the venerable Guru, the supreme Guru, and the preceptor of the highest order.
One should bow with devotion to Gaṇeśa on the right side, to Durgā in front, and to Kṣetrapāla behind; and in the center, one's own chosen deity.
Then, having purified the two hands with the weapon-mantra,
one should perform three claps (tāla) for the binding of the directions and likewise for the fire-enclosure.
Now, regarding the purification of the elements (*bhūta-śuddhi*): it is the cleansing of the elements that constitute the form of the body.
This is considered *bhūta-śuddhi* because of its contact with the imperishable Brahman. (Hbhv 5.63)

Without the purification of the elements (bhūta-śuddhi), all ritual actions such as recitation and fire-offerings performed by the practitioner become fruitless, even if they are carried out according to the rules and completed.
And as for its method:
having formed a "tortoise-cupped" hand gesture with the intellect, one should join oneself from the heart-lotus to the Supreme Self within the thousand-petaled lotus of the head.
One should contemplate that the principles (tattvas), beginning with earth, are dissolved into it.
The left hand is likewise turned upward and bound below by the right;
this is proclaimed as the Kara-kacchapikā mudrā for the purification of the elements (bhūta-śuddhi).
Having dried up this body and burned it, one should bathe it with a rain of nectar;
then, having generated and stabilized it, one should perform the consecration according to the ritual procedure.
Having thus purified oneself and brought oneself to the state of being fit for the worship of Kṛṣṇa,
one should bring the Kṛṣṇa residing in the heart back into that very heart in order to worship him out of affection.
And so it is said in the *Trailokyasaṃmohana-tantra*:
"The wise one should purify the body, together with its sins, by means of the wind residing in the navel;
he should then burn that physical frame with the fire residing in the heart. (Hbhv 5.69)
One should contemplate the pure moon, whose nature is nectar, situated within the thousand-petaled great lotus located on the forehead, as a perfectly full orb.
Therefore, the wise one should dissolve [the body] into ashes with streams flowing from those [syllables];
and with these syllables consisting of the [five] colors, he should contemplate the Goddess as having a body composed of the five elements, as before. Hbhv_5.71.
And so forth. Furthermore, later [it says]:
"Then, having drawn [the breath] back from that [exhalation], the knower of mantras should [do so] with the *praṇava*."
Having placed that radiance within the heart, one should contemplate the imperishable Viṣṇu.
Or else, by means of mere contemplation, having performed the purification of the elements (bhūta-śuddhi),
one should then perform the breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) according to the traditional lineage.
Now, regarding breath control (prāṇāyāma): exhalation (reca) occurs with sixteen measures (mātrās), inhalation (pūra) with thirty-two;
retention (kumbha) occurs with sixty-four—thus should the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇasaṃyama) be performed. (Hbhv 5.74)

Having first expelled the wind and contracted the anal region, one should fill [the body] according to the prescribed method and remain in the *kumbhaka* state according to one's own capacity. (Hbhv 5.75)

There, practicing the *praṇava* or a seed-syllable (*bīja*) or mantra that moves upward, and having performed the recollection of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and the other [constituent parts], one should perform meditation without sloth. (Hbhv 5.76)
And that meditation has been described thus:
[one should meditate on] Viṣṇu, whose crown, armlets, bracelets, finger-rings, necklaces, waist-bands, and ornaments for the feet and hips are radiant;
whose cheeks are touched by great makara-shaped earrings set with gems upon his chest.

I bow to Him who holds in His hands the conch, the discus, the lotus, and the mace; who is stainless, clad in yellow silk garments, radiant with splendor like the rising sun, and seated upon a lotus. Hbhv_5.77 //
And in some [traditions]:

"Rudra is to be meditated upon during exhalation (recaka), Brahmā during inhalation (pūraka), and the venerable Viṣṇu is to be known as the deity to be meditated upon during retention (kumbhaka); the specific place for meditation is learned from the mouth of the Guru. (Hbhv 5.78)
For it is said:
At the location of the navel, one should contemplate the lotus-seated Brahmā, the Grandfather, with a body red and fair, possessing four faces, by means of inhalation (pūraka). (Hbhv 5.79)
One should meditate with breath-retention (kumbhaka) upon the Great-Souled One, dark as the petal of a blue lotus, established in the center of the heart, possessing four arms. (Hbhv 5.80)
The wise one should indeed perform the stainless meditation on the Lord of the Recakas at the forehead, which destroys all sins and resembles pure crystal. (Hbhv 5.81)
Thus,

the Lord Kṛṣṇa— who consists of all the gods, who is the sovereign master, and who is accompanied by his beloved ones— should indeed be meditated upon in every way by those who are single-mindedly devoted. (Hbhv 5.82)
Now, regarding the greatness of *prāṇāyāma*,
as stated in the *Pādma Purāṇa* (3.31.79–83) in the dialogue between Devahūti and Vikuṇḍala:
"Those who are devoted to *prāṇāyāma* do not see the world of Yama."
Even those who have committed evil deeds have their sins destroyed by those very [virtuous acts].
O Vaiśya, sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) performed day after day purify even a direct slayer of a Brahmin, provided they are performed every single day. (Hbhv 5.84)
Whatever austerities are performed, whatever vows and observances are undertaken,
and even the gift of a thousand cows— prāṇāyāma is equal to all of them.
A man who might drink a drop of water from the tip of a blade of kusha grass month after month for more than a hundred years— prāṇāyāma is equal to that.
Whatever great sin there may be, as well as minor and secondary offenses,
a person reduces it all to ashes in an instant through breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma).
Thus, the wise declare that recitation performed without the ritual placements (nyāsa) is demonic and fruitless;
therefore, one should perform the ritual placements according to tradition and according to the prescribed rule. (Hbhv 5.88)

Therein, first, having recollected the seer, meter, deity, and so forth of the Mātṛkā-mantra, and having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the Mātṛkā-mantra upon the head, face, heart, and other parts, one should perform its meditation. Hbhv_5.89.
And that has been said:
"Her face, arms, thighs, waist, and chest were adorned with the fifty letters of the alphabet; she wore upon her crown a crescent moon, and her breasts were full and high."
I take refuge in the Goddess of Speech, who possesses pure radiance and three eyes, holding in her lotus-like hands the mudrā, a rosary of beads, a jar overflowing with nectar, and sacred knowledge.
The wise one should first place the letters beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa* in their pure form upon the forehead and the other limbs, according to the proper sequence.
And that has been explained in detail:

"On the forehead, the face, the cheeks, the eyes, the ears, the nose, the temples, the lips, the teeth, the head, the mouth, the joints of the arms and feet, and the tips [of the fingers and toes]. (Hbhv 5.92)

One should place the letters of the Mātṛkā in sequence upon the two sides, the back, the navel, the belly, the heart, the shoulders, the hump, and the neck; then, preceded by the heart [syllable], upon the pair of hands and feet, and finally upon the belly and the face. (Hbhv 5.93)
Thus,

the wise one should again place those [syllables] together with the *anusvāras* and enriched by the *visargas*— that is, including both the *anusvāras* and *visargas*— in this manner for a fourth time.
Now follows the ritual placement of the *mātṛkās* (*mātṛkā-nyāsa*):
[The letters are placed] at the throat, heart, navel, and secret place; likewise at the anus, the eyebrows, and the head;
situated respectively upon a sixteen-petaled lotus and a twelve-petaled one.
On the ten-petalled, six-petalled, four-petalled, and two-petalled [lotuses],
one should place one syllable at the end of each petal, together with the bindu.
Now, for the Keśava-ādi placement (nyāsa):
having recollected the seers (ṛṣi) and so forth, one should place the phonemes together with the forms [of the deities] beginning with Keśava,
and with the powers (śakti) beginning with Kīrti, in the same manner and sequence as before.
One should assign the four ultimate forms and the powers (śaktis) with [the syllables] beginning with *ya*;
likewise, the seven constituents (*dhātus*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the individual soul (*jīva*), and even Krodha as the end-maker for the Self.
There, he was absorbed in meditation, possessing the brilliance of a hundred rising suns and the pure luster of molten gold,
attended on both sides by the Daughter of the Ocean and the Mother of the Universe.
I bow to Viṣṇu, who is adorned with various ornaments shining with diverse jewels, who wears yellow garments, and who holds a conch, a lotus, the Kaumodakī mace, and a discus in his hands.
Now, as for the glorious forms:
first Keśava, then Nārāyaṇa, and afterwards Mādhava, Govinda, Viṣṇu, and Madhusūdana.
Trivikrama, Vāmana, and then Śrīdhara;
after that, Ṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and likewise Dāmodara.
Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha;
likewise, he who bears the discus, the mace, the Śārṅga bow, the sword, the conch, and the plow.
Muṣalī, Śūlī, Pāśī, and likewise Aṅkuśī;
Mukunda, Nandaja, as well as Nandī and Nara. (Hbhv 5.103)
Narakajit, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Satya, and Sātvata; after that Śauri, then Śūra, and finally Janārdana.
Bhūdharo, Viśvamūrti, Vaikuṇṭha, Puruṣottama, Bala, Balānuja, Bāla, Vṛṣaghna, and Vṛṣa. (Hbhv_5.105)
The forms are Haṃsa, Varāha, Vimala, and Nṛsiṃha.
Now, the powers (śaktayaḥ) are Kīrti, Kānti, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Dhṛti, Śānti, Kriyā, Dayā,
Medhā, Harṣā, as well as Śraddhā, Lajjā, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī. (Hbhv 5.107)
Prīti, Rati, Jayā, Durgā, Prabhā, Satyā, Caṇḍikā, Vāṇī, Vilāsinī, Vijayā, and likewise Virajā. (Hbhv_5.108)
Viśvā, Vinadā, Sunandā, and likewise Smṛti;
Ṛddhi, Samṛddhi, Śuddhi, Buddhi, Mūrti, Nati, and Kṣamā. (Hbhv 5.109)
Rama, Kledinī, Klinnā, Vasudā, Vasudhā, Parā, Parāyaṇā, Sūkṣmā, Sandhyā, Prajñā, Prabhā, and Niśā. (Hbhv 5.110)
The fifty-one powers (śaktis) are considered to be Amoghā, Vidyutā, and so forth;
this placement (nyāsa) beginning with Keśava bestows all prosperity in this world. (Hbhv 5.111)
It leads one to a state of similarity with those who have not fallen away in that [realm], merely by the act of entrusting.
Thus it has been said:
"Having thus meditated upon the Supreme Person,
one should perform the placement [of mantras] day by day with syllables joined with Keśava and the others."
May he be long nourished by intelligence, longevity, mindfulness, fortitude, fame, splendor, fortune, and good luck.
And elsewhere it is said:

"This placement [of mantras] beginning with Keśava bestows upon embodied beings the state of being Acyuta (the Imperishable) by the mere act of placement; this is the truth, the truth—there is no doubt. (Hbhv 5.114)
Thus:
"Whoever performs this ritual placement (*nyāsa*), preceded by the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī, shall soon obtain devotion, liberation, worldly enjoyment, and Kṛṣṇa. (Hbhv 5.115)
And so it has been said:
"The wise person who follows this very procedure, preceded by Ramā, shall attain success."
Having reached the vast expanse of the waters,
he returns once more at the end to the green [earth].
Now, the deposition of reality (tattva-nyāsa):

[It is performed] with the phonemes beginning with *ma* and ending with *ka*, joined with the *bindu*, preceded by "Salutation to Parā" (*namaḥ parāyai*), followed by "Salutation to the Self" (*ātmane namaḥ*). (Hbhv 5.117)
One should sequentially place the names of the principles (tattvas), such as the individual soul (jīva) and so forth, in their respective positions.
Indeed, by means of this placement, the world becomes entitled to perform worship.
Therein, first one should place the individual soul (jīva) and the vital breath (prāṇa) in the entire body;
then, in the heart, the triad consisting of intellect (mati), ego (ahaṅkāra), and mind (manas).
Then, one should place sound, touch, form, taste, and smell on the head,
the mouth, the heart, the secret place, and the feet, respectively.
Then, the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose [should be placed] in their respective positions;
likewise, speech, hands, anus, and genitals in their respective positions. (Hbhv 5.121)
One should [place] ether, air, fire, water, and earth respectively upon the head, the mouth, the heart, the genitals, and the feet. (Hbhv 5.122)

In the heart, one should first place the heart-lotus, measuring twelve, sixteen, or eighteen [finger-breadths], pervaded by the *kalās*; then, one should sequentially assign the solar, lunar, and fiery mandalas together with the phonemes (*varṇas*), accompanied by the letter *ra* and the *bindu*. (Hbhv 5.123)
One should place Vāsudeva with the syllable *ṣa*, joined with *parameṣṭhin* (*ke*) and the syllable *ya*;
one should place Saṅkarṣaṇa at the mouth, accompanied by the *pums-mantra*.
One should place Pradyumna, conjoined with Viśva, in the heart by means of the syllable *la*;
and Aniruddha, enriched by Nivṛtti, in the secret place by means of the syllable *va*;
and Nārāyaṇa, endowed with all [kalās], in the feet by means of the syllable *la* alone. (Hbhv 5.125)

This assignment of the principles (tattva-nyāsa), performed with the seed-syllable of that [mantra] upon the Universal Self as the wrathful Nṛsiṃha, quickly brings about the presence of Kṛṣṇa. (Hbhv 5.126)
And so it has been said:

"The wise who know the reality of the ritual placement (nyāsa) call it the 'placement of reality' because it consists of the pervasion of what is not reality and because it is the cause for attaining that [reality]. (Hbhv 5.127)

Whoever performs the arrangement of the principles (tattva-vinyāsa) certainly becomes purified; for the Blessed One dwells here having entered into that very self. Since he alone is the principles, everything is established within him. (Hbhv 5.128)

Furthermore, one should perform specific breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma) after those [preliminary] breath-controls; while reciting the root mantra in sequence, one should perform two, four, and six cycles of exhalation, inhalation, and retention. (Hbhv 5.129)
Alternatively, one should perform those [breath-control exercises], such as exhalation (recaka) and the rest, sixteen times,
thirty-two times, and sixty-four times respectively, while muttering the Kāma-bīja.
And likewise, in the *Kramadīpikā* (1.39): "The practitioner on the right should exhale through the right [nostril] and fill [the breath] through the left; then again through the central channel."
One should maintain the three [breath-controls] beginning with exhalation (recaka) as they have been described; these consist of the measures (mātrā) known as Kalā, Danta, and Vidyā.
Sanātana, corroborating that very point with the statement from the *Kramadīpikā*, shows a certain specific detail therein: "one should exhale" (*recayet*).
By "the right" (*dakṣayā*), he means by the right channel (*dakṣiṇa-nāḍyā*); "the right one" (*dakṣaḥ*) refers to the wise person (*vidvān janaḥ*).
One should hold [the breath] through the central channel, the *suṣumṇā*.

In this way, there are the three known as exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*). Regarding these three—exhalation and so forth—he states the duration for each in sequence: sixteen *kalās*.
The teeth are thirty-two;
the sciences are sixty-four; the meaning is that [the mantra] consists of that many *mātrās*.
A *mātrā* is the duration of contact with each of the three joints of the fingers, starting from the left little finger up to the thumb.
Or it is the time of touching the circle of the left knee with the left hand while moving clockwise;
in that case as well, a restriction regarding the fingers is stated: "The holding of the nostrils with the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb."
That is to be known as prāṇāyāma, excluding the index and middle fingers.
Thus, in that regard, among those breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas), the number was previously stated for the exhalations (recaka) and so forth;
here, however, the distinction is "in these breath-controls" (HbhvC_5.131).
In that regard, time, number, and so forth are treated right there [in the same context],
both before and after the recitation.
Now, those three have been prescribed by the wise;
he who performs them here sixteen times a day is indeed purified in a month, like a swan.

Sanātana: Regarding the time for *prāṇāyāmas*, it is before (*purataḥ*), at the beginning (*ādau*), and after (*parataḥ*) the recitation (*japa*). As for the number, those three constitute one *prāṇāyāma*; thus, three of those make three *prāṇāyāmas*.
A person who performs sixteen *prāṇāyāmas* every day, that is, daily;

By means of each single month, he is purified from the sin of transgression and becomes pure; this is the general result. Furthermore, everything has already been written above [HbhvC 5.132]. Now follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seats (pīṭha).
Then, one should conceive of one's own body as the very pedestal for worship;
one should install the foundational powers (ādhāra-śakti) and so forth upon the limbs of that pedestal, beginning with the syllable *tāra*.
Therein, however, [he worships] the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti), primordial nature (prakṛti), Kūrma and Ananta,
as well as the earth, the ocean of milk, and the radiant White Island (Śvetadvīpa).
One should place the Śrī-ratnamaṇḍapa and the Kalpavṛkṣa tree within the heart;
then, in a clockwise direction, one should place Dharma and Jñāna upon the two shoulders.
Dispassion and sovereignty [reside] in the two thighs; likewise, unrighteousness in the mouth;
ignorance, lack of dispassion, and lack of sovereignty in the three [other limbs]; and on the two sides [reside] the same. (Hbhv 5.136)
In the heart-lotus, one should likewise [visualize] the lotuses of Ananta, Sūrya, Indu, and Śikhi,
as mandalas in sequence with the syllables consisting of the parts of the *praṇava* together with the bindu.
For therein are the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, as well as the individual self (ātman) and the inner self (antarātman);
and one should likewise [worship] the supreme self (paramātman) with the initial syllables of these [names], accompanied by the bindu.
And [one should worship] the one whose nature is knowledge, conjoined with the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśvarī;
and in its eight directions as well as in the center, the nine Śaktis according to the sequence of the directions.
And they have been described as follows: "Vimalā, Utkarṣiṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, and Yoga are the [first] powers; Prahvī, Satyā, Īśānā, and Anugrahā is remembered as the ninth. (Hbhv 5.140)
Thus, one should place the seat-mantra (*pīṭha-mantra*) above that, as previously described;
thereafter, one should recollect the seer (*ṛṣi*) and the other [limbs] of this eighteen-syllable mantra. (Hbhv 5.141)

And those who are single-mindedly devoted should know the fourfold [stations] beginning with the Ocean of Milk, followed respectively by Śrī Mathurā, Vṛndāvana, its groves, and the nīpa trees. (Hbhv 5.142)
Then follows the ritual placement of the seats (*pīṭha-nyāsa*).
Thus it is said in the *Ādi-puruṣa-rahasya-stotra* of the *Brahma-saṃhitā* (5.56):
"Where that great ocean of milk flows forth from the Surabhis..."
I worship that Śvetadvīpa, where not even a moment known as half a blink of an eye passes; those few virtuous ones who know it here as Goloka are rare wanderers upon the earth.
In the *Kramadīpikā* [1.44–45]:
"Thus, the heart is the Lord Viṣṇu, the self of all beings, accompanied by all;
and the suffix *-ne*, along with Vāsudeva, is conjoined with that which is endowed with the self of all."

The lotus at the base of the yoga, joined with the *ṅe* [case-ending] from the seat (*pīṭha*), and obeisance at the end—this manifest Great Mantra of the Seat is sufficient for all rites of worship. (Hbhv 5.145)
Sanātana says: "Tāra" is the Praṇava;
after that, the word "hṛdayaṃ namaḥ";
and then "bhagavān" and "viṣṇuḥ."
"Pervading all" (*sarvānvitaḥ*) means "endowed with all words" (*sarva-śabda-yuktaḥ*); "the self of beings" (*bhūtātmā*) means "the self of all beings" (*sarva-bhūtātmeti*).
These three, together with Vāsudeva—meaning accompanied by Vāsudeva—are each in the dative case (ending in *ṅe*).
Consequently, the neuter form *sarvātma-saṃyogam* (meaning "union with the self of all") is used according to the archaic usage (*ārṣam*).
And then, at the conclusion of the yoga, there is the "lotus," namely the *yoga-padma*.
At the end of that is the seat (*pīṭha*) itself, joined with the dative case-ending (*ṅe*).
And at the end of that is the salutation, the word *namaḥ*.
Thus, it is established: *Oṃ namo bhagavate viṣṇave sarva-bhūtātmane vāsudevāya sarvātma-saṃyoga-yoga-padma-pīṭhātmane namaḥ*.
And likewise, in the *Śāradā-tilaka*:
"One should utter 'namo bhagavate', and then say the word 'viṣṇave'."
Then one should say: "To Vāsudeva, the self of all beings."
Following the word *sarvātmasaṃyoga*, the word *yogapadma* is repeated;
this mantra, beginning with the syllable *tāra* (oṃ) and ending with the heart-mantra (*hrīḥ*) and the term *pīṭhātmane*, has been taught.
Thus,
in the Sanatkumāra-kalpa,
having first uttered the word "Oṃ namaḥ" (Om, salutation), one likewise [utters] the word "Bhagavate" (to the Blessed One).
Having said "To Vāsudeva," one should likewise utter the word "Sarvātman" (the Soul of All).
Having uttered "saṃyogayoga," one likewise utters the word for the seat (pīṭha).
Joined with the consort of Fire (Svāhā), this is declared to be the seat-mantra (pīṭha-mantra).
Thus [ends the section]. //144-5//
Now, the recollection of the seer and other elements: Oṃ, for this eighteen-syllable mantra, the seer (ṛṣi) is Śrī Nārada, the meter (chandaḥ) is Gāyatrī,
and the deity (devatā) is the son of Nanda, the auspiciousness of all the worlds.
Hrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja),
svāhā is the power (śakti),
and Kṛṣṇa is the primordial nature (prakṛti).
The deity presiding over the fortress;
its application is for the attainment of one's desired object.
And so, in the *Saṃmohana-tantra*, in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā, it is said: "The sage is declared to be Nārada; the meter is said to be Gāyatrī;
Kṛṣṇa, wearing the guise of a cowherd, is proclaimed as the deity. (Hbhv 5.147)
The seed-syllable is known as Manmatha, and the beloved [Goddess] is the power (śakti) of the Fire-eater (Agni).
You alone, O Supreme Sovereign, are its presiding deity.
Its application (viniyoga) is proclaimed for the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life.
Now, regarding the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅga-nyāsa):
one should arrange four limbs with four groups of four syllables each;
and the limb called the weapon (astra) with two [syllables]. Thus, there are indeed five limbs.
And one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of those limbs as all-pervasive upon both hands;
then, some [place] those [limbs] on the five fingers, as well as the consonants and the vowels. (Hbhv 5.150)
And they are said to be:
liquefying, agitating, attracting, subduing, and causing emission; likewise, drying up, deluding, inflaming, burning, and intoxicating. (Hbhv 5.151)
Thus it is said.
Furthermore:
The heart mantra ends with *namaḥ*, while the head and the tuft (*śikhā*) are accompanied by *svāhā* along with their respective limbs.
The armor-mantra is joined with *vaṣaṭ*, and the weapon-mantra is joined with two *huṃ*s and *phaṭ*.
Furthermore, they place the two thumbs, the two index fingers, and likewise the two middle fingers, the two ring fingers, and the two little fingers, in sequence with the five limbs. (Hbhv 5.153)
Furthermore, they simultaneously assign all [the limbs], beginning with the heart and likewise the thumbs and so forth, by means of those five limbs in successive order.
And they perform the placement of the six limbs—the heart and so forth—of that mantra;
and of these, five are placed in the heart and other locations, and one is placed in the directions, respectively.
And the six limbs are described in the *Sammohana-tantra*, in the *Sanatkumāra-kalpa*: "The heart-mantra is held to consist of one syllable; the head is considered to consist of three;
the crest is said to consist of four, and likewise the armor is considered to consist of four."
Likewise, the eye-mantra is considered to consist of four syllables, and the weapon-mantra of two.
Thus, one should place this mantra with both arms from the feet up to the hair;
for three days, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa), and the Praṇava should be placed once. (Hbhv 5.157)
Now follows the placement of the syllables (akṣara-nyāsa):
then, one should place the eighteen syllables of this mantra in their proper order on the teeth, the forehead, the middle of the eyebrows, the two ears, and the two eyes. (Hbhv 5.158)
One should place one [syllable] on the two nostrils, the face, the throat, the heart, the navel, the two hips, the secret place, the two knees, and one on the two feet. (Hbhv 5.159)
The virtuous place [the seed-syllables] beginning with Tārā and ending with Namo, together with the bindu;
others [place them] with the seeds of Śrī, Śakti, and Kāma, according to the sequence of emanation and so forth.
Now, as for the placement of the steps:

having placed the *tāra* (the syllable Om) on the head and the five mantra-words, one should place them in sequence upon the two eyes, the mouth, the heart, the private parts, and the feet. (Hbhv 5.161)
Furthermore, one should place those [mantras] throughout the entire body by means of their pervasiveness;
some, however, assign them along with the initial syllables, ending in "namaḥ. (Hbhv 5.162)
Likewise, there are three [mantras] ending with *svāhā*, which are to be combined with each subsequent one;
having pervaded [the body] from the secret place, the throat, and the head down to the feet.

In this context, for those established in knowledge, the nyāsa regarding the secret [mantras] and other subjects should indeed be performed by Vaiṣṇavas upon their respective castes and bodies, according to each specific caste.
Now, regarding the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seer and so forth:

one should perform the placement of the seven components of this mantra, beginning with the seer, in sequence upon the head, face, heart, breasts, and again on the heart, and once more on the heart. (Hbhv 5.165)

Then, one should display the five mudrās: the one called the bamboo flute, the one called the forest garland, and then the beautiful ones called the Śrīvatsa, the Kaustubha, and the *blī*. (Hbhv 5.166)
Thus, having assumed this body of principles and again performing the binding of the directions,
one should hold the Son of Śrī Nanda by forming the "tortoise" gesture with the hands.
Now, the procedure for meditating upon the Blessed One, the son of Śrī Nanda:
[Krama-dīpikā 3.1–36] Now,
[one should contemplate] the blossoming, excellent *mādhvika* honey overflowing with manifest fragrance...

One of pure intellect should meditate upon the auspicious Vṛndāvana, cooled by trees whose branches are bent low under clusters of flowers and fresh shoots, and entwined by graceful creepers adorned with blossoming new clusters of blossoms. (Hbhv 5.168)
Immediately thereafter, one whose mind is bright and whose heart is pure should contemplate Vṛndāvana.
Of what nature is it? It is cooled, made refreshing, by trees;
and of what kind are those trees? They are those whose fragrance is manifest and preeminent.
That from which honey has dripped and nectar has fallen;
that which is blossomed and fully opened;
and that which is excellent, namely the flower and the fresh sprout.
The cluster of those two is a mass;
by that [mass], their branches were bent.
The shortening of the vowel in *mādhvika* must be tolerated because it was composed by a great poet.
The reading "prakaṭa-saurabhākulita-matta-bhṛṅgolasad" is indeed easy to understand.

Furthermore, by what [are they characterized]? By those lovely and charming *vallaryas*—whether meaning branches at the tips, twigs, or creepers—which are graced by fully blossomed new clusters of blossoms (*mañjarīs*).
Enveloped by those [elements],
it is auspicious (*śiva*), having the nature of well-being, because it is free from affliction and because it brings about supreme welfare. (HbhvC 5.168)
Its interior was made resonant by the humming of bees wandering about, sweet with the tasting of the nectar of blooming jasmine flowers,
and by the cries of birds such as pigeons, parrots, mynas, and cuckoos.
It resounded here and there, agitated by the dancing of the enemies of serpents.
[The breezes] carrying droplets from the moving waves of the daughter of Kalinda, grey with the mass of pollen from the bellies of blossoming lotuses,
and [carrying] the fragrance of the garments of the playful women of Vraja whose passion was kindled—
It is constantly attended by breezes that move restlessly.
With sprouts of coral and fresh shoots, leaves of emerald, clusters of buds made of diamonds and pearls, and various fruits the color of lotuses;
it is the most magnificent tree, constantly served by all the seasons, and the granter of desires.
Even within that, one should meditate upon the uplifted wish-fulfilling tree.
Below it, as radiant as the rising sun atop a range of golden peaks, was a golden ground showering sprays of nectar,
with its floor of blazing jewels made brilliant by heaps of flower pollen.
Furthermore, the wise person, being unwearied, should again recollect that which is free from the six waves.

Having visualized an eight-petaled, stainless lotus upon a most magnificent yoga-throne set within a pavement of jewels, one should contemplate [the deity] in its center, possessing the splendor of the rising sun.
Then one should contemplate Mukunda, who is established in bliss.

His mass of hair is a network of thick, dark blue, and beautifully glossy curls, possessing a luster like a fresh blue lotus or a dense cloud of crushed collyrium, as described in the jewel-like Sūtras.
O King, [he who has] a crest of peacock feathers as lovely as the throat of Śiva.
His crest-jewel is fashioned from the withered blossoms of the celestial tree cherished by the *rolamba* bees;
his ear-ornament is a fresh blue lotus with its filaments bristling upward;
and his forehead is illuminated by the radiance shimmering from his flickering locks of hair.
A forehead mark made with gorocanā, with a fringe of shimmering feathers.
His lovely face possesses the splendor of the full orb of the autumnal moon; his large eyes are like lotus petals;
and he is radiant with the rays from jeweled makara-shaped earrings shimmering with gems.
The cheeks are like mirrors, and the nose is high and beautiful.
Her lower lip is made most beautiful by sindūra; her limbs are illuminated by the splendor of her gentle smile, which possesses the luster of the moon, the kunda flower, and the mandāra;
she is adorned with a collection of wild sprouts and flowers.
With a neck made beautiful and radiant by a jeweled necklace and a conch-shell ornament.
His shoulders were adorned with hanging garlands of *santānaka* flowers frequented by intoxicated, wandering bees;
his full chest was resplendent with a multitude of pearl necklaces.
The sun-like Kaustubha gem, beautiful upon the surface of the sky.
He is beautifully marked with the Śrīvatsa sign; his shoulders are elevated, and his well-formed arms are thick and reach down to his knees;
his abdomen is concave, and his navel is noble and deep.
The line of body hair like a cluster of *vañjula* flowers, resembling a swarm of female bees.
With armlets, bracelets, necklaces, girdles, anklets, and waist-bands fashioned from various jewels,
his slender body was suffused with the glow of divine unguents.
Her orb-like hips are encircled by a lower garment of yellowish hue.

With beautiful thighs and knees, and shanks that follow the natural curve and are pleasing to the mind; with lovely, elevated forefeet that put to shame the beauty of a tortoise; and with a row of nails shining like a fringe of rubies.
His lotus feet are beautiful, adorned with jewel-encrusted finger-guards.
Delightful with the palms of his reddish hands and soles of his feet marked by the fish, goad, lotus stalk, banner, barley, lotus, and thunderbolt;
his limbs fashioned from the very essence of all beauty.
The beauty of whose body surpassed that of the god of love.
By the divine melodies produced by the fingers of his trembling hand as they fill the holes of the flute at his lotus-like mouth,
all sentient beings, far and near, are eternally melted with devotion.
The continuous stream of the continuum, an infinite ocean of the waters of bliss.
With cows whose eyes were fixed upon his lotus-like face, walking slowly and with faltering steps due to the heavy burden of their udders,
and with sprouts of grass still held between the tips of their teeth—
Enveloped by the creeper-like tails of the Rālaṃba birds.
With mouths lovely with frothy milk flowing from teats that were drawn out, filled,
and sucked, and enchanting, deep songs produced by flutes;
And even by the young calves, who pricked up their pair of ears.
With the strikes of their heads, tender with fresh horns, and the falling of their hooves tossing during the exuberant bounds of their play,
they made the ground resonant, while their thick dewlaps dangled as they bellowed loudly.
And he was surrounded by herds of young bulls and young cows.
Even by the great bulls, exhausted by the burden of their massive humps and agitating the circle of the quarters with their lowing,
the flutes were held fast within their upturned ears.
With broad nostrils expanded by the rising nectar of their lowing sounds; // Hbhv_5.187 //
Accompanied by cowherds whose qualities, character, age, amorous play, and dress were identical to his own, who played flutes and lutes with intoxicatingly sweet sounds,
and who were intent on singing songs in low, high, and shrill registers while moving restlessly—
Skilled in performing graceful dances with the vine-like arms.
By those wandering about, their broad hips reaching down to their calves adorned with clusters of dangling tinkling bells,
and wearing charming neck-ornaments fashioned from the claws of hyenas;
It was surrounded by small children with indistinct and sweet voices.
Then, [he beheld] the beautiful cowherd girls, Sulalitās,
whose gait was slow due to the weight of their broad hips and buttocks,
and whose waists were bent by the heavy burden of their breasts.
Of those who possess a line of body hair manifested by the three folds [of the neck].
For those whose limbs and bodies have been made to sprout by the nectar-like essence of that exceedingly sweet and beautiful flute-playing,
the hair on their bodies has risen up, lovely with its multitude of buds.
Of the creepers of song adorned with the Āgamas.
From that ocean of the waters of passion, expanded by the moonlight of her exceedingly beautiful and gentle smile,
[arose] droplets from the breaking of most restless waves.
Of those whose continuous streams of sweat-drops are equal to the [flow from] a water-jar.
With a rain of sharp glances discharged from the bow of her exceedingly lovely and slow-moving eyebrows— Māra’s arrows—
her entire vital organs were shattered and her limbs became overwhelmed with distress.
Of those suffering from the pain of widespread and unbearable trembling.
By those two who were longing for the practice of drinking the nectar of the beauty of his exceedingly lovely and passionate form,
[and] by those rivers flowing with a flood of the water of affection—
With her lotus-eyes trembling with impurity.
[The breasts] are repeatedly attended by swarms of bees greedy for the honey trickling from the full blossoms falling from loosened tresses;
they possess soft voices faltering with the intoxication of passion, and their trembling girdles are heaving.
With the luster of their hips revealed by the ends of their silken garments slipping loose from their waist-knots.
Of those whose faces fill the quarters with the tinkling of jeweled anklets upon their slowly moving, graceful lotus-feet,
and whose petal-like lips quiver— those eyes of Kuṇḍalā, thick with lashes.
Of the lotuses of the pair [of eyes], with shimmering earrings.

Of those women whose faces in all directions were filled with sound by the tinkling of jeweled anklets— which made noise through the gentle striking of their lotus-feet as they stumbled or moved gracefully—
and whose two lotus-eyes, like lakes, had blossoming buds and were thick with excellent lashes.
Of those whose sprout-like lower lips were withered by the heat of the wind from their longest sighs,
and whose lotus-hands shone with various offerings—
Constantly attended on all sides by rows of flowering trees.

[He whose] entire body was worshipped with garlands of full-blown blue lotuses— [lotuses] like their long, tremulous, dark eyes— with those [women] whose sprout-like reddish lips were fading due to the intense heat of the exceedingly long breath-wind; [he who was] the source of manifold diversions.
He bears a captivating garland of bees— his eyes intoxicated with love— which tastes the honey-dew dripping from the lotus-face of his beloved.

"Vyākośam" means fully blossomed; "praṇayāt" means from affection; "unmade" means with intoxication arisen; "akṣiṇī" refers to the two eyes; "madhukṛnmālā" is a row of bees; "bibhrāṇam" means bearing or displaying that [row].

Because her two eyes fall here and there in many ways, she is called "Mālā" (the Garland) due to seeing [them] everywhere. Of what sort? She is one whose habit is to taste the *mādhvī*—that is, the nectar (*makaranda*)—that has flowed forth from their charming and captivating lotus-faces.
For this very reason,
one should visualize before him, outside [the maṇḍala], a captivating assembly of gods, along with cowherds, cowherdesses, and cattle.
Desiring wealth, she was devoted to hymns of praise, preceded by Brahmā, the three-eyed Śiva, and Indra.

Now, with five verses beginning with "gopa," he describes the meditation upon the gods and others who grant the fulfillment of the four aims of human life— known as wealth, virtue, liberation, and desire— as well as the longing for devotion, which is the fifth aim and the most excellent of all.
In front of this Kṛṣṇa, directly facing him,
and to his right, [one should visualize] the multitude of sages who firmly desire the Dharma and are intent on discipline.
Then, on his back, he [carried] Sanaka and the other lords of yogins who were seeking liberation through meditative absorption.
And on his right, one should visualize a multitude of sages;
on his left, those who possess firm aspiration for the Dharma, along with their consorts, as well as yakṣas and siddhas.
And the Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Cāraṇas,
along with the Kinnaras and the foremost Apsarases, seeking the objects of desire, [delighted him] with dance, song, and instrumental music.
One should also visualize the yakṣas and others together with their beloveds— that is, accompanied by their wives—
in what manner?
As those seeking sensual pleasure, who pray for their respective desired objects through dancing and other such means.
One should also remember the principal and most excellent Apsarases, such as Urvaśī and others—[who are] white like a conch, the moon, or a jasmine flower; who know all the Agamas;
and whose mass of matted hair is tawny like a multitude of lightning flashes.
[He is] one who desires unwavering devotion directed toward his lotus feet, having utterly abandoned all other attachments.
The meaning is that it concerns the lotus feet of that Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
he by whom all attachment—that is, clinging—to everything other than devotion has been utterly abandoned (*ujjhitatara*).
[He is endowed with] the seven musical scales (*sapta-rāga*) accompanied by various collections of Vedic hymns.

One should contemplate that son of the Creator, the Lord of Sages, in the great expanse of the sky, delighting him with the rising, heart-captivating melodies (*mūrcchanā*) belonging to the three scales (*grāma*). Hbhv_5.203.
For this very reason, [he sees] this Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is pleasing [him] with his own lute called *kacchapikā*, which is known by the name "Great" (*mahatī*).

With what? With those charming *mūrchanās* (melodic scales) that have reached the three *grāmas*—the collection of the three *grāmas*—which reside within the seven *rāgas* (musical modes), such as *niṣāda* and so forth, or *meghanāda*, *vasanta*, and so forth; these *rāgas* being endowed with various groups of *śrutis*, which consist of thirty-six varieties, that is, a multitude of sounds (*nāda*).
Of what kind? "Uditābhiḥ" means those that have themselves attained manifestation; or, it may be construed as "manifested in the great."

For this very reason, one should properly meditate upon Śrī Nārada, the Lord of Sages, the foremost among the hosts of sages and the son of the Creator, in the sky. As stated in the *Śrī Gautamīya Tantra*:
"Now I shall proclaim the meditation that destroys all sins."
Kṛṣṇa, wearing yellow garments, with eyes resembling lotuses.
With red eyes, lips, hands, feet, and nails, he is auspicious;
his chest is illuminated by the Kaustubha gem, and he is adorned with various jewels.
Adorned with necklaces of pearls shimmering in that abode,
his crown was radiant with the luster of various jewels and possessed divine splendor.
Adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and earrings, with the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest, and graced by beautiful anklets and other ornaments.
Adorned with various jewels, girdles, and finger-rings,
and decorated with wild flowers and a crest made of peacock feathers.
Adorned with a forest garland bound with kadamba flowers,
it resembles the stainless sky, which brings joy to the moon and the stars.
Hari stood in the midst of the cow-pen, holding a flute with both hands and placing it to his mouth, singing with divine melodies. (Hbhv 5.210)
Surrounded by hundreds of maidens as if fallen from heaven,
he was endowed with all auspicious marks and graced with supreme beauty.
It is auspicious, having the form of a blessing for the world,
and is adorned with a necklace (hāra) covered— meaning enveloped— by pearls shining with the luster and brilliance of that Kaustubha gem;
or alternatively, there is a reading "muktābaddha" (strung with pearls).
Adorned with a waist-thread and finger-rings,
it resembles the stainless sky— the expanse of space— which brings joy and happiness through the stars accompanied by the moon;
here, however, the Kaustubha gem occupies the place of the moon.
In place of "stars," there is a garland of *kadamba* flowers;
in place of "the sky," the glorious chest is to be understood.
The meaning is: [it is like] the most beautiful women fallen from heaven.
He was surrounded by a hundred such maidens, the daughters of the cowherds;
here, the word "hundred" implies a number beyond count.
He was the enchantment of all the gopīs and of all the cows as well.
And being licked all around by calves and cows.
By Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Yakṣas; by Apsarases and birds;
by gods, asuras, and humans; and even by stationary beings and serpents.
He was being gazed upon with great wonder by deer and by Vidyādharas,
as well as by Nārada, Vasiṣṭha, and the wise Viśvāmitra.
By Parāśara, Vyāsa, Bhṛgu, and likewise Aṅgiras;
by Dakṣa, Śaunaka, and Atri; and by the perfected Kapila. (Hbhv 5.215)
One should meditate day and night upon Kṛṣṇa, who is joined by Sanaka and the other lords of sages, as well as those who have gone to the world of Brahmā, and others too.
In brief, it is also stated in the Śrī-Sanatkumāra-Kalpa:

"May He protect us— He whose luster is like that of a closing kalāya flower, whose mass of hair shines with the feathers of the enemy of serpents (Garuda), whose charming body is worshipped by the eyes of the gopīs, and who is surrounded by cowherds and herds of cows."

May that Lord, the son of Devakī, whose form resembles the moon accompanied by her glorious lotus-face, who wears yellow garments, and who dispels the weariness of people with the sound of his flute, be our refuge.
Thus, may that Lord, the son of the illustrious Devakī, whose majesty is inexpressible, protect us;
he whose dark luster is like the radiance of a *kalāya* flower. (HbhvC 5.217)
Now follows the inner sacrifice (antar-yāga):
having thus meditated upon that Blessed One and having prayed to him as he pleases,
one should first worship him with all mental offerings.
Those ritual services (upacāra) which are prescribed for external worship according to their respective divisions—
all of those may also be arranged as one pleases for internal worship.
Now, the procedure for the prayer, as stated in the Śrī Nārada Pañcarātra:
"Welcome, O Lord of the gods; be present here, O Keśava."
Accept this mental worship from those who contemplate reality as it truly is.
Thus,
having first worshipped the Lord who abides within his own self by means of both internal and external services, he should, according to the authentic tradition, establish the conch shell.
Now, for the consecration of the conch (*śaṅkha*): having drawn a triangular mandala on the ground to the front-left of oneself,
the wise practitioner should place the conch, washed with the *astra-mantra*, together with its base.

One should cast scented paste, flowers, and unbroken grains into the conch with the heart-mantra; one should fill it with the letters of the mātrkā, arranged in reverse order and ending with the letter *ka*. (Hbhv 5.223)
One should worship the fire-maṇḍala upon that support with the letter *ma* together with a bindu, and the sun-maṇḍala within the conch with the letter *a*. (Hbhv 5.224)
With the syllable *u*, one should likewise worship the lunar mandala in the water;
with the *tīrtha-mantra*, one should invoke the sacred bathing sites (*tīrthas*) and the solar mandala.
Having invoked Kṛṣṇa from the heart-lotus, one should gaze upon him with the Gālinī at the crest;
having looked within with the eye-mantra, one should veil him with the armor-mantra.

One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the root mantra and its limbs upon the water, and then [perform it] upon the directions; having bound [the space] with the weapon mantra (*astra*), one should then transform it into nectar by means of the *dhenu*-mudrā.
Having protected that water with the *cakra-mudrā* and covered it with the *matsya-mudrā*, one should touch the conch and recite the root mantra eight times. (Hbhv 5.228)

Having poured a little of that water into the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, one should sprinkle it three times; with the remainder of that [water], one should sprinkle the various materials for worship as well as one's own body.
The little fingers and thumbs of the two hands are joined to one another;
the index, middle, and ring fingers are pressed together and slightly curved.
This is declared to be the Gālinī mudrā, which is moved over the top of a conch shell.

Then, having removed [the water] from within the conch shell and refilled it with water from the vardhanikā vessel, one should place it before Kṛṣṇa according to the tradition of the virtuous. (Hbhv 5.231)
Then, having worshipped the gurus upon one's own head and Gaṇeśa at the *mūlādhāra* within one's own body,
one should worship the *pīṭha* within oneself according to the procedure for the *pīṭha*-installation (*pīṭha-nyāsa*).
Then, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantra-limbs and so forth upon the limbs of the deity;

thereafter, while reciting the desire-seed-syllable (*kāma-bīja*), one should contemplate the supreme light situated in the three places as being identical in essence with the root mantra, unified with that seed-syllable. (Hbhv 5.233)

Having visualized one's own chosen deity with form through the placement of the five limbs (pañcāṅga-nyāsa), one should then place those five limbs and so forth upon that [deity] just as one has done upon oneself. (Hbhv 5.234)
When the Blessed One and Kṛṣṇa have appeared, the Vaiṣṇavas should perform those respective ritual placements (nyāsa) for the sake of non-difference between the mind and the Blessed One.

Some assign the principles (tattvas) and so forth, as previously described, in their unmanifest forms, sequentially upon the ornaments of the Lord by means of the syllables of the mantra, such as the vowels and *haṃsa*. (Hbhv 5.236)
Then, while visualizing the Blessed One seated upon that throne through external offerings as an internal worship,
the wise one should worship him according to the ritual rules with offerings beginning with the seat and ending with flowers.
Then one should worship the flute in the mouth and the forest garland on the chest;
the Śrīvatsa mark above the right breast, and the Kaustubha gem in that very place on the left.
The Vaiṣṇava, having smeared this [image] with sandalwood paste, should draw twelve tilakas in the shape of lamp-flames using the ring finger, as previously described. (Hbhv 5.239)
As it has been said: having honored him with five handfuls of flowers, one should offer incense, lamps, food offerings, mouth-perfumes, and so forth. (Hbhv 5.240)

Having gratified Kṛṣṇa with songs and other offerings, one who is unable to perform external worship should then entrust the entire [practice] to Him and perform the recitation of mantras (japa). (Hbhv 5.241)
Now, regarding the greatness of the internal sacrifice (*antar-yāga*), it is said in the Vaiṣṇava Tantra:
"Thousands of horse sacrifices (*aśvamedha*) and hundreds of *vājapeya* sacrifices..."
They do not equal even a sixteenth part of a single yoga of meditative concentration.
In the *Bṛhan-nāradīya-purāṇa* (1.11.12), regarding the manifestation of Śrī Vāmana:
"By the mere utterance of His name, all calamities are destroyed."
Whether by hymns of praise or by offerings, what indeed can be said of it through meditation?
In the *Nārada-pañcarātra*, in the dialogue between the Blessed Lord and Nārada:
"O twice-born one, this mental sacrifice removes the fear of old age and disease,
pacifies the flood of all sins, and brings about both existence and non-existence."
Through the yoga of constant practice, one should liberate [the self] from the bondage of the body.
And whoever, O Great-Minded One, should perform this even once with supreme devotion according to the procedure set forth in due order—for him, O Sage, I am pleased. (Hbhv 5.245)

Whatever greatness was previously written regarding recollection (smaraṇa) and meditation (dhyāna), it should be understood that here it is even greater, as these two serve as limbs of the internal sacrifice (antaryāga).
Thus, having first performed the internal worship according to tradition, to the best of one's ability and as long as it brings joy to the mind, one should then begin the external worship.
And so it has been said by Nārada:
"Having meditated and performed the perfect propitiation with sixteen mental services, one should then carry out the external worship. (Hbhv 5.248)
Then, for the outer worship:
"O Blessed One, O Lord, grant me permission for the outer yoga.
Having thus requested permission from Śrī Kṛṣṇa, one should perform the outer worship. (Hbhv 5.249)
In that place, moreover, there are many sites for worship,
and therein are various forms of Śrī as well as śālagrāma stones.
Now, regarding the places of worship, the Saṃmohana Tantra states:
"In a Śālagrāma stone, in a mantra, in a yantra, on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or in images and the like."
The worship of Hari, however, should be performed on bare ground and not otherwise.
In the eleventh book of the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, in the dialogue with Uddhava (11.11.42–46), it is said: "O auspicious one,
the sun, fire, brāhmaṇas, cows, Vaiṣṇavas, the ether, the wind, water,
the earth, the self, and all living beings are my objects of worship."

One should worship me in the sun with the threefold Vedic knowledge, in the fire with oblations, in the foremost of brahmins with hospitality, and in cows, my dear, with fodder and the like. (Hbhv 5.253)
In Vaiṣṇava [worship], [the deity is worshipped] by honoring kinsmen; in the heart, by steadfastness in meditation;
in the air, by the thought of primacy; in water, with substances preceded by water.
On the sacrificial ground, with the heart-mantras and ritual enjoyments, one should worship me—the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña)—within oneself through equanimity toward all beings. (Hbhv 5.255)
Upon these sacrificial hearths (dhiṣṇya), one should worship with a concentrated mind, meditating upon my form—four-armed, peaceful, and endowed with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus. (Hbhv 5.256)
Then, regarding the forms of Śrī, it is said in that very same place (BhP 11.27.12–14): "The image may be made of stone, wood, metal, clay, paint, or sand."
The mind-made and the jewel-made image are considered to be of eight kinds.
The foundation of the temple of the living soul is of two kinds: moving and unmoving.
In the worship of a stationary image, O Uddhava, there is no need for the rites of dismissal or invocation. (Hbhv 5.258)
In an unstable [image], there may be mental visualization; however, in the case of a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), both [visualization and physical action] should occur.
Bathing is for an image that is not to be plastered; otherwise, there is merely wiping clean.
Since they are prescribed in the Gopāla-mantra, the Śrī-mūrtis are required;
nevertheless, for the pleasure of the Vaiṣṇavas, all the Śrī-mūrtis should be depicted. (Hbhv 5.260)
Now, regarding the characteristics of the glorious forms,
in the *Śrī-hayaśīrṣa-pañcarātra*, within the dialogue between the Blessed Lord Śrī-Hayaśīrṣa and Brahmā:
"Vāsudeva, the primordial form, then created Saṅkarṣaṇa."
The supreme is said to have four forms, each of which is divided threefold;
by means of the distinctions beginning with Keśava, the twelve forms are traditionally taught.
One should place a lotus in the right hand and likewise the Pāñcajanya conch above it;
on the upper left is the mace (gadā) and the discus (cakra) is situated below it. This specific variation of the Primordial Form (Ādi-mūrti) is proclaimed as Keśava.
Wherever this has indeed been established in the form of superior and inferior [levels],
that image known as Nārāyaṇa bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In whose left [hands] there is a lotus and likewise the Pāñcajanya conch above;
in whose right upper [hand] there is a mace and a discus situated below—
this is the manifestation of the Primordial Form (Ādimūrti) celebrated as Mādhava.
The discus is situated at the lower right, with the mace positioned above it;
the lotus is located at the upper left, and the conch is established below.
This particular form of Saṅkarṣaṇa is celebrated as Govinda. (Hbhv 5.265)
With a lotus above on the right and a mace situated below,
this variety of Saṅkarṣaṇa is designated as Viṣṇu.
The conch is displayed above the right [hand] and the discus below;
likewise, the lotus is displayed above the left [hand] and the mace below.
This is the variety known by the name Madhusūdana, and it belongs to Saṅkarṣaṇa.
The discus is shown positioned on his left upper [arm], and the conch below;
his left foot rests upon the cosmic egg, while his right foot rests upon the back of Śeṣa.
One should always fashion Vāmana with a thousand-spoked wheel above on the right and the Pāñcajanya conch situated below, measuring seven tālas in height.
Above and to the right is a wheel, and below is a lotus situated;
on his left side stands Padmā, holding a lotus in her hand.
Whether standing or seated, full of passion and playful grace—
this is indeed a variety of Pradyumna, celebrated as Śrīdhara.
The great discus is on the upper right, with Kaumudī situated below it;
the lotus is on the upper left, and the conch shines below it—he who is thus adorned should be known as Hṛṣīkeśa, established as the granter of all desires. (Hbhv 5.273)
In the upper right [hand] is the lotus and likewise the Pāñcajanya conch below it;
in the upper left is situated the discus, and Kaumodī is positioned below that.
This form, named Padmanābha, has been established as the bestower of liberation. (Hbhv 5.274)
In the upper right is the Pāñcajanya conch, and below it the lotus;
in the upper left is the Kaumudī mace, and the King of Weapons (the discus) is situated below.
This specific form of Aniruddha is known as Dāmodara. (Hbhv 5.275)
Among these, however, two auspicious women should be employed, holding a lotus and a lute respectively.
Thus, in order, the twelve lords of the months of the year are Keśava and the others.
Now, regarding the twenty-four forms, it is stated in the Siddhārthasaṃhitā:
Vāsudeva is considered the bearer of the mace, conch, discus, and lotus;
Keśava likewise carries the lotus, the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Nārāyaṇa always bears the conch, the lotus, the mace, and the discus;
likewise, Mādhava carries the mace, the discus, the conch, and the lotus.
The Supreme Person holds the discus, the lotus, as well as the conch and the mace;
likewise, Adhokṣaja bears the lotus, the Kaumodakī mace, the conch, and the discus.
Saṅkarṣaṇa is remembered as bearing the mace, conch, lotus, and discus;
Govinda bears the discus, mace, lotus, and conch with his arms. (Hbhv 5.280)
Viṣṇu bears the mace, the lotus, as well as the conch and the discus;
Madhusūdana likewise bears the discus, the conch, the lotus, and the mace.
Acyuta always bears the mace, the lotus, the discus, and the conch;
Upendra, however, should carry the conch, the Kaumodakī mace, the discus, and the lotus. (Hbhv 5.282)
Pradyumna is said to bear the discus, conch, mace, and lotus;
Trivikrama bears the lotus, the Kaumodakī mace, the discus, and the conch.
Vāmana always bears the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus;
Śrīdhara bears the lotus, the discus, the mace, and the conch with his arms.
Narasiṃha bears the discus, the lotus, the mace, and the conch;
Janārdana holds the lotus, the Sudarśana discus, the conch, and the mace.
Aniruddha has arms shining with a discus, mace, conch, and lotus;
Hṛṣīkeśa should likewise hold a mace, a discus, a lotus, and a conch.
Padmanābha bears the conch, the lotus, the discus, and likewise the mace;
Dāmodara always holds the lotus, the discus, the mace, and the conch.
Hari is he who bears the conch, the discus, the lotus, and the mace;
Viṣṇu is he who carries the conch, the Kaumodakī mace, the lotus, and the discus.
And these forms are to be known according to the sequence of the right lower hands.
And in the Matsya Purāṇa:
"O twice-born ones, this description of the characteristics of images has been declared in brief; even Bṛhaspati would not be able to describe it in detail. (Hbhv 5.290)
Thus,
the glorious Vaiṣṇavas who follow the Pāñcarātra, having reached the culmination of service to Hari,
highly esteem the Śrī-mūrti because all its limbs have become manifest. (Hbhv 5.291)
One's own chosen forms should be worshipped with their respective mantras;
however, no such restriction exists regarding the form consisting of the Śālagrāma stone.
The form of Kṛṣṇa, with two arms, dark as a rain cloud, possessing the triple-bend (tribhaṅgī) posture and a sweet appearance,
is to be served by the deities who are intent on meditation.
Furthermore, various other glorious forms, such as the avatāras and so forth,
should be depicted in front during the procedure for manifestation, according to their respective specific characteristics.

In this context of the daily rites (*nitya-karma*), the procedure for the consecration of an image and its installation is not fit to be written here; however, it shall be written further on. (Hbhv 5.295)
Now, regarding the Śālagrāma stones,
the *Gautamīya-tantra* states:
"In the region of the Gaṇḍakī river, there is the great site of Śālagrāma."
That stone which originates from that [river] is known as a śālagrāma.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"Glossy, black, pale-white, yellow, or likewise blue;
curved, rough, red, very thick, and unmarked. (Hbhv 5.297)
A Kapilā [cow] that is broken like a frog, one with many wheels or a single wheel,
one with a large mouth or large wheels, or again one whose wheels are stuck,
or some whose wheels are bound, or one whose wheels are broken and facing downward. (Hbhv 5.298)
Now, regarding their merits and defects according to the distinctions of color and so forth,
it is said in that very same [text]:
"One who is glossy brings success in mantra, and one who is black bestows fame."
The white one burns away evil; the yellow one bestows the fruit of sons.
A blue [line] bestows fortune; a red one brings about disease;
a constantly crooked one grants protection yet causes constant anxiety; and a curved one brings poverty. (Hbhv_5.300)
A cow that is too large brings death; one that is unmarked brings a life devoid of fruit;
one that is tawny, brindled, broken-horned, or has many wheels or a single wheel [on its hoof] likewise brings misfortune.
She has a large mouth, large wheels, or alternatively, joined wheels.
Whether the wheel is bound or broken, or if it is turned downwards—he who worships [the deity] with such negligence shall obtain only suffering. (Hbhv 5.303)
And in the *Agni-purāṇa*:
"Likewise, the *vyālamukhī* [is formed] when the *viṣaya* is broken and the *cakrika* is bound;
and likewise the *nārasiṃhī* by means of the revolutions of the *vikāra*. (Hbhv 5.304)
A stone that is tawny, marked with whorls of confusion, or marked with whorls of lines, should be known as a giver of suffering; it never bestows happiness.
The *snigdhā*, the *śyāmā*, likewise the *muktāmāyā* or the *sama-cakrikā*, the *ghoṇi-mūrti*, the one called *anantā*, the *gambhīrā*, and the *sampuṭā*. (Hbhv 5.306)
Subtle in form yet formless, appearing face-to-face and bestowing accomplishment,
the auspicious stone of such a kind— measuring the size of an emblic myrobalan fruit and held in the hollow of both hands— should be worshipped with diligent effort.
Whichever form is dear to one, that one should worship with diligence;
when it is worshipped, one obtains the fruit both in this world and in the next. (Hbhv 5.308)
And these defects pertain to worship performed with desire,
as it was stated by the venerable Lord in the *Brahma-khaṇḍa*: "That which is chipped, cracked, broken, split at the side, or pierced..."
A stone originating from Śālagrāma does not bring about any fault.
And in the Śrī-Rudra-Saṃhitā of the Skanda Purāṇa it is said:
"A Śālagrāma that is chipped, cracked, or broken does not incur any fault;
rather, whatever form is desired by a person, he should worship that with diligence. (Hbhv 5.310)
Likewise:
"Either the discus alone, or it joined there with the lotus;
or the forest garland alone, or Hari standing together with Lakṣmī. (Hbhv 5.311)
In that regard, those beginning with *snigdha* (affectionate) are considered primary, while those beginning with *rakta* (attached) are considered secondary;
for others state that in the absence of the primary ones, the secondary ones are indeed to be honored.
Now, regarding the specific designations based on the particular characteristics of those very [stones],
it is said in the dialogue between the Blessed Lord Brahmā and Śrī [Brahmā]:
"O Brahmā, I always dwell in the abode known as Śālāgrāma."
In that very context, listen to my [explanation] of the names of the various types of chariot-wheel marks.
When the two wheels are seen level at the doorway and not receding inward, he should be known as Vāsudeva; he is white in luster and exceedingly beautiful.
When two wheels are conjoined at a single point, the eastern portion is known as Puṣkala;
it is called Saṅkarṣaṇa and is exceedingly beautiful with red lines.
Pradyumna, however, has a subtle wheel and is likewise yellow in luster;
it is hollow, full of pores, and long in shape. (Hbhv 5.316)
Aniruddha, however, is blue in hue, circular, and exceedingly beautiful;
it has three lines at its opening and its back is marked with a lotus.
Keśava bestows good fortune; he who is four-cornered should be known as Śyāma Nārāyaṇa, whose navel-wheel is likewise elevated. (Hbhv 5.318)
One should recognize that which is endowed with long lines and has a broad cavity on the right as having its face turned upward,
and at the door, one should recognize the form of Hari.
He is the bestower of desires, the bestower of liberation, and especially the bestower of wealth;
he is the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), red-hued, and endowed with a lotus and a discus.
Likewise, [the disc] on the back has the shape of a *bilva* fruit and possesses a very large central hole;
Viṣṇu is of black color and is most beautiful upon a thick disc.
He is to be worshipped with celibacy (*brahmacarya*); otherwise, he becomes a source of obstacles.

And in some cases—such as when Kapila, Narasiṃha, or Pṛthu with his two beautiful wheels are present—one must be one who has undertaken the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*); otherwise, the worship will not take place. (Hbhv 5.322)
Narasiṃha has three dots, while Kapila has five dots;
he should be worshipped with celibacy, otherwise he bestows all obstacles.
In the center, there are two large wheels, colored like jujube fruit or lac;
likewise, above the gate, there is a very beautiful line in the shape of a lotus.
Having worshipped the Sphuṭita, Viṣama, Cakra, Nārasiṃha, and Kāpila [yantras], one attains liberation and becomes victorious in battle.
And in the *Pādma Purāṇa*, in the *Kārttikamāhātmya*:
"He whose face is long and endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics, and whose lines are shaped like the mane [of a lion], is indeed considered Nārasiṃha. (Hbhv_5.326)
In the *Brahma-purāṇa* (PadmaP 5.120.61)—"The Vārāha-mudrā is prescribed for the Śakti-liṅga and the odd-numbered Cakras;
it resembles a sapphire, is thick, marked with three lines, and auspicious. (Hbhv 5.327)
And in that very same *Pādmapurāṇa*:

"One who has the form of a boar, with [the body] slightly bent and adorned with discus-lines, is declared to be a 'Vārāha' [type], bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (Hbhv_5.328)

That stone which is of the color of gold, long in shape, adorned with three dots, and known by the name Matsya, should be understood as the Brāhmī; it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (Hbhv_5.329)
And in some places,
the Lord of Gods takes the form of a fish; it is long in shape,
joined with three dots, and beautiful with the color of brass.
The tortoise of Brahmā is likewise elevated on its back, filled with circular whirlpools;
it possesses a greenish hue and is marked by the Kaustubha gem.
And in that very same *Pādma* [Tantra]:
"A stone shaped like a tortoise and marked with wheels is proclaimed as a *kūrma*. (Hbhv 5.332)
The horse-headed one (Hayagrīva) is indeed of the Brahmā type; his form is like a goad, with lines extending toward the wheel and the *śamī* tree;
he is endowed with many wheels and is dark blue as a rain cloud on his back.
And in some cases,
five lines indeed appear in the shape of Hayagrīva’s goad;
they are seen as blue forms, strewn with many dots.
And in that very same *Pādmapurāṇa*:
"Just as there may be a stone marked with a hanging line [resembling] Hayagrīva, so too should this Hayagrīva be worshipped; he becomes the bestower of knowledge. (Hbhv_5.335)
Furthermore:
"He whose face has the form of a horse and likewise has a rosary upon his head,
or who may have the form of a lotus— he is considered to be Hayashirsha."
In the *Brāhma* [Purāṇa], it is said:
"Vaikuṇṭha has the luster of jewels, with a single discus and likewise a banner;
above the gate, there is a very beautiful line in the shape of a lotus. (Hbhv_5.337)
Śrīdhara, however, O Lord, is thus marked with a forest garland;
he has the appearance of a *kadamba* flower and is adorned with five lines.
One who is round and very short is proclaimed to be a *vāmana*;
he resembles the flower of the linseed plant (*atasī*) and is adorned with a dot (*bindu*). (Hbhv 5.339)
And elsewhere:
"The deity named Vāmana, who is short and possesses great splendor, has his wheel above and his wheel below; when worshipped, he bestows the desired object. (Hbhv 5.340)
In the *Brahma* [Kalpa], the god Sudarśana is likewise dark-complexioned and of great splendor;
there are lines of a mace and a discus on his left side, and indeed on his right. (Hbhv_5.341)
In the *Pādma Purāṇa*, within the *Kārttika-māhātmya*:
"That [diagram] which consists of lines arranged in a circular form is known as the Sudarśana; it bestows the fruit of worship. (Hbhv_5.342)
In the *Brahma* [Purāṇa] (PadmaP 5.120.69):
"Likewise, Dāmodara is thick, with a wheel established in the middle;
it has the luster of *dūrvā* grass, is crowded with gates, and likewise has yellow lines. (Hbhv 5.343)
And in that same *Pādmapurāṇa*:
"There are two wheels above and below, and a slit in the mouth that is not too long;
there is also a single vertical line on the wheel—he is known as Dāmodara. (Hbhv 5.344)
And elsewhere it is said:
"Dāmodara should be known as gross, whereas he who has subtle apertures resides in the center of the wheel; when worshipped there, he always bestows happiness. (Hbhv 5.345)
Indeed, he who is of various colors and named Ananta, marked by the coils of a serpent, should be known as Ananta; he bestows the fruit of all worship.
And in that very same *Pādmapurāṇa*:
"He who has an infinite wheel and is distinguished by many marks should be known as Ananta; he bestows the fruit of all worship. (Hbhv_5.347)
On the peak is seen a *liṅga* produced from Śālagrāma,
by which one named Yogeśvara removes the sin of killing a Brahmin. (Hbhv_5.348)
One who is not red-complexioned should daily worship the one named Padmanābha, accompanied by a lotus-umbrella and tulasī; even a poor person shall thus become a lord.
One should point out the net of rays called "Golden," which has the form of the moon,
abounds in golden streaks, and is adorned with the luster of crystal.
Furthermore: "The deity Hṛṣīkeśa is declared to have the form of a half-moon;
by worshipping him, one attains heaven and all desired objects. (Hbhv 5.351)
On the left side, when the wheel is even, that [form] is black in color and marked with a dot;
it is known as Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Likewise, the god Trivikrama is dark-complexioned and possesses great luster;
he has a discus on his left side and a line on his right.
That stone known as Kṛṣṇa, which is adorned with a forest garland (vanamālā) turned clockwise, bestows wealth, grain, and happiness. (Hbhv 5.354)
According to the Gautamīya:
