"If, through the merits of many births, one should obtain a black stone marked with the sign of a cow’s hoof, by that [attainment] one's cycle of birth is brought to an end. (Hbhv 5.355)
Where four lines are seen running along the sides,
and two wheels are in the middle region, that stone is indeed "four-faced" (caturmukhā).
Furthermore, in that very same [chapter] of the *Padmapurāṇa*:
"That *śālagrāma* stone upon which lines produced by *vajra*-insects appear arranged in rows is known as the *viṣṇu-pañjara*. (Hbhv_5.357)
A row of lines coiled like a serpent is Śeṣaka;
when there are two rows in the shape of a lotus with a hanging line in the middle, that is to be known as Garuḍa; Janārdana has four wheels.
Having four wheels, a subtle opening, and a belly marked by a forest garland;
this glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Śālagrāma stones endowed with these characteristics are auspicious;
among them, those that are subtle are remembered as bestowing excellent results.
And so it is said in the Śrī-Bhagavad-Brahma-Saṃvāda at that very place:
"To the extent that a stone is subtle, to that same extent is its great merit;
therefore, one should always worship it for the sake of attaining dharma, kāma, and artha. (Hbhv_5.361)
Even there, O Brahmā, I always dwell together with Śrī in that very [tree] which is like an āmalakī fruit and is exceedingly subtle. (Hbhv 5.362)
Now, regarding the majesty of the Śrī-Śālagrāma stone:
By the mere touch of a Śālagrāma stone, the sins of ten million lifetimes are destroyed;
how much more so the act of worshiping there, which brings about the presence of Hari! (Hbhv 5.363)
In that very same [text], the *Pādme Māgha-māhātmya*, it is said:
"Whoever worships Hari on the discus produced from a *śālagrāma* stone has, every single day, performed the merit of a thousand *rājasūya* sacrifices. (Hbhv 5.364)
That Brahman which the Vedāntas proclaim as devoid of qualities and immutable—grace from that [Brahman] comes to men through the worship of the Śālagrāma stone. (Hbhv 5.365)
Just as fire situated within a large piece of wood becomes manifest when it is being rubbed,
so too does the all-pervading Hari become manifest in the Śālagrāma stone.
O Vaiśya, even those of evil conduct who are otherwise ineligible for [sacred] rites do not go to the abode of Yama if they are worshippers of the Śālagrāma.
He does not delight so much in prosperity nor so much in his own palace as he always delights in the discus-marked Śālagrāma stone.
By him who has worshipped Hari in the form of the Śālagrāma stone, the Agnihotra has been offered and the earth, together with its oceans, has been given as a gift.
Even that lowest of men who is pervaded by sensual desires, anger, and greed,
goes to the world of Hari through the worship of the Śālagrāma stone.
The man who always worships Govinda at Śālagrāma does not fall from heaven until the dissolution of all things.

O Vaiśya, without visiting sacred fords, without giving gifts, without performing sacrifices, and even without spiritual wisdom, a man attains liberation through the worship of the Śālagrāma stone. (Hbhv 5.372)
O Vaiśya, one who worships Acyuta at Śālagrāma does not go to hell, nor to dwelling in a womb, nor to the state of an animal, nor to birth as a worm—even if he were a sinner. (Hbhv 5.373)
He who, knowing the ritual procedure and the mantras for initiation, offers an oblation into the wheel, goes to the abode of Viṣṇu; this I have declared as the truth, the absolute truth.
The worship of the Śālagrāma stone is performed with various food offerings, flowers, incense, lamps, ointments, songs, instrumental music, hymns, and so forth. (Hbhv 5.375)
Whatever man, devoted to devotion, performs [this] in the Kali age,
he rejoices in the presence of Hari for thousands of crores of kalpas.
Whatever fruit is obtained by seeing and worshipping ten million lingas,
that same fruit is obtained here by means of even a single Śālagrāma stone.
Wherever Keśava resides in the form of the Śālagrāma stone,
there dwell the gods, asuras, yakṣas, and the fourteen worlds.
But the man who performs a śrāddha ceremony upon a śālagrāma stone—
his ancestors remain satisfied in heaven for a hundred kalpas.
Wherever there is a Śālagrāma stone, that sacred site extends for three yojanas;
whatever gift, recitation, or fire-offering is performed there becomes ten million times more efficacious.
Within a distance of one krośa all around the vicinity of Śālagrāma,
even a man from Kīkaṭa who dies goes to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
Whoever gives the supreme gift of a Śālagrāma stone discus,
by him the entire earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, has been given.
In the *Skānda-purāṇa*, within the *Kārttika-māhātmya* (Padma-khaṇḍa 5.120.4–43), in the dialogue between Śrī Śiva and Skanda:
"O Mahāsena, the three worlds, including all things moving and unmoving, always remain merged within the Śālagrāma stone along with me. (Hbhv_5.383)
He by whom [a cow] is saluted with reverence, bathed, and likewise honored,
shall obtain merit equal to ten million sacrifices and the fruit of giving ten million cows.
O Brahmin, even one who is constantly attached to sensual desires, if he is devoid of the spirit of devotion yet worships the Śālagrāma stone, he shall become Acyuta himself.
The image of the Śālagrāma stone destroys ten million killings when it is remembered, recited, meditated upon, worshipped, and saluted. (Hbhv 5.386)
Upon seeing a Śālagrāma stone, manifold sins depart, just as herds of deer flee in fear upon seeing a lion in the forest. (Hbhv 5.387)
When a person pays homage during the worship of the Śālagrāma stone,
their sins go to destruction, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun.
Whether attached to sensual desires or filled with anger, whether through devotion or even without devotion, one who performs the worship of the Śālagrāma stone shall attain liberation.
There is no fear of Vaivasvata (Yama), nor likewise of birth and death,
for him who narrates the stories of Viṣṇu before a Śālagrāma stone.
That man who, devoted to bhakti, performs the worship of the Śālagrāma stone with songs, musical instruments, and hymns in the Kali age,
rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu for thousands of crores of kalpas.
Even if men on this earth who are my devotees perform a salutation to the Śālagrāma stone with an absence of [proper] devotion, they shall never experience fear. (Hbhv 5.392)
Those who, arrogant with the power of my devotion, do not bow to me, their Lord, Vāsudeva—they should not be known as my devotees, for they are indeed sinners. (Hbhv 5.393)
"O son, I always dwell upon the Śālagrāma stone;
it was granted as my own abode by the gratified God out of devotion. (Hbhv 5.394)
Whatever fruit is obtained when I am worshipped with thousands of millions of lotuses,
that fruit is multiplied ten millionfold by the worship of a Śālagrāma stone.
I have not been worshipped by those mortals, nor have I been saluted by those men, who have not performed the worship of the Śālagrāma stone in the world of mortals. (Hbhv 5.396)
Whoever performs my worship at the edge of a Śālagrāma stone has, in fact,
worshipped me constantly for twenty-one yugas.
O son, what is the use of worshipping hundreds of lingas if they are devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu, provided that the image of the Śālagrāma stone has not been worshipped?
My offering—whether unworthy leaves, flowers, fruits, or water—attains complete purity once it has come into contact with a Śālagrāma stone. (Hbhv 5.399)
For he who, having been a devotee of Maheśvara, hates the supreme emblem (liṅga) of Vaiṣṇava, indeed goes to hell for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
Even if worshipped but once, human beings attain liberation through an image produced from a Śālagrāma stone, even if they are devoid of Sāṅkhya knowledge.
Whatever fruit is obtained by seeing ten million auspicious marks and by worshipping them,
that same fruit may indeed be attained by [worshipping] even a single mark on a Śālagrāma stone.
Therefore, my dear son, for the sake of pleasing me, my devotees should always perform the worship of the Śālagrāma stone with devotion. (Hbhv 5.403)
Wherever Keśava resides in the form of the Śālagrāma stone,
there dwell the gods, the asuras, the yakṣas, and the fourteen worlds.
If the ancestors are once satiated with a funeral ball (piṇḍa) at the edge of a Śālagrāma stone, they dwell there for him; no limit to that number exists.
For every meritorious deed, my son, there is indeed a measure for its fruit;
however, in the worship of the Śālagrāma stone, the fruit is beyond all measure.
Whoever gives a stone originating from Śālagrāma to a brāhmaṇa who is a devotee of Viṣṇu has, by that act, performed many sacrifices. (Hbhv 5.407)
(From this point onward, the verses are not seen in the original source.
In this world, the stone originating from Śālagrāma is difficult for humans to obtain;
it is not acquired without merit, especially in the Kali age. (Hbhv_5.408)
That person is blessed in the world, and his life is fruitful, in whose house the pure Śālagrāma stone is worshipped. (Hbhv 5.409)

That person who, having fully restrained the collection of the senses, performs the worship of the Śālagrāma stone with devotion, partakes in the merit of a horse sacrifice for every single flower offered.
Whether at the proper time or at an improper time, whether with devotion or without devotion, whoever performs the worship of the Śālagrāma stone partakes in merit.
Even through hatred, greed, hypocrisy, or deceit,
one is liberated from sin upon seeing the deity born from the Śālagrāma stone.
Whether one is impure, of wicked conduct, or devoid of truth and purity,
by touching a Śālagrāma stone, one becomes pure instantly.
Whoever daily offers a hundred *prasthas* of sesame seeds with devotion attains that same fruit by worshipping the Śālagrāma stone. (Hbhv 5.414)
O son, a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a root, water, or dūrvā grass and unbroken rice grains,
when offered upon a śālagrāma stone, become equal to Mount Meru.

Even one who performs the worship of the maṇḍala (cakrapūjā) devoid of the prescribed ritual and lacking the ritual actions and mantras, obtains the full fruit as declared in the scriptures. (Hbhv 5.416)
And in that very same [text], elsewhere it says:
"But he who, having placed the leader of mountains upon his shoulder, carries the path—by him all the three worlds, including the moving and the unmoving, would be carried. (Hbhv 5.417)
Whatever sin a man commits, such as the killing of a Brahmin or any other,
the worship of the Śālagrāma stone quickly consumes it all.
In the worship of the Śālagrāma stone, there is no need for ritual offerings, nor mantras, nor recitation, nor meditative cultivation; there is neither praise nor ceremonial service.
Wherever there is a Śālagrāma stone, that sacred site extends for three yojanas;
there, every act of giving and every burnt offering becomes ten millionfold in merit.
The man who performs a śrāddha ceremony upon a śālagrāma stone—
his ancestors remain satisfied in heaven for a hundred kalpas.
Within a distance of one *krośa* all around the vicinity of Śālagrāma,
even a man from Kīkaṭa who dies goes to the realm of Vaikuṇṭha.
And in the *Padma-purāṇa*:
"Whoever gives the supreme gift of the discus-marked Śālagrāma stone, by him the entire circle of the earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, has been given. (Hbhv_5.423)
In the Garuḍa Purāṇa: "The ancestors and human beings always abide in sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā and Puṣkara."
Sacrifices, wisdom, and even the Meru mountains marked with wheels dwell in the house of one [who possesses these].
In the *Pādmapurāṇa*, within the *Kārttikamāhātmya* in the dialogue between Śrī Yama and Dhūmrakeśa:
"Those men by whom Hari has been worshipped upon a *śālagrāma* stone—having purified their sins, they shall attain enlightenment for the sake of liberation. (Hbhv_5.425)
In the month of Kārttika, Hari bestows the state of having the same form (sārūpya) upon one in Mathurā; indeed,
when Kṛṣṇa is worshipped on a Śālagrāma stone with the ancestors in view, he shall deliver those ancestors to his own world.
And in the Bṛhannāradīya [1.38.67–68], at the conclusion of the narrative of Yajñadhvaja:
"Wherever Keśava resides in the form of the Śālagrāma stone, there the asuras, bhūtas, vetālas, and the like do not cause harm. (Hbhv 5.427)
Wherever there is a Śālagrāma stone, that is a sacred ford (tīrtha) and a forest of austerity (tapo-vana),
because the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana is ever-present there.
If those Śālagrāma stones are worshipped— whether twelve or a hundred— with devotion, then the fruit shall be even greater.
Now, regarding the specific fruit resulting from their abundance,
it is stated in the *Māgha-māhātmya* of the *Padma-purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Devadūta and Vikuṇḍala (3.31.124–126):
"O Vaiśya, there are twelve stones indeed produced from the *śālagrāma* stone."
I shall tell you of the merit belonging to him by whom [the deity] has been worshipped according to the prescribed rule.
Whatever merit would result from worshipping twelve million lingas with golden lotuses at twelve different times, that same merit shall be obtained in a single day.
Furthermore, he who worships with devotion a hundred *śālagrāma* stones shall dwell in the world of Hari and, upon returning here, is born as a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).
In the *Skānda-purāṇa*, within the *Kārttika-māhātmya* (Padma-khaṇḍa 6.120.31–33), in the dialogue between Śrī Śiva and Skanda:
"Listen to me regarding the merit of that Vaiṣṇava who constantly worships exactly twelve stone slabs originating from Śālagrāma. (Hbhv_5.433)
By worshipping ten million thousand liṅgas on the bank of the Ganges,
that which would take eight yugas to achieve through residing in Kāśī is accomplished in a single day.
Moreover, what need is there for much? Indeed, when a Vaiṣṇava man performs worship, even the gods beginning with Brahmā cannot calculate the extent of his merit.
Now, regarding the prohibition of buying and selling that [Śālagrāma]: in that very same place (*Padma Purāṇa* 3.31.144–146) it is said:
"The man who sets a price upon a Śālagrāma stone..."
The seller, the one who consents, and he who initiates the examination [are all at fault].
All of them go to hell until the dissolution of the world at the call [of Brahmā];
therefore, O Brahmin, one should utterly avoid the buying and selling of the Discus.
Now, regarding the prohibition of consecration,
it is stated in that very same [text]:
"In the case of a Śālagrāma stone, however, no consecration is required at all."
Having first performed a great worship, the wise one should then worship her.
Thus,
among the various bases [of worship], just as with the sun and other deities, the Śālagrāma stone alone shall be the supreme base for Hari, even more so than [his] embodied forms. (Hbhv 5.439)
Now, regarding the superiority of all bases,
it is stated in that same *Pādma* [3.31.115–117]:
"In the heart, in the sun, in water, or likewise in images and on sacrificial altars..."
Having fully worshipped Hari, those men go indeed to the station of Viṣṇu.
Alternatively, Vāsudeva should always be worshipped by those seeking liberation upon the disc-marked stone of Śālagrāma, which is fashioned by the *vajra-kīṭa* insect.
For that is the abode of Viṣṇu, O Vaiśya, which destroys all sins, bestows all merit, and grants liberation to everyone. (Hbhv 5.442)
In that very same *Kārttika-māhātmya*, within the dialogue between Yama and Dhūmrakeśa, it is stated:
"O Prince, worship of him is prescribed in an image made of stone,
wood, metal, plaster, paint, or sand."
The form of Śrī is traditionally remembered as eightfold: consisting of mind and consisting of jewels.
In the Śālagrāma stone, however, there is the direct service of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
Vāsudeva, the teacher of the world, is eternally present there. (Hbhv 5.444)
In the *Skānda Purāṇa*, within the *Kārttika-māhātmya* during the dialogue between Śrī Śiva and Skanda:
"O best of gods, Hari does not reside in an image made of gold, nor in one made of jewels, nor in one made of stone;
rather, Hari always dwells within the *śālagrāma* stone. (Hbhv_5.445)
Therefore it has been said:

"The tulasī from contact with whose feet destroys the sin of killing; the water at His feet destroys theft; the food offering destroys the evil resulting from drinking excessive liquor; and [the dust] destroys the sin born of union with the wife of one's guru."
The mind is dependent on the Lord Śrī, one’s state of being is with the devotees of Hari, and the sin born from their association is removed;
such is this extraordinary and world-transcending majesty of the Nṛsiṃha residing in the Śālagrāma stone.
Who, even one who has taken refuge in Śrī Caitanya, is able to count the waves of the ocean of majesty of the Blessed One in the form of the Śālagrāma stone? (Hbhv 5.447)
Now, regarding the necessity of the worship of the Śālagrāma stone,
it is stated in the Padma Purāṇa:
"He who eats anything whatsoever without having worshipped the Śālagrāma stone..."
And he is born as a worm in the excrement of outcasts and the like for an entire kalpa.
And in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"He whose body is pierced by the tips of the peaks of Mount Gaurava, yet in whom no inclination arises toward the worship of the Śālagrāma stone— " Hbhv_5.449.
Thus, the illustrious Blessed One, who is essentially present in all *śālagrāma* stones,
is to be worshipped by the twice-born, by women, by *śūdras*, and by those devoted to the Blessed One.
Likewise, in the *Skānda Purāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Brahmā and Nārada concerning the *cāturmāsya* vow and the worship of the *śālagrāma* stone, it is stated:
"Brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, or even virtuous śūdras have the qualification for the *śālagrāma*; never others. (Hbhv 5.451)
In that very same place, elsewhere it is said:
"Whether they be women or Śūdras, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, or others, by worshipping the stone discus (śilā-cakra), they attain the eternal state. (Hbhv_5.452)
Thus, whatever statement is clearly heard that serves as a prohibition, that should be understood by those who perceive the truth as being directed against non-Vaiṣṇavas. (Hbhv 5.453)
Just as I am to be honored by a Brahmin alone, whether he be pure or impure,
contact with the hand of a woman or a Śūdra is more unbearable than even a thunderbolt.
By the mere recitation of the *praṇava*, by the worship of a *śālagrāma* stone, and by sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Śūdra shall fall into the state of a Caṇḍāla. (Hbhv 5.455)

Sanātana confirms that very point through the words of Śrī Nārada: "O Brāhmaṇa... [and so forth]. For virtuous Vaiṣṇavas, even if they are Śūdras, in the worship of the Śrī Śālagrāma stone—that is, in the worship of the Śālagrāma stone—[there is no restriction].
"Of others" means of other *śūdras* who are destitute.
For this very reason, it is said concerning the *śūdra* in the *Vāyu Purāṇa*: "He should be a giver without asking; he may practice agriculture for the sake of his livelihood."
One should constantly listen to the Purāṇas and worship the Śālagrāma.

Thus, because this statement contradicts the declarations of the great Purāṇas that "I am to be worshipped by Brāhmaṇas alone," it should be understood as a fabrication devised by certain Smārtas who are dominated by envy. Furthermore, if this were established by logic and possessed a valid foundation, then non-Vaiṣṇavas and Śūdras, as well as women of that nature, would not be permitted to perform his worship.
It must be established that this [practice] is to be performed by those who have received the initiation of Viṣṇu according to the prescribed rules;
for even among Śūdras and outcastes (antyajas), those who are Vaiṣṇavas are indeed not called "Śūdras" and so forth.
And thus it is said in the Nāradīya:
"O protector of the earth, even a *śvapaca* who is a devotee of Viṣṇu is superior to a twice-born [Brahmin]," as stated in the *Itihāsa-samuccaya*. Furthermore, in the same work:
"One should not [look upon] a Śūdra, nor a Niṣāda, nor likewise a *śvapaca*, if they are devotees of the Blessed One."
Because of that commonality of birth, he certainly goes to hell.
Thus it is said; and in the Padma Purāṇa:
"Those Śūdras who are devotees of the Blessed One are indeed Bhāgavata men."
Among all castes, those Śūdras who are not devotees of Janārdana [are the lowest].
Thus, this and more will be clearly explained in detail later in the section on the majesty of Vaiṣṇavas.
Furthermore, by the power of initiation from the Lord, even Śūdras and others certainly attain equality with Brāhmaṇas.
And so it is said there: "Just as [base metal] attains the state of gold," and so forth.
This has indeed already been written previously in the section on the greatness of initiation (*dīkṣā-māhātmya*).
For this very reason, there is the speech of Devahūti in the third book [of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa]: [BhP 3.33.6]—
By merely hearing or reciting its name, by bowing down to it, or even by remembering it at any time,
even a dog-eater immediately becomes fit for the sacrificial bath.
How much less, O Blessed One, could it be from seeing you?
Thus,
it means that he becomes fit— that is, capable— for the *savana* (soma-pressing) and for sacrifice.
For this very reason, Vaiṣṇavas are counted together with Brahmins in one and the same category.
And so it is said in the *Haribhaktisudhodaya*, in the dialogue between the Blessed Lord and Brahmā:
"Holy fords, the Aśvattha tree, cows, brāhmaṇas,
and likewise My devotees— these five should be known as My own bodies."
Thus, in the description of the great King Śrī Pṛthu in the fourth book [of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, 4.21.12]:
"His commands were never thwarted anywhere, and he held the single scepter over the seven continents."
Except for a Brahmin family, except for one of the Acyuta lineage.
Thus, in the speech of the Great King [BhP 4.21.37]:
"May your splendor never prevail through great supernatural powers."
In a family of twice-born men who had conquered the gods through endurance, austerity, and sacred knowledge, he was born himself from a royal lineage.
Thus [it is said].

Here, from that splendor of the royal family which arose through the great commentaries and the supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) of the venerable Śrī Svāmipāda, there arose among the families of the twice-born (*dvija*), the Brahmins,
those Vaiṣṇavas who were unconquered and worthy of worship by the gods.
May it never arise in their family; may it never come into being at any time. In what kind of [family]?
"Even without external prosperities, he shines resplendently by means of self-restraint and other virtues himself.
And in the *Purañjana* narrative (*BhP* 3.26.24), it says:
"O hero's wife, I placed self-control in him for you."

Whoever has committed an offense against anyone other than a member of the family of the gods of the earth shall not see him free from fear and joyful in the three worlds— unless he is before the enemy of Mura, or otherwise before a servant of that enemy.
Thus it is said.
Regarding that, the same commentary states: "O wife of the Hero!
He who has committed an offense against you..."

In that regard, O Brāhmaṇa, I have maintained self-restraint (*dama*)— that is, I exercise punishment (*daṇḍa*)— toward anyone other than those from a brāhmaṇa family, and toward anyone other than the servants of Murāri;
such statements are indeed many in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata and other scriptures.
Thus, indeed, the equality of Vaiṣṇavas with Brāhmaṇas is established.

Furthermore, by such statements as "from a Brāhmaṇa endowed with the twelve qualities" (BhP 7.9.10), the superiority of Vaiṣṇavas—even those born of low castes—over Brāhmaṇas is most clearly indicated.
For this very reason, the venerable Lord Hayagrīva stated in the *Śrī-hayaśīrṣa-pañcarātra*, at the conclusion of the *Śrī-puruṣottama-pratiṣṭhā*:
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the image-protectors (mūrtipas) should be given as half of that for the preceptor (deśika);
half of that for the Vaiṣṇavas; and half of that for the twice-born (dvijans).
Thus,
it is entirely logical that the Blessed One is worshiped by all others.
Likewise, in the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*, within the narrative of Priyavrata, even the religious hunter (dharmavyādha) is said to have performed the worship of the Śrī Śālagrāma stone.
Then, having heard those words of the Dharma-fowler, he stood there amazed; and the fowler, having brought them both, showed them to you.
The two elderly men, having washed their garments, sat upon their seats before their own gurus,
as did the well-worshipped Śālagrāma stone near them.

Thus, the established practice here is that, especially in this Middle Country and particularly in the South, the authority of the most eminent Śrī-Vaiṣṇavas is the standard; this is the general direction.
In this way, the eligibility of Vaiṣṇavas for the recitation of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam and other such matters should also be understood.
Since injunctions and prohibitions do not apply to the devotees of the Lord—as evidenced by such scriptural statements as "Of the gods, sages, beings, ancestors, and men...

(BhP 11.5.41)—and since no fault whatsoever can arise from the renunciation of ritual action and so forth, this has been clearly taught by such statements as "One should perform those actions... (BhP 11.20.9) and "When the Lord shows grace to someone... (BhP 4.29.46).
All of this will be clearly explained in detail later on in the *Śrī-Vaiṣṇava-Māhātmya* (HbhvC 5.454–455).

Here, the term "dog-eater" (*śvādatva*) refers specifically to the particular caste of those who eat dogs; for according to the etymology "one who eats a dog" (*śvānam atti*), the present tense is used, which—as in the case of the term *kravyād* ("meat-eater")—implies that it is one's habitual practice.
If, however, the intention were to prescribe an expiation for an occasional act of eating, then the past tense would have been employed.
This is also contradicted by the maxim that "conventional usage (rūḍhi) sets aside etymological derivation (yoga).
For this very reason, they have explained it as "śvapaca" (dog-cooker).
Furthermore, in this context, *savana* refers to the Soma sacrifice.

Therefore, O Blessed One, from the mere hearing of His name or any one of these means, there occurs immediately the destruction of the sins of *prārabdha-karma*—both those already commenced and those that initiate the state of being born into a low caste which is unfavorable to the fitness for the *savana* (the sacrificial bath). This is understood from what was said by the Blessed One to Uddhava: "Therefore, devotion fixed upon Me purifies even dog-cookers (*śvapāka*) from their very birth" (*BhP* 11.14.20). This statement is made for the sake of the *kaimutya* argument (the principle of "how much more so"), yet here "fitness" refers merely to the cessation of the *prārabdha-karma* sins that cause one to attain the status of a dog-cooker.
However, for the purpose of the *savana* (the ritual extraction of Soma), the addition of another quality (*guṇāntarādhāna*) is indeed required—
just as, although Brahmin boys possess the capacity at birth, there is still a requirement for the *sāvitra* and *daikṣya* initiations;
since the attainment of right conduct (*sad-ācāra*) occurs only upon such initiations like the *sāvitra*, engagement in the *savana* would not be appropriate [prior to them].
Therefore, intending that the purport lies merely in its being worthy of worship, the authors of the *Ṭīkā* have also stated: "By this, the state of being worshipful is indicated.
Nevertheless, by virtue of its removing the defects of birth (*jāti-doṣa*), the quality of destroying even those karmas already set in motion (*prārabdha*) is clearly established;
indeed, it should be diligently upheld by Vaiṣṇavas, just like the *śālagrāma* stone.
And she is always to be honored as being endowed with the marks of the wheel on her palms and soles.
In that same *Brāhma* [Purāṇa] it is said:
"The deity born from Śālagrāma and the deity born from Dvāravatī—wherever there is a conjunction of these two, there is liberation; of this there is no doubt. (Hbhv_5.457)
In the *Skānda Purāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Brahmā and Nārada, it is said:
"O tiger among sages, wherever a stone marked with the discus stands before a *śālagrāma* stone, there all prosperities increase. (Hbhv_5.458)
In that very same work, elsewhere it is said:
"He who daily worships twelve *śālagrāma* stones, joined with [stones from] Dvāravatī, is glorified in Vaikuṇṭha. (Hbhv 5.459)
Now, regarding the characteristics of the marks of the auspicious Dvārakā discus, it is stated in the Śrī Prahlāda-saṃhitā: "One [mark] is Sudarśana; by two [marks], Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is remembered."
With three [syllables] he is named Trivikrama, and with four, Janārdana.
Vāsudeva is said to consist of five [syllables], Pradyumna of six;
Baladeva consists of seven, while Puruṣottama consists of eight.
With nine [faces] he is the Ninefold Array (Navavyūha), with ten he is the Ten-formed (Daśamūrtika);
with eleven he is Aniruddha, and with twelve he is the Twelve-fold Self (Dvādaśātmaka).
In other systems involving many wheels, he is proclaimed as Infinite (Ananta).
Now, regarding the majesty of the twelve-spoked discus, it is said in the Vārāha Purāṇa:
"Whatever stones are marked with the discus of Viṣṇu..."
By the mere touch of them, one is liberated from all sins.
In the Gāruḍa [Purāṇa]: "But stones such as the Sudarśana and others, when worshipped, grant all desires. (Hbhv_5.464)
And in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Whether with devotion or without devotion, if a person worships the mark of the discus (cakrāṅka), even if he be of very wicked conduct, he is liberated; there is no doubt in this. (Hbhv 5.465)
And in the *Dvārakā-māhātmya*, regarding the description of Śrī Brahmā and others who had gone to Dvārakā, it is said:
"This indeed is Cakra-tīrtha, where the stone is marked with the discus;
it grants liberation to sinners in this world, being worshipped even in the land of the Mlecchas. (Hbhv 5.466)
Now, regarding the distinction of fruits according to the distinction of the discs among those very [stones],
the *Kapila-pañcarātra* states:
"A single disc made of stone from Dvāravatī is most auspicious."
That which is named Sudarśana bestows exclusively the fruit of liberation.
With two [verses], Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
with these [three verses], he who is the form of Acyuta grants the fruit of Indra’s realm.
Vāsudeva has four arms and four discs; he bestows the fruits of the four aims of life and removes the fear of birth and death.
With six [syllables], he is indeed Pradyumna; he bestows fortune and splendor.
With seven, he is Balabhadra, the increaser of lineage and fame.
The Supreme Person grants all that is desired by means of eight [circles],
while Nṛsiṃha, with nine circles, bestows unsurpassed fruit.

Aniruddha bestows sovereignty with ten [repetitions], while he who is remembered as the one who descends in ten incarnations (Daśāvatāraka) grants a kingdom with ten; with eleven, he bestows sovereign power.
This Nirvāṇa consists of twelve aspects; it bestows happiness and is well-honored.
Now, regarding the defects and virtues according to the distinction of colors and so forth, as well as [the criteria for] being worthy or unworthy of worship, it is stated in that very same [text]:
"The black [smoke] always brings death, and the smoky [smoke] is indeed terrifying."
A variegated [halo] brings about ill-health, while a blue one causes the loss of wealth.
A cracked [image], when worshipped, will certainly bestow the miseries of poverty;
a pale one brings great suffering, while a broken one causes separation from one's wife. (Hbhv 5.475)
The white-colored [deity] bestows the ultimate and most excellent happiness of sons, grandsons, wealth, and sovereignty; therefore, one should worship him.
In the Śrī-Prahlāda-Saṃhitā:
"A black cow always brings death; a tawny one causes fear; a brindled cow bestows disease and affliction; and a yellow cow destroys wealth. (Hbhv_5.477)
Those that are smoke-colored lead to the loss of wealth; those that are broken destroy one's wife;
likewise, those with holes, those that are triangular, those with uneven circles, and those shaped like a half-moon—these are indeed not fit for worship.
According to Gārgya and Gālava,
the twelve-spoked wheel is auspicious and bestows happiness;
it is excellent and brings well-being to men when it is either circular or square.
That which is triangular, uneven, perforated, or likewise broken, and that which has the shape of a half-moon, is not worthy of worship;
no fruit whatsoever arises from worshipping such [a site]. (Hbhv 5.480)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Abode," in the *Śrī Bhagavad-bhakti-vilāsa* composed by Śrī Gopāla Bhaṭṭa.
6. The Sixth Chapter: The Playful Bathing Ritual (Snāpanika-vilāsa) of the Snāpanika [section].
By the grace of Śrī Caitanya, for one who desires to perform that beautiful festival of Gokula in that very form, the procedure for the worship of the image is now described.
The self-manifested and the installed are considered the two types of images;
Kṛṣṇa is self-manifested, while the others are installed by means of consecration.
And as it is stated in the *Padmottara-khaṇḍa* [PadmaP 6.253.4–7]:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe the abode for the worship of Hari;
its installation is proclaimed to be of two kinds: that which is self-manifested (*svayam-vyakta*) and that which is established. (Hbhv_6.3)

Having fashioned an image of Hari out of stone, clay, wood, metal, or other materials, its installation is indeed performed according to the rites prescribed in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Āgamas. (Hbhv 6.4)
Listen to me as I explain that which is called "establishment" (sthāpana), for it is self-manifested; in that [image], Viṣṇu himself is present for men on earth. (Hbhv 6.5)
The Lord Himself is manifest in stone and wood; indeed, that is remembered as "self-manifest" (svayam-vyakta).
Because a self-manifest form is difficult to obtain, the most excellent of Śrī-Vaiṣṇavas, having installed it according to the prescribed rites, should worship the image thus established. (Hbhv 6.6)
In the *Haribhaktisudhodaya*, it is said:
"By means of [devotion to Hari], a man not only delivers his own lineage, but the entire world;
through worship of the Deity (arcā), men obtain their desired fruit, which is difficult to attain even through sacrifices and other rites."
Just as one who relies upon a wish-fulfilling creeper that grants all desires relies upon an image.
Now, regarding the propitiation of the Śrī-mūrti and the purifications of the self and so forth:
one should wash the Śrī-mūrti, which is worthy of cleansing, with auspicious scented water and other such substances; as for any other [image], one should wipe it clean with the root mantra.

Having touched the heart of the Śrī-mūrti, one should recite one's own mantra eight times. In this way, there is the propitiation of the form; from that propitiation comes the purification of oneself.
This is the first [purification], while the second consists in being free from distraction.
"Purity of place and purity of materials were described previously;
thus, by way of these different types, there shall be a fourfold purity. (Hbhv 6.10)
And it was said by the venerable Nārada:
"Having taken water with a flower, one should sprinkle all the ritual implements;
then, having placed the deity in a vessel, one should perform the bath for removing impurities. (Hbhv 6.11)
One should also perform the purification of substances such as flowers and unbroken rice (akṣata) by means of mantras and so forth;
one should carry out the purification of the image through washing, the application of water, and the like.
Then, with undistracted mind, one should practice the purification of oneself and the purification of the site.
Thus it is said.
Some desire the supreme purity of mantra and the purity of mind;
thus, there are six meritorious purities according to the tradition. (Hbhv 6.13)
Now, for the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā):

on a pedestal made of copper or other materials, smeared with sandalwood paste and the like, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus provided with a pericarp, enriched with three concentric circles, and possessing sixteen filaments. (Hbhv 6.14)
Having drawn the worship-diagram (pūjā-yantra), which has six spokes, is quadrangular, and is adorned with four gates, one should perform the worship of the seat (pīṭha) therein.
On the pedestal, to the left of the Blessed One, one should worship the venerable gurus, the sandals of the guru,
the ancient perfected ones such as Nārada, and other Vaiṣṇavas.
And on the right, one should worship Durgā, Gaṇeśa, and Sarasvatī;
there, one should perform the worship according to the previously described ritual placement (*nyāsa*). (Hbhv 6.17)
Then, in the center, one should place the Foundation Power (Ādhāra-śakti) and so forth; in the intermediate directions, Dharma and the rest;
in the four cardinal directions, Adharma and the rest; and again in the center, Ananta and the others.
One should worship the Śaktis on the nine [or] eight petals and in the pericarp;
likewise, one should worship the Pīṭha-mantra above that, as previously described.
Then, upon that pedestal, one should establish the Śrīmūrti with the root mantra;
having taken up a handful of flowers, one should contemplate the form of one's chosen deity.
Then, having offered three handfuls of flowers with the root mantra,
one should contemplate the supreme identity between oneself and the form of one's chosen deity.
Now, since placing the feet firmly on the ground is prohibited during the worship of the deity following the invocation and other rites,
one should perform the invocation and so forth while keeping the feet placed upon the ground.
One should perform the invocation (āvāhana) at that place which is to be invoked and serves as the locus;
however, in the case of installing a Śālagrāma, there is neither invocation nor dismissal (visarjana).
And so it has been said:
"Just as there is neither dismissal nor invocation in the case of a stationary [deity], so too in the worship of the Śālagrāma, there is indeed no invocation or dismissal. (Hbhv 6.24)
Just as the Lord Hari has manifested in the Śālagrāma stone, he is not manifest in that same way elsewhere— in the sun and other such objects, nor even in Vaikuṇṭha— though he is omnipresent.

Now follows the ritual procedure for invocation and so forth, as well as the mudrās for invocation and so on: having displayed these, the wise one performs the invocation (āvāhana), and likewise the installation (saṃsthāpana), the bringing near (sannidhāpana), and the confinement (sannirodhana). (Hbhv 6.26)
One should perform the sakalīkaraṇa and the avaguṇṭhana according to the prescribed rule,
as well as the amṛtīkaraṇa and likewise the paramīkaraṇa.
Likewise, regarding the purpose of invocation and so forth, it is stated in the Āgama:
"Invocation is the respectful act of bringing the Lord face-to-face."
Through devotion, his dwelling is established by means of the *saṃsthāpana* mudrā.
The perception of belonging, as in "I am yours," is bringing [the mind] into proximity;
maintaining it until the completion of the task is confinement. (Hbhv 6.29)
The unification of all is said to be the manifestation of all its limbs;
for the absolute manifestation of the density of bliss is indeed the "covering" (avaguṭhana).
The act of making [the object] immortal (amṛtīkaraṇa) consists in its being encompassed by all the limbs [of the ritual];
that which is called "making supreme" (paramīkaraṇa) is the ultimate accomplishment of one's desired goal.
Now, regarding the greatness of the invocation (āvāhana), it is said in the Nārasiṃha Purāṇa:
"Having invoked [the deity] with the words 'O Narasiṃha, come!', [one should worship] with unbroken grains and flowers."
By this much alone, O Indra among kings, one is liberated from all sins.
Thus, one should perform the placement of the limbs and so forth upon the deity according to tradition as before;
then, the wise one should display the mudrās, such as those of the conch and the discus.
And so it is stated in the *Tattvasāgara*:

"Having displayed the mudrās for the invocation and so forth, and then again having performed the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) upon the deity, one should display the mudrās. (Hbhv 6.34)
Now, regarding the mudrās, it is said in the Āgama: "The mudrā for invocation, that for installation, and likewise another for bringing [the deity] into close presence."
And another which effects complete cessation, and the supreme one which effects the ritual integration of the limbs.
Likewise, one should subsequently display these eight [mudrās]: the Avaguṇṭhanī, the Amṛtīkaraṇī, and another, the Paramīkaraṇī, as well as the other six previously mentioned.
The conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, the pestle, and the Śārṅga bow;
likewise the sword, the noose, and the goad, and similarly Vainateya.
During the worship of Kṛṣṇa, the practitioner should likewise display the Śrīvatsa, the Kaustubha gem, the flute, the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons, and the forest garland. (Hbhv 6.38)
Furthermore, a seal (mudrā) shaped like a bilva fruit should also be employed constantly;
thus, one should display these seventeen seals once again. (Hbhv 6.39)
Having smeared one's hands with *ganda*, one should employ the mudrās everywhere;
the fool who acts otherwise will not attain accomplishment and shall not partake of the fruit. (Hbhv 6.40)
Now, regarding the majesty of the mudrās, it is said in the Agastya-saṃhitā:
"By means of these seventeen mudrās, the wise practitioner [should perform the rite]."
O best of Brahmins, whoever should constantly worship me and yet delude the Lord of the Gods,
even he shall cause him to flee and thereby obtain his desired object.
In the *Kramadīpikā* (2.58), concerning the *bilva-mudrā*:
"Whatever has been done here or in the past by mind, speech, or body— whether unintentionally or intentionally— all that accumulation of evil deeds," [is purified by this mudrā].
The person who knows this mudrā exhausts [all obstacles]; the hosts of gods bow to him, and all people constantly come under his influence. (Hbhv 6.42)
Then, having offered a seat and so forth, one should cast three handfuls of flowers over the deity;
having given a flower for the purpose of a seat, one should perform the welcome according to the ritual procedure.
During the ritual services such as the offering of seats and so forth, the wise one should display sixteen mudrās in their proper sequence:
the well-known ones beginning with the lotus and the svastika, across the sixteen [services].
One should offer the *arghya*, *pādya*, *ācamanīya*, *madhuparka*, and again the *ācamanīya* to Śrī Kṛṣṇa according to the prescribed ritual.

And likewise, in the Smṛtyarthasāra: "The invitation, the seat, the water for the feet, the water for the guest-offering, the water for sipping, the bath, another sipping, the cloth for wiping, and the sacred thread. (Hbhv 6.46)

One should offer water for sipping (ācamana), fragrance, flowers, incense, and a lamp; then, having offered the food oblation (naivedya) and water for sipping once more, one should bow, offer praise, and dismiss [the deity]. (Hbhv 6.47)
And elsewhere:
"First, having offered a handful of flowers, thereafter comes the worship of the feet;
then the water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (argha), the water for sipping (ācamana), and the honey-mixture (madhuparka), as prescribed. (Hbhv 6.48)
Having performed anointing and massaging, one should perform the great bath;
then, having offered the garment for the consecration, one should cause Hari to be honored with the waving of lights.
Thus:

one should offer the water of honor (arghya) upon the head of the venerable image, the water for washing the feet (pādya) at the feet, the water for sipping (ācamanīya) in the mouth, and there indeed the honey-mixture (madhuparka) three times. (Hbhv 6.50)
In all ritual services, such as the offering of water for the feet and so forth,
those devoted to the Blessed One desire that a handful of flowers be offered separately at the beginning of each.
Now, regarding the greatness of offering a seat and so forth, it is said in the Narasiṃha Purāṇa:
"Having offered a seat, as well as water for honor (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), and water for sipping (ācamanīya)..."
By means of the rite for the God of gods, one is liberated from all sins.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"By the gift of seats, one finds a place everywhere;
likewise, the man who offers water for the feet obtains the fruit of the gift of a cow. (Hbhv 6.53)
Then, by the giving of such an offering, one is liberated from all sins;
likewise, O best of Brahmins, is the giver of water for rinsing the mouth.

Likewise, by offering the water of sacred fords (tīrtha) and again providing water for the deity’s sipping (ācamana), a person becomes free from all sins and attains the heavenly world; indeed, the giver of water for sipping becomes stainless. (Hbhv 6.55)
By the giving of the honey-mixture (madhuparka), one attains the supreme state in this very world.
And in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"Having performed the ritual for the madhuparka, O Brahmin, he who offers the madhuparka goes to the supreme abode; of this there is no doubt. (Hbhv_6.57)
Then, having requested the deity for the bath, one should place the sandals before him;
with the *mahā-vidyā* and other mantras, one should then lead him to the bathing place.

As before, the wise one should offer a seat, water for the feet, and water for sipping right there; then, having presented the offering, he should display the mudrā that effects the transformation into nectar.
Then one should install the deity in the form of a Śālagrāma stone,
or else one's own chosen mobile image of Śrī within the bathing vessel.
Now, regarding the vessel for bathing, it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"He who, having fashioned [an image] in a copper vessel, should worship Madhusūdana..."
One obtains the fruit of worship for every day for a hundred years.
Whoever worships Mādhava with devotion, seated upon an aśvattha leaf,
daily obtains the merit arising from ten million lotuses.
The man who, having placed Hari upon a plantain leaf, worships him,
shall have Keśava, together with his beloved, drink from him for ten thousand years.
Those who behold with devotion even once Him who stands upon a lotus leaf,
the beloved of her whose abode is the lotus— they have attained the fruit that is difficult to obtain.
Thus,
one should then perform the consecration with a conch shell accompanied by the sounds of a bell and other instruments,
while intermittently offering incense with the root mantra and the eight-syllable mantra. (Hbhv 6.65)
In that regard, first of all, one should with devotion slowly perform an oil massage for Śrī Hari using divine substances such as fragrant oils and the like.
Now, regarding the substances for anointing and their greatness, it is said in the Skanda-purāṇa:
"Having taken Mālatī and Jāti, or again, other fragrant [flowers]... (Hbhv_6.67)
Likewise, those men who, out of devotion, take various other kinds of flowers and bathe the Lord of Gods during the festival on the day of Hari; Hbhv_6.68 //
For the Self-Existent One has declared that the fruit [of this] is indeed equal to the gift of the earth;
moreover, for one who [anoints with] divine medicinal herbs combined with flower-oil... (Hbhv 6.69)
Having cast saffron into the midst [of the paste], Hari performs the oil-anointing of Viṣṇu;
with his body covered in horripilation, Mādhava joyfully holds [the image] upon his own lap together with his beloved for a hundred *manvantaras*.
And in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "By giving divine, fragrant, and pure scented oils to Keśava, a person rejoices together with the Gandharvas. (Hbhv 6.71)
Then follows the bathing with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta):
thereafter, one should bathe [the deity] in sequence with milk held in a conch shell,
and separately with curd, ghee, honey, and sugar.
Those dear to him do not always desire bathing with the five nectars and so forth;
however, they cause it to be performed by means of those [substances] at specific times, places, and so on.
Now, regarding that measurement,
in the *Brahmapurāṇa* it is said:
"Where there is an image of the gods, there should follow the anointing with ghee."
Twenty-five palas of that [medicine] should be given with faith.
One hundred and eight *pala*s should always be given;
however, for a great ablution (*mahā-snāna*), the number is two thousand *pala*s.
That ghee by which it flows out in all directions when it is to be given.
Thus, the wise should understand that even in the case of milk and other substances, the count is to be known in this same way;
and the measurement in palas is to be understood from the statements of Yājñavalkya and others. (Hbhv 6.77)
For instance: five *kṛṣṇala*s make one *māṣa*; sixteen of those make one *suvarṇa*; and four *suvarṇa*s are designated as one *pala*. (Hbhv 6.78)
Thus it is said.
Furthermore:
"For the purpose of bathing, the milk of a cow is fragrant, whereas that of a buffalo and other such animals is contemptible. (Hbhv 6.79)
And in the Viṣṇudharmottara: "The bathing of Viṣṇu with milk pacifies physical suffering, destroys mental anguish, and likewise bestows the ocean of milk."
In the Agni Purāṇa:
"Whatever fruit is obtained from properly giving a hundred cows to Brahmins, one obtains that same fruit by bathing Viṣṇu with a prastha of ghee; of this there is no doubt. (Hbhv 6.81)
It is said that the image was bathed with water mixed with ghee by Indradyumna, who had obtained the earth consisting of the seven continents.
Having bathed the Lord of the Worlds with ghee every month on the eighth day of the bright fortnight and having worshipped him thoroughly, one is liberated from all sins.
Whatever sin a person commits, whether knowingly or unknowingly,
he washes it away at the twilight rite when he is gratified by the sprinkling of clarified butter.
Those worlds where rivers flow with milk and the mud is made of milk-rice,
men go to those worlds by bathing Hari in milk.
And in the *Viṣṇudharma*, in the dialogue between Śrī Pulastya and Prahlāda:
"O tiger among Daityas, bathing Hari with the sacrificial oblation of cow-products on the twelfth and fifteenth days destroys even the greatest sins. (Hbhv 6.86)
Just as curds and other such transformations arise from milk,
even so does the bathing of Hari with milk fulfill all desires without exception.
In the *Nārasiṃha*:
"He who bathes the Lord of Gods, whose banner is Garuḍa, with milk—purified of all sins, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. (Hbhv 6.88)
Having bathed Viṣṇu once with curd— He who is stainless and of pleasing appearance—
one attains the world of Viṣṇu, served by the best of the gods.
O bull among men, bathing with curd should be known as a pacifier of bad dreams and a destroyer of inauspiciousness; it bestows an increase in auspicious fortune. (Hbhv 6.90)
The man who performs the worship of Hari’s image after it has been bathed with honey,
having rejoiced in the world of Agni, shall dwell again in the city of Viṣṇu.
Having performed a bath with honey, one attains good fortune;
likewise, by using sugarcane juice, one obtains friends throughout the world.
And in the *Śrī-Dvārakā-Māhātmya*, within the dialogue between Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya and Indradyumna:
"Those men who perform a bath with milk upon the head of Viṣṇu are said to obtain, drop by drop, the merit born of a horse sacrifice. (Hbhv_6.93)
Clarified butter is ten times more [efficacious] than milk; honey is ten times more than that;
and sugar is ten times more than honey. (Hbhv 6.94)
O best of kings, the water with flowers, the water with fragrance, the water with mantras, and likewise the water with *darbha* grass, each increases tenfold.
O King, the juice of grapes and the juice of mangoes are equal to the merit of a hundred horse-sacrifices;
likewise, the water of sacred fords yields the same fruit. (Hbhv 6.96)
Whoever performs the ritual bathing of the Lord Kṛṣṇa according to their ability obtains that fruit which has been proclaimed; one who is free from desire shall attain liberation.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"A person who, having personally brought sacred waters from holy fords (*tīrtha*), performs an oil-bath [for an image], is liberated from all sins. (Hbhv 6.98)
Now, regarding the greatness of incense during bathing and fumigation, it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"He who burns aloe-wood at the time of Kṛṣṇa’s bath..."
Having entered the cavity of the nostril, it burns away the sins of ten thousand lifetimes.
Immediately thereafter, one should cause the deity to be anointed with substances suitable for use, such as oils and the like, which serve as the means for removing [impurities]. Hbhv_6.100.
Now, regarding the application of unguents and its greatness, it is stated in the Nārasiṃha Purāṇa: "One should apply an unguent made from the powders of barley and wheat with warm water."
Having washed the Lord of the gods of gods, one shall attain the world of Varuṇa.
And in the Viṣṇudharmottara: "By rubbing Janārdana with flour of wheat and barley mixed with powdered *lodhra*, one likewise attains strength and beauty. (Hbhv_6.102)
Having offered powdered lentils mixed with powdered saffron to the God of gods, one rejoices together with the Gandharvas.
In the Vārāha [Purāṇa]: "Furthermore, one should perform anointment with the powder of kalāyaka or with the flour of ground grain,
combined with fragrant flowers."
If one desires supreme accomplishment, one should be devoted to my practice.
Thus it is said.
Then, one should apply a brush made of uśīra and other materials to the joints of the limbs of the glorious form, for the purpose of removing impurities and so forth. (Hbhv 6.105)
Now, regarding the *kūrca* and its greatness, it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"By giving a *kūrca* made of *uśīra* grass, one is liberated from all sins."
By giving a brush made of cow-hair, one dispels all sufferings;
by giving a chowrie-brush, one attains unsurpassed prosperity.
Then follows the bath with pure water: having first bathed [the image] with lukewarm water, one should bathe it again with consecrated, fragrant,
and cool water held in a conch shell.
Thus it is said in the Eleventh Skandha [BhP 11.27.30]:
"When one has the means, one should always bathe [the deity] with waters scented with sandalwood, uśīra, camphor, saffron, and agallochum, while reciting mantras. (Hbhv_6.108)
Now, regarding the measurement of water,
it will be stated in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
"One hundred palas of water should be given for bathing, and twenty-five for an oil massage."
A great ablution (mahā-snāna) is proclaimed to consist of two thousand palas.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states:
"Worship with food at night, water, flowers, and so forth, does not merit the status of a formal bath."
Viṣṇu:
One should not perform rites for the gods while holding water received at night. (Hbhv 6.111)
Hārīta says:
These waters entered Varuṇa at night;
therefore, one should not draw them at night.
Now, regarding the greatness of the ceremonial bath (snapana), it is said in the Nārasiṃha Purāṇa: "Then,
having removed the old garland and having bathed Keśava with water..."
O King, by beholding the form of Narasiṃha, one is liberated from all sins.

Having obtained the fruit born of the gift of a cow, and having reached the city of Narasiṃha by means of a celestial vehicle resplendent with garments, he rejoices for an imperishable duration of time.
Furthermore:
O lord of men, by bathing Narasiṃha with devotion using water, one is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. (Hbhv 6.115)
Having bathed Narasiṃha with water scented with camphor and agallochum,
one rejoices in the world of the Moon and thereafter shall dwell in the city of Viṣṇu.
Furthermore:
By means of water with *kuśa* grass and flowers, one may attain the world of Viṣṇu; by water with jewels, the world of Savitṛ; and by golden water, the world of Kubera. (Hbhv 6.117)
In the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"By the offering of water with jewels, one obtains unsurpassed prosperity;
by the offering of water with seeds, one shall obtain the fruitfulness of one's actions. (Hbhv 6.118)
By the offering of flowers and water, a person becomes illustrious;
by the offering of fruit and water, one finds that one's actions bear fruit.
In the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*:
"Whoever bathes the One Reclining on the Waters with fragrant water attains the world of Brahmā for as long as fourteen Indras endure. (Hbhv 6.120)
In the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"Those men on earth who bathe Janārdana with water mixed with *tulasī* and worship him with devotion are truly blessed. (Hbhv_6.121)
In the Agni Purāṇa:
"Having properly bathed Govinda with the Great Bath (mahā-snāna), whatever desire a person prays for, that he shall obtain without a doubt. (Hbhv_6.122)
In the *Padma Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Pulastya and Bhagīratha:
"The number of merits belonging to one who always performs bathing and worship of Keśava is not within the range of knowledge. (Hbhv_6.123)
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"He who offers fragrance for the purpose of bathing the God of gods, women everywhere and at all times come under his control. (Hbhv 6.124)
Likewise, by the gift of flowers in this world, one becomes endowed with fruit;
by giving a bath with musk, one shall obtain all desires. (Hbhv 6.125)
By the gift of all medicinal herbs, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice;
by giving the preeminent nutmeg fruit, one finds that one's ritual action has borne fruit.
Now, the group known as *sarvauṣadhi* consists of murā, māṣī, vacā, kuṣṭha, śaileya, the two types of rajanī, śaṭī, campaka, and musta. (Hbhv 6.127)
And regarding fragrance, it is stated in the *Āgama*:
"Fragrance is said to consist of sandalwood, camphor, and black agallochum. (Hbhv 6.128)
Now, regarding the greatness of the conch (śaṅkha) in the Skanda Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śrī Brahmā and Nārada:
"He who bathes Keśava with water residing within a conch..."
A human being obtains the fruit of giving a hundred tawny cows.
I suspect that whoever, having taken water from a sacred ford,
bathes Mādhava on the twelfth day, would deliver a hundred lineages by means of even a single drop.
The righteous person who takes the milk of a tawny cow, places it in a conch shell, and bathes Janārdana with it, shall obtain the fruit of ten thousand sacrifices.
O Nārada, he who places milk produced from another cow into a conch shell and bathes the Lord of Gods with it shall obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Having placed water together with unbroken rice grains and flowers in a conch shell, one should bathe the Lord of the Gods; this shall destroy sins accumulated over a long time. (Hbhv 6.133)
Whoever prepares water with unbroken rice grains, flowers, and sandalwood in a conch shell and bathes the deity with it shall dwell for a long time in my world.
He who, having poured scented water into a conch shell, bathes Keśava while reciting "Namo Nārāyaṇāya," is liberated from the perils of rebirth.
O lover of the Kali age, all water— whether from a river, a pond, a well, a lake, or other sources— becomes as sacred as the water of the Gaṅgā when placed in a conch shell.
O best of brahmins, by the command of Vāsudeva, all the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) that exist in the three worlds reside within the conch; therefore, one should always worship the conch.
Having placed water together with flowers, sesame seeds, and unbroken rice grains into a conch shell,
one offers this *arghya* to the God, which yields the fruit of the entire earth including its oceans.
Whoever performs a circumambulation with a conch after having offered the *arghya* water has,
by that act, circumambulated the earth with its seven continents.
Even by the mere sight of Śaṅkha, sins go to destruction; how much more so when he is touched? They perish just as snow does at the rising of the sun.
Whoever carries a conch shell during the daily, occasional, or optional rites of bathing, worship, and anointing shall dwell for a long time in Śvetadvīpa.
Having bowed and holding a conch shell in his hand, the Vaiṣṇava who bathes Govinda with this mantra gains infinite merit. (Hbhv 6.142)
O Pañcajanya, you are the mantra born of the ocean in ancient times, held in the hand by Viṣṇu and honored by all the gods; homage be to you!
By your roar, the clouds, gods, and asuras are terrified;
O Pāñcajanya, who possesses the radiant splendor of ten thousand moons, homage be to you!
The wombs of the wives of the enemies of the gods dissolve in a thousand ways by your roar in the netherworld; O Pāñcajanya, salutations be to you!
And in the Vārāha [Purāṇa]:
"He who should perform an ablution in water reaching up to the navel with a right-spiraling conch and water mixed with sesame seeds... (Hbhv 6.146).
Furthermore, if a person with a one-pointed mind [bathes] in a river flowing eastward,
the sin committed throughout their entire life perishes at that very moment.
Whoever, with a mind fixed on Kṛṣṇa, receives with his head water contained in an udumbara vessel by means of a right-spiraling conch,
the sin committed in that person's birth perishes at that very moment.
In the scripture:
"The three qualities of the conch are its largeness, its smoothness, and its translucence. (Hbhv 6.149)
The defect of whirlpools and ripples does not arise from the application of gold,
provided that there is no hole in the tube by its very nature.
Thus,
the sounding of a bell is highly recommended at the time of bathing,
because it is always most dear to the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu. (Hbhv 6.151)

One should always employ this [mantra], consecrated by its own mantra, during the invocation, the offering of water (arghya), the incense, and the presentation of flowers and food offerings. (Hbhv 6.152)

Then, having uttered the mantra of that [deity], the sound of "Victory! (jaya-dhvani), and the mantra "O Mother of Mantras, svāhā," and having performed worship while ringing the bell, one should offer incense at a low level.
Except at the time of worship, there is no benefit in moving it;
nor should one who desires accomplishment perform worship without it.
Now, the greatness of the bell is described in the Skanda Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śrī Brahmā and Nārada:
"He who makes the sound of the bell at the time of bathing and performing worship..."
Listen now to the fruit of merit for one who stands before that Vāsudeva.
For thousands of millions and hundreds of millions of years,
he dwells in the world of the gods, attended by hosts of apsarases.
The bell made of all musical instruments is always dear to Keśava;
by sounding it, one obtains merit arising from ten million sacrifices.
He who bathes Govinda with the sounds of musical instruments, the resonance of drums, songs, and auspicious chants, shall indeed become one liberated while living.
But in the absence of musical instruments, at all times during the period of worship,
men should produce the sound of a bell, for it embodies the essence of all musical instruments.
The bell, consisting of all musical instruments, is beloved by the God of Gods;
therefore, with every effort, one should cause the sound of the bell to be made.
For thousands and hundreds of manvantaras,
Keśava, the Lord of Gods, becomes pleased by the sound of the bell.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, in the dialogue between the Blessed Lord and Prahlāda:
"Listen, O Lord of Daityas, I shall declare the supreme majesty of the bell. O Prahlāda, there is no devotee of mine equal to you in the three worlds. (Hbhv 6.162)
"A bell engraved with my name stands before me, worshipped in the house of a Vaiṣṇava; know that I am there, O son of a Daitya. (Hbhv 6.163)
If anyone should place before me a bell marked with the figure of Vainateya and joined with the Sudarśana,
I shall dwell within that person's body.
But he who sounds the bell marked with the emblem of Vainateya during the incense offering, the lustration ceremony, the bathing, the time of worship, or the anointing; Hbhv_6.165.
O child, before me every day one receives the fruit of each of these: ten thousand cows, a hundred cows, and that which arises from a hundred cāndrāyaṇa fasts. (Hbhv 6.166)
Worship performed even outside the prescribed rites becomes fruitful for men;
pleased by the sound of the bell, I bestow my own state.
A bell marked with the sign of the elephant’s enemy (the lion) and provided with a wheel destroys,
through its sounding, the fear of birth and death.
O Lord of Daityas, seeing the bell marked by Garuḍa, I always feel joy every single day, just as a man who has acquired wealth feels upon obtaining Lakṣmī.
Just as the gods experience joy day and night upon seeing the nectar of immortality,
so too do they feel joy when the Suparṇa [image] is situated atop the bell-tower.
With their own hands, they produce the sound of a bell out of their own devotion;
during the time of my worship in the Kali age, the fruit is that of ten million moons.
And elsewhere it is said:
"Whoever should place the discus upon the top of the staff of the bell, [he has established] Garuḍa, who is indeed dear to Viṣṇu, as established throughout the three worlds. (Hbhv_6.172)
But whoever hears the sound of the wheel and bell at the time of death,
even if burdened by ten million sins, the servants of Yama perish.
When the sound of the bell is made for Hari, all defects are dissolved;
it becomes a festival for the deities, the lords of sages, and the ancestors. (Hbhv 6.174)
In the absence of even the son of Vinatā or the discus,
there is no doubt that Hari bestows grace upon his devotees by the sound of the bell.
In whatever house there is always a bell joined with the enemy of serpents (a peacock), there is no fear of snakes, nor of fire or lightning. (Hbhv 6.176)
How can the name of the Bhāgavata be sung by that embodied being in whose house there is no bell and no conch shell before Lord Hari?
Thus, for the pleasure of the Blessed One, the Vaiṣṇavas have diligently taken up the bell accompanied by the glorious Garuḍa, adorned above with a discus. (Hbhv 6.178)
During the ritual bath, the sounding of conch shells and other instruments, the chanting of Hari’s names,
singing, dancing, and the recitation of the Purāṇas and similar texts are highly commended.
Now, regarding the greatness of musical instruments and the like during the bath, the Skanda Purāṇa states:
"At the time of Kṛṣṇa’s bath, however, there is the sounding of conch shells and other instruments."
He performs [this] in the Brahma-world and dwells there for one day of Brahmā.
When the time for bathing has arrived, dancing and singing before Kṛṣṇa purify one here; indeed, it is stated in the Ṛgveda that this is accomplished through the mouth.
In that very same *Śrī-Brahma-Nārada-Saṃvāda*:
"The worship of Vāsudeva, accompanied by the playing of the mṛdaṅga drum and the paṇava cymbal, and joined with dance, bestows liberation upon men. (Hbhv 6.182)
Singing, instrumental music, dancing, and likewise the recitation of sacred texts—these are always dear to Keśava during the time of worship of Kṛṣṇa. (Hbhv 6.183)
But in the absence of dance, instrumental music, and so forth, one should perform the recitation of a book;
for at the time of worship, O son, this always bestows delight.
However, in the absence even of a book, [one should recite] the Thousand Names of Viṣṇu.
The King of Praises, O best of men, and the liberation of the lordly elephant.
O highly fortunate one, at the time of worshiping the Lord, the Gītā, the Stotras, the Anusmṛtis, and the five hymns (pañcastavāḥ) bring great joy to Hari. (Hbhv 6.186)
Always setting aside songs and instrumental music at the time of worshiping Hari, one should recite the *Viṣṇu-sahasranāma* with great devotion. (Hbhv 6.187)
In the *Dvārakā-māhātmya*:
"At the time of Kṛṣṇa’s bath, whoever utters the cry of 'Victory!', and performs song and dance accompanied by the clapping of hands... (Hbhv 6.188).
O Lord of Men, acting with the movements of a madman, laughing and talking as he pleases, he does not lie on his back in his mother's lap.
Now, regarding the majesty of the Thousand Names,
it is said in that very same work:
"At the time of bathing the Lord, one should recite the Thousand Names."
For every single syllable, one shall obtain the merit arising from [the gift of] a hundred Kapila cows.
In the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"Having offered praise to that Great-Souled One with the Thousand Names, a person attains freedom from all misfortunes; of this there is no doubt. (Hbhv 6.191)
In the *Skānda-purāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Brahmā and Nārada, it is said:
"The human being who recites the thousand names of Viṣṇu at the time of worship obtains the fruit of the meritorious Vedas. (Hbhv 6.192)
O divine sage, the fruit that is proclaimed for reciting even a single verse of the *Sahasranāma* cannot be attained even by hundreds of sacrifices.
Whatever worship of Hari has been performed deficient in mantras or deficient in ritual action—
all that becomes entirely complete through the recitation of the Thousand Names.
Furthermore:
Having recited the Thousand Names of Viṣṇu in the presence of Viṣṇu, one abandons the great affliction consisting of sin committed through knowledge or ignorance. (Hbhv 6.195)
Even sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, though committed through intentional action, surely go to dissolution; what then need be said regarding other sins? (Hbhv_6.196)
All undertakings, even those conceived only in the mind, are accomplished for one who,
having risen at dawn, recites the Thousand Names of Viṣṇu.
In that very same Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Arjuna Saṃvāda:
"By him indeed the Vedas have been studied, and all the gods have been fully worshipped;
for one who studies the Thousand Names, liberation stands in the palm of his hand. (Hbhv 6.198)
Even while committing thousands of sins and eating here and there,
one who recites the *Nāmasahasra* does not perceive any foul odor.
O Guḍākeśa, when the Kali age has arrived, there is no other dharma whatsoever apart from the Thousand Names; this which I have spoken is the truth.
O Arjuna, I derive no pleasure from sacrifices, gifts, austerities, or hymns of praise;
indeed, I find no satisfaction in anything other than the Thousand Names.
Those who indeed do not know the hymn called the *Nāmasahasra* in the Kali age wander through the world as men excluded from all dharmas. (Hbhv 6.202)
In whosever house this hymn called the *Nāmasahasra* is written and worshipped in my presence, I indeed accept their worship.
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, in whichever house my thousand names always remain written down, Kali does not enter there.
Therefore, O son of Kuntī, you too, being my devotee with your mind fixed on me,
shall attain all desires by reciting my thousand names.
In the past, I was propitiated by Brahmā, the creator of the world;
from that, I obtained my supreme thousand names, which bring the highest benefit to the world.
Previously, it was obtained by Nārada from the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin);
then it was proclaimed by Nārada to the sages of perpetual celibacy (ūrdhvaretas).
O mighty-armed one, it was proclaimed by the sages in the world of the gods, and it was expounded for human beings in the world of mortals by Vyāsa. (Hbhv 6.208)
Through fierce and great austerity, the high-souled Śaṅkara attained,
by my grace, that which is the most excellent among secrets.
This thousand names of mine was indeed given by Rudra to Bhavānī;
it is renowned throughout the three worlds, and I have recited it for you.
O Pārtha, this thousand names of mine removes all suffering without exception;
it instantly produces joy and is meritorious, like nectar to the gods. (Hbhv_6.211)
O Dhanañjaya, this Thousand Names of yours has been extracted by me from the essence of the eighteen Purāṇas and fully proclaimed to you. (Hbhv 6.212)
Lord Śaṅkara alone knows the greatness of the Thousand Names;
whoever recites or even hears the greatness of the Thousand Names shall never be tainted by a thousand offenses. (Hbhv 6.213)
Now, regarding the majesty of the Śrī Bhagavad-gītā, as spoken by Śrī Vyāsa in the Avantī-khaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa: "The Gītā should be well-sung; what is the use of other extensive scriptures?"
She who herself issued from the lotus-face of Padmanābha.
Since the Gītā consists of all scriptures, embodies all deities,
and comprises all dharmas, one should therefore practice it thoroughly.
Whoever recites the chapter on the Gītā before a Śālagrāma stone dwells for thousands of Manvantaras in the city of Brahmā.
Having repeatedly slain the entire world and having plundered all that is moving and unmoving, one who studies the Gītā is in no way defiled by sins whatsoever. (Hbhv 6.217)
By him who constantly practices the Gītā, all sacrifices have been offered, ten thousand cows have been given, and the imperishable state has been attained. (Hbhv 6.218)
Whoever recites a chapter of the Gītā, or even a single verse or half-verse,
being completely liberated from the sins of worldly existence, goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
I shall now describe the merit of that twice-born man who constantly recites this chapter called "The Universal Form," which reveals the majesty of the God of gods. (Hbhv 6.220)
Whatever merit is gained from studying the Vedas along with the ancient Itihāsas, one obtains that same merit by means of a single verse; there is no doubt in this matter.
He who recites the Viśvarūpa hymn and its manifestation (vibhūti) constantly brings satisfaction to the entire world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass. (Hbhv 6.222)
Indeed, Keśava forgives thirty-two offenses for that mortal who recites the chapter on the Gītā day after day. (Hbhv 6.223)
Having written it out, he indeed bestows the Gītā scripture upon the Vaiṣṇavas;
and day by day he worships Hari here—of this there is no doubt. (Hbhv 6.224)
Having extracted the very essence of the four Vedas, Viṣṇu revealed the Gītā-śāstra for the benefit of the three worlds. (Hbhv 6.225)
Having drunk the water of the Gaṅgā that is the Gītā— the entire essence of the nectar of the Mahābhārata issued from the mouth of Viṣṇu— rebirth is no longer found.
By one who always desires virtue, wealth, pleasure, and even liberation, the Gītā uttered from the mouth of Kṛṣṇa should be heard and studied. (Hbhv 6.227)
The man who daily recites this scripture of the Gītā every day,
being liberated from all sins, goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Now, regarding the majesty of reciting the Purāṇas and so forth, as stated in the *Padma Purāṇa* in the dialogue between Devadūta and Vikuṇḍala (*PadmaP* 3.31.94–96):
"Those who investigate the scriptures and those who are devoted to the study of the Vedas..."
And those who cause the Purāṇa-saṃhitā to be heard and those who recite it; // Hbhv_6.229 //
Those who expound the Smṛtis, those who awaken others to the Dharma, and those who are established in the Vedāntas—it is by them that this world is sustained. (Hbhv 6.230)
By the greatness of their respective practices, all those whose taints have been destroyed go to the world of Brahmā, where delusion is not found.
In that very same [text], in the dialogue between Śrī Śiva and Umā:
"Even for one who has reached the end of the Vedas and knows the meaning of all the scriptures, if he has not heard the Purāṇas, there is no perfect vision of the goal for such a person. (Hbhv 6.232)
O beautiful lady, I consider the meaning of the Purāṇas to be superior to the meaning of the Vedas;
for by distorting the Purāṇa, one may fall into the womb of an animal.
And in the *Bṛhan-nāradīya-purāṇa* (1.1.57, 60–61):
"O best of the twice-born, the merits accumulated by those lowest of men who declare that the Purāṇas are merely figurative exegesis (*arthavāda*) go to ruin."
O best of the twice-born, those who declare that the Purāṇas— which expound all dharmas—
are merely figurative speech (arthavāda), are destined for hell.
O best of the twice-born, he who desires to acquire merits here without effort should listen to the Purāṇas with devotion; of this there is no doubt. (Hbhv 6.236)
Indeed, his sins accumulated in the past go to destruction;
certainly, his intellect becomes fixed upon the hearing of the Purāṇas. (Hbhv 6.237)
Moreover:
Even while the Purāṇa is being recited, one who is bound by the noose of sin proceeds with a mind attached to other verses, showing disregard for it. (Hbhv 6.238)
Then,
having displayed the mudrā of bathing, one should gently wipe the limbs with a pure, fine cloth and offer divine garments.
In accordance with the costumes and other requirements of the Madhyadeśa region, some here devotedly provide garments such as tunics and turbans. (Hbhv 6.240)
And likewise, in the Matsya Purāṇa:
"One should have each respective image fashioned, enriched with the ornaments characteristic of that particular region. (Hbhv_6.241)
In the eleventh book [BhP 11.27.32]:
"My devotee, endowed with love, should adorn me as is appropriate. (Hbhv_6.242)
And in the future, one should worship Viṣṇu with garments that are dear to oneself,
as well as with other auspicious, divine, and fine silk cloths. (Hbhv 6.243)
And one should offer to Hari garments that are variegated, substantial, pure, fumigated, hairless, and new.
One should adorn [the body] with many garments and various items such as bodices; it is the consensus of the wise that this should be done immediately after enjoying [the pleasures]. (Hbhv 6.245)
Now, regarding the majesty of wiping the limbs with a cloth: in the *Dvārakā-māhātmya*,
it is said that one should wipe Kṛṣṇa, whose body is still wet from bathing, with a cloth.
There shall be the cleansing of even that sin acquired through hundreds of thousands [of lifetimes].
Now, regarding the greatness of the offering of garments, it is said in the *Nārasiṃha-purāṇa*:
"Having clothed Acyuta with two variegated garments out of devotion..."
Having dwelt in the world of Soma, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Śiva and Umā:
"Having given garments that are very pure, substantial, soft, beautiful, new, and with their fringes intact to Hari... (Hbhv 6.248)
As many threads as there are in the measurement of the cloth,
for that many thousands of years one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara* (3.341.176–178):
"By the gift of a *rāṅkava* woolen blanket, one obtains all desires;
he who would give a pair of cotton garments to Janārdana... (*Hbhv* 6.250).
For as many threads as there are in that [cloth] measuring one cubit,
for that many thousands of years he is honored in the world of Viṣṇu.
O Brahmins, just as its great value, its origin in a noble land, and its subtlety [are established], so too has the great fruit been declared.
Furthermore, in that same work, elsewhere (3.341.179–185), it says:
"By the gift of white cloth, one obtains unsurpassed prosperity;
by [cloth] dyed with saffron, one enjoys great good fortune. (Hbhv 6.253)
Likewise, O best of the twice-born, by giving [a gift] dyed with saffron, one becomes beloved of women; by giving what is dyed with indigo, or any other dye except red,
