one becomes righteous in soul and free from all diseases.
Whoever offers to the God silken garments that are very soft and light shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Whoever should give blankets made of the wool of the *rāṅkava* deer, as well as beautiful ones made of *kadali* fibers,
to the God of gods, shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
By giving garments made of bark that are variegated with various patterns,
as well as new and bright white clothes, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
And in the *Dvārakā-māhātmya* it is said:
"Having perfumed [the image] with very soft, fine garments produced from various lands, one honors Mādhava with great devotion."
He dwells in the abode of Hari for as many Manvantaras as there are threads [in the cloth].
Furthermore, regarding the prohibition on offering clothing, it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Clothing dyed with indigo, as well as that which is worn out, or likewise that which has been worn by another,"
He who would give [this] to one who is a god among gods is indeed joined with sins.
Regarding this, there is an exception stated in that same work:
"In the case of woolen cloth and silk fabric, the indigo dye is not considered a fault. (Hbhv 6.260)
Then, having displayed the mudrās of the sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta) and the offering of the garment, and having caused [the disciple] to put them on;
then, having offered the sacred thread, he should display that mudrā as well.
Now, regarding the greatness of offering the sacred thread (*upavīta*):
by giving a three-stranded sacred thread, white or yellow, made of silk thread or other materials, to Govinda, one becomes a master of the Vedānta. (Hbhv 6.262)
In the Nandipurāṇa:
"By the gift of a sacred thread to the gods or to a Brāhmaṇa, one becomes a learned scholar of the four Vedas with a purified intellect; there is no doubt in this matter. (Hbhv 6.263)
Now, regarding the water for the feet, the tilaka,
and the water for sipping: first, having offered the water for the feet, one should fashion a beautiful vertical *puṇḍra* mark on the forehead of Kṛṣṇa and then offer the water for sipping.
Then, having offered divine ornaments to the deity, one should clothe [the image] with ornaments as is appropriate and display its mudrā.
Now, regarding the greatness of offering ornaments,
in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śiva and Umā:
"Having given an excellent ornament joined with jewels and pearls..."
Having given an ornament according to one's own ability, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Furthermore:
"He who would give even a single *guñjā* seed's weight of gold upon the head of Viṣṇu shall dwell in the abode of Indra until the dissolution of the world at the time of the final call. (Hbhv 6.267)
Therefore, O Goddess, an ornament should always be given to Viṣṇu;
through supreme devotion, O auspicious one, Nārāyaṇa will become pleased.
In the Nandi Purāṇa:
"He who gives an ornament to a Brahmin or to a deity shall go to the world of Varuṇa, adorned with various ornaments."
Born upon the earth through [the power of] *kāya*, one becomes a king who is a lord of an island.
In the Viṣṇudharmottara:
By the gift of earrings, a man becomes one who retains what he hears;
he obtains the merit of a horse sacrifice and also attains good fortune. (Hbhv 6.270)
By the gift of ear-ornaments, one attains learning everywhere.
By the gift of a head-ornament, one becomes blessed upon the surface of the earth and rules over the Vasundharā, which is encircled by the four oceans. (Hbhv 6.272)
In that very same third section:
"By the gift of ornaments, one becomes preeminent upon the earth;
[one obtains] beautiful, variegated jewels made of gold, O best of the twice-born. (Hbhv_6.273)
By giving various kinds of ornaments, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice;
by the gift of a toe-ring, one becomes the lord of the Guhyakas.
By the gift of foot-ornaments, one finds a place everywhere.
By the gift of a girdle for the hips, one rules the earth girt by the oceans with enemies destroyed; there is no need for deliberation on this point. (Hbhv 6.276)
By giving a small bell to Hari, one attains great good fortune;
by the gift of a finger-ring for the hand, one shall attain supreme good fortune.
In the same way, by the gift of armlets, one becomes a king upon the earth;
by the gift of bracelets, one becomes the destroyer of the enemy's faction.
And by giving neck-ornaments, one becomes a knower of the meaning of all scriptures;
furthermore, O best of the twice-born, women come under his control.
Having given the foremost *pratisarā* charms, one is not overcome by malevolent spirits.
Furthermore, in that very same [text]:
"O divine ones, artificial ornaments should likewise be given;
having given what is fashioned in imitation, one is quickly endowed with nourishment. (Hbhv 6.281)
In the *Padma-purāṇa*:
"By fashioning golden ornaments of the conch, discus, mace, and so forth, and placing them on the feet and other limbs [of an image], one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. (Hbhv 6.282)
In the Nārasiṃha [Purāṇa]:
"The man who worships Viṣṇu with divine golden ornaments— necklaces, armlets, earrings, crowns, bracelets, and so forth— " (Hbhv 6.283).
Completely liberated from all evil and adorned with every ornament,
the wise one shall dwell in the world of Indra for as long as Indra reigns— fourteen [aeons].
In the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"O Vāsava, for him whose image of Viṣṇu stands adorned with golden ornaments and especially with jewels and pearls, day after day... (*Hbhv* 6.285).
O Lord of the Gods, it has been told to me by Brahmā that his residence shall indeed be in the world of Hari for thousands of millions of kalpas.
O Śakra, that man who, even once, beholds Kṛṣṇa adorned with golden ornaments with devotion during the Kali age, purifies his lineage unto the seventh generation.
Thus:
"The virtuous desire that ornaments be worn abundantly after one has bathed and applied ointments; and that flowers follow the application of ointments and the wearing of ornaments. (Hbhv 6.288)
Then, having supplicated the Lord as before and offered the pure sandals,
one should lead him back to the place of worship with music, song, a parasol, and other honors.
Having offered the seat and other items as before, one should offer fragrance with its respective mudrā;
then, having placed sandalwood along with a tulasī leaf into a conch shell— Hbhv_6.290.
Now, regarding fragrance, it is stated in the Āgama:
"The paste of sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor is here called 'fragrance'. (Hbhv 6.291)
In the *Garuḍa-purāṇa*:
"Two parts of musk, four of sandalwood, three of saffron, and one of camphor—this is the 'Fourfold' (catuḥsama) compound. (Hbhv 6.292)
Camphor, sandalwood, frankincense, and saffron constitute the "fourfold equal" (catuḥsama);
this is declared to be the universal fragrance, beloved by all the gods.
In the Vārāha [Purāṇa]: "Camphor, saffron, excellent tagara,
rasya, sandalwood, as well as aguru and guggulu."
The wise one should offer these auspicious and beautiful ointments.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara* and the *Agnipurāṇa*:
"One should worship the Lord of the World with fragrant substances—mura, māṃsī, camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood—as well as with other auspicious materials. (Hbhv 6.295)
In the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā*:
"One should anoint [the image] with sandalwood mixed with camphor and agallochum; especially musk is desired by the wielder of the discus. (Hbhv 6.296)
In the *Skānda-purāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śrī Brahmā and Nārada:
"Sandalwood is more meritorious than other fragrances; aloe-wood is superior to sandalwood; black aloe-wood is better than that; and saffron is even greater than that. (Hbhv 6.297)
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"O best of the twice-born, no other unguent than this should be given;
sandalwood is proclaimed to be the foremost of all unguents. (Hbhv 6.298)
In the Nāradīya [Purāṇa] it is said:
"Just as food offerings made of rice are always desired by Viṣṇu, so too, according to what was spoken by Śuka in the Purāṇa, are Tulasī and sandalwood. (Hbhv 6.299)
And in the *Agastya-saṃhitā*:
"Rubbing a piece of *tulasī* wood and placing it upon the head of Rāma is not equaled by camphor, agallochum, musk, or saffron. (Hbhv 6.300)
Now, regarding the greatness of anointing,
in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, within the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada concerning the greatness of the conch:
"They anoint the Lord of Gods after having placed sandalwood paste upon the conch."
The Supreme Self bestows supreme joy for a hundred years.
In the *Garuḍa-purāṇa*:
"He who constantly anoints Janārdana with sandalwood paste adhering to a *tulasī* leaf obtains his desired fruit. (Hbhv 6.302)
In the *Nārasiṃha*:
"O King of kings, by anointing the form of Acyuta with a paste of saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood out of devotion, one shall dwell in heaven for ten million kalpas. (Hbhv 6.303)
In the Viṣṇudharmottara and Agni Purāṇas:
"Anointed with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, usīra, and padmaka, Hari, when worshipped with devotion, bestows excellent enjoyments. (Hbhv 6.304)
Kāleyaka, turuṣka, and excellent red sandalwood.
O Supreme Person, meritorious gifts bestowed upon men become [fruitful]. (Hbhv 6.306)
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"By anointing him with sandalwood paste, one shall attain the world of the Moon;
likewise, one is liberated from physical and mental sufferings. (Hbhv 6.307)
By anointing this [image] with saffron, a person is honored in the world of the Sun;
likewise, that human being attains supreme good fortune in the world.
By anointing this [image] with camphor, one shall attain the world of Varuṇa and likewise be liberated from physical and mental sufferings. (Hbhv 6.309)
By giving the finest musk, one shines with glory;
by giving powdered *jātī* fruit, one enjoys the fruition of one's actions.
Having anointed Janārdana with delightful aloe-wood essence, one obtains incomparable good fortune in the world and supreme strength. (Hbhv 6.311)
Likewise, one would obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice by [anointing] with the resin of the Bakula tree;
and by anointing the Lord of the World with fragrant sandalwood mixed with Bakula and agallochum, one would obtain the fruit of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice.
Having unified all [these] and having anointed Janārdana,
one undoubtedly attains the fruit of the principal horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha).

O Lord of Gods, as many atoms as there are in all the substances used for anointing— from those made of earth onwards— that person who should anoint the Lord with the celebrated ointments [attains that merit].
For that many years in the worlds, that man becomes a mover at will,
having produced the fragrance of hair from musk.
One enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice in which all desires are fulfilled.
For one who bestows fragrant substances and those prepared with perfumes,
the state of a Gandharva is certain, as is supreme good fortune.
Now, regarding the majesty of the sandalwood from the wood of the sacred *tulasī*,
as spoken in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa* in the dialogue between the venerable Nārada and King Dhundhumāra:
"He who daily offers sandalwood from the *tulasī* tree to Hari..."
O best of men, he indeed dwells in heaven for infinite eons.
In the Kali age, he who, with devotion, offers tulasī and sandalwood to Mahāviṣṇu and worships him with mālatī flowers shall never again become a suckling at a mother’s breast.
For one who offers sandalwood produced from *tulasī* wood to Hari, it shall burn away every sin committed throughout hundreds of previous births. (Hbhv 6.320)
Tulsi wood and sandalwood are desired by all the gods,
and especially by the ancestors, just as they are always beloved by Hari.
But when the time of death has arrived, for one who has tulasī wood and sandalwood upon his body, Hari, having become present within him, leads him to Hari.
O King, sandalwood from Mount Malaya and black aloe-wood shine only so long as the meritorious sandalwood of tulasī wood is not seen. (Hbhv 6.323)
The fragrance of musk and the scent of camphor remain [superior] only so long as the sandalwood from the *tulasī* leaves is not offered to Viṣṇu.
O Dhundhumāra, those mortals who in the Kali age offer tulasī wood and sandalwood to Viṣṇu do not return to this earth again.
For that man who, having become a devotee of the Blessed One, does not always offer *tulasī* and sandalwood to Viṣṇu in the Kali age, is not truly a devotee.
In the *Prahlāda-saṃhitā*:
"There is no Vaiṣṇava on earth equal to him in this world, who offers sandalwood from a *tulasī* plant to Kṛṣṇa. (Hbhv 6.327)
In the Kali age, a person who anoints Viṣṇu with devotion using sandalwood paste produced from Tulasī wood rejoices in the presence of Hari.
Whoever makes an anointing with sandalwood produced from *tulasī* wood for the pleasure of Viṣṇu shall obtain the fruit of a gift of a tawny cow.
Whoever uses sandalwood produced from *tulasī* wood is liberated,
especially at the time of death, even if he has committed sins.
Whoever offers Tulasī wood and sandalwood to the ancestors,
he indeed provides them with satisfaction for a hundred years at the Śrāddha rite.
And in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"One whose limbs are anointed with *tulasī* and sandalwood performs the worship of Kṛṣṇa;
by that worship for even a single day, one obtains the merit of a hundred years. (Hbhv_6.332)
Listen to the fruit of merit for him in whose house there resides the sandalwood of tulasī wood for the purpose of anointing Kṛṣṇa. (Hbhv 6.333)
The merit that arises from giving eight measures of sesame seeds during the northern course of the sun—
merit equal to that is produced through the grace of the wielder of the discus.
Thus, in the absence of sandalwood (*malayaja*), that which comes from the *kadamba* tree should be given because of its coolness;
just as [in the absence of *devadāru*], sandalwood is used because of its fragrance. (Hbhv 6.335)
In the Gāruḍa:
"Sandalwood from Malaya is best for Hari; in its absence, that which grows on Devadāru [is recommended]."
Now, regarding substances prohibited for use as unguents, the *Viṣṇudharmottara* states: "The *padmaka* tree causes poverty, and red sandalwood causes ill health."
Others might cause the affliction of mental derangement, such as the disorder of the mind known as uśīra.
Thus, those who desire happiness in this life should not give lotuses and the like; however,
if the primary [gift] is unavailable, all of that should be given by those devoted to the Blessed One.
Then, immediately after applying the ointment to the Blessed One,
the wise one should perform fanning with various fans and chowries.
And regarding the greatness of fanning, it is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"Having anointed the Lord of the World, one should fan Him with a palm-leaf fan."
By that action, a person attains the world of Vāyu.
Whoever fans Janārdana, the God of gods, with chowries,
undoubtedly obtains the fruit of giving a prastha of sesame seeds.
Then, O King of kings, with great devotion he wards off the heat of the God of gods with a fan or a cloth, like the wind. (Hbhv 6.342)
In that family, however, the fear of the hell-being in the realm of Yama subsides;
O protector of the earth, there is no further falling away from the world of the wind.
A person should please Kṛṣṇa with the wind from a moving fly-whisk.
O Lord of Gods, he indeed praises his own head with his own mouth;
for this should be understood as occurring during the hot season, when the virtuous do not even apply sandalwood paste because of its coolness in the months of Pauṣa and Māgha. (Hbhv 6.345)
And so it has been said:
"In the cold, that which is cooling should not be given. (Hbhv 6.346)
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Bathing," in the *Śrī-Bhagavad-bhakti-vilāsa* composed by the venerable Gopāla Bhaṭṭa.
8. The Eighth Chapter: The Graceful Conclusion of the Morning Worship (Prātar-arcā-samāpana-vilāsa)
I bow to Lord Śrī Caitanya, by the power of taking refuge at whose feet even a pauper can gather a collection of jewels from a multitude of mines.
Then, having offered incense, one should present the smoke while holding it low with that mudrā,
chanting the name of Kṛṣṇa and ringing the bell with the left hand. (Hbhv 8.2)
And so it is stated in the *Bahvṛca-pariśiṣṭa*:
"In a secluded place, during the offering of incense, when fanning the limbs with incense, and during all lustration ceremonies (*nīrājana*), one should chant the names of Viṣṇu. (Hbhv 8.3)
One should raise a cry of victory, proclaim compassion, as well as sounds of auspiciousness and praise for the Seed of the World. (Hbhv 8.4)
And elsewhere:
"Then one should offer incense with the sounding of bells, musical instruments, and cries of 'Victory!', having worshipped the place of the incense with the left index finger of Hari. (Hbhv 8.5)
In this regard, the mantra is:
"Produced from the sap of the lord of trees, rich in fragrance, this is the most excellent incense; worthy of being smelled by all the gods, may this incense be accepted. (Hbhv 8.6)
Now, regarding incense, the Vāmana Purāṇa states: "Ruhikā, kaṇa, dāru, sihlaka, and white aguru."
Conch shells, the fruit of the *jāti* flower, and incenses are indeed dear to Śrīśa.
In the Root Tantra,
one should prepare the supreme incense by casting guggulu, agallochum, śīra, white clarified butter, honey, and sandalwood onto the glowing embers of heartwood.
And in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"O Lord of the Dānavas, likewise those incenses which possess auspicious fragrances should be offered to Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, by those who know the Dharma. (Hbhv_8.9)
Now, regarding incenses, that which is derived from living beings is prohibited for the purpose of incense.
In that very context, there is this exception:
"In incense, one should avoid all products derived from living beings, except for musk."
In the Kālikā-purāṇa: "One should never offer yakṣa-incense to Madhava. (Hbhv 8.12)
In the Agni Purāṇa:
"A wise person should not offer incense made from sallakī, nor grass, nor that which is prepared from the sap of bark-shavings, nor anything devoid of its constituent parts, to Kṛṣṇa. (Hbhv 8.13)
Now, regarding the greatness of incense,
in the *Nārasiṃha Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya and Satanīka, it is said:
"Guggulu known as Mahiṣa, combined with clarified butter and sugar..."
O King of Men, the devoted one offers incense to Narasiṃha.
Perfumed and freed from all evil in every direction,
he reaches the world of Vāyu by means of a radiant celestial chariot accompanied by throngs of Apsarases, and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"O King of kings, those men in the Kali age who incense Kṛṣṇa with black agallochum mixed with camphor become equal to Kṛṣṇa himself. (Hbhv 8.16)
Having incensed Janārdana with well-prepared guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter as fragrant incense, a person goes to his state of eternal auspiciousness.
By constantly offering agallochum, camphor, and divine sandalwood with their fragrance out of devotion to Hari, one shall deliver a hundred generations of one's lineage. (Hbhv 8.18)
In the third section of the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Incense is likewise supreme, bestowing the fruits of all rites.
By offering incense made of *turuṣka*, one obtains the fruit of the *Vahnistoma* sacrifice. (Hbhv 8.19)
By giving a primary artificial [image], one obtains all desires;
by giving one made of fragrant substances, one obtains the Gosava sacrifice.
Having given camphor resin, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice;
having given bdellium in the spring, one attains the Vahnistoma sacrifice.
In the summer, by offering the essence of sandalwood, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice;
by the gift of turuṣka resin during the rainy season, one attains preeminence.
By the gift of camphor in autumn, one obtains the merit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
In the winter, by means of the musk of the deer, one obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice;
in the cool season, by means of the essence of agallochum, one obtains the fruit of the universal sacrifice.

The giver of incense attains the supreme state and enjoys prosperity. Just as a streak of incense smoke constantly rises upward, so too does a person, through the gift of incense, always ascend to higher realms. (Hbhv 8.25)
And in the *Prahlāda-saṃhitā*:
"He who offers incense to Hari with the fire of *tulasī* wood obtains merit equal to a hundred sacrifices and the fruit of ten thousand cows. (Hbhv 8.26)
Thus,
one should properly incense the glorious abode of the Blessed Lord;
then, the Vaiṣṇava should himself devotedly partake of the remains of that incense.
And likewise, in the *Brāhma* [Purāṇa], in the question posed by Gautama to Ambarīṣa: "O King, you devotedly partake of the remnants of Kṛṣṇa’s incense;
O King, having performed the *ārātrika* rite for Viṣṇu, you bow with your own head. (Hbhv 8.28)
Now, regarding the greatness of incensing the abode of the Blessed Lord:
that Vaiṣṇava who indeed incenses the temple of Śrīdhara with incense arising from black agallochum is liberated from the ocean of hell. (Hbhv 8.29)
The greatness of using the remnants of incense is described in the *Padma Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Gautama and Ambarīṣa:
"Just as one becomes stainless when washed by hundreds of millions of sacred fords (*tīrthas*),"
In the same way, the residue of incense makes the body of Hari stainless.
No fear exists for him— whether from the earth, the heavens,
or the netherworld— for his body is perfumed with the residue of Kṛṣṇa’s incense.
Indeed, no calamities or misfortunes ever befall that embodied being who always perfumes his body with the remains of what has been offered to Hari.
Neither unhappiness, nor fear, nor suffering born of mental afflictions, nor even that born of disease,
shall befall him who partakes of the remains of the incense of Viṣṇu, whose deeds are marvelous.
Having used the incense, the remains of the offerings, and the water from the feet of Hari, there shall be no fear whatsoever of cruel beings, nor any fear of thieves. (Hbhv 8.34)
And in the *Haribhaktisudhodaya*:
"The scent of the remains of incense offered to Hari, when smelled from all sides, shall remove the poison of karma for those bitten by the serpent of worldly existence. (Hbhv 8.35)
Thus,
even by merely seeing the incense, others also obtain all the fruit arising from the offering of incense and so forth; and that will be explained further ahead.
Then, likewise for illumination, having offered this lamp while sounding the bell as before,
one should intensely illuminate [the deity] from the lotus of the feet up to the lotus of the eyes by means of the mudrā.
Regarding this, the mantra in the *Gautamīya* is as follows:
"O you who are well-illuminated, of great splendor, who dispel darkness in every direction!"
May this lamp, which possesses light both external and internal, be accepted.
Then, if one is able, one should light a lamp with camphor or ghee;
if those are unavailable, even with fragrant oil made from cow-products.
And so it is stated in the Nāradīya-kalpa:
"One should offer with faith to Hari, together with his entire retinue, incense consisting of guggulu mixed with clarified butter, and a lamp lit with cow's ghee. (Hbhv 8.40)
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"O King, a lamp should be offered with ghee or, alternatively, with oil. (Hbhv_8.41)
And in the Mahābhārata:
"The first option is with sacrificial oblations; the second is with the juices of medicinal herbs. (Hbhv 8.42)
Now, regarding what is prohibited concerning lamps, it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"A lamp should never be offered with fat, marrow, or similar substances. (Hbhv 8.43)
In the Mahābhārata:
"One who desires nourishment should not [use] fat, marrow, bone, or exudations. (Hbhv 8.44)
In the third section of the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"One should carefully avoid a lamp with blue or red wicks. (Hbhv 8.45)
In the Kālikā-purāṇa it is said:
"O Bhairava, a lamp-tree should be made of metal or other such materials;
the lamp should be placed upon trees, but never on the ground. (Hbhv 8.46)
Now, regarding the majesty of the lamp, in the Skanda Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada:
"Having lit a lamp with camphor for the God of gods..."
One obtains the merit of the horse sacrifice and uplifts one's entire lineage.
In this very place and elsewhere it is said:
"O protector of the earth, he who offers a lamp before Kṛṣṇa casts off all sin and obtains a fruit that is the nature of light. (Hbhv 8.48)
In the Vārāha [Purāṇa]:
"O Goddess, for one who, established in devotion to me, offers a lamp, there shall be no blindness for him during seven births, O beautiful one. (Hbhv 8.49)
But for one who, endowed with faith, should offer a lamp to me in all directions,
his rebirth is ordained in regions that are self-luminous.
Just as the light given in the *Hari-bhakti-sudhodaya* spreads forth radiance upon one’s own light,
so too does the light of Hari remove the darkness of sin for the giver. (Hbhv 8.51)
In the *Nārasiṃha*:
"If a person should light a lamp with ghee or oil for Viṣṇu according to the rules and with devotion, hear the fruit of his merit. (Hbhv 8.52)
Having abandoned all evil, possessing a radiance equal to a thousand suns,
he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu by means of a luminous celestial chariot.
And in the *Prahlāda-saṃhitā* it is said:
"O son of a Daitya, he who offers a lamp to Hari with the very fire of *tulasī* attains the merit of thousands of lakhs of lamps. (Hbhv 8.54)
Thus,
afterwards, the Vaiṣṇava should indeed venerate that lamp with devotion by bowing his head;
by even the mere sight of it, others as well obtain that same fruit, just as they do from the incense.
Furthermore, some Vaiṣṇavas desire that this lamp be waved before the head of the Śrīmūrti here, just as in the great lustration ceremony (mahā-nīrājana).
And likewise, in the *Rāmārcana-candrikā*, regarding the lamp following the incense: "The *ārātrika* [lamp] should be provided with an uneven number of many wicks;
having worshipped it, one should offer it to Rāmacandra, placing it on the left and in the middle. (Hbhv 8.57)

Then one should offer a handful of flowers with the words "Homage to Dīpeśvara," and after scattering them and worshipping with musical instruments, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) over the head of the Lord.
Thus it is said;
for this very reason, they desire that he be saluted by them with both hands, and that his name be "Ārātrika" and so forth, and that the wicks also be numerous and equal. (Hbhv 8.59)

In this very context, within the temple of the glorious Blessed One, the greatness of offering lamps—both those offered during the month of Kārttika and those offered otherwise—is written down as a secondary topic. (Hbhv 8.60)
Now, regarding the greatness of offering lamps in the temple of the Blessed Lord, as stated in the first section of the Viṣṇudharmottara [1.166.17ff]:
"There has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift superior to the gift of a lamp."
Having fashioned a beautiful lamp-tree in the temple of Keśava,
it shines exceedingly with splendor, reaching toward the heavens on all sides.
Those men who offer garlands of lamps in the abode of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow become equal to the moon upon reaching heaven.
Having constructed a beautiful lamp-house resembling a peaked pavilion,
and having established a shrine for Keśava, that man shines in the world like Śakra.
O Yādava, just as a lamp becomes radiant,
so too the donor shines eternally radiant in the world upon the heights of heaven.
Just as eyes are fruitful in a place where there is a lamp,
so too do those who possess the vision of fruitfulness become givers of lamps.
Now hear the fruit of the merit of that man who, every fortnight, offers a lamp to Kṛṣṇa on the eleventh and twelfth lunar days. (Hbhv 8.66)
He ascends a divine celestial chariot, richly adorned with gold, jewels, and pearls, enchanting, exceedingly beautiful, and filled with rows of lamps.
By offering lamps made from wicks produced from lotus fibers and fueled with fragrant oil, a person becomes free from disease and fortunate. (Hbhv 8.68)
The gift of a lamp is certainly of great merit even among other deities;
how much more so, then, for the infinite and high-souled Vāsudeva?
In that very same third section:
"One should offer a lamp, which bestows sight and likewise bestows an upward rebirth;
just as the flame of a lamp moves upward, so too does the donor attain an upward rebirth. (Hbhv 8.70)
As many times as a lamp burns in a temple for the duration of a blink of an eye,
for that many thousands of years is one honored upon the heights of heaven.
In the *Bṛhan-nāradīya*, while recounting the account of Yajñadhvaja’s previous birth to Vitihotra, it is said:
"O best of the twice-born, a lamp was placed there for the sake of sexual pleasure;
by that act, my evil karma was entirely brought to an end. (Hbhv_8.72)
And in the *Viṣṇudharma*:
"When one possesses independence, a lamp placed in one's own hand within the temple of Viṣṇu yields great fruit; it does not lead to hell. (Hbhv 8.73)
In the *Nāradīya-purāṇa*, in the words of Śrī Rukmāṅgada addressed to Mohinī:
"O woman of excellent complexion, let alone vast amounts of wealth for the purpose of giving;
one may go to heaven by the gift of a lamp, [which causes] distress to the heart. (Hbhv_8.74)
O fortunate one, even in its absence, the illumination of another lamp should be performed with a spirit of devotion, for it is superior to all other forms of giving.
Thus,
even at a specific time, the greatness of offering a great lamp with devotion in the temple of the Blessed One is also described here. (Hbhv 8.76)
Now, regarding the majesty of the great lamp,
in the first section of the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"O protector of the earth, a great wick should always be offered, for it yields great fruit."
Especially during the dark fortnight, and there too, it is particularly so.
The new moon day (amāvasyā) and the twelfth day (dvādaśī) are specified as yielding great fruit;
this applies to whichever dark fortnight occurs after the month of Āśvayuja has passed.
O King, on that auspicious new moon day, and especially on the twelfth day,
a measure of oil should be offered at the right side of the deity.
O King, one who has fasted and subdued the senses should cause a wick made of eight *palas* to be offered there, wrapped entirely in a new cloth.
O Mahāmati, having given these two great lamps once,
after enjoying the heavenly world for a very long time, when one is born again upon the earth, ||| Hbhv_8.81 |||
Then one becomes possessed of fortune, endowed with victory and wealth, and is born preeminent within one's own kingdom, country, and likewise in the city. (Hbhv 8.82)
And in that family, O tiger among kings, there shall be one with a radiance like a lamp;
he becomes resplendent in battles and in quarrels.
Likewise, one gains renown in the world through the good qualities of those with good qualities;
moreover, even he who gives but a single [gift] to these two most beloved ones [attains such fame].
O great sinless one, O Yādava, a person attains in the human state everything that has been described to you;
likewise, he attains it in heaven during the time of enjoyment.
O King, the gift of even an ordinary lamp yields great fruit;
how much more so, then, for a great lamp—for which there is no limit? (Hbhv 8.86)
Now follows the prohibition against giving lamps with wicks made from red, coarse, worn-out, or dirty cloth, or even cloth that has already been used for a wick:
One should never give red, coarse, worn-out, or indeed dirty cloth, nor one that has already been used, for the purpose of making a wick. (Hbhv 8.87)
Thus:
One who desires merit should never, whether by oneself or through another, take away the lamps offered to Śrī Hari, nor should one ever extinguish them or cause them harm. (Hbhv 8.88)
Now, regarding the fault of extinguishing the lamp and so forth, it is stated in the first section of the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"Having offered a lamp, it must not be taken away by one who understands that ritual act."
Extinguishing a lamp and causing injury are indeed censured.
Indeed, he who commits violence through that action becomes one with blooming eyes;
the stealer of a lamp becomes blind, and the one who extinguishes it becomes one with parched eyes.
And in the *Viṣṇudharma*, regarding the denizens of hell, the venerable Dharmarāja spoke:
"In former times, while intoxicated by the pride of youth and devoid of discernment, you stole a lamp from the house of Govinda. (Hbhv 8.91)
Therefore, today they have fallen into a terrible hell, intensely tormented by hunger and thirst,
and torn apart by cold winds.
In that very place, in the words of Śrī Pulastya, it is said:
"Therefore, O best of the twice-born, one should offer lamps in the sanctuary of Viṣṇu;
having offered them, one should not extinguish them, nor should one deprive them of oil. (Hbhv 8.93)
And one who extinguishes a lamp is born mute and blind after death;
indeed, he is cooked in the hell of blinding darkness, which is so difficult to traverse.
Regarding the prohibition against offering lamps on the ground,
the *Kālikā Purāṇa* states:
"O Bhairava, a lamp-tree should be made of metal or other such materials."
A lamp should be offered upon trees, but never upon the ground.
Then, having offered the food offering (naivedya), and having performed the handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali), the seat (pīṭha), the foot-washing (pādya), and the sipping of water (ācamana),
one should offer the food to Kṛṣṇa in vessels according to the prescribed rule.
Now, the procedure for the offering of food (naivedya):

having recited the Astra-mantra and sprinkled water over the naivedya, one should protect it with the Cakra-mudrā and sprinkle it again with water consecrated by the recitation of the Vāyu-bīja. (Hbhv 8.97)
Having dried up that defect with it, one should visualize the fire-seed syllable on the right palm; then, joining the other [hand] upon its back, it is displayed.
One should burn away his dried-up defects with the fire arising from that [mantra] using the heart-mantra;
thereafter, one should contemplate the seed-syllable of nectar upon the palm of the left hand.
Placing the palm of the right hand upon its back, one should display it;
having offered the oblation with that [gesture], one should sprinkle it with a stream of nectar.

Having sprinkled that [object] with water over which the root mantra has been recited, and having contemplated it all as being of the nature of nectar, one should touch it and recite the root mantra eight times.
Having rendered that [offering] nectar-like by means of the *dhenumudrā* and with water and other substances,
and having worshipped both that and Kṛṣṇa, one should take up a handful of flowers.
Having prayed to Śrī Kṛṣṇa and meditated on the light emerging from His mouth,
one should unite it [with the leaf] and offer this leaf while touching it with the left hand.
Taking water mixed with fragrance and flowers in his right hand, he should recite the root mantra ending with *svāhā* and pour that water upon the ground. (Hbhv 8.104)
Raising that offering, which is accompanied by *tulasī* and rich with leaves, with both hands, one should devotedly present it to the Bhāgavata with his mantra. (Hbhv 8.105)
And this is the mantra for the offering:
"O Hari, I offer this oblation to you; please enjoy it. (Hbhv 8.106)
Thus,
while reciting "Thou art the bed of nectar, svāhā," he should offer water for rinsing the mouth to Hari according to the rules with his left hand.
One should display the *grāsa-mudrā*, which resembles a full-blown blue lotus.
One should display the *prāṇādi-mudrā* with the right hand, using the mantras beginning with *Tārā* and their respective names, ending with the fourth case and *svāhā*. (Hbhv 8.108)
Then, touching the two ring fingers with the two thumbs of his hands,
he should display the *mudrā* of the offering while reciting its mantra.
And this mantra is found in the *Kramadīpikā* (4.62): "The one born of Nanda, joined with water, the mantra, and the bindu; obeisance to the self consisting of the side, Rāma, and the wind, and Ni."
The self-born [Agni] is joined with *ruddha* and *ṅe*, while Anila is joined with *yuta* and *ami*, and both are associated with *nivedya* and the side of the month (*māsapārśva*). Hbhv_8.110.
Regarding the mantra of the offering as their own chosen mantra, those who are single-mindedly devoted recite it while extending the *grāsa-mudrā*. (Hbhv 8.111)
And they did not contemplate the emergence of radiance from Kṛṣṇa’s mouth;
with charming conversation, they joyfully fed Hari.
And elsewhere it is said:
"Well-prepared rice cooked with milk, white milk-rice as cool as the moon's rays, cakes and soups,
things to be licked, drunk, and well-sucked, white ambrosial fruits, *ghārikā* and other such delicious foods."

Enjoy this abundant clarified butter, the fuel for the fire, that which brings luster to the eyes, the savory seasoning of cardamom and black pepper, and the array of vegetable dishes— a meal like that of the gods.
Furthermore, in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:

"With supreme devotion, accompanied by the ringing of bells and the sounds of 'Victory!', the wise man should offer food offerings (*naivedya*) to Hari, as well as the waving of lights (*nīrājana*) and a lamp-seat (*dīpāsana*). (Hbhv 8.114)

Now, regarding the vessels for the food offering (*naivedya*), in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, within the dialogue between the venerable Brahmā and Nārada, it is said: "I shall describe the food-offering vessel for the Great-Souled Keśava."
A vessel made of gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, or even clay, as well as one of palāśa wood or a lotus leaf, is exceedingly dear to Viṣṇu. (Hbhv 8.115)
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"By the gift of leaves, moreover, one does not go to hell. (Hbhv 8.116)
Regarding the measurement of the vessel, the Devīpurāṇa states: "A vessel of thirty-six finger-breadths is proclaimed to be the best."
The medium-sized [bowl] is three parts less than that, and the smallest is twelve finger-breadths;
one should never have a bowl made that is deficient by eight finger-breadths.
Then, regarding the foods to be eaten,
in the eleventh skandha (11.27.34): "Molasses, milk-rice, clarified butter, saṣkulyas, apūpas, and modakas."
If available, one should arrange as an offering saṃyāva, curd, and soups.
Furthermore:
(11.11.41) Whatever is most desired in the world, and whatever is exceedingly dear to oneself—that one should offer to me; that conduces to infinity.
In the eighth Skanda [Purāṇa] (8.16.52):
One should offer food-offerings that are superior in quality, which grant satisfaction to the Supreme Person.
And in the Baudhāyana-smṛti:
"One should prepare an offering for Viṣṇu with various kinds of food and drinks, as well as delightful edibles and the like; and in the absence of those, with milk-rice (pāyasa)."
Only [that which is] combined with clarified butter.
In the Vāmana Purāṇa:
"Barley, wheat, and rice grains prepared with sacrificial oblation (havis), as well as sesame, mung beans, black gram, and paddy—these are dear to Hari. (Hbhv 8.122)

In the *Garuḍa-purāṇa*: "One should prepare with faith for Hari the four kinds of meritorious food, rich in qualities and like nectar, whether it has been prepared in one's own home or otherwise. (Hbhv 8.123)
In the Bhaviṣya [Purāṇa]:
"Flowers, incense, as well as lamps and very pleasing food offerings—namely, sugar-candies, *laḍḍukas*, *śrīveṣṭakas*, *kāsāras*, *aśokas*, and *vartikas*. (Hbhv 8.124)
Svastikas, ullāsikas, milk, sesame, veṣṭakas,
kilāṭikas, and also ripe fruits such as oranges and the like.
O King, having offered other various kinds of edible foods according to the prescribed rule, one should cause such things as these to be given with devotion. (Hbhv 8.126)
In the Vārāha [Purāṇa]:
"O Goddess, O Mādhavī, that devotee of the Lord by whom [the deity] is gratified with food remains gratified for many births. (Hbhv_8.127)
May this auspicious vessel, filled with all kinds of rice and endowed with all flavors, be offered to me by means of the mantra; may nothing else whatsoever touch it.
The fruits of the iṅgudī and bilva, jujubes and emblic myrobalans, dates and āsana fruits, as well as mānava and parūṣaka fruits.
And likewise *śāloḍḍambarikā*, as well as the fruits of the *plakṣa*, the *paippala*, the *kaṇṭakīya*, the *tumburu*, and the *priyaṅgu*. (Hbhv 8.130)
Marica, śiṃśapāka, bhallātaka, ramardaka, grapes, pomegranate, and indeed the piṇḍa-kharjūra; Hbhv_8.131 //
Sauvīra, as well as kelika and auspicious fruits, the piṇḍāraka fruit, and the punnāga fruit as well. (Hbhv 8.132)
The śamī, the kavīra, the kharjūraka with its large fruit, the fruit of the kumuda, and likewise the fruit of the vaheḍaka. (Hbhv 8.133)
The aja and karkoṭaka, as well as the fruits of the tāla;
the kadamba and kaumuda—these are the two kinds of land-lotuses.
After that, there is the bamboo known as Piṇḍikaṇḍa, and further,
the nīpa known as Madhukaṇḍa, as well as the buffalo-horned bamboo (māhiṣakaṇḍa).
The karamardaka tuber, as well as that of the blue lotus (nilotpala), lotus stalk (mṛṇāla), the lotus root of the Puṣkara, and likewise the fruit of the śālūka; Hbhv_8.136 //
These and many others— stems, roots, and fruits—
are those which have been prescribed by me as fit for consumption.
Then there is the potherb of radish, likewise the potherb of tamarind,
as well as the potherb of peas and likewise that of mustard.
The vegetable of vaṃsaka, indeed the vegetable of śāka, and the vegetable of kalambikā,
as well as the vegetable of fresh ginger and the vegetable of pālaṅka.
Ambiloḍaka and śāka, kāśa and likewise kaumāraka,
the leaf of the śukamaṇḍala, and the two types of taruvānaka.
The leaf of the *carasa* tree, as well as the *madhukoḍḍumbara*,
and these and many others by the hundreds and thousands—
all those which have been enumerated by me are indeed suitable for ritual action.
And I shall explain the uses of rice, O Mādhavī;
listen to all of that with a focused mind, O beautiful one. (Hbhv 8.142)
And [he offered] red rice that was fragrant and pleasing to both the righteous and the unrighteous,
long-bearded great śāli rice, and excellent saffron petals.
O beautiful one, village rice, sea-rice, rice with its stalks, and rice with its awns,
as well as two kinds of barley, should be known as suitable for my ritual use.
Mung beans, black sesame seeds, horse gram, wheat,
great mung beans, and mung beans— these eight [types of legumes] overcome indigestion and are wholesome for digestion.
These fans, said to be suitable for ritual action, are accompanied by beloved ones;
indeed, I accept all these dear devotees of the Lord.
Furthermore:
"Those products of the cow—curd, milk, and ghee—which are to be consumed by me alone," (Hbhv 8.147)
And in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada:
"The food offering for the God of gods consists of divine sacrificial oblation, rice with thorns, mixed with clarified butter and sugar, as well as barley-gruel and milk-rice. (Hbhv_8.148)
In the absence of food offerings, however, one should present fruits;
and in the absence of fruits, even grasses, shrubs, and medicinal herbs.
If medicinal herbs are unavailable, one should offer water;
if even that is unavailable, it is traditionally taught that in all such cases, a mental offering is superior.
In the Skanda Purāṇa, the venerable Nārada spoke to Mahendra:
"Those who have heard of the Tulasī leaf being offered before Mādhava shall dwell in the world of Viṣṇu along with their ancestors until the end of the kalpa. (Hbhv 8.151)
Now, regarding the items prohibited as food offerings (*naivedya*), the *Hārīta-smṛti* states:

"Nothing that is unfit for consumption should be used for an offering; even among things otherwise fit for consumption, the milk of goats and buffaloes, as well as five-nailed animals and fish, are excluded. (Hbhv 8.152)
Regarding the majesty of Dvārakā:
those who sow indigo fields or eat radishes shall have no escape from hell, even after hundreds of millions of kalpas.
In the Vārāha [Purāṇa]:
"The meat of buffaloes, sheep, and goats is declared to be unfit for sacrifice."
Furthermore:
One should avoid buffalo milk, as well as its curd and ghee.
In the third section of the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:

"One should not offer as a food-offering (*naivedya*) anything that is unfit to be eaten, nor anything unpleasant, nor that which is infested with hair or insects, nor that which is otherwise prohibited. (Hbhv_8.156)
Fruit accompanied by mouse-droppings, that which has been blown upon or sneezed over,
as well as *uḍumbara*, *kapittha*, and *dantaśaṭha*—
such things as these should never be offered to the deity. (Hbhv 8.157)
Now, regarding forbidden foods,
it is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"The eggplant (*vṛntāka*), the *jālikā* vegetable, safflower (*kusumbha*), and *aśmantaka* [mushroom], likewise..."
One should avoid onions, garlic, white exudations, and resins.
Having eaten gṛñjana, kiṃśuka, kukuṇḍa, as well as uḍumbara and alābu, a twice-born man indeed falls [from his caste]. (Hbhv 8.159)
O Lord of Men, one should never eat the remnants of food from which the essence has been extracted at a Vaiṣṇava rite.
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Hari remains far away from him who does not eat the eggplant (vṛntāka)."
Furthermore, elsewhere it is said:
"With the two arms, the two feet, the two knees, the chest, the head, the eyes, the mind, and speech—this is declared to be the eight-limbed prostration. (Hbhv 8.162)
With both knees, the two arms, the head, speech, and the mind—this is the five-limbed prostration; these two [types of prostration] are the most excellent for acts of worship. (Hbhv 8.163)
Therefore it is said in the Yāmala: "Where there is liquor, as well as meat, and likewise eggplant and radish—one should never offer these; therein lies the exclusive devotion to Hari. (Hbhv 8.164)
Now, regarding the greatness of the offering of food (naivedya), it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"One should offer pleasing foods before Kṛṣṇa."
For that long, the ancestors indeed experience eternal satisfaction for the duration of a kalpa.
O Lord of Men, for one who indeed bestows pleasant fruits upon a friend,
his desire becomes fruitful and he is reborn until the end of the aeon.
In the *Nārasiṃha*:
"Having offered as an oblation rice cooked with milk (*śālyodana*) mixed with clarified butter and sugar, as well as barley gruel (*yāvaka*) and milk-rice (*pāyasa*), to Narasiṃha. (Hbhv 8.167)
O King, for as many years as there are grains of rice in those heaps,
those devotees of Viṣṇu shall enjoy great pleasures in the world of Viṣṇu.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The giver of food attains satisfaction and goes to the heavenly world;
likewise, by giving food for the purpose of distribution, he remains unwearied."
By satisfying the three worlds, one obtains that merit at that very moment.
By giving rice accompanied by a fan, one obtains inexhaustible food and drink for the ancestors and attains heaven. (Hbhv 8.170)
Likewise, by giving *paramānna*, one attains eternal satisfaction;
one reaches the world of Viṣṇu and likewise uplifts one's lineage.
By the gift of rice cooked with ghee, one obtains long life;
by the gift of rice cooked with curd, one attains unsurpassed prosperity.
By the gift of milk-rice, one shall obtain long life;
and by the gift of sugarcane, one enjoys supreme good fortune.
One shall become a partaker of jewels and go to the heavenly world;
by the gift of molasses, one obtains the fruit of establishing the sacred fires.
Likewise, by the gift of molasses, one shall obtain whatever desired object is wished for.
By offering sugarcane juice with devotion, one attains supreme good fortune;
and he who offers honey obtains all his desires. (Hbhv 8.176)
One who offers that very same [food] with joy shall obtain the Rājasūya sacrifice;
one who offers barley-gruel obtains the Agniṣṭoma,
and likewise, one who offers cakes obtains the Atirātra.
By the gift of foods made from split pulses, one shall obtain all desires;
by offering oblations filled with ghee, one attains long life.
By the gift of sweetmeats (modaka), one obtains one's desired objects.
By the gift of various kinds of foods fit for eating, one attains heaven;
by the provision of meals, one obtains unsurpassed satisfaction. (Hbhv 8.180)
Likewise, by the offering of foods to be licked, one attains good fortune;
and by the presentation of foods to be sucked, one acquires strength and a fine complexion.
A giver of boiled grain with sour gruel shall obtain the fruit of the Vahnyādheya sacrifice;
likewise, by the gift of salt, one may attain the Vājapeya (Vahniṣṭoma) sacrifice.
One who offers wealth mixed with honey, parched grain,
and especially flour-cakes, shall attain the Vahniṣṭoma sacrifice.
One who offers leafy vegetables obtains the merit associated with those who have retired to the forest;
likewise, by giving a green fruit, one attains that very same fruit.
By giving delightful vegetables, one is born free from sorrow;
likewise, by giving fans and other such implements.
The twice-born who offers bulbs and roots attains birth in a noble family; likewise, one who offers blue lotuses and vidārī roots [attains the same]. (Hbhv 8.186)
By giving a bulbous root, one obtains the auspicious fruit of the forest-dweller;
by giving cucumber or gourd, one shall obtain the fruit of a white lotus.
Having offered jujube and wild plum, as well as the *pāraivata*, *kalam*, *parūṣaka*, *abhra*, breadfruit, and coconut; Hbhv_8.188 //
Bhavya, mocā, likewise ucca, kharjūra, and then dāḍima; āmrātaka, sruvāmla, uṭaphala, māna, and priyālaka.
The rose-apple, the wood-apple, and the myrobalan, as well as the jasmine, the vīṇātaka, the orange, the citron, and also seeds and fruits that are light; Hbhv_8.190.
Thus, he who offers such divine fruits,
as well as the most excellent tubers, with devotion to the God of gods, [attains these rewards].
The one who offers grapes attains the fruitfulness of their action, as well as the heavenly world,
and obtains the reward of good health.
By worshipping the Lord of Gods with mangoes, one obtains the foremost of flavors as well as supreme good fortune; one shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
Furthermore:
the mocaka, panasa, jambu, as well as other kumbhālī fruits,
the prācīnāmalaka, and those of the madhuka and udumbara trees are excellent.
Even if it has been ripened through effort, the excellent plantain fruit is to be accepted.
And in the *Haribhakti-sudhodaya* it is said:

"Whatever small amount of food offering is saturated with the nectar of devotion to the Lord, the Blessed Lord quickly causes that very thing to nourish His own happiness for those who give it. (Hbhv 8.195)
Then, as before, one should offer various excellent fruits, and thereafter water that is fragrant, cool, and clear.
Now, regarding the *panakas* and their greatness, it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
By offering fragrant and especially cool beverages to the God of gods, one obtains the merit of a horse sacrifice.
Combined with cinnamon, cardamom, *nāgakesara*,
and camphor, along with sugar, honey, and jaggery, they are endowed with excellent fragrance, color, and quality.
By offering panakas together with bījapūra, nāraṅga, and sahakāra fruits,
one obtains the merit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
By offering coconut water, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
There, where rivers that flow with all desired objects are eternally delightful,
those who provide drinks go to dwell among women endowed with every virtue.

Thus, having presented the offering in this manner and given the food, one should then withdraw the curtain; going outside, one should perform the recitation and meditation according to one's capacity. (Hbhv 8.201)
Then, while engaged in meditation, he was joined by Brahmā, Śiva, and other sages seated all around him,
and was respectfully fanned by Lakṣmī with her hands whose bracelets were tinkling.
With a face laughing at the playful jests of the *marmas*, the illustrious Rāmeśvara eats the six flavors from a golden vessel, making those sitting in the row laugh.
Thus,
those who are single-mindedly devoted should meditate upon the meal of Kṛṣṇa while he was in Gokula with his companions, being fondled by Yaśodā. (Hbhv 8.203)
Now, regarding the fire sacrifice (homa):
one should perform the daily obligatory fire sacrifice according to one's capacity;
however, if one is unable to perform the fire sacrifice, one should perform a recitation (japa) four times the required number.
Some indeed think thus: "One must certainly perform the daily fire-oblation (nitya-homa) at all times;
for that is considered the rule to be followed when one is unable to perform the fire-oblation of the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa). (Hbhv 8.205)
Previously, a certain portion of the ritual for initiation and the ritual for fire-offerings (homa) has been written;
those who desire them should learn their full details from the respective scriptures.
Having contemplated the completion of the meal and having sipped water for rinsing the mouth, the wise person should recite: "Thou art the covering of nectar, svāhā. (Hbhv 8.207)
One should release that radiance into the mouth of the deity by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā*;
one should not cause the radiance to exit as if it were a transfer to another location. (Hbhv 8.208)
Then, after the offering to Bali,
the wise one should remove the curtain according to the ritual rules and present a portion of the food offering to the Blessed One Viṣvaksena.
And likewise, in the *Pañcarātra*, there is the word of the venerable Nārada:
"A hundredth part of that *naivedya* should be given to Viṣvaksena;
and the water for the feet and the *prasāda* should be given to Caṇḍeśvara at the *liṅga*. (Hbhv 8.210)

The procedure for that is as follows: from the primary vessel, starting from Īśāna, one should take out a portion of the food offering (naivedya) for the Supreme Being, the Parameṣṭhin, who is the embodiment of all deities. (Hbhv 8.211)
"Obeisance to you, Viṣvaksena, who are engaged in the service of Śrī Kṛṣṇa";
having spoken thus, one should offer the cloth moistened with the holy water on the left side of Śrī Hari.
Or else, it may be a hundred-thousandth part; otherwise, it would be fruitless.
And afterwards, having recited the verses beginning with "balir," the Vaiṣṇava should offer a hundredth part of that to all the Vaiṣṇavas.
And those two verses are as follows:
"Bali, Vibhīṣaṇa, Bhīṣma, Kapila, Nārada, Arjuna, Prahlāda, Ambarīṣa, Vasu, the son of Vāyu, and Śiva. (Hbhv 8.215)
May Viṣvaksena, Uddhava, Akrūra, Sanaka and the others, Śuka and the rest—
may all these Vaiṣṇavas receive this grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Although this [reflection] would be possible only through the application of a mirror,
nevertheless, due to Kṛṣṇa’s affection for his devotees, it may occur even here.
Now, regarding the greatness of the *bali-dāna*, it is stated in the *Nārasiṃha-purāṇa*:
"Then, with the remainder of that food, [one should offer] to the attendants on all sides."
Whoever offers a bali-oblation mixed with flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata), [attains the fruit].
Then, being satisfied by that Vaiṣṇava strength, the gods bestow peace, prosperity, and even health upon him.
Then, having smeared the ground with a mouthful of water and so forth,
one should again offer three mouthfuls of water to Kṛṣṇa; thereafter, one should give him a tooth-cleansing stick.
Having again given water for sipping (ācamana) to the venerable hands and the venerable face,
and having offered a cloth for wiping, one should wipe all the limbs.
Having caused him to put on other garments and having again provided another seat, one should offer water for the feet and water for sipping once more, as before. (Hbhv 8.222)
One should offer sandalwood and agalloch powder for the cleansing of the hands, as well as camphor and other fragrances for the mouth, betel leaf, and tulasī. (Hbhv 8.223)
Now, regarding the greatness of betel (mukha-vasadi) in the third section of the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"Having given a nut of the areca palm (*pūga-jāti-phala*) as well as a leaf of the betel vine (*jāti-patra*),"
Likewise, the fruit of the *lavaṅga*, *phala*, *kakkola*, *mela*, and *kata*.
By [giving] a sprout of betel vines, one shall attain the heavenly world, as well as incomparable good fortune in this world and unsurpassed beauty. (Hbhv 8.225)
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"O leader of men, Hari is always pleased with that person who affectionately offers betel leaf along with camphor and areca nut to Kṛṣṇa. (Hbhv 8.226)
Then again, having offered divine fragrances and perfumes as desired,
one should anoint Śrī-Kṛṣṇa with various divine unguents through the practice of uninterrupted devotion.
One should most excellently fashion beautiful vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) with high-quality pigment of the appropriate color in their proper places, and apply fragrant unguents for Kṛṣṇa.
And likewise, in the Āgama, in the context of meditation:
"Adorned with a shining vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) made of gold upon the forehead, the heart, the belly, the throat, and many parts of the sides. (Hbhv 8.229)
Thus,
one should cause Śrī Kṛṣṇa to put on divine garments— such as tunics, turbans, girdles, and other excellent clothes— that are most wonderfully variegated.
Then, having clothed him in divine crowns and other ornaments according to his preference,
and having adorned him with various divine garlands, one should embellish him.
Then, having offered the services of a great king, as well as other royal honors such as the fly-whisk, the parasol, the sandals, and so forth,
one should present a mirror.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"By offering the royal insignia in a temple according to the prescribed place and time, one becomes a king himself; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (Hbhv 8.233)
In that regard, such is the greatness of the *cāmara*: by the gift of a *cāmara*, one becomes illustrious upon the earth,
is liberated from sins, and likewise goes to the heavenly world.
Regarding the greatness of the parasol,
it is said in that very same place:
"The parasol should have many ribs and be joined with a *jhallarī* and cloth."
It was provided with divine garments and equipped with a golden staff.
He who offers an umbrella to Kṛṣṇa, surrounded by a hundred thousand umbrellas,
is sought after by all the immortals and sports together with his ancestors.
In this very world, or elsewhere, the best of the twice-born, having given an umbrella, becomes a king;
he does not suffer the pain born of enemies and, as a conqueror of foes, shall fear no battle. (Hbhv 8.237)
By the gift of sandals, one ascends a celestial chariot;
possessing the splendor of an immortal, one wanders through the worlds as one pleases.
Regarding the greatness of the banner,
it is stated in that very same source:
"By giving an excellent banner to Viṣṇu, one shall become like a banner throughout the worlds."
A person attains the world of Śakra for many groups of years.
Furthermore:
"O best of the twice-born, it is fitting that one who has offered a golden banner to Keśava, whose emblem is Garuḍa, shall be honored in all the worlds. (Hbhv 8.240)

Whatever greatness regarding the raising of the banner was previously written concerning his grace, all that should be understood here as well; likewise, this [following] is what pertains to this place.
Furthermore, in the *Bhaviṣya-purāṇa*: "A wise man should make the staff on Viṣṇu’s banner golden;
the banner near Garuḍa should also be yellow. (Hbhv 8.242)
Regarding the greatness of the fan, it is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"By the gift of its surface and its handle, one shall attain supreme bliss. (Hbhv 8.243)
Regarding the greatness of the canopy,
it is said in that very same source:
"By the gift of a canopy, one is liberated from all sins."
He attains supreme peace wherever he is reborn.
By giving the greatness of swords— namely, excellent blades— one is not overcome by enemies;
by giving that preeminent binding [of weapons], one obtains the fruit of establishing the sacred fires.
Furthermore:
By likewise giving a spittoon, one is born as a bestower of auspiciousness;
by the gift of a footstool, one finds a secure position everywhere. (Hbhv 8.246)
By the gift of a mirror, one becomes handsome and confident;
likewise, by polishing it, one is born fortunate.
Whatever one may give to the God of gods, endowed with devotion, that very gift becomes inexhaustible; he goes to the heavenly world.
Furthermore, in the *Vāmana Purāṇa*, in the speech of Śrī Prahlāda to Śrī Bali:
"The wise know that those offerings of gifts which are given to Janārdana by those who are faithful and devoted to Him become inexhaustible. (Hbhv_8.249)
In this case as well, some maintain that after offering three handfuls of flowers,
one should display the ten previously mentioned mudrās, beginning with the conch.
Thus, there were songs, instrumental music, and dances,
performed by others in various charming ways or executed by himself.
One should satisfy Śrī Kṛṣṇa with songs, instrumental music, and dances.
Furthermore, one who is seated there should not look upon the devotees performing dances and other acts that are prohibited;
nor should one walk past them sideways, thereby interposing oneself between them and the Lord.
And thus it has been said:
"O Indra among kings, he who, while sitting, gazes with delight upon a Vaiṣṇava dancing, shall become lame in birth after birth. (Hbhv 8.253)
Furthermore:
"Among those who are dancing and singing, both the devotees and Keśava, he who passes by them unseen goes to the womb of an animal. (Hbhv 8.254)

The man who causes singing, instrumental music, dance, and the sounding of conchs and trumpets to be performed in the temple of Viṣṇu during the twilight hours—
especially at all times— becomes able to go wherever he desires and assume any form at will.
Served by hosts of apsarases skilled in fine music,
and traveling in a magnificent, variegated, and resplendent celestial chariot,
he reaches heaven after heaven and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
In the *Skānda Purāṇa*, within the dialogue between Viṣṇu and Nārada, it is said:
"O Sage, he who performs song, instrumental music, dance, dramatic performance, and the narration of Viṣṇu’s stories—that meritorious soul is established above the three worlds. (Hbhv_8.257)
In the *Bṛhan-nāradīya*, in the dialogue between the venerable Yama and Bhagīratha:
"O Lord of the Earth, listen to the fruit obtained by one who, filled with devotion, dances or sings songs in the temple of a deity. (Hbhv_8.258)

joined with the eight families, that man thereafter becomes a partaker of liberation.
In the *Liṅga-purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya and Ambarīṣa:

The fruit of all the Vedas arises for him; there is no doubt in this matter.

In the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa*, in the dialogue between the messenger of Viṣṇu and Śivaśarman:

In the *Viṣṇuśarman* [section] of the *Śrī-Bhagavad-ukti*:
"If your mind is drawn toward the art of music by passion, then, fixing your intellect upon Me, you should sing My sacred stories. (Hbhv 8.271)
On this earth, that devotee who constantly and loudly sings the *Haribhaktisudhodaya* alone is sufficient to destroy the sins of all people.

When a devotee, singing with a sense of joy, sheds tears of merit, that constitutes bathing in the waters of all sacred fords and the purification of one's own impurities. (Hbhv 8.273)
In the Vārāha [Purāṇa]:
"A Brāhmaṇa, constantly singing for the sake of Vāsudeva, [should do so] properly through the application of rhythm (tāla) or again through the coordination (sannipāta). (Hbhv 8.274)
Having gone to the abode of Kuvera, he indeed rejoices at his pleasure for nine thousand and nine hundred years.

Furthermore:
"O sages, this sequence of songs of the Sage has been declared to you;

One who is devoted solely to Vāsudeva through action, mind, and speech attains the same world as Hari (sālokya) and becomes superior even to the hosts of Rudras. By singing and dancing [to Him], one attains Him; therefore, they know that song is supreme. (Hbhv 8.279)
In the first book, in the words of Śrī Nārada (1.6.33):

In the twelfth book (12.12.49–50),
in the words of the Blessed Sūta:
"For those are false words, they are unreal, and they are worthless talk."
That which the Blessed One Adhokṣaja does not speak—
that alone is truth, that indeed is auspiciousness,

That alone is lovely, radiant, ever-new; that alone is the perpetual great festival for the mind;
that alone is the drying up of the ocean of sorrow for human beings.

In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Having given a song, those who know the Dharma rejoice together with the Gandharvas;

"O Nārada, I do not dwell in Vaikuṇṭha, nor in the hearts of yogis; wherever My devotees sing, there I abide. (Hbhv_8.284)
People perform worship and other rites for them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
through that, I attain supreme joy, which I do not experience in the same way from my own worship.

"A Brahmin is remembered as one who is other [than those devoted solely to rituals] because of his skillful means regarding actions.

"He who dances with a joyful soul, through various moods and with great devotion..."
It burns away his evils, even those accumulated over hundreds of other births.
From the dancing devotee of Viṣṇu, who exults in the *Hari-bhakti-sudhodaya*, much inauspiciousness is joyfully cast out from the earth by his feet,

In the Vārāha [Purāṇa]:
"O lady of beautiful hips, he who dances according to the summary of what was declared in the Purāṇas [remains] for thirty thousand and thirty hundred years."

"By offering dance, one undoubtedly attains the world of Rudra;

"By the frequent clapping of hands before the Lord of Śrī while He dances, all the birds of sin residing within the body fly away. (Hbhv 8.292)
One who knows the true principles of playing the lute according to the treatises on music, who is proficient in the *śrutis* and *jātis*,

"By giving musical instruments to a brahmin, one attains the world of Śakra;

Among musical instruments as well, the lute (tantrī-vādya) is always dear to the God;

Therefore, if one is capable, one should again perform worship; if able, one should once more worship Kṛṣṇa along with his retinue using perfumes and so forth,
and having worshipped him with the five offerings (pañcopacāra) by means of the root mantra, one should present the arghya offering.
Then, having performed the *nīrājana* rite and offered three handfuls of flowers with the root mantra,
one should perform the great *nīrājana* amidst the sounds of great musical instruments and cries of victory.
For that purpose, one should kindle an *ārātrika*—consisting of many uneven wicks—in an auspicious vessel, using either camphor or ghee. (Hbhv 8.298)
Now, regarding the greatness of the *nīrājana* rite,
as related in the *Skanda Purāṇa* in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada:

Whoever performs the *ārātrika* rite shall dwell in heaven for ten million eons.
O best of sages, he who with devotion performs the *ārātrika* (luminous waving) rite over the head of Keśava using camphor shall enter the imperishable Viṣṇu. (Hbhv 8.300)
In that very same place, elsewhere it is said:
"O King, those humans who perform the *ārātrika* rite for Kṛṣṇa with camphor and radiant lamps shall dwell in the world for seven kalpas. (Hbhv 8.301)
In that very same [text], in the Śrī-Sivomasaṃvāda:
"Whatever worship of Hari has been performed, even if deficient in mantras or deficient in ritual actions, it all attains completeness when the Nīrājana is performed, O Śivā. (Hbhv 8.302)
In the *Haribhaktisudhodaya*:

"By performing the *nīrājana* rite for Viṣṇu with the beautiful array of lamps on the festival of lights, one conquers the transformation of darkness; and when that is conquered, what is worldly existence? (Hbhv 8.303)
And elsewhere it is said:
"Tens of millions of killings of Brahmins and tens of millions of illicit sexual unions—Viṣṇu’s face at dawn burns them away by its mere sight. (Hbhv 8.304)
Thus,
whatever greatness of the lamp has been previously written,
that should be understood to apply everywhere as well, for these two are generally non-different.
Therefore, having risen with reverence, this great *nīrājana* should be beheld by all like a lamp, as well as that *ārātrika* which is worthy of worship. (Hbhv 8.306)
Thus it was said by the venerable Pulastya in the *Viṣṇudharma*:
"One who beholds the incense and the *ārātrika* lamp and bows with both hands, having delivered ten million ancestors of his lineage, goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. (Hbhv_8.307)
And in the Mūlāgama:

"The brahmin who beholds the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) of the God of gods, the Wielder of the Discus, shall become a brahmin for seven births and, at the end, attain the supreme state. (Hbhv_8.308)
Now, regarding the majesty of sounding conch shells and other instruments,
in the *Bṛhan-nāradīya-purāṇa*, within the dialogue between the venerable Yama and Bhagīratha, it is said:
"O King, a man who makes the sound of a conch shell in the temple of Keśava..."
Completely liberated from all evil, he rejoices together with Brahmā.
Those who utter the sound "kara" in the temples of Keśava are all liberated from sin and become lords of celestial chariots for two eons.
O King, listen as I describe the fruit that a man obtains by making the sound of cymbals and the like in the temple of Viṣṇu. (Hbhv 8.311)
Completely liberated from all evil, surrounded by hundreds of celestial palaces,

With kettledrums, clay drums, cymbals, and muraja drums, along with ḍiṇḍimas, they delight the Lord of Gods; hear now the fruit of their merit. (Hbhv 8.313)
Accompanied by hosts of celestial women and honored with all objects of desire,
they reach the heavenly world and rejoice there for five kalpas.
Thus [it is said].
Then follows the *nīrājana* with the water-filled conch;
thereafter, the water-filled conch is placed above the head of the Blessed One.
Having whirled it three times, one should again perform the lustration ceremony for the Lord.
And its greatness is described in that very same *Dvārakā-māhātmya*:
"Having placed water in a conch shell and whirled it over Keśava..."
He dwells in the presence of Viṣṇu in the Ocean of Milk until the end of the kalpa.

"These two lustrations (nīrājana) and the offering of betel-leaf (tāmbūla) come after;
some desire them [to follow] the offering of the mirror. (Hbhv 8.317)
And so it is stated in the Pañcarātra:
"One should again offer water for rinsing the mouth and likewise a rubbing-paste for the hands;
one should also offer betel with camphor and perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana). (Hbhv 8.318)
Having offered his crown and other ornaments, the wise one should likewise display a mirror, having prepared the parasol and the fly-whisks.
And in the *Garuḍa-purāṇa*:
"Then, having given [food] to one who has eaten, one should offer water scented with camphor for sipping (*ācamana*), betel leaf, and the cleansing of the hands with sandalwood paste. (Hbhv 8.320)
Then, having offered a handful of flowers with devotion, one should display a mirror;
the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) should be performed again, using camphor if one has the means.
Therefore, it is said in the *Vāyu Purāṇa*:
"An oilless *ārātrika* (lustration lamp) causes the deity to become devoid of moisture;
therefore, having first pacified [the deity] with oil, one should perform the worship again. (Hbhv 8.322)
Therefore, in the *Dvārakā-māhātmya*, it is said:
"Having performed all the worship and other rites right there, one who performs the *ārātrika* ceremony over the blazing head of Kṛṣṇa rejoices in the presence of Kṛṣṇa. (Hbhv 8.323)
Thus it is said:
some desire the prostration after the lustration (nīrājana), then the circumambulation, then the hymn of praise, and then the singing, dancing, and so forth. (Hbhv 8.324)
Thus, according to their respective traditions, people proceed toward devotion to the Lord; for indeed, everything performed with devotion is auspicious.
Then, having offered three handfuls of flowers over the Deity, the devoted one should perform praise with various sweet hymns. (Hbhv 8.326)
Now, regarding the method of praise, it is said in the Mahābhārata:
"Desiring to propitiate Kṛṣṇa, I wish to utter these words."
By this [work], both detailed and concise, may Madhusūdana be pleased.
Thus, at the commencement of the praise, one intent on praise should recite this verse;
and when that [praise] is completed, he should proclaim this verse. (Hbhv 8.328)
Thus, Viṣṇu, the source of knowledge and austerity, who is himself without origin, has been proclaimed;
may the Lord Janārdana, worshipped by this sacrifice of speech, be pleased with me. (Hbhv 8.329)
In the *Pūrvatāpanī-śrutis* [GTU 1.34–45]:
"Oṃ! Salutations to the one whose form is the universe, the cause of the universe's maintenance and end;
salutations again and again to Govinda, the Lord of the universe, who is the universe itself. (Hbhv 8.330)
Homage to the one whose form is consciousness, whose nature is supreme bliss; homage again and again to Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Gopīs, Govinda. Hbhv_8.331
Homage to the lotus-eyed one; homage to the one garlanded with lotuses; homage to the one whose navel is a lotus; homage to the Lord of Kamalā. Hbhv_8.332 //
Salutations again and again to Govinda, who is delightful with his peacock-feather crown, whose intellect is unimpeded, and who is the swan in the lake of Ramā’s mind. Hbhv_8.333 //

who wanders along the banks of the Yamunā, and who wears swinging earrings.
Salutations again and again to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who wears a garland of lotus-faces of the cowherd girls, who is skilled in the art of dance, and who protects those who bow before him. Hbhv_8.336 //

to the ender of Pūtanā’s life, and to the one who took away the pleasure of Tṛṇāvarta.

O Keśava, remover of afflictions, O Nārāyaṇa, O Janārdana,
O Govinda, supreme bliss, O Mādhava, lift me up!

there are such Vedic [texts], as well as Purāṇic, Tantric, and even new hymns concerning Kṛṣṇa. (Hbhv_8.344)

"By means of hymns composed by himself with unerring characteristics and well-formed syllables, that tiger among Brahmins shall therefore obtain his desires. (Hbhv 8.345)

one who praises the immeasurable majesty [of the Lord] with beautiful words strung together by devotion shall become a vessel for the Lord’s compassion, which is difficult even for Brahmā and others to obtain. (Hbhv 8.349)

whatever greatness of the hymn has been written or should be written regarding the bath, and whatever greatness of its recitation there is—all that should be understood here as well. (Hbhv 8.355)

Thus it was said by the Blessed Lord in the eleventh book [BhP 11.27.45]: "Having praised Him with various hymns and praises—whether from the Purāṇas or even in the vernacular—one should prostrate like a staff, saying: 'O Blessed One, be gracious! (Hbhv 8.358)
Now, the procedure for prostration is described in that very same place [BhP 11.27.46]:
"Placing the head at my feet and with the arms crossed around each other..."
O Lord, protect me who have sought refuge, terrified as I am by the ocean of the crocodile of death.

"With the two arms, the two feet, the two knees, the chest, the head, the eyes, the mind, and the speech—this is declared to be the eight-limbed prostration. (Hbhv 8.360)
With the two knees, the two arms, the head, speech, and the intellect—this five-limbed prostration is the most excellent among all forms of worship. (Hbhv 8.361)

having placed the Garuḍa on the right, the wise man should perform it behind him;

"Prostration is remembered as a sacrifice, and the best among all sacrifices."

"The destination which one attains by prostrating like a staff upon the ground and worshipping with salutation cannot be reached even by hundreds of sacrifices."

"He who, pressing his knees upon the ground and placing his head on the earth, bows down to the Lord of Gods, shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice. (Hbhv 8.368)

"Thousands of millions of sacred fords and hundreds of millions of sacred fords do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of a prostration to Nārāyaṇa. (Hbhv 8.369)

In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Having saluted the Lord of the World, one shall likewise have one's purpose fulfilled;

"Those men who constantly bow before the God who is without beginning or end, and who shatters the Daityas and Dānavas, do not behold Yama. (Hbhv 8.374)

do not go anywhere other than to Viṣṇu through their bathing [in him].

"Even a single prostration made to Kṛṣṇa is not equal to the final purificatory baths of ten horse-sacrifices."
One who has performed ten horse-sacrifices returns to birth again;
but one who bows to Kṛṣṇa does not return to further existence.

Sandalwood, even as the residue of incense, removes the sin of killing a Brahmin.
In that very same [text], regarding the greatness of the conch:
"Whatever water situated in the conch has been whirled over Keśava, he who always honors it with his head—what need has he for bathing in the Gaṅgā? (Hbhv 9.4)
There is no burning, no exhaustion, no affliction, and indeed no fear of the fires of hell for one upon whose head the water from a conch shell has been poured and gazed upon by the eyes of Kṛṣṇa.
Neither the grahas, nor the kuṣmāṇḍas, nor the piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas,
upon seeing conch-water on the head, flee in the ten directions.
Having whirled that water, which was contained within the conch, over Kṛṣṇa’s head and then sprinkling it upon one's own head,
one attains liberation through the grace of Viṣṇu.
The Vaiṣṇava who, having whirled the temple of Hari over his head with water from a conch shell, sprinkles it, shall have no inauspiciousness in that house. (Hbhv 9.8)
O tiger among sages, wherever the water used for the royal consecration of a king, or the water from the feet of Hari, remains, there all prosperities increase.
In that very same [text], it says further:
"O King, whoever’s body is touched by the water from Viṣṇu, he obtains the fruit born of bathing, characterized as the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of a sacrifice. (Hbhv 9.10)
In that very same *Śrīśivokti*:
"One who is burdened by ten thousand murders is purified by the water from the feet of the Lord, as is one by the water from his conch; of this there is no doubt. (Hbhv 9.11)
And in the *Bṛhad-Viṣṇu Purāṇa*:
"Water that has always been touched by the glance of Keśava is more purifying than a hundred sacrifices, even more so than a holy place (*tīrtha*)."
One cuts away evil by [offering] that which is mixed with *tulasī*,
especially that which has been fashioned on a stone slab marked with a discus.
Then,
having offered the water from the sacred fords and the water from the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa to the Vaiṣṇavas,
he himself should first bow down with devotion, offer it, and then place it upon his head.
The ritual procedure for his mantra has already been written in connection with the morning bath;
now, however, a certain amount of the specific details regarding drinking are being written.
And it was said: Oṃ, the ancient, wide-spread, pure filter, by which one who is purified crosses over evil deeds.
Purified by that pure and holy [practice],
may we cross over evil and enmity.
