Thus, with reverence, one should listen to the scriptures of devotion, and therein,
specifically, to the Śrīmad Bhāgavata, repeatedly hearing the stories of Kṛṣṇa’s divine play.
Now, regarding the majesty of the Vaiṣṇava scriptures:
In the Skanda Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śrī Brahmā and Nārada, it is said:
"Those who hear and read the Vaiṣṇava scriptures..."
Blessed are those men in the world with whom Kṛṣṇa is pleased.
Those men who honor the Vaiṣṇava scriptures in their home become liberated from all sins and are praised by the gods.

O best of Brahmins, even at the cost of one's entire possessions, the collection of the scriptures must be undertaken by Vaiṣṇavas with great devotion for the sake of pleasing the Wielder of the Discus. (Hbhv 10.370)
O Nārada, in whosever house the Vaiṣṇava scripture remains written,
there the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself dwells.
Whoever recites even a single verse from the ancient Vaiṣṇava scriptures, or half a verse,
or even a quarter-verse, shall obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
O best of Brahmins, this Vaiṣṇava scripture is difficult to obtain even for deities, sages, and yogis; what then can be said of human beings? (Hbhv 10.373)
In that very same Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Arjuna Saṃvāda: "O tiger among the Kurus, those men who constantly worship and recite my scriptures always come as guests to me. (Hbhv 10.374)
I think of that man who expounds my teaching and reflects upon my scriptures; of him I think constantly as if he were myself, without a doubt. (Hbhv 10.375)
Now, regarding the majesty of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, it is said in that very same work:
"For those for whom the Bhāgavata scripture is dearer than life itself in the Kali age..."
For them, no affliction arises even in a hundred eons of Yama.
Those who always maintain the Bhāgavata scripture in their home—
their ancestors, filled with joy, clap their hands and leap for them.
O brahmin sage, for as many days as the Bhāgavata scripture remains in the home,
for that long the ancestors drink milk, clarified butter, honey, and water.
Those men who always worship the Bhāgavata scripture in their home please the gods until the dissolution at the end of the kalpa.
Those who indeed offer the Bhāgavata scripture with devotion to a Vaiṣṇava dwell in the world of Viṣṇu for thousands of crores of kalpas.
It is better to have even half a verse or a single quarter-verse of the Bhāgavata in one's home than hundreds or thousands of other collections of scriptures.
He in whose house the Bhāgavata scripture does not remain during the Kali age shall never again return from the noose of Yama.
How is he to be known as a Vaiṣṇava? In the Kali age, that brāhmaṇa in whose house the Bhāgavata scripture does not reside is the lowest of outcasts.
O Brahmin, wherever the Bhāgavata scripture may be found in the Kali age,
there Hari goes along with the gods, O Nārada.
In that place, O best of sages, all sacred fords, rivers, streams, and lakes abide wherever this scripture of the Bhagavata remains.
In that house where the Bhāgavata scripture remains worshipped, all sacred fords and all sacrifices accompanied by excellent sacrificial fees are present.
Moreover:
"That man who constantly recites the Bhāgavata Purāṇa shall obtain for every single syllable the merit arising from the gift of a Kapilā cow. (Hbhv 10.387)
One who daily recites or listens with devotion to even half a verse or a single quarter-verse originating from the Bhāgavata shall obtain the fruit of [giving] a thousand cows.
O Sage, the person who, being self-restrained, daily recites this verse from the Bhāgavata,
obtains the fruit of the eighteen Purāṇas.
In that very same [work], in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Bhagīratha:
"For that evil-minded man who creates an obstacle to the scripture of the Bhāgavata does not find favor; he causes a hundred lineages to fall. (Hbhv 10.390)
In the *Pādmapurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Gautama and Ambarīṣa:
"O Ambarīṣa, listen daily to the *Bhāgavata* proclaimed by Śuka; recite it yourself as well, if you desire the destruction of worldly existence. (Hbhv 10.391)

In whosever house a verse from the Bhāgavata, or even half a verse or a single quarter-verse, remains written, Hari—the God of gods, Janārdana—dwells there forever; of this there is no doubt. (Hbhv 10.392)
In the *Dvārakā-māhātmya*, within the dialogue between Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya and Indradyumna:
"He who recites the scripture of the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavata* in the presence of Kṛṣṇa sports together with yogis, accompanied by hundreds of millions of his ancestors. (Hbhv 10.393)
In the Gāruḍa [Purāṇa]:
"This is the meaning of the Brahma-sūtras, the definitive determination of the meaning of the Mahābhārata;
it takes the form of a commentary on the Gāyatrī, augmented by the meaning of the Vedas. (Hbhv 10.394)

This work, known as the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata, is the personification of the Sāman among the Purāṇas, directly proclaimed by the Blessed Lord; it consists of twelve skandhas, is joined with one hundred chapters, and contains eighteen thousand verses. (Hbhv 10.395)
In that very Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, in the First Canto [BhP 1.1.2, 1.3.40–41]:
"Herein lies the supreme dharma, free from deceit, for the virtuous who are devoid of envy;
here is the reality to be known, which bestows auspiciousness and uproots the threefold suffering."
In the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam composed by the great sage, what need is there for others?
For here, the Lord is immediately captured within the hearts of the skillful who desire to hear it, at that very moment.
The venerable sage composed this Purāṇa named Bhāgavata, which is equal to the Veda and recounts the deeds of the Lord of Excellent Praise (Uttama-śloka). (Hbhv 10.397)
For the ultimate welfare of the world, he caused his son—the best among those who possess self-mastery—to grasp this great, auspicious, and propitious work;
it is the very essence extracted from the essence of all the Vedas and Itihāsas. (Hbhv 10.398)
Furthermore:

"When Kṛṣṇa had departed for his own abode along with dharma, knowledge, and the rest, this sun of the Purāṇas has now arisen for those whose vision is lost in the Kali age. (BhP 1.3.43) [Hbhv 10.399]
Furthermore:
"Knowing that the world does not understand devotion to Adhokṣaja as the direct means for the cessation of misfortune, the wise one composed the Sātvata-saṃhitā. (BhP 1.7.6–7)
Indeed, when this [narrative] is heard regarding Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, devotion arises in a person that removes sorrow, delusion, and fear. (Hbhv 10.401)

In the second [chapter], in the words of Śrī Śuka (BhP 2.1.9–10): "O royal sage, although he was firmly established in the state beyond the qualities (nirguṇya), his heart was captivated by the pastimes of the Lord of Excellent Renown (uttama-śloka), such that he studied this narrative. (Hbhv_10.402)
Other ancient texts shine among the assembly of the virtuous only so long as the Bhāgavata, that ocean of nectar, is not heard. (Hbhv 10.403)
And in the twelfth [skandha]:
"Other Purāṇas continue to shine among the assembly of the virtuous only so long as the Bhāgavata, that ocean of nectar, is not heard. (Hbhv 10.404)
For the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata is held to be the essence of all Vedānta;
for one who is satiated by its nectar-like rasa, there can be no delight in anything else whatsoever.
Just as the Gaṅgā is among those who flow downward, as Acyuta is among the gods, and as Śambhu is among the Vaiṣṇavas, so is this [Purāṇa] among the Purāṇas. (Hbhv 10.406)
The Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam is the stainless Purāṇa, beloved by the Vaiṣṇavas,
in which the one supreme, stainless knowledge of the state of the Paramahaṃsas is sung;
therein, freedom from action (naiṣkarmya) is revealed, accompanied by knowledge, detachment, and devotion.
By hearing this, reciting it well, and being intent on reflecting upon it with devotion, a person shall be liberated.
Therefore it has been said [BhP 1.1.3]:
"The fruit fallen from the wish-fulfilling tree of the Vedas, joined with the essence of nectar, has issued from the mouth of Śuka."
O connoisseurs of rasa on this earth, O seekers of the divine! Drink again and again the nectar of the Bhāgavata, which is the very abode of bliss.
Furthermore [BhP 1.2.3]:
He who is His own self-manifest power, the essence of all the Vedas, the singular lamp of spiritual knowledge for those desiring to cross over the blinding darkness—
Out of compassion for those wandering in saṃsāra, I approach that son of Vyāsa, the teacher of sages, who has revealed that ancient secret.
Now, regarding the greatness of the speaker of the Blessed Lord’s scripture:
one should worship with devotion, as if he were a guru, the Vaiṣṇava who speaks the dharma of the Blessed Lord, recites the scripture of the Blessed Lord, and bestows knowledge. (Hbhv 10.410)
In the *Nārada-pañcarātra*, in the speech of Śrī Śāṇḍilya to the sages:

"He who knows the teacher who expounds Vaiṣṇava knowledge to be like Viṣṇu himself, and worships him with speech, mind, and body—he is a knower of the scriptures; he is indeed a Vaiṣṇava. (Hbhv 10.411)
Indeed, even one who merely recites a single quarter-verse of a *śloka* is always worthy of worship;
how much more so one who expounds the true nature of the Blessed Viṣṇu!
Furthermore:
"Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman; he is attained through knowledge of him. The means to that knowledge is the scripture, and the scripture comes from the mouth of the Guru. (Hbhv 10.413)
For this reason, the attainment of Brahman is always dependent upon the guru;
for this very cause, O brahmins, the guru is remembered as the most venerable.
For the Lord of the World, out of compassion, having assumed a body made of clay, uplifts the submerged worlds with the scripture as his hand.
Therefore, one who fears the terror of saṃsāra should cultivate devotion toward the guru,
who, through knowledge of the scriptures, shall dispel the darkness of ignorance.

He who proclaims the scripture—which removes evil, is meritorious, pure, and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; which grants peace, possesses great purpose—he is the Teacher of the World. (Hbhv 10.417)
Now, regarding the greatness of hearing the narrations of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes and their power to purify sins and other defilements,
it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada:
O best of Brahmins, there is no doubt that the great sin of those who hear the story of Hari, accumulated over hundreds of millions of years, is destroyed. (Hbhv 10.418)
In that very same place, elsewhere it is said:
"Visiting all hermitages and bathing in all sacred fords do not bring such fulfillment to men as does a discourse on Nārāyaṇa. (Hbhv 10.419)
In the *Bṛhan-nāradīya-purāṇa* (1.39.2), at the conclusion of the narrative of Yajñadhvaja:
"Oh, the stories of Hari in this world destroy sin and bestow merit, especially for those who hear them and those who speak them, and particularly for His devotees. (Hbhv 10.420)
In the First Skandha [BhP 1.2.17]:
"For those who hear His own stories, Kṛṣṇa—whose hearing and chanting are meritorious—standing within the heart as the Friend of the virtuous, shakes off all inauspicious things. (Hbhv_10.421)

And in the eleventh book, in the hymn to the Lord (BhP 11.6.9): "O Worshipful One, the purification of men who are possessed of evil intentions does not occur through knowledge, sacred learning, study, charity, austerity, or ritual acts."
O Bull among beings, may [this] come to pass through your fame, which has been nourished by hearing it with increased, true faith. (Hbhv 10.422)
In the tenth book [BhP 10.1.13], in the speech of Śrī Parīkṣit to Śrī Bādarāyaṇa:

"This hunger, though extremely difficult to bear, does not afflict me even though I have abandoned all other water, as I drink the nectar of the stories of Hari flowing from the lotus of your mouth. (Hbhv 10.423)
And in that very same [text] of the Skanda-purāṇa: "The life-story of Viṣṇu bestows prosperity, destroys all calamities, pacifies all suffering, and wards off malevolent planets. (Hbhv 10.424)
Now, regarding the fact that this very [text] brings about all auspiciousness in an eminent manner, it is said therein:
"The noble conduct of Yaśodharmajaya should be heard by those who desire fame, dharma, and victory."
O celestial sage, those with a mind set on righteousness perform it for the sake of destroying evil and for the sake of attaining heaven.
The life-story of Viṣṇu, which bestows long life, health, fame, and increases merit, should be heard constantly by one of virtuous intellect. (Hbhv 10.426)
The life-story of Viṣṇu brings about the increase of one's family, victory, the destruction of enemies, and strength; it bestows the fruit of all goals at all times. (Hbhv 10.427)
In the First Skandha [BhP 1.2.8]:
"If dharma well-practiced by men does not produce delight in the stories of Viṣvaksena, it is indeed nothing but mere exhaustion. (Hbhv 10.428)

In the third canto, in the dialogue between Śrī Vidura and Maitreya (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.6.37): "They say that for men, the singular attainment of speech is the discourse on the qualities of Him who is the crest-jewel of those of excellent renown."
And one should apply oneself to the nectar of the discourse when it has been presented by the learned, according to the sacred tradition.
In the second [chapter], in the words of Śrī Śaunaka (BhP 2.3.17):
"This sun, rising and setting, indeed steals away the lifespan of men;
yet that moment of his passage which is spent in conversation concerning the One of Excellent Fame is truly gained. (Hbhv 10.430)
In the third instance, in the words of Śrī Vidura (BhP 3.5.13):
"That [faith], increasing in one who is faithful,
produces detachment from other things for a person."
For one who is blissful through the constant recollection of Hari's feet,
it swiftly brings about the dissolution of all suffering.
In the fourth canto, at the conclusion of the account of Śrī Pṛthu, in the words of Śrī Maitreya (BhP 4.23.12):
"With his intellect severed from other objects and having realized the nature of the Self, he became free from desire; by that very wisdom, he cut asunder this world and abandoned it."
A disciplined practitioner remains vigilant through the stages of yoga only so long as they do not take delight in the stories of the elder brother of Gada (Kṛṣṇa).
And in the eleventh book, in the words of Uddhava addressed to the Blessed Lord (BhP 11.6.44): "O Kṛṣṇa, Your divine play is the supreme auspiciousness for men;
having obtained it as nectar for the ears, people abandon all other desires. (Hbhv 10.433)

Regarding the fourth [chapter], in the words of the Blessed Lord spoken to Pracetās (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 4.30.19): "Even for men who dwell in homes and perform virtuous deeds, if their time is spent in my news, those homes are not considered a cause of bondage. (Hbhv_10.434)
In that very same [text], the Skanda Purāṇa states:
"O child, whatever is desired here by men regarding dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, one obtains all that by constantly hearing the narrative of Hari. (Hbhv_10.435)
And in the twelfth book, in the words of Śrī Śuka (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 12.4.40):
"For one desiring to cross over the ocean of saṃsāra, which is exceedingly difficult to traverse, there is no other raft than the Blessed One, the Supreme Person."
For a person afflicted by the forest fire of manifold sufferings, there can be no [remedy] other than the enjoyment of the nectar of the stories of the Divine Play (līlā).
In the *Dvārakā-māhātmya*:
"For one to whom the stories of Kṛṣṇa are always dearer than even his own life, nothing whatsoever is difficult to attain in this world or in the next. (Hbhv 10.437)
In the second book [of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, 2.3.12]:
"Knowledge is that wherein the cycle of the waves of the modes has ceased;
it is the serenity of the self, as well as non-attachment to the modes."
Furthermore, this path of devotional yoga (bhakti-yoga) is esteemed as the way to liberation;
who, being at peace, would not take delight in the stories of Hari?
In the tenth book, in the *Śruti-stuti* (BhP 10.87.21):

"Those who have exerted themselves by circling the great ocean of the nectar of Your deeds— You who have assumed a physical form for the sake of making known the reality of the Self, which is otherwise difficult to comprehend— "
O Lord, some who have abandoned their homes through association with the swans of Your lotus feet do not even long for liberation.
In the third book, in the dialogue between Śrī Kapila and Devahūti (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.25.34): "Some, devoted to service at my feet and intent on my will, do not desire identity with me."
Those devotees who, being attached to one another, praise my heroic deeds; // Hbhv_10.440 //
In the second [chapter], it is stated by Śrī Sūta [BhP 2.2.37]:
"Those who drink the nectar of the stories of the Blessed One, the Self of all beings, collected in the cups of their ears..."
They purify their minds defiled by sense objects and go into the presence of his lotus-like feet.
In the third chapter, during the hymn of praise to Kapiladeva (BhP 3.5.45): "O Lord, those whose hearts have become pure through increased devotion by drinking the nectar of Your stories..."
Having attained awakening, the essence of which is dispassion,
may they proceed directly to the unimpeded celestial abode.
In the *Skānda-purāṇa*, within the *Amṛtasāroddhāra* section on the instruction of Śrī Yama’s messengers:
"Those who hear the story of Viṣṇu and those who read the story of Hari do not behold [the world] for ten thousand kalpas; they have gone to eternal Brahman. (Hbhv_10.443)
For one whose mind is constantly delighted by conversations concerning Viṣṇu, prosperity never departs; his goal remains established in the palm of his hand.
In the twelfth [chapter] (BhP 12.3.15): "But that recitation of the qualities of the One of Excellent Verses, which is sung repeatedly, destroys all inauspiciousness."
Desiring pure devotion toward Kṛṣṇa, one should constantly and repeatedly listen to that very [text]. (Hbhv 10.445)
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"O protector of the earth, wherever a Vaiṣṇava narrative exists, there Hari goes, just as a cow is devoted to her calf. (Hbhv 10.446)
In the *Śrī-Viṣṇudharma*, as spoken by the Blessed Lord,
and in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between the Blessed Lord and Arjuna: "One who constantly recites my stories and delights in hearing my stories..."
I shall not abandon that man whose mind finds delight in stories concerning me.
In the tenth book, in the hymn of praise by Brahmā (BhP 10.14.3):
"Abandoning all effort toward knowledge, they live merely by bowing down and listening to Your message as it is proclaimed by the virtuous."

Those who, established in their respective stations, have largely conquered the senses through body, speech, and mind according to the Vedas— even by them you have been conquered throughout the three worlds.

In the third [canto], in the hymn by Śrī Sanaka and others (BhP 3.15.48): "They do not even consider Your favor to be ultimate, much less anything else that carries fear through the raising of Your eyebrows."
O Lord, those who have taken refuge at Your feet are skilled in Your narrative,
whose fame is a sacred ford worthy of praise, and they are connoisseurs of its aesthetic flavor.
In the fourth canto, within the praise offered by the Siddhas to the Blessed Lord (BhP 4.7.35):
"But this elephant of my mind, scorched by the forest fire of afflictions, has plunged into the river of the nectar cleansed by Your stories."
Afflicted by thirst, he plunged in and did not remember the forest fire;
he was as if immersed in a forest endowed with the Brahman, from which he does not emerge.
Therefore it was said in the First Canto by Śrī Śaunaka and others (BhP 1.1.19):

"We, however, are not satiated with the heroic exploits of the One of Excellent Renown, for as we listen, they become sweeter and sweeter at every step for those who know the aesthetic essence. (Hbhv 10.451)
Furthermore:
"Who indeed, being a connoisseur of flavor, could ever be satiated with the narration of Him who is the sole supreme refuge?"
Even those lords of yoga, headed by Brahmā (Bhava-padma), have not reached the end of the qualities of the One who is beyond all qualities.
In the third [skandha], Śrī Vidura says:
"He performs his pastimes and carries out various activities through different incarnations for the welfare of the twice-born, the cows, and the gods."
The mind is never satiated, even as we listen to the nectar-like deeds of the crown jewel of those with excellent renown.
And in the tenth book, Śrī Parīkṣit said:

"O Brāhmaṇa, who indeed would ever be satiated while hearing the meritorious stories of Kṛṣṇa, which are like honeyed wine, which remove the impurities of the world, and which are ever-new to one who knows what has been heard? (BhP 10.52.20).
Therefore, King Śrī Pṛthu prayed:
"O Lord, I do not desire even that place where the nectar of Your lotus feet is not present."
"Let that which has issued from the mouth of the Great One within my heart enter my ears; this is my boon. (Hbhv_10.455)
Therefore, it is stated with certainty in the *Padma Purāṇa*, in the *Māhātmya* of Vaiśākha (PadmaP 5.85.41), by Śrī Nārada to Ambarīṣa:
"I do not see any other merit that is so conducive to mutual excellence and that increases the highest degree of supreme satisfaction."
The virtuous, enjoying a state of supreme devotion, worship those of infinite qualities, who are mines of infinite bliss, by means of forceful resolve.
In the first book, Śrī Sūta said:

"Whatever stories are to be told concerning the Lord of vast deeds, which take His qualities and actions as their subject matter—those should be cultivated by men who desire to attain the Supreme. (BhP 1.18.10) [Hbhv 10.457]

And at the conclusion of the Tenth Canto, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa [Vedavyāsa] stated [BhP 10.90.49]: "Thus, by the Supreme Lord, who has assumed a body for the sake of His pastimes in order to protect His own path, there are imitations corresponding to that [human condition]."
One who desires to follow the conduct of the feet of that best of the Yadus should hear of his deeds, which are the ploughshares for tilling away [the seeds of] karma.
Now, regarding the fault of abandoning the discourse of the Blessed Lord:

therefore, while the discourse of Kṛṣṇa is available, one should abandon listening to other discourses, as well as the failure to listen to Him, aversion toward Him, and even the sense of being satisfied with something else. (Hbhv 10.459)
In the third book, in the dialogue between Kapila and Devahūti (BhP 3.32.19):

"Surely those who, struck down by fate, abandon the nectar of the stories of the Infallible One and listen instead to the tales of the wicked, are like excrement-eaters who reject ambrosia and consume filth. (Hbhv 10.460)
In that very description of Śrī-Vaikuṇṭha (BhP 3.15.23):

"Those who, being attached to other objects, do not go to [Vaikuṇṭha] because they listen to wicked stories that destroy the intellect and distract from the narration and study of the deeds of Him who destroys all evil."
Alas, those very teachings which have been heard by men whose fortune is destroyed— having had their essence extracted—
cast them instead into the refuge-less darknesses.
Furthermore, in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, it is said:
"O best of sages, Yama is forever the master of those lowest of men who do not listen to the Vaiṣṇava scripture when it is being recited. (Hbhv_10.462)
Those who, having encountered a Vaiṣṇava discourse, neither listen to it nor rejoice in it, lose their merit, lifespan, fame, righteousness, and even their progeny. (Hbhv 10.463)
O celestial sage, he who does not listen to the story of Hari, which destroys all sins,
shall perish very soon, along with his very roots.
In the second book, as spoken by Śrī Śaunaka [BhP 2.3.20]:
"Those cavities which do not hear the exploits of the Wide-Striding One (Urukrama) within the hollows of a man's ears..."
Though possessing a tongue like a frog,
she does not sing the hymns of the Wide-Strider.

In the third canto, in the *Śrī-Brahma-stuti* (BhP 3.9.7): "Those whose intellects have been struck down by destiny, whose senses are turned away from Your association— which pacifies all that is inauspicious— "
Overcome by greed and with minds enslaved by passion, these wretched ones constantly perform unwholesome deeds for the sake of a mere tiny fragment of sensual pleasure.
I grieve for those who are themselves objects of pity— the ignorant ones who,
through their sin, are averse to the narrations of Hari.
The unblinking god (Time) consumes the lifespan of those whose speech, conduct, and mindfulness are in vain.
And as stated by Śrī Maitreya in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (3.13.50):
"Who indeed in this world is a knower of the essence of human goals who would abandon the nectar of the Lord's stories for the sake of ancient tales?"
Having drunk the nectar that removes worldly existence with the cupped hands of their ears,
alas, who would not become dispassionate, were it not for another man?
In the fourth [canto], in the *Śrī-Pṛthu-stuti* (BhP 4.20.26):
"One who hears Your auspicious fame, which is beautiful to hear, even once by chance upon meeting with noble persons..."
How could one who knows virtue desist from [protecting] a creature without [offering] a victim, since Śrī herself chose him with the desire to gather virtuous qualities?
At the beginning of the tenth book, in the question of Śrī Parīkṣit [BhP 10.1.4]:
"From that medicine for worldly existence, which is sung by those whose thirst has ceased, and which is delightful to the ear and the mind..."
What man, other than a slayer of animals, would turn away from the chanting of the virtues of the One of Excellent Renown?
Therefore it was said by the gods in the Fifth Canto [BhP 5.19.23]:
"Where there is no river of the nectar of the stories of Vaikuṇṭha, nor saintly devotees who take refuge in them..."
That world where there are no great festivals of sacrifices to the Lord of Sacrifice, nor even the realm of the Lord of the Gods— that indeed should not be resorted to.
Therefore, being attached to discourse concerning the Blessed One,
one should always practice such discourse on the Blessed One and repeatedly inquire of those who relish it, for the sake of increasing mutual joy. (Hbhv 10.471)
In the Tenth Canto [BhP 10.13.2]:
"This is the natural disposition of the virtuous who possess the essence—
that even when their speech, hearing, and minds are directed toward external objects..."
The news concerning Acyuta was as fresh at every moment for the women as it was for the libertines. (Hbhv_10.473)
Therefore, in that very same place [BhP 10.87.11], it is said:

"Those who were equal in learning, austerity, and character, and who regarded their own, their enemies, and those in between as equals, even though they were desirous of hearing, performed the proclamation of the teaching as one. (Hbhv 10.474)

Furthermore, for the sake of increasing mutual affection, one should personally inquire of virtuous persons who know them regarding the greatness of the teaching of the Blessed Lord’s dharma, as well as the Vaiṣṇava duties, even while they are being performed. (Hbhv 10.475)
A wise person must certainly explain the teachings of the Lord to a Vaiṣṇava who inquires with faith; otherwise, he would partake in fault. (Hbhv 10.476)
Thus it has been said:

"In the Kali age, one who, though being a devotee of the Bhagavat, does not proclaim the Vaiṣṇava dharma to one who asks as a devotee of Viṣṇu, goes to a merit that lasts for a hundred years. (Hbhv 10.477)
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, it is said:

"O best of the twice-born, that foremost of brāhmaṇas who bestows the Vaiṣṇava dharma upon a Vaiṣṇava obtains a fruit greater than that which one gains from gifting the earth together with its oceans. (Hbhv 10.478)
Furthermore, in that very same [text]:
"And he who gives knowledge and instruction in the Dharma to one who is ignorant—that is remembered as equal to giving the entire earth. (Hbhv 10.479)
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara* (3.341.50):
"That best of men who causes the story of Him to be heard by His devotees obtains, by that deed, the fruit of the gift of a cow. (Hbhv 10.480)
In the *Padma Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between the divine messenger and Vikuṇḍala (PadmaP 3.31.97):
"Even the gods worship him who, having understood it himself, bestows knowledge arising from the Vedas and the Śāstras—knowledge that tears asunder the bonds of worldly existence. (Hbhv_10.481)
In the *Bṛhan-nāradīya-purāṇa* (1.1.63): A person who is devoted to the company of the virtuous, the worship of the gods, sacred discourses, and beneficial instruction;
At the conclusion of the body, possessing splendor equal to the Infallible One, he proceeds to that supreme station of Viṣṇu.
Now, as for the duties toward the Blessed Lord—those duties of the illustrious Lord are manifested through the characteristics of His devotees;
herein, some of the principal ones are written down, though others also exist. (Hbhv 10.483)
Although these have indeed been well-known in works such as the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata,
they are nevertheless being collected together here with effort, along with their means of accomplishment.
And they were spoken of by Candraśarman in the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa* and the *Dvārakā-māhātmya*:
"Listen, O Kṛṣṇa, to what must be done by me from this day forward:
one must never eat on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), and a vigil (jāgara) must always be observed. (Hbhv 10.485)
A great festival must be celebrated, and you should perform daily worship;
even if one has eaten as little as half a pala, one should eat again on the following day.
Out of love for you, I shall observe eight twelfth-day vows accompanied by religious observances; I shall practice devotion to the Lord with my very life and my wealth. (Hbhv 10.487)
The thousand names, which are dear to you, should be recited constantly;
indeed, I must always perform worship with *tulasī* leaves. (Hbhv 10.488)
A garland made from the wood of the tulasī plant must always be worn by me;
and when your vigil has arrived, dancing and singing must be performed.
I shall apply an ointment made from sandalwood produced from Tulasī wood before you, and I shall proclaim your virtues.
I must go to Mathurā every year;
there, I should listen to its stories and likewise read the sacred texts.
I shall diligently bear the water from [the Lord's] feet upon my head at all times,
and, firm in my vow, I shall also partake of the consecrated food offerings.
I shall reverently bear upon my head your floral remains (nirmālya);
and having offered to you whatever is desired, I shall joyfully consume it. (Hbhv 10.493)
"In such and such a manner should you act that your satisfaction may arise;
this truth, O Kṛṣṇa, I have proclaimed before you. (Hbhv 10.494)
In the Seventh Canto [BhP 7.7.30–32], Śrī Prahlāda states:
"By service to the guru, by devotion, by offering all that is gained,
by faith in his stories, and by chanting of his qualities and deeds..."
Through meditation upon his lotus feet, and by means of beholding his liṅga, worship, and so forth.
"The Lord Hari, the Sovereign, dwells within all beings"—
thinking thus, one should properly honor all beings with those same desires in one's mind.
And in the eleventh [canto], Śrī Kavi-Yogeśvara [Śukadeva] said:
"Know those means for the attainment of the Self which were indeed proclaimed by the Blessed One for men who lack knowledge—those are the Bhāgavata [means]. (BhP 11.2.34) [Hbhv 10.497]
In that very context, the awakened Lord of Yoga [in BhP 11.3.23–30] stated:
"First, one should practice non-attachment of the mind toward everything, and attachment toward the virtuous;
and one should truly manifest compassion, friendliness, and humility toward all beings as is appropriate."
Purity, austerity, forbearance, silence, self-study, straightforwardness, celibacy, non-violence, and equanimity toward the perception of dualities.
Everywhere one should observe the self and the Lord, solitude, homelessness,
clothing made of rags from a secluded place, and contentment with whatever comes by chance.
Faith in the scripture of the Bhagavat and lack of censure toward others as well;
the restraint of mind, speech, and action; truthfulness; and both tranquility and self-control. (Hbhv 10.501)
Hearing and chanting about Hari, whose deeds are wonderful, as well as reflecting upon His births, activities, and qualities, and performing every action for His sake— Hbhv_10.502.

Whatever has been sacrificed, given, performed as austerity, or recited, whatever conduct is dear to oneself, and the offering of one's wife, children, home, and even life to another—[this is the highest gift]. (Hbhv 10.503)
Thus, one should cultivate friendship toward those humans who have Kṛṣṇa as their soul and their lord,
and likewise offer service to both types of great and virtuous men.
The mutual recounting of the purifying glory of the Blessed One, mutual delight, mutual satisfaction, and mutual cessation of the self [from worldly objects]. (Hbhv 10.505)
And by the Blessed Lord [BhP 11.11.34–41]:
"Beholding, touching, and worshipping My liṅgas and My devotees;
service, praise, and the chanting of the qualities and deeds of those who are humble. (Hbhv 10.506)
O Uddhava, faith in hearing my stories, meditation upon me, the relinquishing of all gains, and the offering of oneself through service—these are the means. (Hbhv 10.507)
The recounting of my birth and deeds, the celebration of my festivals, and festivals in my temple through song, dance, instrumental music, and assemblies; Hbhv_10.508.
Pilgrimage and the performance of offerings on all annual festival days;
Vedic and Tantric initiation; and the observance of my vows. (Hbhv 10.509)
There is a natural faith in establishing my worship, and an effort made collectively in the work of building gardens, groves, pleasure parks, cities, and palaces. (Hbhv 10.510)
Serving my household with sincerity, like a servant, by means of sweeping, smearing, sprinkling water, and drawing mandalas. (Hbhv 10.511)
Absence of pride, absence of hypocrisy, and not proclaiming one's own deeds;
one should not even make use of the light of a lamp offered to me.
Whatever is most desired in the world, and whatever is exceedingly dear to oneself—one should offer all that to me; that conduces to infinity.
Furthermore:
"Constant faith in my nectar-like stories, the perpetual chanting of my praises, steadfastness in worship, and the glorification of me with hymns. (BhP 11.19.20–23) Hbhv 10.514.
Reverence in service, salutation with all one's limbs, worship of my devotees as superior to [all other] worship, and a mind directed toward me in regard to all beings. (Hbhv 10.515)
Gesturing with the limbs for my sake, praising my qualities with speech, offering the mind to me, and the renunciation of all desires. (Hbhv 10.516)

The renunciation of wealth, as well as of enjoyments and pleasures, for my sake; and whatever is sacrificed, given, offered in fire, recited, or whatever vow and austerity is performed for my sake—[all this is for me]. (Hbhv 10.517)
Moreover, it is said further on [BhP 11.29.9–12]:
"One should perform all actions for my sake, remembering me gradually, with the mind and heart dedicated to me, and with delight in the self and the mind fixed upon my dharma. (Hbhv 10.518)
One should resort to holy places frequented by virtuous devotees of mine,
as well as the deeds performed by my devotees among gods, asuras, and humans.
Or, separately, he should cause great festivals for me to be held during the sacred sessions and festival processions, accompanied by song, dance, and the like, with the splendor of a great king.
One whose mind is pure should perceive me alone—unveiled both externally and internally—in all beings, and likewise perceive the Self within oneself, like the sky. (Hbhv 10.521)
Now, the majesty of the dharma of the Blessed Lord has been described; and it was said by Śrī Prahlāda in the Seventh Canto (BhP 7.7.33):
"In this way, those who have conquered the six internal enemies practice devotion to the Lord."
That by which delight is obtained in the Blessed One, Vāsudeva.
In the eleventh [canto], Śrī Nārada says:
"For the true Dharma—whether heard, recited, meditated upon, honored, or approved—purifies instantly even one who has wronged all the gods. (BhP 11.2.12) [Hbhv 10.523]
In that very context, the illustrious Kavi-Yogeśvara [Śukadeva] stated [in Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.2.35]: "O King, by relying upon which a man would never be negligent;
even while running or closing his eyes, he would neither stumble nor fall in this world. (Hbhv_10.524)
"By one who, through devotion arising from that [devotion], learns the Bhāgavata duties from the illustrious Prabuddha-Yogeśvara,
and is intent upon Nārāyaṇa, the difficult-to-cross *māyā* is easily transcended. (Hbhv 10.525)
And by the Blessed Lord [BhP 11.19.24]:
"O Uddhava, for those humans who thus surrender their very selves through these duties, devotion to Me arises; what other goal remains for them? (Hbhv_10.526)
Furthermore, it is said ahead [BhP 11.29.20]:

"O Uddhava, not even an atom of the destruction of My dharma has been resolved by Me at its very commencement, because it is perfectly free from the guṇas and devoid of desire for rewards. (Hbhv 10.527)
If a virtuous assembly is not available, the knower of the scriptures should recount the stories of the Blessed One at home, or in his own residence, or in a temple, to one who is eager to listen.
Now, regarding the majesty of glorifying the narrations of the divine pastimes of the Blessed Lord:
it was said by the Blessed Lord to Arjuna in the Skanda Purāṇa: "He who recites my stories in the presence of Vaiṣṇavas..."
In this world one obtains enjoyments, and likewise liberation; of this there is no doubt.

In the first book [BhP 1.5.22], Śrī Nārada said: "For this [is the fruit] of a man's austerity, sacred learning, well-performed sacrifice, and eloquent speech, as well as of his intellect and charity."
The meaning established by the poets as unchanging is this: the description of the qualities of the One of Supreme Fame.
Furthermore:

"Indeed, for those whose minds are afflicted, this description of Hari’s deeds is seen as a boat across the ocean of worldly existence, arising repeatedly from the desire for contact with the objects of the senses. (BhP 1.3.35) [Hbhv 10.531]
In the eleventh book, Śrī Śuka also says [BhP 11.31.28]:
"Thus, the most peaceful heroic deeds and childhood pastimes of the Lord Hari..."
A person who recites these teachings heard elsewhere and here shall attain supreme devotion toward the state of the Paramahaṃsas.

Therefore, it was said by Śrī Prahlāda in his hymn of praise to Nṛsiṃha (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.9.18): "O Nṛsiṃha, I am that very person who sings the playful stories of You— the beloved friend, the well-wisher, and the Supreme Deity— as sung by Viriñca."
Chanting your praises, I cross over all difficulties with ease, liberated from the qualities of material nature through association with the *haṃsas* who dwell at the abode of your pair of feet.
The cowherd girls also sang:
"The nectar of Your story, praised by poets, is the life-sustainer for those scorched by suffering and the remover of all impurities."
Those people who give much are proclaimed on earth as those for whom the auspicious and glorious hearing [of the Dharma] has spread far and wide.
Even in this case, that same greatness which exists in hearing it should be understood to apply to its chanting;
for indeed, hearing is accomplished by chanting itself.
In the absence of the study of the scriptures, one should recount among one's kinsmen the stories of the virtuous— both those renowned in the world from ancient times and those of the present day.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "Association with the Holy," in the *Śrī Bhagavad-bhakti-vilāsa* composed by Śrī Gopāla Bhaṭṭa.
11. The Eleventh Chapter: The Grace of Completing the Daily Duties;
the Completion of the Daily Duties.
I take refuge in Śrī Caitanya, whose power is most wonderful;
by his grace, even a wicked person becomes a devotee of the Lord. (Hbhv 11.1)
Then, at the final portions of the day, having performed his circumambulation outside the temples of the gods,
the twice-born man should perform the twilight worship according to the prescribed rule.
In the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Aurva and Sagara [ViP 3.11.100–1, 105]:

"O King, having properly performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), a wise man should worship the evening twilight at the end of the day according to the prescribed rule, and the morning twilight when it is joined with the lunar mansions (*mṛkṣa*), accompanied by the sun. (Hbhv 11.3)
Attendance upon the king at all times during the twilight periods is required,
except in cases of childbirth, ritual impurity, confusion, illness, or fear.
O King, those evil-minded ones who do not attend upon either the morning or the evening twilight go to the Tāmisra hell. (Hbhv_11.5)
Thus,
having performed the evening rites according to the customs of his stage of life (*āśrama*),
he should, as before, perform the worship of the Blessed One with devotion. (Hbhv 11.6)
If, due to attachment to devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, one should omit rituals such as the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana),
there is no possibility whatsoever of the fault of falling from one's status.
Now, regarding the avoidance of the downfall resulting from the omission of ritual duties for those devoted to the Blessed Lord,
it is stated by the Blessed Lord in the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"If there should be an omission of ritual action for men who perform My work..."
Three million great seers perform their ritual duties for them.
And in the Ādi-purāṇa:
"The sages devoted to the Blessed One perform rituals for those who remember my names, having abandoned all ritual action. (Hbhv 11.9)
Thus,
for one who possesses mild faith and devotion but has not yet attained maturity,
this karma is elaborated because he is entitled to some degree of ritual action. (Hbhv 11.10)
Since a devotee of mature faith has no further obligation toward ritual actions, he certainly does not incur a fall; this should be written down before him.

The wise have prescribed various methods of worship at each of the three junctions of the day, distinguished by differences such as meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and so forth, for the sake of swiftly attaining their respective desired goals. (Hbhv 11.12)
Now, specifically regarding the procedure for worship at the three times of day,
I shall describe the method of propitiation according to the *Śrī-Gautamīya-Tantra*, particularly for the morning time.
One should meditate upon Vṛndāvana as the best, served by sacred trees and other such features.
With *punnāga* trees, *nāga* trees, and *panasa* trees, as well as with *kāñcana*,
*bakula*, *bilva*, and wild *kurvaka* trees.
In the midst of that, one should meditate upon a sandbank abounding in *campaka* flowers, with trees bent down by blossoms that bear the flowers of every season.
Adorned with incense, lamps, canopies, and flower garlands,
it was decorated with strings of pearls, banners, and wild flowers.

In the midst of that, seated upon a lotus throne in the shade of a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), he is well-established, enriched by the song of his flute, and adorned with all ornaments. (Hbhv_11.17)
Surrounded by a forest garland and encircled by hundreds of cowherd girls,
[he was attended] by gods, asuras, siddhas, gandharvas, and throngs of apsarases.
Kṛṣṇa, who possesses a pure smile, was being praised by yakṣas, hosts of vidyādharas, birds dwelling upon the earth, and brahman-sages.
Adorned with various kinds of cowherds and wild animals and birds,
he was being licked affectionately by hundreds of millions of cattle.
Divine and beautiful, like a blue lotus, it is the abode of Indirā;
its face is like the full moon, and its eyes resemble lotus petals.
His hands and feet possess the luster of lotuses and are beautifully adorned with excellent rubies;
he is the refuge of all the worlds and the beloved of the very life-breath of the gopīs.
Having meditated thus, one should always worship with the sixteen types of offerings;
one should present milk together with curd and sugar.
One should offer a morsel of food to the cowherds in a golden vessel and [another] in a bronze one;
thus, with concentration and devotion, one should worship while reciting the mantra. (Hbhv 11.24)
At midday, I shall explain the worship that grants the accomplishment of all aims,
performed at the base of a golden mountain adorned with minerals.
Abounding with virtuous trees, resounded by the songs of auspicious birds,
and adorned with ponds filled with lotuses, water lilies, and other such flowers.
On that delightful sandy bank, in the shade, upon a lotus-seat within a golden pavilion beautifully adorned with canopies and other ornaments.
In a delightful place adorned with garlands and the like, beautified by gems and flowers, and interspersed here and there with clusters of gold and jewels; Hbhv_11.28 //
Seated upon his lion-throne, the slayer of Kaṃsa was at ease,
adorned with necklaces and garlands of exquisite pearls.
Having meditated thus, one whose self is perfectly purified should worship with jasmine flowers;
one should offer the food for the ritual oblation in a vessel of pure silver.
Having conquered his senses, he should offer morsels of food to his friends and the cowherd girls,
and thus meditate upon Devakī’s supreme bliss while seated comfortably.
I shall now describe the ritual for the night worship of the Beloved of Rukmiṇī,
beneath a wish-fulfilling tree laden with all kinds of flowers and fruits.
Hari stands in the center of a jeweled pavilion, wearing divine yellow garments,
his limbs anointed with divine sandalwood paste, and adorned with divine ornaments.
Adorned with many divine garlands, the lotus-eyed one,
beautiful and with a lovely smile, stands in the midst of a jeweled pavilion.
Adorning all the worlds with his own form and innate splendor,
he is the beloved of the hearts of the gopīs, possessing the radiance described [in scripture].
Having worshipped Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the leader of all, with fragrant flowers, one should offer pure, cooked milk shining in a vessel. (Hbhv 11.36)
Having thus worshipped with the mind, one should recite the mantra with concentrated focus;
during worship at the three times of day, one should recite it one thousand and eight times.
This is declared by the wise to be the daily procedure for the mantra of Kṛṣṇa.
Immediately following that, after the description of the concise three-time worship, [it says]:
"Having worshipped well with the mind at the three junctions of the day,
the self-controlled one should daily recite the mantra one thousand and eight times."
If one lacks the capacity [to perform the ritual], one should likewise recite the mantra eight hundred times daily.
Thus [it is said].
Now, regarding the rites to be performed at night, the Vaiṣṇava, having then completed the fire-oblation (homa) according to tradition, [should proceed].
Having performed singing, dancing, and so forth with devotion, one should pray to the Lord.
And so it has been said:
"O Lord Keśava, by your powerful foot, mark the path; come to the place of rest together with your beloveds."
Having thus prayed and offered him the two sandals, one should bring the Lord to his bedchamber and arrange the ritual services appropriate for that place.
In that regard, one should especially offer thick milk with sugar,
betel leaf with camphor, and divine garlands and ointments.
Having thus propitiated the Blessed One with devotion according to one's own ability, the virtuous person should offer all actions and their fruits for His pleasure. (Hbhv 11.43)
Now, the procedure for surrendering all actions throughout day and night is described in the eleventh book [BhP 11.2.36]:
"By means of the body, speech, mind, or senses..."
Or, because its nature follows from the essence of the intellect,
whatever one does entirely, one should dedicate that to Nārāyaṇa, saying "to Nārāyaṇa. (Hbhv 11.44)
Furthermore, in this regard:
"Whatever action has been performed by me, whether good or evil, O Blessed One Viṣṇu, accept all of that as my supreme act of worship. (Hbhv 11.45)
Moreover:
"Whether sleeping or sitting near water, in a house, by day or by night, and as one goes along,"
Whatever little merit has been performed by me,
may Janārdana be pleased by that which has been done.

Therefore, it was said by the Blessed Lord to Brahmā in the Third Canto (BhP 3.9.41): "The highest good for men is accomplished through meritorious works, austerity, sacrifices, gifts, and yogic concentration; this is my pleasure, according to the opinion of those who know the truth. (Hbhv_11.47)
Thus,
one should constantly worship the Blessed One according to the prescribed rule,
with wealth acquired by righteous means, for the sake of attaining the complete fruit. (Hbhv 11.48)
Now, regarding the means for attaining the fruit of worship, the tenth book [of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, 10.84.37] states:
"This is the path leading to well-being for the twice-born householder."
When a person performs a sacrifice with pure wealth acquired through faith, [that is the highest form].
And in the *Agastya-saṃhitā*:

"A twice-born man should perform acts such as giving, fire-offerings, and worship with means acquired through righteous means; for if he does not do so, he goes downward even while performing them with devotion. (Hbhv 11.50)
Thus,
the fortunate one should worship the Lord with his own pure substances, accomplished through effort;
if he is unable to provide the materials for worship, he should burn incense or at least observe the act of worship.
Now, the means for one who is incapable [to perform worship] to obtain the merit of worship is stated in the Agastya-saṃhitā:
"If one is unable to perform the propitiation, one should give the materials for worship."
One who is unable to give at all should perform the act of honoring and beholding [the object of worship].
O best of sages, that alone is sufficient for crossing the ocean of existence;
he who does not possess even one [of these] surely goes downward, and not otherwise.
Moreover, in that very same [text]:
"But the wise person who, with devotion and effort, having personally prepared everything, performs the complete rite of worship, obtains the full fruit. (Hbhv 11.54)
He who worships according to the rules with devotion, even by means of materials brought from others, would obtain only half the fruit of the worship; he would not receive the full result.
Furthermore, in the *Padma Purāṇa*, within the *Kārttika-māhātmya* from the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā (6.112.21):
"A man who, for the sake of religious duty (*dharma*), asks for wealth from another—Dhanada shall obtain the fruit arising from that meritorious deed of his. (Hbhv 11.56)
Now, regarding the greatness of seeing [the Lord],
in the *Pādma Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between the venerable Pulastya and Bhagīratha:
"Those people who see Janārdana when he has been worshipped or is being worshipped..."
That fruit is constantly obtained from the gift of a hundred tawny cows.
In the Āgneya [Purāṇa]:
"Whoever should behold Hari with devotion while he is being worshipped or has already been worshipped, and whoever should rejoice with faith, he too shall obtain the fruit of sacrifice. (Hbhv 11.58)
Whoever beholds Hari with faith while he is being worshipped according to the prescribed rite shall obtain the entire fruit of the sacrifice; there is no doubt in this matter. (Hbhv 11.59)
Having seen the God thus worshipped, one should rejoice while dancing;
with a mind free from doubt and purified, one attains the Supreme Brahman.
Now, regarding the necessity of constantly beholding the form of the Blessed Lord, it is said in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"To that extent do men of dull intellect wander in the cycle of worldly existence."
As long as they did not behold the form of the great-souled Keśava.
And in that very same *Pādmapurāṇa*:
"Whatever is offered, sacrificed, or chanted by Vaiṣṇavas who do not behold Hṛṣīkeśa being worshipped, reaches the Daityas. (Hbhv 11.62)
Furthermore, in that very same work, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada concerning the description of the ritual for worship, it is said:
"In whatever place people go and do not see an image endowed with the Vedic dharma, they are to be punished by the servants of Yama. (Hbhv 11.63)
Now, regarding the greatness of giving material gifts for the sake of the Blessed Lord, it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Whatever is given to a devotee of Viṣṇu with Viṣṇu in mind [is of great merit]."
That gift is declared to be stainless, the sole means for achieving liberation.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa:
Whatever is to be given, dedicated to Īśāna, to a Brāhmaṇa, to Prabhava, or to Viṣṇu—that is recorded as having infinite fruit. (Hbhv 11.65)
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*—[though not found there]—it is said:
"By means of great compassion, the Nārāyaṇabali should be performed for one who has become a preta or one who has fallen [from grace]; by that, favor shall be bestowed upon him. (Hbhv 11.66)
The God who is without beginning or end, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace, the imperishable Puṇḍarīkākṣa—in Him, what is given does not perish. (Hbhv 11.67)
Whatever is given in any manner whatsoever to Janārdana, the God of gods, know that it is indestructible; Janārdana alone is the worthy recipient.
In that very third chapter (not found):
"O best of the foremost gods, what is given with ordinary devotion is indeed received by the feet; but what is offered through approaches of exclusive devotion is received upon the head. (Hbhv 11.69)
The Blessed One Viṣṇu is infinite; whatever is given to him by those who are free from desire is said to be truly inexhaustible.
O best of the twice-born, the Lord accepts with his feet what is offered by one who still possesses desire; he accepts with his head what is given by one free from desire.

Likewise, it was stated by Śrī Nārada in the Mokṣa-dharma: "That which Brahmā and the sages themselves, as well as Paśupati, and other foremost among the wise—the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas—[have declared]. (Hbhv_11.72)
The Nāgas, Suvarṇas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and likewise the royal seers,
constantly partake of offerings of both sacrificial oblations and raw flesh according to the prescribed rites; yet all of this remains at the feet of that Lord.
Whatever actions are performed by those whose intellects are directed toward a single goal,
the Lord himself indeed accepts them all with his own head.
In the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"Even by giving a single cow along with her calf according to the prescribed rites, a man who intends it for Kṛṣṇa certainly attains his heart's desire. (Hbhv 11.75)
In the Nārasiṃha-purāṇa:
"He who gives a milch cow of black color to Viṣṇu, having obtained the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice, shall go to Hari. (Hbhv 11.76)
Free from all sins and adorned with every ornament,
he shall attain the divine realm that is the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara* (3.341.76): "By giving a milch cow at the temple of Vāsudeva for the purpose of providing curds, milk, and ghee, one attains the world of cows."
Having given a cow for the honey-mixture offering, one shall obtain a great fruit.
Having likewise constructed a reservoir of water, one is liberated from all sins.
Having established a reservoir of water endowed with trees possessing flowers and fruits,
and having adorned it with gardens, clusters of lotuses, and charming hermitages,
one attains Śvetadvīpa and does not return from there again.
He who causes a beautiful market street to be constructed before the gods becomes a king in the worlds, having conquered his enemies and possessing great magnanimity.
Having likewise constructed a city, one attains universal sovereignty;
those who provide a palanquin go to Amarāvatī.
Givers of horses shine like the sun in heaven, established in the celestial realm;
through the gift of a supreme sage, a man does not fall from the worlds for a long time, even after the passing of Śakra.
He becomes a righteous king, a lord of the earth upon this world.
O twice-born ones, by giving a book concerning the stories of Viṣṇu in a temple of Viṣṇu, a man attains the world of Brahmā, remaining there for a very long time. (Hbhv 11.85)
Likewise, the man who here bestows other books as well attains the world of Sarasvatī for a very long time.
Having made one who is well-supported his reciter in a temple of the gods, a person,
having obtained the fruit of the gift of knowledge, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
By the gift of a conch shell to Viṣṇu, one attains the world of Varuṇa;
and having returned to human birth, one is born with a renowned reputation.
Likewise, by the gift of a bell, one attains great renown;
and by giving a gabled pavilion, one becomes a lord of a city.
Having given a new, firm, and auspicious altar for the sake of divine rites,
one attains the state of the earth, for the altar is indeed the earth.
That man who causes an ornamental archway (toraṇa) to be constructed in the temple of the God of gods,
for him indeed the gates to the worlds shall remain wide open.
That person who gives implements for craftsmanship suitable for the temples of the gods, or musical instruments, shall attain the status of Gaṇeśa.
The person who gives a new and auspicious water-jar for the sake of the work of the gods attains the world of Varuṇa and is liberated from all sins.
The man who offers four water-pots at a temple indeed enjoys the earth girdled by the four oceans. (Hbhv 11.94)
O best of Brahmins, by giving even a single water-pot with a well-composed mind, one becomes a righteous king upon the earth; of this there is no doubt.
By giving a water-jar, one attains the world of Varuṇa;
by the gift of a water-pot, one obtains the fruit of a sacrifice.
Having offered even a small measure for the sake of service to Hari,
one enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice in which every desire is fulfilled.
By the gift of a palm-leaf fan, one shall attain supreme bliss;
likewise, by giving a vessel for garlands, a vessel for incense, and a vessel for perfumes, one shall become a fit recipient for all desires. (Hbhv 11.98)
Having given vessels made of copper or indeed of precious metals,
one becomes a vessel for desires, for sacred sciences, and for wealth.
By the gift of beds and seats, one finds eternal stability;
by the gift of a canopy, one shall obtain all desires.
By the gift of gold, a person shall obtain all desires;
by the giver of silver, one obtains beauty, especially that which is difficult to find on earth.
By the gift of jewels, one attains authority in the worlds;
by the gift of a draft ox, one obtains the fruit of ten cows.
The gift of elephants, cows, buffaloes, camels, and mules is proclaimed to be a thousandfold greater than the gifts previously mentioned. (Hbhv 11.103)
O best of the twice-born, by giving a dwelling, one attains the world of Varuṇa;
likewise, through the gift of a cow, one enjoys that very same world.
He who gives away a camel, or even a donkey, or a mule,
reaches Alakā and rejoices together with the lords of the Yakṣas.
By giving [the flesh] of wild forest animals as well as birds,
one obtains the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and likewise becomes fortunate.
By giving a male slave, one is born in a happy world, not fallen from one's desired state;
likewise, O Brahmins, by giving a female slave—of this there is no need for deliberation. (Hbhv 11.107)
Those who bestow a courtesan skilled in dance and song,
being completely liberated from all suffering, go to Amarāvatī.
By offering a dance, one likewise attains the world of Rudra without a doubt.
By the gift of spectacles, one is honored in the world of Śakra;
likewise, by giving song, one undoubtedly attains the world of Brahmā.
Those who offer a drum become possessed of renown.
Having given grains, seeds, various crops,
and even coins, one shall attain that very state of being worthy of worship by the gods.
By giving delightful vegetables, one is reborn free from sorrow;
likewise, by giving condiments and various utensils for their sake.
By giving a flowering tree, one becomes the ruler of a region;
likewise, by giving a fruit-bearing tree, one becomes the ruler of a city.
Likewise:
"That man who gives fragrant substances for the perfuming of the cloth here to the God of gods shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. (Hbhv 11.115)
By the gift of a *kaṅkata* comb, one is born hairless;
by providing a beard-grooming brush, one attains supreme auspiciousness. (Hbhv 11.116)
Having given whatever is wonderful and marvelous, one shall obtain ultimate happiness.

Furthermore, regarding the fruit of offering garments, ornaments, and so forth to Kṛṣṇa, that has already been described in various places previously in the context of the application of ritual services (upacāra). (Hbhv 11.118)

Various modes of ritual service (upacāra) for the worship of the glorious Blessed One are recognized by the Vaiṣṇava followers of Tantra according to the distinctions of one's capacity, power, and so forth. (Hbhv 11.119)
Now, regarding the various modes of service in the Āgama:
the seat, the welcome, the water for honor (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), and the water for sipping (ācamanīyaka).
And the honey-mixture, water for sipping, the bath, garments, and ornaments.
One should perform the offering of fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, and food, as well as prostration; these are the sixteen services that constitute the command for worship.

The ten services (upacāra) are, in sequence: the water for honoring (arghya), the water for washing the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamana), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), another sipping of water (ācamanīya), and those beginning with fragrance (gandha) and ending with the food offering (naivedya). Hbhv_11.122.
The five-fold worship consists of offerings beginning with incense and ending with the presentation of food.
Three types of such worship have been taught; one should perform at least one of them.
And in some cases:
the seat, the invitation, the water for the feet, the respectful offering, the water for sipping, the bath, the garment, the ornament, the fragrance, the flower, and the incense. (Hbhv 11.124)
The lamp, the food offering, and the handful of flowers; thereafter, the circumambulation, the prostration, and the dismissal—these constitute the sixteen [services]. (Hbhv 11.125)
Some say there are sixty-four modes of service for my worship;
among those many varieties, one particular mode is described here.
In the early morning, Kṛṣṇa, who had been sleeping happily,
was awakened by the chanting of the Vedas, the playing of lutes and musical instruments, and even by the hymns of bards.
Then there are the words of victory, salutations, auspicious rites, and the evening lamp-offering;
as well as the seat, the tooth-stick, and the water for washing the feet, the guest-water, and the water for sipping.
Then follows the offering of water for sipping (ācamana) enriched with honey-mixture (madhuparka), the presentation of sandals,
the cleansing of the limbs, anointing with oil, rubbing with unguents, and bathing with water.
One should bathe the limbs and the two garments with milk, curd, clarified butter, honey, and sugar, as well as with water purified by mantras. (Hbhv 11.130)
Furthermore, the sacred thread, water for rinsing the mouth, ointment, ornaments, flowers, incense, a lamp, and the removal of obstructing sights; Hbhv_11.131 //
An offering of food, mouth-freshener such as betel, an excellent bed,
grooming of the hair, divine garments, and a great crown.
Then there is the anointing with divine fragrances, the Kaustubha and other ornaments,
various divine flowers, and the auspicious *ārātrika* ceremony.
The mirror, the festival of arriving at the pavilion by means of a comfortable vehicle,
the sitting upon the lion-throne, and again the worship with water for the feet and other offerings.
Again, by the offering of incense and so forth, one should present the supreme food offering as before;
and thereafter, divine betel-leaf and the great lustration ceremony (mahānīrājana) once more.
The waving of the yak-tail fan and the parasol, singing, instrumental music, and dancing;
circumambulation, prostration, and praise offered to the two lotus feet of Śrī. Hbhv_11.136.

Placing those two upon one's head, wearing the remains of offerings made at sacred sites (tīrtha-nirmālya), eating the remnants of their food, and sitting in a place designated for the service of their feet. Hbhv_11.137.
At night, there was the preparation of the bed with various divine means;
the offering of hands, and the great festival of arriving at the place of rest.
The offering of a bed and a seat, preceded by the washing of the glorious feet, followed by the presentation of perfumes, flowers, and betel, and the festival of the waving of lights (nīrājana).
Massaging the feet while he lies on his remaining side, and so forth—
these sixty-four services are proclaimed in their proper order.
Whatever daily rites and other duties one performs oneself according to the tradition of the virtuous, one should cause those very same acts to be performed for Śrī Kṛṣṇa as well.
Therefore, whatever further details such as the ritual services (upacāra) and so forth have not been written here,
one should understand all of them in accordance with worldly custom.
And in the absence of the aforementioned ritual services, the Blessed One should always be honored by the devotee with whatever offerings are available, even if they are merely mentally visualized.
Now follows the procedure for the inclusion of the entities mentioned as metaphors in the Tantra for one who has not yet attained meditative concentration.
But even in the absence of physical substances, the rites should be performed with flowers, unbroken rice, and barley.
When the absence of the materials for the offering of flowers has occurred,
the fulfillment of the substances may be achieved with pure water alone.
Whatever among the ritual materials and substances may be difficult for a wise person to procure,
all that should be mentally envisioned through the intellect by means of scattering flowers.
And regarding these services, one should avoid stinginess with wealth;
whatever among them is incomplete, one should mentally provide for it.
In the Agastya-saṃhitā, within the section on the majesty of Śrī Tulasī:
"Whatever deficiency there may be in the means for the worship of Rāma, that is completely fulfilled by being joined with even a single leaf of Tulasī. (Hbhv 11.148)
And in the eleventh book, in the dialogue between the Blessed Lord and Uddhava (11.26.15):

"For a devotee free from deceit, my sacrifice is performed with well-known materials in images and the like, or indeed with whatever is obtained, and even by means of devotion within the heart. (Hbhv 11.149)
Then, having requested permission from the master and prostrated before him like a staff,
he should eat his evening meal according to the rule and sleep comfortably while recollecting the master.
Now, the procedure for the bed is stated in the Āgama:
"He is devoid of qualities, partless, the bearer of the form of the universe, and imperishable."
May that Mādhava protect me, who reclines in the midst of the Ocean of Milk, which is without beginning or end, eternally infinite, and resplendent with the jewels upon his hoods.
May the one whose banner is Garuḍa— the self of all and the possessor of all powers— protect me, along with my body, both internal and external, from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
Thus, having placed protection foremost, one should sleep while recollecting Viṣṇu.
Furthermore, elsewhere it is said:
"Having performed the rite of purification with water and having washed his feet, he should sip water twice while remembering the Lord of the Universe, the Lord of Vraja, the Beloved of Śrīvallabhī."
Having wiped her pair of feet with his garment while she was drinking for a long time his speech— which was like a shower of nectar— and having led her to the bed, he should immediately go to sleep.
Furthermore:
"Whoever constantly remembers Rāma, Skanda, Hanumān, Vainateya, and Vṛkodara while in bed, their bad dreams perish. (Hbhv 11.155)
Moreover, in the Skanda and Padma Purāṇas (PadmaP 5.9.44–47):
"He who approaches his wife only during the proper season and is devoted solely to his own wife should always be known here as a householder who is a celibate. (Hbhv 11.156)
The season consists of sixteen nights; among them, four are censured.
Those nights that are even-numbered yield sons, while those that are odd-numbered yield daughters. (Hbhv 11.157)
Having avoided the malefic Moon and having left behind Maghā and Mūla,
being pure, he should approach his wife especially under a constellation with a masculine name;
thus he shall procreate a pure son who accomplishes the goals of human endeavor.
In the *Viṣṇu-purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Aurva and Sagara (3.11.111–127):

"O King, having performed the purification of his feet and other limbs and having eaten in the evening, the householder should then go to a bed made of a single piece of wood that is not cracked. (Hbhv 11.159)
One should not occupy a bed that is not spacious, nor one that is broken, uneven, or dirty; nor one that is infested with insects, nor one that is uncovered.
O King, for a man who sleeps, the head is recommended toward the eastern direction or the southern; however, if it is otherwise, it brings about disease. (Hbhv 11.161)
O Lord of the Earth, approaching one's own wife during her season is commended;
specifically at an auspicious time when the lunar mansion is masculine, on the nights of the "eldest" (the first) and the "pair" (the second and third) following the onset of menstruation.
One should not approach a woman who has not bathed, nor one who is ill, nor one who is menstruating;
nor one who is undesirable, nor one who is angry, nor one who is ill-omened, nor one who is pregnant.
One should not [approach] a woman who has given her fee, nor one who desires another, nor one who is without desire, nor the wife of another;
nor one emaciated by hunger, nor one who has overeaten; and he himself must be endowed with these same qualities.

A man, having bathed, wearing garlands and perfumes, being joyful, neither overcome by fatigue nor afflicted by hunger, and being full of desire and passion, should engage in sexual intercourse. (Hbhv 11.165)
The fourteenth day, the eighth day, the new moon, and the full moon—
these, O King of kings, as well as the sun's transit into a zodiac sign, are the sacred festival days (parvan).
O King, a man who indulges in oil, women, and meat on these sacred festival days goes to the hell named Viṇmūtrabhojana.

One should not engage in sexual intercourse with another's wife, nor with one who is not a woman, nor when medicines have been administered; furthermore, one should not engage in sexual intercourse with gods, twice-born men, or gurus, nor should one remain outside the stages of life (āśrama).
O Lord of the Earth, one should never [defecate] at a shrine, on a crossroads, at a sacred bathing place, nor in a cow-pen, at a four-way junction, in a cemetery, in a grove, or in bodies of water.

O King, a wise man should never engage in sexual intercourse during the prescribed festival periods, nor on the remaining days of those periods, nor during the two twilights, nor when oppressed by the urge to urinate or defecate. (Hbhv 11.170)
One should never approach another's wife even in thought; how much less so in speech? For those who engage in sexual misconduct, there is not even a bond of bone with them.
Upon death, one goes to hell, and here in this world one’s lifespan is diminished;
for men, taking pleasure in another's wife brings fear in both places.

Thinking thus, a wise man should approach his own wives when they are in their season, provided they are free from the aforementioned defects; he may also do so even outside the season if they are desirous.
Thus,
although those ritual acts may not be useful for devotion,
nevertheless, their mention has been made because they are necessary for householders.
Thus, by worshipping Śrī Kṛṣṇa every day from rising in the morning until going to bed, one will achieve all goals and become dear to Him.
Now, regarding the greatness of the worship of the Blessed Lord, it is said in the Śrī Kūrma Purāṇa:
"There is no Vedic rite more meritorious than the propitiation of Viṣṇu."
Therefore, one should constantly worship Hari, who is without beginning, middle, or end.
In that very place, in the direct words of the Blessed Lord addressed to Bhṛgu and others:
"Those twice-born who shall always worship Me with devotion in the Kali age, according to the rite seen in the Vedas, they shall go to that abode. (Hbhv 11.177)
In the Viṣṇu-rahasya:
"Those men on earth who perform the worship of Śrī Viṣṇu go to the eternal, supreme abode of Viṣṇu’s bliss. (Hbhv 11.178)
Thus it is said;
and in that very same passage from the words of the Blessed Lord:
"The yogis who are perfectly devoted to meditation do not bring me complete satisfaction."
O celestial sage, those devoted to the yoga of action become such as they are.
For the yoga of action is indeed my preferred means over the higher yoga when it is well-practiced;
through men who are devoted and free from envy, satisfaction may arise for me.
Those men who constantly worship while themselves devoted to the yoga of action, and those who constantly meditate upon me—for them, ritual action is considered superior. (Hbhv 11.181)
O divine sage, for one devoid of action, even meditation does not bestow liberation;
nor do the wise know me truly as meditators do without [action].
Those who are properly devoted to the yoga of action attain me through meditative absorption.

For just as devotion (bhaktiyoga) is the supreme fulfiller of desires for men, so too is it my own great source of satisfaction— highly meritorious, auspicious, and the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Whatever merit those absorbed in meditation obtain for me in a year,
that is attained here in a single day by men devoted to the yoga of ritual action.
In the Ādipurāṇa:
"Meditation is not like action; its fruit is not like action;
renunciation is not like action; and austerity is not like action."
There is no merit equal to action, and no destiny equal to action.
In the Nāradīya [Purāṇa]:
"O Supporter of the Earth, Hṛṣīkeśa is to be grasped through devotion, not by riches;
Viṣṇu, when fully worshipped with devotion, grants one's heart's desire. (Hbhv 11.186)
Therefore, O Brahmins, devotion to the wielder of the discus should always be practiced;
for even by a common person, the Lord of the World, when worshipped, becomes the destroyer of afflictions.
In the *Haribhakti-sudhodaya*:
"Even service performed for the sake of hypocrisy or derision delivers people; it is not fruitless like other actions. Who indeed could be more compassionate than this? (Hbhv 11.188)
In the *Brahma-vaivarta*:
"O twice-born one, just as that god, when propitiated, becomes the granter of liberation, so too does the consumer of oblations (fire) burn even one who touches him unintentionally. (Hbhv 11.189)
Through the propitiation of Hari, one becomes wealthy, possessed of sons, an enjoyer of pleasures, renowned, free from fear, intelligent, wise, and learned. (Hbhv 11.190)
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Sanatkumāra and Mārkaṇḍeya:
"For men, the worship of Viṣṇu is a dharma superior to all other dharmas;
it yields the fruit of all sacrifices, austerities, fire-offerings, and ritual ablutions at sacred fords. (Hbhv 11.191)
By worshipping Viṣṇu, one shall obtain that fruit multiplied ten millionfold;
therefore, with every effort, one should worship Nārāyaṇa here in this world.
In that very same [text], in the dialogue between Śrī Śiva and Umā:
"The man who would give all the earth, including the oceans, to a preeminent brahmin, obtains that same fruit by worshipping Viṣṇu even once. (Hbhv 11.193)
He who worships Viṣṇu continuously for even half a month should be known as Puruṣottama; he is a devotee of Viṣṇu, without a doubt. (Hbhv 11.194)
Whoever worships Viṣṇu when the sun has reached the meridian shall obtain that merit which belongs to the giver of a great earth filled with wealth.
He who, having risen in the morning, constantly worships Viṣṇu,
obtains the supreme fruit of a thousand Agniṣṭoma sacrifices.
Whoever, having become purified, worships Viṣṇu at the time of twilight,
obtains the rare fruit of the Gomedha sacrifice.
Thus, by worshipping Keśava with devotion at all times— whether at the prescribed times or not— a person shall attain all their desires.
How much more so for one who would constantly worship him who is honored by all the gods;
blessed and having fulfilled his purpose, he shall attain the world of Viṣṇu.
Moreover:
"By initiation alone, men indeed attain liberation from Kṛṣṇa;
how much more so those men who always worship Acyuta with devotion? (Hbhv 11.200)
In that very same work, in the dialogue between Śrī Brahmā and Nārada, it is stated:
"In this most terrible cycle of existence, agitated by the fear of birth and death, the worship of Vāsudeva is remembered by the learned as the means of liberation. (Hbhv 11.201)
He indeed is a man of merit in this world, and by him his lineage is truly adorned—
he by whom Viṣṇu has been propitiated, the support of all living beings.
The constant worship of Hari yields a fruit for men that is superior even to sacrifices, austerities, and all auspicious deeds. (Hbhv 11.203)
In the Kali age, those overcome by the impurities of the age do not know Hari as the Supreme;
yet those who worship that Lord are indeed those who have accomplished all their duties. For there is no higher good for human beings than the propitiation of Viṣṇu.
Therefore, in this age of darkness, one should constantly worship Hari;
for when the God of gods, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace, has been worshipped, [all obstacles are removed].
Since Hari is omnipresent, all the gods are worshipped when he is worshipped;
when Keśava— the lord of all the worlds, who is saluted by gods and asuras,
and the slayer of Keśin and Kaṃsa— is worshipped, a man does not go to hell.
He by whom [the Lord] has been worshipped even once, or saluted even with ease,
goes to the supreme abode which is honored even by the gods.
The constant worship of the Lord Śārṅgin, the God of gods and the Protector of all the worlds, is the true fruit of birth.
Right there at the beginning:
"In this truly essence-less cycle of existence, this alone has been determined to be the essence:
the worship of Hari, the Lord of all the worlds, with faith. (Hbhv 11.209)
Furthermore:
"In whatever place the stories of Viṣṇu are constantly told, where Vaiṣṇavas reside, and where men who always worship Hari remain—those indeed are beyond the reach of the Kali age. (Hbhv 11.210)
In the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*, it is said:
"Alas, what does the worship of Hari not accomplish for men?
It bestows sons, friends, wives, kingdoms, heaven, and even liberation. (Hbhv_11.211)
It removes evil, destroys diseases, casts out mental afflictions, swiftly increases merit, and grants one's heart's desire. (Hbhv 11.212)
