They do not at all take notice of what they have acquired for themselves, as they have attained all their goals simply through being followers of the Blessed One.
And in the twelfth [skandha], regarding Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya, it is stated by Śrī Śiva in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* (12.10.6):
"The brahmin-sage desires no blessings anywhere, nor even liberation;
he has attained supreme devotion for the imperishable Supreme Person. (Hbhv_11.578)

Therefore, it was said by Bādarāyaṇi concerning the Blessed Lord in the fifth book [BhP 5.14.43]: "He who renounced his sons, kinsmen, wealth, and wife—which are difficult to abandon—even though he was entreated for them; and who possesses a glancing glance sought after by the best of the gods, which brings grace."

The king did not desire that which was appropriate for great beings whose minds are devoted to the service of the Slayer of Madhu; even non-existence would have been insignificant [compared to such service].
And in the eleventh [book], the Blessed One [said]: "Neither the station of Brahmā, nor the abode of Mahendra, nor universal sovereignty, nor lordship over the worlds of taste."
One who has dedicated their self to me does not desire the perfections of yoga or even non-returning [to saṃsāra] as anything other than me.
Therefore, it was said by the venerable Rudra in the Sixth [Book]:
"For men who carry devotion toward Vāsudeva, the Blessed One, there is no need for any other support here for knowledge, detachment, or heroism. (BhP 6.17.32) [Hbhv 11.581]
And in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, Śrī Prahlāda said:
"What need has he for dharma, wealth, or pleasure? Liberation stands in his hand, he whose devotion is fixed upon You, the root of all the worlds. (ViP 1.20.27) [Hbhv 11.582]
Therefore, it is said in the Nārasiṃha Purāṇa: "Since leaves, flowers, fruits, and water are always available without being purchased..."
Since the Ancient Person is easily attained through devotion,
for what purpose is effort exerted for the sake of liberation?
Therefore, it is said in the First Canto [of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa]:
"Even sages who delight in the Self and are free from all bonds offer causeless devotion to the One of Wide Strides; such are the qualities of Hari. (BhP 1.7.10)
The attainment of the realm of Śrī-Vaikuṇṭha is described in the Vāmana Purāṇa:
"Those who possess unswerving devotion for Him who holds the discus and mace in His hands..."
They go inevitably to that place where Hari, the Lord of Yoga, resides.
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"The sage who is constantly devoted to recitation, possessed of firm devotion and conquered senses, goes to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu even while dwelling in his own home. (Hbhv 11.586)

And as it is said in the description of Śrī Vaikuṇṭha in the Third Canto (BhP 3.15.25): "Those who, by following the lead of the Lord of the Senses, go to that realm which is far beyond even the immortals, and whose character is the object of our longing."
Their limbs bristling with thrill from the emotion, tears, and agitation caused by their mutual conversation regarding the illustrious husband; Hbhv_11.587.
And in the tenth book, during the hymn of praise by Brahmā (BhP 10.14.5): "O Infinite One, here in this world many yogīs,
through their own actions performed with their desires dedicated to You..."
Having awakened through devotion alone brought forth by the narrative, O Acyuta, they attained Your supreme goal.
In the *Bṛhan-nāradīya*, in the dialogue concerning the pleasing of the Blessed One [1.1.50]:
"Viṣṇu, who consists of all the gods, is the destroyer of the suffering of those seeking refuge;
the Lord is affectionate toward His own devotees and is pleased by devotion alone, and not otherwise. (Hbhv_11.589)
In the seventh book, in Śrī Prahlāda’s "Instruction for Children" (BhP 7.7.51–52):
"O sons of the asuras, neither the status of a twice-born, nor divinity, nor the state of a seer is sufficient to please Mukunda; neither conduct nor great learning [is sufficient]. (Hbhv 11.590)
Neither charity, nor austerity, nor sacrifice, nor purity, nor vows please Hari; he is pleased only by stainless devotion—everything else is a mere mockery. (Hbhv 11.591)
And in the *Śrī-Nṛsiṃha-Stuti* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.9.9): "I consider wealth, noble birth, beauty, austerity, sacred learning, vitality,
splendor, influence, strength, manliness, and intelligence— [all these] united together— "
For these do not lead to the propitiation of the Supreme Person; yet the Blessed One was pleased by the devotion shown even to the leader of the elephant herd.
Elsewhere too [in the *Padyāvalī* 8]:
"What is the conduct of a hunter? The age of Dhruva? The learning of a lordly elephant? What indeed is the beauty of a hunchback? And what is that wealth of Sudāmā?"
What was the lineage of Vidura? What was the prowess of Ugra, the lord of the Yādavas?
Mādhava is pleased solely by devotion, not by virtues; he is one for whom devotion is dear.
Therefore, it has been said by the Blessed Lord in the *Śrī Bhagavad-gītā* (9.26):
"Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water—that offering of devotion from one of purified soul, I accept. (Hbhv_11.594)
In the first book, the illustrious Hanumān said:
"Neither birth, nor greatness, nor good fortune, nor speech, nor intellect, nor physical form is a cause for satisfaction."
O friend, alas, that elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa caused even us forest-dwellers, though we were released by them, to suffer!
Regarding the state of bringing about union with the Blessed Lord, it is said in the Śrī Bhagavad-gītā (11.54):
"But by unswerving devotion alone, O Arjuna, may I be known as I am in this way."
To know it, to see it in its true nature, and to enter into it, O scorcher of the foe.
And in the eleventh book, in the dialogue between the Blessed Lord and Uddhava (BhP 11.14.25):
"Just as gold, when smelted by fire, casts off its dross and again assumes its own form,"
And the self, having shaken off the latent tendencies of karma through the yoga of devotion to me, then worships me.
Furthermore:

"O Uddhava, by means of unswerving devotion, he approaches Me—the Supreme Brahman, the cause of all, the Great Lord of all worlds, and the source of the origin and dissolution of everything. (BhP 11.18.45)
Regarding the power to subjugate the Blessed Lord, it is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*, within the *Kārttika-māhātmya* during the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Śaunaka:
"Hari bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon those who worship Him elsewhere; [but here, He grants even more]."
And because it brings Hari under one's control, it bestows devotion.
In that very same Vaiśākha-māhātmya (5.85.39),
in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Ambarīṣa: "O King, he is free from illusion through devotion, not by means of illusion."
It is established by virtuous persons; you yourself know that.
And in that very same place, in the eleventh book [BhP 11.14.20–21]:
"Neither yoga, nor Sāṅkhya, nor religious duty, O Uddhava, nor Vedic study, nor austerity, nor renunciation accomplishes Me as does my intense devotion. (Hbhv_11.601)
For indeed, neither dharma endowed with truth and compassion, nor knowledge accompanied by austerity, can properly purify a self that is devoid of devotion to me. (Hbhv 11.602)
The state of being the supreme human goal in itself is described in the third *skandha* of the *Śrī-Kapila-bhāgavatam* [BhP 3.29.13]:
"Even union with the Lord— whether as residence in the same realm (*sālokya*), equal opulence (*sārṣṭi*), proximity (*sāmīpya*), similarity of form (*sārūpya*), or oneness (*ekatva*)— "
People do not accept what is being given to them without serving me.
In the ninth book, within the narrative of Ambarīṣa, it is stated by the Blessed Lord:

"Those who are fulfilled by service to Me do not desire the fourfold attainment beginning with *sālokya* (residing in the same world) that is obtained through My service; how much less anything else that is subject to the ravages of time? (BhP 9.4.67)
Thus,
whatever greatness of the devotees of the Blessed One has been described previously,
that should also be understood as belonging to devotion itself, for it truly arises through devotion to them alone. (Hbhv 11.605)

In the same way, the greatness of the worship of its constituent parts, of the Śrīmad-bhāgavatam, and of other [sacred names] should be understood here, since they serve as limbs of devotion. (Hbhv 11.606)
Now, regarding the eternality of devotion to the glorious Blessed Lord:
as long as a person on earth does not take as their sole essence the extraordinary nectar-like flavor of the discourse concerning devotion to Viṣṇu, [so long shall they wander].
For that long, one undergoes those many sufferings born of numerous bodies, afflicted by hundreds of births, old age, and death.
In the tenth book, in the hymn of praise to Brahman (BhP 10.14.4):
"O All-pervading Lord, those who cast aside devotion, the path to the highest good, and strive only for the attainment of mere intellectual knowledge,"
For them, only the afflictions themselves remain,
and nothing else, just as for those who thresh coarse husks.
In the eleventh [chapter] (BhP 11.5.2–3):

"From the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet of the Puruṣa, the four castes—beginning with the Brahmins—were born separately along with the stages of life (āśramas), distinguished by their qualities (guṇas). (Hbhv 11.609)
Those who do not worship this Puruṣa, the Lord who is the manifest source of the self, and instead despise him, fall downward, fallen from their station.
Therefore it has been said by the Blessed Lord [Gītā 7.15]:
"The evil-doers, the deluded, the lowest of men, do not take refuge in Me;
their wisdom carried away by illusion, they have resorted to a demonic nature. (Hbhv_11.611)
Whatever permanence has been previously described for the various limbs of devotion, by each and every one of those very factors is its supreme permanence established in this [work].

Furthermore, the characteristics of devotion to Him—such as hearing [the scriptures] and so forth—are well-known from the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavata* and other texts; nevertheless, some of them are now being written down here. (Hbhv 11.613)
Now, regarding the characteristics of glorious devotion (*bhakti*), the general characteristic is found in the third canto of the *Śrī-Kapila* [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.25.32]:
That which is the spontaneous activity of the mind fixed solely upon the sattva of the gods— who are characterized by qualities and whose actions are based on revealed scripture—
is causeless devotion to the Lord (Bhāgavata), and it is superior even to spiritual perfection.
Now, regarding the characteristics of devotion as a means for attaining excellence, the *Gautamīya Tantra* states:
"Toward the deity, toward the mantra, and likewise toward the preceptor who bestows the mantra..."
Kṛṣṇa is pleased with one who possesses this eightfold devotion.
Affection for those who are his devotees, rejoicing in their worship, a well-disposed mind, constant worship, and the avoidance of hypocrisy for his sake—[these constitute the service]. (Hbhv 11.616)
There is passion for hearing stories about that, physical agitation for its sake, constant recollection of it, and one who subsists on its name. (Hbhv 11.617)
Indeed, that man in whom this eightfold devotion exists, even if he be a barbarian,
is a sage, a speaker of truth, and shall be renowned.
Indeed, this eightfold devotion, even if it exists in a barbarian,
makes that man a sage, a speaker of truth, and one possessed of fame.
In the seventh book, in the speech of Prahlāda (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.5.23–24):

"Hearing and chanting about Viṣṇu, remembering Him, serving His feet, worshiping Him, offering prayers to Him, becoming His servant, making friends with Him, and surrendering one's very self. (Hbhv 11.620)
If, therefore, devotion characterized by these nine marks were to be truly offered to the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu by a person,
I consider that to be the highest form of study.
In that very place, in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Yudhiṣṭhira (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.11.11):
"Hearing and chanting about Him, remembering His movement among the great ones, serving, worshiping, bowing down, becoming His servant, friendship, and self-surrender. (Hbhv 11.622)
In the *Pādma Purāṇa*, within the *Kārttika-māhātmya*, in the dialogue between Śrī Yama and Dhūmraketu:
"Hearing, chanting, worship, dedication of all actions, remembrance, service, obeisance, love, and the surrender of one's own self unto Hari. (Hbhv 11.622)
In that very same section, within the dialogue between Śrī Śiva and Pārvatī [Padma Purāṇa 6.224.23–27]:
"The primary Vaiṣṇava rite is said to be the marking with the conch and discus of Hari, the wearing of the vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), and the formal acceptance of their mantras. (Hbhv 11.623)
Worship, recitation, meditation, as well as the remembrance of His name, glorification, hearing [His name], salutation, and service at His feet. (Hbhv 11.624)
Serving the water from his feet, eating what is offered to him,
and serving his devotees— this constitutes the completion of the vow of the twelfth day (dvādaśī).
The planting of *tulasī*, devotion to Viṣṇu— the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow— is declared to be sixteenfold for the sake of liberation from the bondage of worldly existence.
Thus it is said.
Furthermore:
"O Blessed One, the sight of your form, the touching [of it], and the cultivation of the sacred field."
Smelling the remains of incense and the like, and wearing the remains of offerings (nirmālya).
Dancing before the Blessed One, as well as playing the lute and other instruments, enacting the pastimes of Kṛṣṇa and so forth, and service to the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam. (Hbhv 11.628)

The wearing of a rosary of lotus seeds, keeping vigil on the eleventh day and other such occasions, the construction of temples and so forth—other [practices] are to be understood according to the scriptures. (Hbhv 11.629)
The teachings of the Blessed One and the characteristics of devotees have been written down;
all of those should be understood as the characteristics of devotion itself, for there is no characteristic other than devotion.
Among those, the discerning should distinguish between the secondary and the primary factors for the attainment of love, as well as those that are external and internal. (Hbhv 11.631)

The various divisions of devotion, according to the distinctions of the devotee's disposition and so forth, should be understood from works such as the *Muktāphala*; enough with writing about them here. (Hbhv 11.632)

When love-devotion (*prema-bhakti*) has been perfected, all goals become its servants of their own accord, and the Lord Himself becomes exceedingly submissive; its auspicious characteristics are now described.
Now, regarding the characteristics of loving devotion (*prema-bhakti*),
it is stated in the *Nārada-pañcarātra*:
"A sense of ownership toward Viṣṇu that is exclusive, and a sense of ownership overflowing with love— "
This is called devotion by Bhīṣma, Prahlāda, Uddhava, and Nārada.
Thus [it is said].

Now, the rarity of glorious devotional service (*bhakti*) and the greatness of loving devotion (*prema-bhakti*), which is superior even to the greatness of devotional service— [these shall be described].
Since it is certain that the fruit of devotion is indeed love alone, it is already established.
As one enumerates even a few of the external and internal signs of the attainment of love,
it is its very greatness that is being inscribed.
In the Seventh Canto, in the "Instruction for the Child" of Śrī Prahlāda (BhP 7.7.34–36):
Having heard of his incomparable deeds, qualities, and heroic exploits performed through his pastime-forms...
When, with hair standing on end from excessive joy, with tears and a faltering voice, one utters songs with great longing, cries out, or dances; // Hbhv_11.637 //
When, as if seized by a planet,
he laughs, cries out, meditates, or salutes people,
sighing repeatedly he says: "O Hari, Lord of the World!"
Thinking "I am Nārāyaṇa," he is free from shame.
Then the person, with all bonds liberated,
his disposition and form imitating that state of being,
has the latent tendencies of his seeds burnt away by the Great One.
Having approached Adhokṣaja through the practice of devotion, // Hbhv_11.639 //
And in the eleventh canto, following the Śrī-kavi-yoga (BhP 11.2.39–40): "Hearing the auspicious births and deeds of the one who holds the discus in his hand, which are celebrated in the world..."
Singing songs and names that have that as their meaning, one should wander without shame and without attachment.
One who observes such vows, having developed affection through the proclamation of his own beloved name, becomes intensely moved in heart; he laughs, weeps, cries out, and sings aloud.
Like one who is insane, he dances, excluded from the world.
In that very place, the *Śrī-Prabuddha-Yogeśvarottara* [BhP 11.3.31-32] states:
"Remembering and causing one another to remember Hari, who removes the flood of sins, they bear their bodies with horripilation through the devotion that has arisen. (Hbhv 11.642)
In some places they weep through meditation on Acyuta; in other places they laugh, rejoice, and speak in ways beyond the world;
they dance, sing, and practice the discipline of the Unborn.
But having reached the supreme state, they become silent and utterly tranquil.
And in the *Śrī-Bhagavad-Uddhava-Saṃvāda* (BhP 11.14.23–24):
"How could one whose sins are to be destroyed be purified without the hair standing on end, without a melting heart, and without a stream of tears of bliss, if it be without devotion? (Hbhv 11.644)
His voice becomes faltering, his mind melts away; he weeps incessantly and sometimes laughs;
devoid of shame, he breaks into loud song and dances.
Endowed with devotion to me, he purifies the world.
But if one is unable to practice the aforementioned devotion, one should take refuge in the lotus feet of the Blessed One with the attitude of one who has sought shelter, for they destroy all fear.
Now, regarding taking refuge, in the venerable Bhagavad-gītā [18.66]:
"Renouncing all duties, come to Me alone as your refuge."
I shall liberate you from all evils; do not grieve.
And in the eleventh book, in the dialogue between the Blessed Lord and Uddhava (BhP 11.12.14–15):
"Therefore, O Uddhava, casting aside injunction and counter-injunction, as well as engagement and withdrawal, and what is yet to be heard and what has already been heard," (Hbhv_11.648)
Go for refuge with your whole being to me alone, the self of all embodied beings; through me, you shall indeed be free from fear from every quarter.
And its permanence is stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"Even though one has attained human birth, which is more difficult to obtain than that desired by the gods..."
Those by whom Govinda has not been taken as refuge have long deceived themselves.
And indeed, eighty-four hundred thousand times,
those men wandering through the various states of living beings obtain a human birth through the cycle of rebirths.
Even that [effort] of those wretched people who pride themselves on their own selves became fruitless,
because they did not take refuge in the two feet of Govinda.

Now, the greatness of taking refuge has been stated in the *Rāmāyaṇa* by the illustrious Lord Raghunātha in the context of Vibhīṣaṇa’s arrival: "He who takes refuge even once and entreats, saying, 'I am yours'— "
"I grant him fearlessness at all times; this is the vow of Hari."
"In the Nārasiṃha [Purāṇa], it is said: 'O Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, I have sought refuge in you, Janārdana, the God of gods.
Whosoever has thus come for refuge, I deliver him from suffering. (Hbhv 11.654)
In the context of offenses against the Name, Śrī Sanatkumāra said to Śrī Nārada in the Padma Purāṇa:
"Those devoid of all proper conduct, deceitful-minded, outcastes who deceive the world, devoted to hypocrisy, egoism, drinking, and backbiting— sinful, low-born, and cruel."
And those others who are devoted to wealth, wives, and sons—the lowest of all—even they, O twice-born one, become liberated if they take refuge in the lotus feet of Śrī Govinda. (Hbhv 11.655)
In the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"O Śaunaka, it has been stated again and again that men who take refuge in the one named Nārāyaṇa do not encounter misfortune; this is the truth. (Hbhv 11.656)
In the *Bṛhan-nāradīya-purāṇa*, in the section concerning the Kali age:
"He who has gone for refuge to Govinda—the ultimate reality and the primordial cause of all worlds, the worthy protector—does not perish. (Hbhv 11.657)
In the Śāntiparvan [MBh 12.111.26–27], within the discourse on the duties of kings (*rājadharma*) in the conversation between Bhīṣma and Yudhiṣṭhira, it is said:
"O bull among men, he who remains devoted to the beloved welfare of Jiṣṇu (Arjuna), O King, is that very same invincible Vaikuṇṭha, the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*), for you as well. (Hbhv 11.658)
Those who take refuge here in this Nārāyaṇa Hari with devotion cross over all difficulties; of this I have no doubt.
In the third book, in the dialogue between Vidura and Maitreya (BhP 3.22.37):
"How do physical, mental, divine, human, and elemental afflictions trouble one who has taken refuge in Hari? (Hbhv 11.660).
In the *Vāmana*, within the dialogue between Śrī Prahlāda and Bali:
"Those who have taken refuge in Hari— the infinite, whose beginning and middle are unknown,
Nārāyaṇa, the preceptor of the gods, the bestower of auspiciousness, and the most excellent— "
The wise do not enter that pure realm, which has the gait of the king of birds and is the abode of the Lord of Kamalā, where the King of Dharma acts as its sovereign.

Those who take refuge in the Lord of Śrī, the destroyer of the fear of worldly existence, who holds the conch, discus, and lotus in his hands, who wields the Śārṅga bow, whose banner bears the king of birds, and who grants boons;
For those who partake in liberation, there is no fear.
In the *Bṛhannāradīya*, at the conclusion of the section on expiations (*prāyaścitta-prakaraṇa*):
"In this most terrible cycle of existence, which is overwhelmed by the sleep of delusion, those who go to Hari for refuge have achieved their purpose; of this there is no doubt. (Hbhv 11.663)
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Those who have gone for refuge to Acyuta through action, mind, or speech—Yama has no power over them; they are partakers of the fruit of liberation. (Hbhv 11.664)
In the Tenth Canto [BhP 10.14.58]:
Those who have taken refuge in the boat that is the sprout-like foot of Murāri, whose great state is of meritorious fame;
The ocean of existence is but a cow's footprint for those whose feet are set upon that supreme state which is not a station for calamities.
In the first [verse]:

"O Sūta, those sages who take refuge at his feet and whose conduct is tranquility instantly purify those who touch them, just as the waters of the celestial river are purified by constant service. (Hbhv 11.666)
In the second [canto], in the words of Śrī Śuka (BhP 2.4.18):
"The Kirātas, Hūṇas, Āndhras, Pulindas, Pulkaśas, Ābhīras, Śumbhas, Yavanas, Khasas, and others..."
Salutation to that Sovereign Lord, by taking refuge in whom even other sinful beings are purified.
In the third canto, as spoken by Maitreya (BhP 3.23.42):
"What is difficult for those men of unrestrained minds to achieve, by whom the feet of the Lord of Holy Places—the refuge that transcends all calamities—have been taken as shelter? (Hbhv 11.668).
In the tenth book, in the hymn by the wives of the Nāgas (BhP 10.16.37):
"Neither the vault of heaven, nor the sovereignty of Brahmā,
nor universal dominion, nor lordship over the waters [is desired]."
O Perfect One, I do not desire the perfections of yoga or even non-rebirth if they are devoid of you.
And in the eleventh canto, in the Śrī-Karabhājana-Yogeśvara-uttara (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.5.41):
"O King, he is not a servant nor a debtor to the gods, sages, spirits, kinsmen, men, or ancestors."
He who has gone for refuge with his whole being to Mukunda, the worthy refuge, having abandoned all other action.
Therefore, it was said by Uddhava to the Blessed Lord (Bhagavān): "O Lord, for one who is struck by the threefold suffering and scorched on the terrible path of worldly existence... [BhP 11.19.9]
I see no other refuge than the pair of your feet, which are like a parasol raining down the nectar of immortality.
Thus should the wise understand the characteristic of taking refuge:
that which consists of taking exclusive shelter in Kṛṣṇa through speech, heart, and body. (Hbhv 11.672)
Now, regarding the characteristics of taking refuge:
[one takes refuge in] Govinda, Paramānanda, Mukunda, and Madhusūdana.
Having abandoned all else, I truly know nothing other, I do not worship anything else, nor do I remember anything else.
I do not bow to him, nor do I praise him, nor do I behold him with my own eyes;
I have no longing for him, I do not sing his praises, nor indeed do I go anywhere without Hari.
Thus it is said;
and some say that the state of having gone for refuge is of six kinds,
and upon investigation, it generally culminates in the mode of friendship.
And that has been stated in the Vaiṣṇava-tantra: "The resolve for favorability, the avoidance of hostility,
the conviction that [the Lord] will protect, and likewise the choosing of Him as the protector;"
In the wretchedness of surrendering oneself, there is a sixfold taking of refuge.
Thus, saying "I am yours" with speech, knowing it likewise with the mind,
and taking refuge in that state with his body, the one who has come for shelter rejoices.
Thus it was said in the Tenth Canto by Akrūra to the Blessed Lord (Bhagavān):
"Who else but a fool would seek refuge in anyone other than You—the one who is dear to His devotees, whose word is truth, the well-wisher, and the grateful? (BhP 10.48.26)
He gives everything to his friends who serve him with longing;
he is one for whom there is neither increase nor decrease, even regarding his own self.
In the third [canto], Śrī Uddhava says [BhP 3.2.23]:
"Aho! That wicked Bakī, who out of a desire to kill him made him drink the deadly poison from her breast—"
He attained the state appropriate for a nurse; other than him, to what other compassionate one shall we go for refuge?
Thus:
Now, the various types of conduct for the illustrious Vaiṣṇavas, which follow the practices of the learned (śiṣṭa), are to be performed; they are here written down in brief. (Hbhv 11.680)

Now, regarding the rules of conduct, as stated in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa* within the dialogue between Aurva and Sagara at the commencement of the description of the conduct of householders (*gṛhasthācāra*):
"One should worship the gods, cows, brāhmaṇas, perfected beings (*siddhas*), elders, and teachers."
And one should perform the twilight devotions at the two times of day, and likewise attend to the sacred fires.
A self-controlled man should always wear unsoiled garments, as well as auspicious medicinal herbs and gems associated with Garuḍa.
With hair that is glossy and clean, fragrant and wearing beautiful attire,
he should not take even a little of another's property, nor should he speak even the slightest unpleasant word.
One should not speak what is pleasant if it is untrue, nor should one proclaim the faults of others;
likewise, O bull among men, one should not take pleasure in hostility toward another's wife.
One should not mount a corrupted vehicle, nor should one rely on the shadow of a noble family.
Together with those who are hated, outcasts, madmen, many enemies, and other such "insects," with harlots, the husbands of harlots, and those who speak base lies— Hbhv_11.686.
A wise person should not cultivate friendship with those who are excessively wasteful, who delight in slander, and who are deceitful; nor should one travel the road alone.
O Lord of Men, one should not plunge into the force of a flood of water;
one should not enter a burning house, nor climb to the top of a tree. (Hbhv 11.688)
One should not grind one's teeth, nor should one wrinkle the nose;
one should not yawn with the mouth uncovered, and one should suppress sneezing and coughing.
A wise person should not laugh loudly, nor should he emit wind with sound;
he should not bite his nails, nor cut grass, nor scratch the earth.
A wise person should not bite his beard, nor should he crush clods of earth.
O Lord, one should not gaze upon the celestial luminaries when they are defiled by impurities.
One should not utter the sound "huṃ" regarding a corpse or its odor, for the smell of a corpse arises from Soma.
One should always avoid at night crossroads, the *ciñcā* tree, cemeteries, groves, and the proximity of wicked women.
A wise person should not step over the shadow of a venerable deity, a twice-born, or a celestial body.
One should not travel alone through a deserted forest, nor should one dwell in an empty house.
One should avoid from afar hair, bones, thorns, impurities, offerings, ashes, and chaff, as well as ground that is still damp from bathing.
A wise person should not resort to various worldly objects, nor should they take pleasure in crookedness.
One should not approach a wild beast, nor should one remain for long with those who have risen [from their seats],
nor with those who eat as they please, nor with those who are averse to the gods, nor from afar should one avoid those who have transcended the duties of the social classes and stages of life.
O Lord of Men, a wise person should likewise avoid excessive wakefulness and sleep, as well as standing and sitting, and similarly avoid [excessive] reclining and physical exertion. (Hbhv 11.699)
A wise person should avoid from afar those who have fangs and those who have horns.

O King of kings, a wise man should not bathe in dew, nor in the presence of a headwind or the sun; he should not sleep naked, nor should he perform ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśet) while naked. (Hbhv 11.701)
One should not sip water for purification with one's lower garment untucked, nor should one omit the worship of the gods and other deities;
nor should one perform the recitation of mantras for the twice-born while wearing only a single garment.
Furthermore:

One should not shake out one's hair, nor should one rinse the mouth immediately upon rising; one should not step over a foot with a foot, nor should one carry anything toward an object of worship. (Hbhv 11.703)
One should not pass by the left of temples, crossroads, auspicious objects, or those worthy of worship; likewise, one should not do so in reverse order with respect to the right.
A wise person should not discharge saliva, feces, or urine while facing the moon, the sun, fire, water, the wind, or those worthy of worship. (Hbhv 11.705)
One should not urinate while standing; likewise, one should not urinate on paths.
One should never step over phlegm, feces, urine, or blood.
Spitting phlegm or expelling feces is not recommended at mealtime, nor during offerings, auspicious rites, recitations, fire oblations, or in the presence of a great assembly. (Hbhv 11.707)
A wise man should not despise women, nor should he place his full trust in them;
he should not be envious of them, nor should he ever entrust them with authority.
A wise man devoted to right conduct should not depart from his home without having paid homage to auspicious flowers, jewels, clarified butter, and those worthy of worship. (Hbhv 11.709)
A wise person should observe a suspension of study during unseasonable thunder and similar phenomena, on sacred festival days, during periods of impurity, and likewise during eclipses and the like.
One who desires protection for the body should always go with an umbrella against rain and heat, with a staff in the night or in forests, and wearing sandals. (Hbhv 11.711)
A wise person should wander about without looking upward, downward, or into the distance;
a man should walk while looking at the surface of the earth only as far as the length of a yoke.
Furthermore: "One should not speak that which, though pleasant, is considered by one to be unbeneficial;
rather, that which is beneficial should be spoken, even if it is extremely unpleasant, provided it is devoid of malice. (Hbhv 11.713)
A wise person should practice only that which is beneficial for living beings both in this world and in the next, whether by deed, by mind, or by speech.
In the *Bṛhan-nāradīya-purāṇa*, in the section concerning right conduct (1.25.35–43):
"A twice-born man should indeed say 'This is I' when performing a salutation;
likewise, he should do so during a *śrāddha* ceremony, a vow, a gift, or the worship of the deities."
One should not offer salutation to one who is performing a sacrifice or a libation.
Likewise, one should not speak to someone who is bathing, running, impure,
eating, or whose head is anointed with oil.

One who carries food obtained as alms, one who sports while standing in the midst of water, and one who, when saluted, does not return the salutation—such a person is not to be saluted; he is to be regarded exactly like a Śūdra. (Hbhv 11.717)
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*,
in the dialogue between Madrāla and Sālarka:
One should avoid idle chatter, falsehood, and harshness of speech.
O son, [abandon] false scripture, false doctrine, and the service of the wicked.
Grooming the hair, looking into a mirror, cleaning the teeth,
and the libation to the deities— these should be performed only in the forenoon.
One should avoid seeing, touching, or conversing with a woman in her courses.
A man should not bathe his head frequently without a specific reason;
and having bathed his head, he should not touch any part of his body with oil.
The king must yield the path to Brahmins, to one afflicted by suffering,
to one superior in learning, to a pregnant woman, to one burdened by a load, and to one who is great.

And [one should not give] to those who are mute, blind, or deaf; to one who is intoxicated or insane; to a promiscuous woman, to one who has committed enmity, to a child, or to one who has fallen from their status.
One should not wear shoes, garments, or garlands that have been worn by others;
one should likewise avoid the sacred thread, ornaments, and mouthfuls of food [left over by others].
A wise person should never stand with his arms or legs akimbo;
nor should he dangle his feet, nor shake his robe. (Hbhv 11.725)
One should neither mock nor revile fools, the insane, those addicted to vices, the deformed, the deceitful, those with missing limbs, or those who are low-born. (Hbhv 11.726)

One should not raise a staff against another, even for the sake of instructing a son or a pupil; and one who has completed his Vedic studies (snātaka) must never apply ointments unless he has first bathed.
Nor should one wear dyed garments or even those of variegated colors,
O son; after the rite of shaving, at the conclusion of sexual union with a woman,
and upon reaching the ground of a funeral pyre, a wise man possessing cloth should bathe.
A wise person should not carry water and fire at the same time;
he should not point out a cow suckling her calf, nor should he drink water from his cupped hands.
At all times for purification, whether they be many or few, one should not delay for the sake of cleanliness; nor should one blow upon fire with the mouth.
Flies and the like, as well as insects, are not considered defiled by contact with the hand; goats and horses are pure when touched; and the mouth of a calf is pure. (Hbhv 11.731)
The milk flowing from a mother’s breasts is pure, as is a bird that causes fruit to fall;

however, having touched a woman in her courses, one who is impure due to childbirth, those who are naked, those who stay with a woman in labor, or those who carry a corpse, one should bathe for the sake of purification. (Hbhv 11.732)
Having touched a human bone that still has marrow, a person becomes pure by bathing;
however, if it is free of marrow, he becomes pure simply by sipping water (ācamana) and then touching a cow or looking at the sun.

One should not converse with a hateful person, nor with a woman devoid of heroism, nor with those who revile the deities, guests, the true scriptures, sacrifices, perfected beings, and so forth. (Hbhv 11.734)
Having conversed by means of touch, one becomes pure by looking at the sun; likewise,
having looked upon a woman in her courses, an outcaste, a fallen person,
a rogue, one who follows a false dharma, a woman who has recently given birth, a eunuch, one who is naked, or a dweller in another's house.
Those who carry out the dead and those who take pleasure in the wives of others—
this indeed is the purification that the wise must perform for themselves.
Furthermore:

"And whatever action one performs, my son, such that one's own self does not feel revulsion toward it—that should be done without hesitation, provided it is not something to be concealed from great people. (Hbhv 11.737)
In the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira:

"A righteous king should employ all those twice-born men who do not perform the morning twilight devotion (*pūrva-sandhyā*) nor the evening twilight devotion (*paścima-sandhyā*) in the work of Śūdras. (Hbhv 11.738)

O King, one who desires his own welfare should always perform the voiding of urine at a distance from the dwelling, the washing of the feet at a distance, and the disposal of food remnants at a distance. (Hbhv 11.739)
One should not touch one's head while impure from food remnants, for all the vital breaths (prāṇas) are dependent upon it.
One should avoid seizing the hair or striking the head;
nor should one ever scratch the head with both hands. (Hbhv 11.740)
Furthermore:
He should feed married women, pregnant women, the elderly, children, and the sick with well-prepared food first, and the householder himself last. (Hbhv 11.741)
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, he who eats while others look on and without having given [to them], eats only sin when the ox-driver and others have grown old. (Hbhv 11.742)
One should avoid curd and parched grain at night, and roasted grains during the day.
Furthermore:
One should not pull at garlands, nor wear them outside [the house].
In the home, doves are auspicious, as are parrots together with mainas.
In the *Vyāsagītā* of the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Whether it be a blade of grass, or a vegetable, or a root, or even water—if a living being takes these from another, he falls into hell. (Hbhv 11.745)
A wise person should not accept gifts from a king, nor from a Śūdra, nor even from one who has fallen from his caste; likewise, he should avoid begging from others and shun those who are censurable.
One should not be a constant beggar, nor should one beg from that very same person again; for such a foolish beggar robs him of his very life. (Hbhv 11.747)
O best of the twice-born, one should not steal the property of the gods, especially not that of the Brahmins; nor should one ever seize the property of a Brahmin, even in times of distress.
They say that poison is not truly poison; the property of a Brahmin is called poison.
Therefore, one should always avoid the property of a deity with great effort.
Having committed a sin, one should not perform a vow under the pretext of dharma;
by concealing his sin with a vow, such a Brahmin who deceives women and Śūdras will be censured by those who discourse on the Veda, both in this world and after death. (Hbhv 11.750)
Offense against a guru is ten million times more severe than offense against a god; and atheism and the denial of knowledge are ten million times more severe than that. (Hbhv 11.751)
Furthermore:

A twice-born man should not dwell anywhere else except in that auspicious region between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, extending from east to west and situated between the two oceans. (Hbhv 11.752)
Or where a black antelope constantly roams by its very nature,
or where there are famous, sacred rivers— there a twice-born man should dwell,
O best of the twice-born, avoiding the riverbanks for half a krośa.
Furthermore:
By fire, by ashes, and especially by water;
by a doorway, by a pillar-path, and by the feet—the line is divided.
One should not report to anyone a cow wandering in another's field.
A wise person should never describe to another a halo around the sun, nor a rainbow, nor one produced by fire, nor even the moon;
they should not state the lunar day of the fortnight, nor point out the constellations. (Hbhv 11.755)
One should not obstruct what is being given to gods, gurus, or brahmins.
That man who reviles his gurus, the gods, or the Veda along with its supplements,
is cooked in the Raurava hell for more than a hundred times ten million kalpas.
One should remain silent during criticism and not utter any reply;
one should depart while covering the ears and must not even look at the person.
A wise person should avoid the secrets of others and keep them concealed;
one should never engage in disputes with one's own kin.
O best of the twice-born, one should not call a sinner "sinful," nor should one call a sinless person "sinful."
One should not look at the rising sun or the moon with the intention of observing omens.

One should not look at [the sun] as it is setting, nor when it is reflected in water, nor when it is obscured, nor when it is in the middle [of the sky], nor when it is hidden by a cloth, nor when it has moved beyond the horizon.
One should not look at a naked woman or man, nor feces or urine, nor those who are outcaste, deformed, or Cāṇḍālas, whether they are impure or pure. (Hbhv 11.762)

One should not touch a cow that is still tied up, nor one that is intoxicated, even if it is no longer in a state of madness; one should not touch one's wife while she is eating, nor look at her while she is urinating.
One should not look at one who is agitated or yawning, nor at one who is not seated on a seat as is comfortable;
nor at one's own reflection in water, nor at a mongoose, nor at a hole.
One should not give instruction to a Śūdra, nor kṛsara, milk-rice, or curd;
nor should one give him leavings, ghee, honey, a black antelope skin, or sacrificial oblation.

One should not cause pain to anyone; one may strike a son or a disciple, but one should not despise oneself and should avoid dejection with effort. A wise person should neither treat disciples with excessive honor nor speak ill of himself.
One should not call a river a river, nor a mountain a mountain;
one should not dwell with such a person, nor should one abandon a fellow-dweller.
One should not smear one's body with the oil remaining after anointing the head;
nor should one touch the private hairs or one's own bodily apertures.
One should not resort to fickleness of hand, foot, speech, or eye;
one should never strike water with the feet or ever with the hand.
One should not destroy fruits with bricks, nor fruits with a fruit;
one should not learn the speech of barbarians, nor should one drag a seat with the foot.
One should not eat food on one's lap, nor should one cause a cow to lie down;
one should not play with dice, nor run about, nor engage in disputes with women.
One should not cut one's nails or hair with the teeth; one should not wake a sleeping person;
one should not expose oneself to the morning sun; and one should avoid the smoke from a funeral pyre.
One should not sleep alone in an empty house, nor should one remove one's own sandals.
One should not spit without cause, nor should one cross a river by swimming with one's arms.
A wise person should never wash his feet with his foot itself; he should not warm his feet over a fire, nor should he place them upon a bronze vessel.

One should not deceive the gods, brahmins, or even a cow. While impure from eating, one should not touch brahmins, cows, fire, or the sun with one's hand; nor should one touch food with the foot, nor should one touch an image of a deity.
One should not cross a flowing river without touching it;

one should not bypass a sacred tree (*caitya*) or a *brahma* tree, nor should one cut them down. One should not discharge phlegm into the water, nor should a wise person leap over a fire, nor should he ever place it beneath himself.
One should not place it at one's feet; one should discard it at night when it is bound with sesame seeds.
One should not descend into a well, nor should one ever speak while impure.
One should not throw fire into fire, nor should one extinguish it with water;
likewise, one should not personally announce to others the death of a friend or their suffering.
Furthermore, one should not engage in selling anything that is either forbidden for sale or even permitted for sale.

One may plow the boundary at a site of merit, a place for water, or a field; however, one should never, even under any circumstances, break an established agreement that is accompanied by a solemn oath.
A wise person should not cause beasts, predators, or birds to fight one another;
nor, having had craftsmen perform their tasks, should he deceive them.
A Brahmin should avoid external perfumes and entry through side doors; he should not frequent assemblies alone, and he should avoid large gatherings.
One should not fan oneself with a garment, nor should one sleep in a temple;
nor should one ever pass between fire, a cow, a Brahmin, or others [who are worthy of respect].
One should not intentionally step upon the shadow of Brahmins or even of cows;
nor should one allow the shadow of oneself to be stepped upon by those who have fallen from their caste and the like, nor by those afflicted with disease.

One should not drink buttermilk with milk, nor should one sow seeds upon seeds; likewise, the milk of a cow whose calf has died, camel’s milk, the milk of a cow within ten days of calving, sheep’s milk, and the milk of a cow in heat— Manu declared these to be undrinkable.
Furthermore, a twice-born man should always give a guest either the word "hanta" (be welcome), or the finest [food], or alms according to his ability; he should thus perceive him as the Supreme Lord.
They say that alms consist of a single morsel; four times that is the "excellent" (puṣkala);
and four times that again is desired as the "hanta-kāra."
In the Mārkaṇḍeya [Purāṇa]:
"One should not eat without first having given food—whether it be a meal, or even a morsel, or even alms—to others according to one's own means. (Hbhv 11.787)
In the Kāśī-khaṇḍa it is said:
"One should not eat while sitting on a high seat, nor should one throw impure things into the fire.
He who, devoid of knowledge, eats at another's śrāddha after having already performed a śrāddha [himself], [incurs sin]."
The donor gains no fruit from the śrāddha, and the recipient shall instead partake of the misdeed.
One should never pluck out body hair or nails with the teeth;
one should avoid cutting fingernails with the fingers or using the hand itself for that purpose.
One should not go through side doors to one's own house or the house of another; one should avoid from afar bribes, gambling, acting as a messenger, and wealth acquired through improper means.
One should cast spittle and phlegm far away from the house.
Having removed five lumps of earth, one should bathe in another's reservoir;
for if one does not remove them, one becomes a sharer in a fourth part of the sin of that [reservoir's] maker. (Hbhv 11.791)
But that which one eats on the palm of the hand, that which is eaten with a hissing sound,
and that which is eaten with fingers spread apart— these are like beef for him. (Hbhv 11.792)
In the Atri-smṛti:
"The milk of a cow that has either undersized or oversized udders, or one that grazes on forbidden food, should never be offered in sacrifice nor ever drunk. (Hbhv 11.793)

One should avoid the milk and the dung of goats, cows, and buffaloes—even if one might otherwise consume their impure flesh—and likewise avoid their milk and dung when performing offerings to the gods (havya) or the ancestors (kavya). (Hbhv 11.794)
Using a finger [to eat], chewing a tooth-stick, likewise consuming visible salt, and even the eating of clay—these are equal to the consumption of cow-flesh. (Hbhv 11.795)

Regarding this, there is an exception stated in the *Manu-smṛti*: "The two most wonderful salts, namely sea salt and rock salt, are to be accepted even though they are [prohibited] by direct perception; the prohibition, however, applies to other [types of salt]. (Hbhv 11.796)
In the Atri-smṛti:
"The shadow of a wood-apple tree during the day and the eating of curd at night, as well as a cotton tooth-stick—these take away one's fortune even from Indra. (Hbhv_11.797)
And in the Viṣṇu-smṛti: "A Śūdra who drinks the milk of a tawny cow (kapilā) shall go to hell;
a Brāhmaṇa should drink what remains from the oblation (homa-śeṣa); otherwise, he would be a mere beast. (Hbhv 11.798)
Furthermore, whatever has been written here in this letter that deviates from what is stated in various treatises,
that should be forgiven by the great-souled ones.
Such are the conducts of the virtuous, and there are many others as well;
they are to be known from the world and the scriptures, and should indeed be observed by Vaiṣṇavas.
Their eternality and greatness have also been written here previously;
through the eternality and greatness of right conduct, [the goal] is well accomplished. (Hbhv 11.801)
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Conclusion of Daily Duties," in the *Śrī Bhagavad-bhakti-vilāsa* composed by the venerable Gopāla Bhaṭṭa.
